A request a fast client sent within `lent::WAITED` ran on the worker that
answered the last (D42), but any later one was handed to whichever thread
of the blocking pool was free, and the pool wakes its idle threads in
turn. A session moved between threads at nearly every transaction of a
client that thinks between them. What a statement allocated on one thread
was then freed on another, so every serving thread took the locks of
every arena of the allocator, freed chunks were merged across threads,
and the session's state went cold in each processor's cache.

So a connection's first request opens its home (`native/home.rs`), one
long task of the blocking pool that runs each of the connection's
requests until the connection ends or goes idle. The connection's task
still reads a slow client's request, takes a permit of SERVER.WORKERS for
it, and waits for the loan back (`native/lent.rs`). It then hands the
request to the home instead of the pool, and the home parks between
requests holding no permit. Statements are bounded, queued, cancelled and
timed out as before, and a fast client's next request is still read by
the worker itself.

A home per connection, not a fixed set of threads each serving many
connections, because a statement may wait for a row lock another
connection holds. On a shared thread the holder's commit could queue
behind its waiter, and stealing work to undo that moves the session
again. With a thread each, no session waits behind another's statement,
and an idle home costs a parked thread. A session's end, a Reset and a
ChangeUser still run on any free thread, once a connection or rarely.
This helps any allocator, since each one's per-thread caches serve a
thread that both takes and frees.

#### D768. Homes share the places of waiting workers, and retire once idle as long as the pool keeps a thread

A home holds one of the MAX_WORKERS places of the connections that keep a
thread of the pool (`Services::hot`), which a worker waiting on its client
for the next request takes too. So the pool's bound, twice MAX_WORKERS
beside the logins' threads (`runtime.rs`), still leaves a thread for every
statement SERVER.WORKERS allows. A connection that finds no place runs
each request on any free thread, as every request ran before. A worker at
home waits on its client without taking a second place.

A home with no request for `home::KEPT`, ten seconds, retires, giving its
thread and place back, and the connection opens another at its next
request. Ten seconds is how long the runtime keeps an idle thread of its
pool, so an idle connection gives back its thread when the pool would
have. A connection idle that long pays one move of thread, and idle
connections never keep active ones out of the places.

#### D769. A request is handed to a home under one lock, which decides its retirement too

The connection's task and its home share one slot and a condition
variable. The task puts a request in the slot unless the home has retired.
The home takes it, or retires under the same lock once its wait times out
with the slot empty, so no request is ever left with a thread that has
gone. A home whose thread ends otherwise, by a panic or because the runtime
stops before it ran, retires as its thread's guard is dropped, dropping any
request left in the slot. That gives the loan back failed, so the
connection ends rather than waits. A request a retired home refuses is
handed back, and runs on a new home or on any free thread.

#### D773. A comparison with an uncorrelated subquery of one row at most is a semi join with its row

DELIVERY takes the least new order of a district and deletes it, which a
driver may write as one statement, `NO_O_ID = (SELECT MIN(NO_O_ID)
...)`. The subquery was run once and its value compared with
every row of the district's NEW_ORDER rows read whole, as no index probe
was made of a value not known as planned. A conjunct of WHERE or HAVING
that compares a value of the row with a column of an uncorrelated scalar
or row subquery is true of a row exactly when the subquery has a row and
the comparison with it is true: of no row the value is null and the
comparison unknown [X3.135-1986 §5.11 GR1, §5.24 GR2]. So, of a subquery
that gives one row at most by its shape, an ungrouped set function's or
one fetched first (`LogicalPlan::one_row_at_most`), the node's rows are
those of the semi join of its input with the subquery's rows on the
comparisons (`optimizer/unnesting/scalar.rs`). A subquery that could give
more would raise its cardinality error, which no join raises, so it is
left. As the other semi joins are (D541), it is made only of a pure
subquery that cannot raise, and of comparisons that cannot, and the
subquery may stand nowhere else in the condition. Of several such
subqueries the right is the product of their rows, itself one row at
most, so that STOCK-LEVEL's `OL_O_ID < (...) AND OL_O_ID >= (...)`
bounds one probe from both sides. The planner then probes the input's
index from the subquery's row (D774), by an equality or as a range of
keys (D776).

#### D774. A semi join of a few right rows probes the left's table from them, by the distinct values its equalities compare

A semi join probed an index of the right's table from the left's rows
when those were few (D540), but a set of a few keys, an IN of a
subquery of UNNEST or of VALUES or an EXISTS equating the key with an
array's elements, is the right, and the left read its table whole to hash
it or probe it. A semi join's rows are the left's rows some right row
matches, each once. Of a right of one row at most, they are the left's
rows of the inner join of the right with the left on the condition. Of a
condition whose conjuncts that read the right are each an equality of a
left column and a right one, they are the left's rows of the inner join
of the distinct values of the right's columns compared with the left: a
left row's values make the one row of them it matches. That join is
planned as any inner join, its index probes priced against the read of
the left's table they replace (D35, D386), and taken when it probes an
index of the left's table from each of its rows (`physical/semi/probed.rs`);
else the semi join is planned as before. An antijoin is not, as the rows
it keeps are those no probe finds. Its rows come in no order of the left's.

Three judgements kept such a semi join from being made, or its probes
from being typed. An array constructor by enumeration raises nothing, as
its elements are cast as bound and their number checked then [ISO/IEC
9075-2:2023 §6.49 SR2, GR2], so it no longer keeps a subquery nested
(`functions/arrays.rs`). A CAST of a constant raises only what casting
that constant raises, judged as it is planned (`logical/raises.rs`).
And a column of a projection, of an UNNEST or of a grouping has the
declared type of the expression, the collection's element or the
aggregate that gives it, where those are known
(`physical/indexed/typed.rs`), so a probe compares a key with a value of
its type.

#### D775. The object rows of a searched UPDATE or DELETE may be a semi join, which keeps the table's rows alone

The object rows of a searched UPDATE or DELETE were planned with every
subquery left nested (D318), so a join would not make the plan other than
an access to the table changed. An IN of a few keys' subquery, or an
EXISTS of one, was then run for each row of the table, and the plan read
the table whole. A semi join's rows are its left's alone, each once, so
they are the object rows the condition selects. These plans are now
optimized with the semi joins (D541, D773) made, and the others still
left (`db/compiled.rs`, `plan_written`), so the table's index is probed
from the few keys (D774). No access to the table reads the rows such a
plan keeps, so their ids are not given with them. A plan that is no
table access is planned again of the object table's scan located, each
row followed by its id (`storage::located`), which the semi joins,
filters and projections over it keep last (`db/compiled/located.rs`).
Its rows are read and the ids taken off them (`exec/entries.rs`). A
plan whose object scan lies under another node is planned as before. An
updatable cursor's plan is planned as before.

#### D776. An index join bounds the key's column after its equalities by values of the outer row

STOCK-LEVEL's join of DISTRICT and ORDER_LINE equates the warehouse and
the district and keeps the lines of `OL_O_ID < D_NEXT_O_ID AND OL_O_ID >=
D_NEXT_O_ID - 20`, a few orders' lines of the district's many. A
probe of the equalities alone read every line of the district, each then
judged by the bounds. Where the index's next column after those its
equalities give is compared by order with an outer column, or with a sum
or difference of one and a constant that raises nothing by the declared
types (D373), the probe reads the keys between the bounds alone
(`JoinProbe::Range`, `physical/indexed/bounded.rs`). A bound is taken
only of a column of exact numbers or datetimes, of the outer value's
kind, whose comparison the index's order answers exactly [X3.135-1986
§5.11 GR2, GR5], so the conjuncts it answers are judged of no pair again;
a null bound matches no key, as its comparison is unknown. Each bound
keeps the default share of a range of the rows the equalities find, and
the probes are priced so against the read they replace. Two bounds of
one outer column, as `D_NEXT_O_ID - 20` and `D_NEXT_O_ID`, keep instead
the share their constants' distance is of the column's distinct values.
A kept plan may hold such a join (D418).

Four steps bring such a join to the probe. A filter over a product, and
a join's condition, that raises nothing by its columns' declared types
is split among the operands and hashed as any (D15, D373), where the
judgement by expressions alone kept it whole. A column the inner table's
own filter fixes makes an index's prefix also where the index's next
column is bounded by the outer row (D761, `physical/indexed/fixed.rs`),
as the order of a subquery's row bounds it. A join enumerated with no
equality of two columns stated takes those implied (D387), so the
bounds' table may still be probed by key (`enumerate/realize.rs`). And a
range join is priced against the probes too, the columns the inner
table's filter fixes among their keys, net of the inner table's read
they replace, as the range join's own price leaves its operands' reads
out (`physical/range/planned.rs`).

#### D777. An UNNEST is estimated by its collections' elements, when each is a constant, a slot whose value is given or a constructor of its values

An UNNEST was estimated at `UNNEST_FANOUT` rows for each row of its input,
whatever its collections held, so the probes of a few host arrays' keys
were weighed at rows the arrays did not have. Of collections that are
each a constant array or multiset, or a slot whose value the planner is
given, as a prepared statement's or a kept body's are (D45, D414), or a
constructor by enumeration, whose elements are as many as its values
[ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §6.49 GR2, §6.52 GR2], the estimate is each input
row times the elements of the longest, a null one none [§7.6 SR8f,
SR8h], and at least one
(`physical/cardinality/nodes.rs`). A JSON table and GRAPH_TABLE, planned
as UNNEST is, keep the default.

#### D778. A lateral derived table that reads the rows before it is bound as a collection derived table of the multiset of its query's rows

A `<lateral derived table>`'s query may reference the table references
before it in its FROM clause [ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §7.6 SR5, SR20a], and
its table is its query's [SR10], so its rows are its query's for each
row before it. A collection derived table is lateral the same way, and
is already planned over the rows it reads (`binder/unnest.rs`), after a
comma or as the second operand of CROSS, INNER and LEFT joins. It reads
none of a RIGHT or FULL join's first operand [§7.10 SR4].

So a lateral derived table that reads a column before it is bound as one
(`binder/subquery/lateral.rs`). Its one collection is the multiset of its
query's rows, each the ROW of its columns, as a `<table value constructor
by query>` makes it [§6.52 SR1e, GR3], spread into its columns. Unlike
that constructor's, its query may have an ORDER BY, which orders nothing
but says which rows OFFSET and FETCH keep. The collection is a subquery
whose outer references are the columns it reads, so it is computed again
for each row before it, its plan made once. One that reads nothing
before it is bound as the derived table it then is, planned as any.

#### D779. An UNNEST of a subquery of one row at most raises only what the subquery's plan raises, so a lateral of a set function may be a semi join's right

A semi join or a decorrelated subquery evaluates its right for bindings
the original might not have read, so neither is made of a plan that can
raise an error (D15, D317). Every subquery was taken as raising, as a
scalar subquery of more than one row raises a cardinality violation
[ISO/IEC 9075:1992 §7.11 GR1]. So an IN of a lateral derived table's
rows (D778), the least key of each district, was read row by row of the
whole table, a filter over a scan.

A collection of an UNNEST that is a subquery of one row at most now
raises what its outer expressions and its plan raise
(`optimizer/unnesting/pure.rs`), which the plan's one row says no
cardinality violation is among. Of that plan, a set function that
gathers an element of each row, as COLLECT does
(`AggregateFunction::gathers`), raises nothing of one row at most if its
argument and filter raise nothing, as one element is within any bound on
a multiset's elements. ROW of its values raises nothing. So the multiset
of a lateral's query of one row, as of an ungrouped MIN, raises nothing
more than MIN does, and the IN is a semi join.

Such a collection is estimated at one element, not `UNNEST_FANOUT`
(`physical/cardinality/nodes.rs`), so the semi join's right is as many
rows as the rows before the lateral, and its few rows probe the key
(D774). A probe takes a value only of a column whose declared type is
known to be of the key's kind. A lateral's column is a field of the row
type its UNNEST spreads [ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §7.6 SR8n], so its type is
that field's (`physical/indexed/typed.rs`), of a subquery's column the
type of its plan's column.

#### D785. A grouping by no column, of set functions none DISTINCT, is made as its one group, with no key, hash or work area

A grouping by no column has one group, even of no rows [X3.135-1986
§5.23 GR1, §5.25 GR1]. It was made as any grouping. Each row was keyed,
the key hashed and looked up in the pass's map, and the pass took a work
area. A `SELECT SUM(k) ... WHERE id BETWEEN ? AND ?` paid that for each of
its rows, though every row is of the one group.

Such a grouping is now made whole (`exec/group/streamed.rs`, `whole`).
Its set functions are fed every row and finished, of no rows too, as the
grouping is opened, as a grouping by key makes its groups. A row made
only once it was pulled raised the warning of a null it eliminated after
its statement's diagnostics were taken, so that statement lacked it and
the next one had it. Nothing is keyed, hashed or held. This holds
whichever way the planner asked for the grouping, hashed or streamed.

- A grouping with seeds (made before any row), or with a set function
  that is DISTINCT or an inverse distribution, is still made by key. Those
  need the key, the bag of values taken, or the sort of values.
- The one row is made as it is first asked for, within that one ask, so
  no set function's state outlives it (D551).

#### D786. A search keeps a decoded key only once a second entry has its bytes

A search kept the last key it decoded, and its bytes, so the entries of
one key are decoded once (D501). It copied each key it decoded to keep it,
though in a range of a unique key no second entry ever takes the copy.

A search now keeps the bytes of the last key it decoded, and the key only
once a second entry has those bytes (`index/blink.rs`, `Decoded`). The
entries of a unique key are decoded and never copied. Entries of a key not
unique are decoded twice, for the first two, and take the kept key after.
What each entry is given is the same key as before.

#### D787. A projection of columns each named once, in ascending order, is made in the row it is given

A projection of columns alone took its values out of the row it was given
into a new row (D31). Each row of an index range read for a few of its
columns paid a second allocation and a free for that.

A projection whose columns are each named once, in ascending order, now
swaps them to the front of the row it is given and cuts the rest off
(`exec/project.rs`, `in_place`). The column named `i`-th is at a place no
earlier than `i`, and no later column is at a place before its own, so no
swap moves a value still to be taken. Other projections make a row as
before. A column past the row is refused the same way in both.

#### D821. An index scan compares each row's key with its entry's as the bytes the index holds

An index scan rechecks each row it reads by the key of its entry, since an
index holds the entries of versions a reader may not see (D34, D501). The
built-in btree decoded every entry's key into values for that check, one
allocation and a decode per entry, a few percent of a range read's time.

An index may now hand its entries with their keys as the bytes it holds
(`Index::search_encoded`, by default none). The btree does so for a range
none of whose keys must be checked against the probe. Each entry is lent
from the scan (D809), its row id cut off, and is passed on uncopied and
undecoded (`index/blink/encoded.rs`).
A scan that reads each entry's row and checks it in place, by a key of
its columns as they are, by no sort key and with no projection, takes
them (`exec/scan/encoded.rs`). It encodes the row's key columns into one
buffer kept for the scan and compares the two as bytes
(`entries::fetch_encoded`). Equal bytes are of equal values. Bytes not
equal are decoded and compared as values, as before, so the scan keeps
exactly the rows it kept. Covering scans, scans deciding a condition, and
every other index read take decoded keys as before.

The check stays even for an equality on a whole unique key. A row whose
key an update moved from 5 to 6 has entries under both, and a reader
whose snapshot sees 5 finds its row by the entry under 6, which the
check alone refuses.

#### D805. A pool finds its files with no lock and no reference count moved

Each page a pool writes, and each it reads from its file, finds the file
by number. The files were kept behind one reader-writer lock, and the
file's `Arc` was cloned out of it, so every such call wrote the lock's
reader count and the file's reference count. Threads writing pages of
different tables passed both cache lines between them, and a profile
of contended cache lines at 32 threads put it among the shared lines of
row updates. Files are only ever added to a pool, so each is now set
once in a slot never changed again. Slots come in chunks made as files
are added, and each chunk is set once in a fixed table
(`disk/buffer/sources.rs`). A lookup loads two `OnceLock`s and borrows
the file for as long as the pool lives. The chunk and table sizes are a
capacity bound, not a tuning. A pool registers at most 1,048,576 files,
and one added past that is given a number no file has, so every use of
it is refused.

#### D790. A correlated subquery probed by a unique key is decorrelated only once its probes cost what its build would

A subquery run EXECUTOR.DECORRELATE_AFTER_RUNS times is decorrelated
(`exec/subquery.rs`). It runs once without its equalities with outer
references and builds every row it gives into a keyed table. For a
scalar subquery over a table's key, such as a price read by an item's
id, that build is the whole table, made again by each statement that
runs the subquery past those runs. A run whose plan is kept as one probe
of a whole unique key (D675) costs a single descent instead.

So the runner keeps such a subquery probed past those runs
(`exec/subquery/probed.rs`). It decorrelates it only once its probes,
each weighed as `PROBE_ROWS` rows built, reach the rows the build would
hold, as planning estimates them. The runs so far stand for the runs to
come. Up to that point the probes cost no more than the build, and past
it a build is as likely to pay as not. A subquery whose run is any other
plan is decorrelated after EXECUTOR.DECORRELATE_AFTER_RUNS runs, as
before. A probe plan is kept from the first run even when decorrelation
is due before a plan could be learned, since a unique probe needs no
learning.

#### D791. A probe of a unique key is weighed as the rows of a build it costs as much as, measured

D790 weighs each probe a subquery made as `PROBE_ROWS` rows of its
decorrelated build. That weight is measured, not chosen. The `probed`
sweep of `bench/joins.rs` (`bench/joins/probed.rs`) runs a scalar
subquery over a table's primary key for 100 outer rows of an UNNEST,
never decorrelated, and the same subquery over a copy of the table with
no index, decorrelated at its first run, over tables of 1,000, 10,000
and 100,000 rows. The probes a second and the build's rows a second
give the rows that cost one probe. They came to 15.6, 18.8 and 11.3.
`PROBE_ROWS` is their geometric mean, 14.9, rounded to 15.

The spread moves the break-even point by less than a factor of two,
and the decision falls well to one side in the cases that matter. An
order of at most 15 lines probes an item table of 100,000 rows, and its
runs weighed at any weight from 4 to 64 come to at most 960 rows, far
fewer than the build would hold.

#### D780. A session keeps its own copy of the definitions' snapshot, taken again only once one is published

Each statement took the database's snapshot of its definitions by
reading the lock it is published under and copying its `Arc`. Both write
a line every session shares, the lock's count of readers and the
snapshot's count of references, twice a statement. At eight threads of
point queries each statement waited on those lines moving between
processors, and the cost of a query grew with the threads running.

So the database counts each snapshot it publishes, moving the count
after the snapshot is in place (`database/published.rs`). A session
keeps a copy of its own of the last snapshot it took, the `State` cloned
with its count. A statement reads the count, one word written only as
definitions change, and takes its session's copy while the count is the
same. Only once a change was published does the session read the lock
and copy the snapshot again. The count is read before the lock, so a
copy is never counted newer than it is. A statement of a session then
writes to no line another session's statement writes. A copy costs one
clone of the `State` per session per change of definitions, and its
shared parts stay shared. `Database::snapshot` keeps reading the lock for
the work that is not a session's statement.

#### D781. A prepared statement keeps its own copy of what its place keeps, copied again only once the place changes

Statements prepared alike in many sessions share the place their plans
are kept in (D610). Every execution read the place's lock and copied the
`Arc`s of the kept plan and the tables it reads, so the lock's count of
readers and those counts of references were written by every session's
executions.

So a place counts the changes of what it keeps, under its lock
(`prepared/shared.rs`), and each prepared statement keeps a copy of its
own, with the count it was copied at. An execution reads the count and,
while it is the same, takes what it needs from its copy. The copy holds
its own `Arc`s of the parsed statement, the cursor specification, the
physical plan and its tables, so taking them changes no count another
session changes. A plan kept is still kept in the place, under its lock,
and found by the other sessions at their next execution, which copies it
then. A place shared keeps its point: a plan is bound, planned and
learned once for all the sessions. The copy is behind a lock of the
statement's own, which no other session takes.

#### D782. What every transaction writes is alone on its cache lines, apart from what others read

A counter every transaction writes shared its cache line with fields
every transaction reads. The count of active transactions sat beside the
clock and the table of what cancels each transaction's statements. The
clock's counter of ids sat beside the durable timestamp every snapshot
reads. So a transaction beginning took the line from every other
transaction reading the field beside it, though they shared no data.

So each such value is alone on its cache lines (`sync/alone.rs`):
`Alone` aligns a value to 128 bytes and pads it out. The size is derived:
a cache line is 64 bytes, and an adjacent-line prefetcher fetches lines
in aligned pairs, so a write to either line of a pair takes both. The
clock's counters of ids and commits, its stable and durable timestamps,
the count of active transactions, each shard of what cancels the
statements of open transactions, each shard of the transactions
holding log records, and each shard of the ends of open transactions,
which row waits wait on, are alone. Their shards are found by an XXH3 map of
their own, not SipHash.
Nothing changes in what they hold or when, only where they lie.

#### D783. A transaction that changed nothing in a table takes nothing its store's transactions share as it begins or commits there

A transaction joining a table made the list its changes spill to at
once, reading the store's work areas under their lock and copying their
`Arc`. Committing there, it made another list for the rows to stamp,
and stored its status. A transaction that claimed no status, a reader,
took the lock of the statuses' map for writing to find it was not there.
A reader thus wrote the work areas' lock and count, and the map's lock,
at each transaction, for nothing it kept.

So a transaction's list of changes is given the work areas only as its
first change is pushed (`mvcc.rs`, `Open::changes_in`). A commit in a
table where it changed nothing stores its status alone, with no list. A
status claimed in no slot is looked for in the map only when the map
holds one (`mvcc/status.rs`). The latest snapshot and the horizon the
statuses keep are each alone on their lines, so raising one moves no
line a commit reads the slots by.

D870 does the same for the lists a commit makes in a table it wrote.

#### D784. A table's open transactions are kept in shards, by id, each alone on its cache lines

A table kept the bookkeeping of the transactions open in it in one map
under one lock. Every transaction took it for writing to begin and to
end there, and every read of a row took it to find its bookkeeping. So
every reader of a table wrote the lock's count of readers at each row
it read, and waited behind every begin and end.

So the map is in shards (`mvcc/opens.rs`), 32, chosen by the
transaction's id, each under its own lock, alone on its lines with a
count of what it holds. Transactions running at once fall in different
shards, as ids are given in turn, so one's begin, reads and end take no
line another's do. What asks of every transaction open in the table,
the newest but one or the oldest, for versions undone changes appended,
looks at each shard in turn. A transaction beginning while it looks did
not read what it is asked for. Whether any is open, which every
transaction's end may ask, is read from the counts alone, with no lock.

#### D805. A pool finds its files with no lock and no reference count moved

Each page a pool writes, and each it reads from its file, finds the file
by number. The files were kept behind one reader-writer lock, and the
file's `Arc` was cloned out of it, so every such call wrote the lock's
reader count and the file's reference count. Threads writing pages of
different tables passed both cache lines between them: a profile of
contended cache lines at 32 threads put it among the shared lines of
row updates. Files are only ever added to a pool, so each is now set
once in a slot never changed again: slots in chunks of 1,024 made as
files are added, each chunk set once in a fixed table of 1,024
(`disk/buffer/sources.rs`). A lookup loads two `OnceLock`s and borrows
the file for as long as the pool lives. A pool registers at most
1,048,576 files; one added past that is given a number no file has, so
every use of it is refused.

#### D815. A fast client's request takes nothing every worker shares: the permit kept while none waits, the stage and the user read with no lock

Between two requests of a fast client, its worker gave up its permit to
run statements (D42) and took it again, taking the limit's lock twice
and waking a waiter's notifier. Before each request it asked whether the
server still serves, through the lock of the server's watch, and whether
its user still is one, through the database's snapshot. As a statement
began and ended it set its connection's state in CONNECTIONS under the
lock of every connection's row. Every worker wrote each of those lines
at every request.

So the limit counts its waiters, alone on their line (`limit.rs`). A
worker lends its permit as it waits on its client for at most
`lent::WAITED` (`Permit::lend`). It gives the permit up only if another
waits for one, and else keeps it to run the request that comes. A waiter
that comes meanwhile is let in once some worker ends its next request,
or its wait, which is at most `WAITED` away; a worker whose client does
not come in time gives its permit up. The server's stage is a byte alone
on its line beside the watch (`server/stage.rs`), written as the stage
moves. Whether the connection's user is a user is asked of a snapshot
only once one was published since it last was (`native/seen.rs`,
`Database::publications`).
A connection's state is an atomic its row shares, set with no lock.
The session's settings told in Status are read from its own snapshot
(D780).

#### D795. A transaction's end writes the shared collection state only when it changes, and what every transaction reads never shares a line with what every one writes

Every writing transaction's end took the lock of the database's set of
tables awaiting collection twice, copied the set, and stored whether it
held any. Each also stored the table's last change instant, lowered the
table's earliest garbage timestamp with an atomic minimum, and asked
whether a collection was due by taking the read lock of the table's open
transactions. Each of these wrote a cache line every other writer then
read. The flags every transaction reads (whether the database takes
changes, whether tables await collection) sat beside counters every
transaction writes, so reading them missed as well.

Now a table carries whether it is in the set (`TableLock::noted`), kept
with the set under its lock. An end that would leave the set as it is,
a table not yet due left noted or a table gone left out, takes no lock,
and the set is copied only while it holds any. Whether tables await
collection, the change instant and the earliest timestamps are stored
only when they change, and `due_at` asks whether a transaction is open
in the table from D784's shard counts, with no lock. The database's
flags every change reads (whether it takes changes, whether it is held,
whether tables await collection) and the count of changes logged, which
every commit raises, each sit alone on their cache lines (D782). The
checkpoint's gate has 64 stripes, so threads at once seldom share one.

What is collected, and when, is unchanged. A table passed over is still
in the set for a later end to collect, and an end that collects it still
asks under the lock whether garbage came meanwhile (D445).

#### D796. A log appender whose block is written before those ahead of it files it, and whoever publishes up to it publishes every filed block that follows and wakes their appenders at once

D741 parked an appender whose block was written before those ahead of
it under its block's start, and the appender publishing up to it woke it
alone. That one then published its own block and woke the next. A run of
blocks written early was published one wake-up after another, each
appender waiting for the one before to be scheduled. At 32 sessions on
16 processors, one appender descheduled before its write stalled every
appender after it, and about one context switch in three of oltp
update_index was an appender parked there. The server then used fewer
processors at 32 sessions than at 8, and committed fewer transactions.

An appender whose block is written before those ahead of it now files
the block, its end and its thread, and waits. The appender that
publishes up to a filed block publishes it as well, and every filed
block that follows on from it, under the lock of the filed blocks, and
then wakes their appenders together. A run of blocks written early costs
one wake-up's wait. An appender in turn publishes its block with one
atomic step and takes the lock only when blocks are filed. The order in
which blocks are published, and what a reader sees, is D30's.

#### D806. A read by key that keeps its leaf reads a copy of it while the leaf's frame is unchanged

A read by key that keeps its leaf from read to read (`get_near`, D500),
as a fetch of rows by id from an index's entries does, found the next
row in the same leaf without a descent, but still read the page from
the pool and parsed it for each row. Each such read looked up the
frame's hint, wrote its latch's reader count and told the eviction
policy. Once the leaf
answers two reads in a row, the read now copies it, with the stamp of
its frame (D502), into what it keeps. Later reads take the copy while
the frame's version and page are as stamped, which is two loads and no
write, and the stamp of the tree's retirements as before. Any write of
the leaf moves the version on before it changes a byte, so a copy read
is the leaf as it is. A copy that is no longer current is dropped and
the leaf read again from the pool, and copied again if it answers.
Reads of keys of other leaves copy nothing, so a probe of scattered
rows costs no page copy.

#### D807. A thread keeps 256 inner node copies across its trees, the one to give way chosen by a clock bit

The copies of D502 were sixteen per thread, found by a scan and replaced
in turn. They are shared by every tree a thread reads, so a transaction
touching several tables, each with a root and a level below it, cycled
through them and read its inner nodes through their latches again. A
thread now keeps 256, found by page in a map. Each has a clock bit, set
when a descent reads it (Corbató, 1968). The copy to give way is the
first the hand finds with its bit clear, clearing the bits it passes.
At 8 KiB pages that is at most 2 MiB a thread. A copy taken again of a
page whose bytes no descent still holds is written into the old copy's
bytes, so re-reading a changed node allocates nothing.

#### D808. A leaf's copy is parsed once, and a read of it steps to the slot after the last found

A read from the copy of D806 parsed the copy's header again and checked
that the leaf answers for the key, a comparison with its first key and
its high key, before it looked at the slot after the last one found.
The copy does not change while it is kept, so its header is now parsed
once, as the copy is taken, and kept beside it. Each later read rebuilds
the node from those fields with no header read and no check made again
(`engine/tree/node/parsed.rs`). It compares the key with the one at the
slot after the last found first. A match is the key's entry in a leaf
that holds it, so the leaf answers for it and the read takes the value
with that one comparison. Any other key is checked against the leaf's
range and searched for as before.

#### D809. A scan keeps the entries it took from a leaf in one buffer, and lends them

A scan copies the entries it wants from a leaf under the leaf's latch,
so it holds no latch between entries (D31). Each entry was copied into a
key and a value of its own, two allocations, and a key of a node with a
shared prefix was put back together into its own. Each leaf of a
forward scan also gave the scan a new lower bound. An index's range
reader looks at each entry once and keeps only the row id and, for a
checked or decoded probe, the key decoded. A scan now copies a leaf's
entries into one buffer of bytes with each entry's places beside them,
both reused from leaf to leaf, and writes its lower bound into the bytes
of the one before (`engine/tree/scan/ready.rs`). `Scan::next_entry`
lends each entry until the scan is used again, and an index's entries
are read through it, so a range allocates nothing per entry once the
buffer has grown to a leaf's. The iterator gives owned entries as
before, copied from the buffer, for readers that keep them. Each entry
is lent with what the scan reads the tree through, so an index search
decodes keys by the types of the index the search holds. It no longer
clones the types' `Arc`, whose count every search on every thread
wrote, and a search moves the index it is given into what it holds
rather than clone it.

#### D792. A SELECT ... INTO of a kept program keeps the plan of the change its delta table reads

A kept program's INSERT, searched UPDATE and searched DELETE keep their
plans (D406). A SELECT ... INTO whose one table reference is the delta
table of such a change ran that change bound and planned anew at each
execution (`db/delta.rs`), though the change is the same statement each
time, its values the frame's slots. That made binding and planning the
largest cost of a body that reads what it changed, such as a stock or
district update read back through FINAL TABLE.

So such a SELECT ... INTO keeps its change's plan in the place the
program keeps its own statements' plans (`routines/program/host.rs`).
`select_into` passes those plans to the delta table's statement
(`run_delta_table`), which runs it as the program would run it alone,
by `Keeping` as a prepared statement's change. The SELECT around the
delta table is still bound and planned as it runs, as its rows are the
change's. A MERGE as the delta table's statement, or a SELECT ... INTO
of other table references besides, keeps nothing, as before.

#### D793. A kept SELECT ... INTO keeps its query over a delta table, a kept INSERT its query's plan, and a kept write probes by an array's element

A profile of order entry at two clients, on a build with D792, still
found three plannings at each run of a kept body, about a sixth of the
server's cycles; at eight clients, binding and planning were more than a
quarter. The SELECT around a delta table was bound and
planned at each execution (`select_into`). A searched UPDATE found by
an element of an array, as an order's stock update is
(`S_I_ID = NO_ITEMS[LOOP_COUNTER]`), planned its object rows at each
execution. Its kept binding held the element as a call of two slots,
which no probe took, so its plan made with slots was a scan. Its plan
made with values had the element folded into a probe, so the two never
had one shape, and it stopped learning (D613). An INSERT's query, the
order lines' over the arrays, was planned at each execution too, as the
query of a kept INSERT always was.

A SELECT ... INTO of a kept program over a delta table now keeps its
query as a prepared query is kept (`prepared/plans/delta.rs`). The
program keeps, beside each statement's plans, the plans of that query
and a transition table of its own. Each run refills that table with the
rows the change gives, in place, so the query bound once over it reads
each run's rows. Its physical plan is kept or learned as a prepared
query's (D45, D422). A run of the same statement that keeps nothing
gives its rows a table of their own, as before, so a plan kept never
reads another run's rows.

A probe of a kept write's object rows takes a column compared with an
`<array element reference>` of slots and constants
[ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §6.25], the element's value placed as each
execution places a slot's (`physical/probe.rs`). Such an element can
raise array element error [§6.25 GR2b], which a probe kept from D613
never takes. The search condition is evaluated for each row of the
table [§14.14 GR5], and the element is the same at every row, so it
raises at every row or at none. A probe by it reads the rows a scan
would find, as long as it raises nowhere. An execution whose element
raises therefore places nothing. It runs a plan made with its values,
which leaves the failing element unfolded, as folding leaves any
failing expression, and scans, raising as the scan does
(`Kept::places`). The planner takes such a comparison as one a probe
may answer only for a kept write's plan made with slots
(`answerable`). No test yet tells that guard apart. A table with rows
raises at the probe as at the scan, and an emptied table is planned
again as it drifts (D422) before the kept probe could run over it. Only a write's object rows take such a probe. A query's
kept plan, and each other probe, take none, as before.

A kept INSERT's query keeps its physical plan as a query's is kept, kept
at once if it is one probe of a unique key, else learned
(`db/write/inserted.rs`). One that reads the statement's instant is still
planned at each execution, as that instant is no slot its plan reads.
Nor is one kept whose statement EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs, which counts the
plan it makes.

Those plans read leaves no kept plan held before. A transition table is
one shape with itself, so a plan over the delta query's own table
learns, and a filled plan reads it as refilled. Rows of values are one
shape when they have as many rows of as many expressions, and an UNNEST
when its collections are alike over an input of one shape
(`physical/kept/shape.rs`). Each is filled as its expressions are
(`physical/kept/filled.rs`).

A correlated subquery of such a plan, the price of each order line's
item, learned its plan anew at each execution, since each execution's
runner is its own (D675). A kept plan now keeps what its subqueries
settled, kept or planned at each run, beside it (`KeptSubqueries`,
`exec/subquery/planned.rs`). Each execution's runner starts from that,
and a run whose values do not fit the slots is planned alone, as before.
What it keeps goes with the plan, so it is made again whenever the plan
is.

A prepared CALL keeps its binding as a prepared INSERT does
(`routines/call.rs`). It is bound once with its `?`s as slots, unless the
binding holds a value, and each execution fills its arguments' slots
with its values before they are evaluated [§9.18 GR3]. The binding was
made with the definitions of then, so a change of the procedure or of
a privilege binds it again (D45).

`binder::bindings()` counts the bindings a thread made, as
`physical::plannings()` counts its plannings. `tpcc_plans.rs` now runs the
driver's procedures, FINAL TABLE reads and order arrays included, and
asserts that no CALL binds or plans anything in a steady state. The
procedures it ran before had neither, so it passed while each run bound
and planned these statements.

#### D810. A checkpoint tells how long it took, how long writers waited for it, and the pages it wrote

The `checkpoint_taken` event carries what the checkpoint took, in
microseconds. `micros` is the whole. `shut_micros` runs from the gate
asked shut to opened again, the engines' capture inside it, which is how
long writers waited. `sync_micros` is the checkpoint record's sync, and
`finish_micros` the captures made durable, the image recorded and the log
truncated. `pages` counts the pages written to the tables file
meanwhile, written back or captured, so a writer's own evictions count
too. An operator sees what a checkpoint costs the work going on without a
profiler, and a change that spreads that cost is measured by it.

#### D811. A commit closes its side file and writes its file in runs of granules

A commit wrote each held granule to the side file as an op of its own,
and copied each granule into the file with a write of its own: for a
checkpoint of a gigabyte, a quarter of a million ops, frames and system
calls each way. Now granules next to each other go as one run, up to
`RUN_BYTES`: one op closing the side file, which recovery already reads
as a run, and one write into the file. `RUN_BYTES` is 64 KiB, by a sweep
from 64 KiB to 64 MiB on a drive with power-loss protection and one
without. It gave the shortest commits on both, by a little, and past
4 MiB they lengthen again, so the best does not move with the drive and
it is a constant, not a setting.

#### D812. Withdrawn: a checkpoint's commits are not spread, as spreading them cost throughput

The checkpoint job once spread its commits over three quarters of the
time since the last checkpoint began, waiting after each write for its
share of the span. It flattened the work going on through a commit, but
an A/B against commits made at once gave less throughput in all, on a
drive with power-loss protection and one without. A smoother window
does not pay for work lost, so commits are made at once again, and
D811's runs are what shortens them.
A checkpoint's captures are made durable as writers go on (D590), but
the commit's copying takes a core and the drive while it runs, and the
work going on loses the same share of both for the seconds it takes. The
checkpoint job asks the commits to take about `SPREAD` of the time since
the last checkpoint began instead: after each write, the commit waits
until its share of the span is due (`disk/shadow/pace.rs`). The cost is
the same, spread thin, and the job is done before the next checkpoint
is due. The first checkpoint has no last to measure from and
goes at once.

A checkpoint asked for, by `Database::checkpoint`, a backup or a close,
goes at once, as its caller waits for it. A close tells a spread commit
going on to hurry, so it waits for no span. `SPREAD` is three quarters,
by a sweep of none, a quarter, a half and three quarters on a drive with
power-loss protection and one without. Three quarters gave the flattest
work going on on both, so the best does not move with the drive and it
is a constant, not a setting. A quarter of the time is left before the
next checkpoint is due, and a next one due sooner only starts later.
#### D665. A chain of inner hash joins may read its leaves first, each filtered by Bloom filters of the others' keys, before its joins

A hash join's runtime filter (D369) goes from its build to its probe
side, so a selective condition on the table a chain probes never shrinks
the tables it builds. Predicate transfer, as Yang, Zhao, Yu and Koutris
(CIDR 2024) define it, reads the chain's tables first, each filtered by
filters of the keys of the tables read before it, so a condition on any
table shrinks the others. The planner plans a phase, `Plan::Transfer`,
over a chain once the rest of the plan is made, and EXPLAIN shows it as
`PredicateTransfer` above the chain.

- A chain is inner hash joins, LEFT outer joins of no condition of an
  operand's own, and the filters and projections over them, its leaves
  the plans below. A LEFT join's key transfers from its left operand to
  its right alone, as a left row no right row matches is still a row of
  the join, with nulls [ISO/IEC 9075:1992 §7.5 GR4]. A key on which nulls
  match transfers in no chain with a LEFT join, as a row it made with
  nulls would match it. A leaf has the same number for the planner
  and the executor, its place in a walk of left inputs before right ones,
  past the operators EXPLAIN ANALYZE counts.
- A step is a key of a hash join that is a column of a leaf on each side.
  Its filter holds the keys of the rows one leaf kept and judges the
  other's column, as a runtime filter does (D369): a range of an exact key
  and a blocked Bloom filter of the keys' hashes. A row it drops matches
  no row of the other leaf, so no row of the chain holds it. The joins then
  run in their planned order over the rows kept, so the chain gives the
  same rows in the same order.
- No operator of the chain or of its leaves may raise an error or a
  warning (`Plan::can_raise`), so no operator raises on fewer rows than it
  would (D15), and no leaf is the operand of a guard (D373), whose part
  can raise.
- The phase reads each leaf whole, so a chain under a limit not of a sort
  is planned as it was, and so is one inside a part run in parallel,
  whose morsels the phase is no step of. The chain must give batches,
  every table it reads read by batch, its rows asked for in no order.
- A plan with a phase is never kept for a prepared statement's next
  executions (D422): a phase is of no shape a kept plan compares alike.
- PLANNER.PREDICATE_TRANSFER, ON by default and of a session's scope,
  plans phases; OFF plans none, as to compare the two.

#### D666. Predicate transfer goes along a maximum spanning tree of the chain's leaves rooted at the largest, up and back

The steps run along a tree of the chain's leaves, as LargestRoot in Zhao
et al., Robust Predicate Transfer (SIGMOD 2025), builds it: a maximum
spanning tree of the leaves joined by keys, each edge weighed by the keys
its two leaves share, rooted at the leaf of the most estimated rows. Each
leaf sends to its parent after the leaves below it, then each parent
sends to its leaves before they send to theirs. For a chain acyclic once
its equalities are classes, one pass up and one back reduce each leaf to
the rows some row of the chain holds. A key of a cycle that is no edge of
the tree transfers nothing; its join still filters as any. A chain whose
keys leave a leaf unjoined has no tree and no phase.

#### D667. A transfer step is kept where its keys are at most half the values it judges, and the phase is planned where it pays

A step's filter holds at most as many keys as its leaf's rows kept and
the values of its column, by the leaf's table's statistics. The step is
kept only where those are at most half the values of the column it
judges, so it is expected to drop at least half of that leaf's rows, as
RPT+ (Qiao, Boncz and Zhang, PVLDB 2026) builds a filter only where it is
expected to drop rows. A leaf's rows are reduced by each step taken
before, its keys taken as spread alike and independent (Selinger et al.,
1979). The phase is planned if the rows its steps are expected to drop,
each worth half a row read, outweigh an insert into and a probe of a Bloom
filter of each row of each step, a tenth of a row read each, and the
phase's own cost, a fixed number of rows read (`PHASE_ROWS`). Of the chain's first leaf, only the
rows dropped past those a filter of the other leaf as planned would drop
are counted, as its scan is told the runtime filters of the builds joined
with it already (D369).

#### D668. A phase holds its leaves within its work area, reads a leaf past it again with its filters, and stops a filter that keeps most rows

The executor takes the chain's leaves out of it and takes the steps in
order. The leaf a step's filter is made of is read, told every filter made
for it so far as a hash join tells its scan (D369), and its batches held
with the rows kept, charged to the phase's work area (D38); a leaf held
already is judged by the filters made for it since. Each leaf then goes
back into the chain, held, or told its filters, and the chain runs over
them. A leaf past what is left of the work area is not held: its filter is
made of its key's vector alone as it is read, and it is read again in the
chain, told every filter made for it, as Robust Predicate Transfer streams
its largest relation. A filter that keeps more than nine in ten of the
rows of its first batches stops judging them (D369), and the step back
along its edge is not taken, as RPT+ drops a transfer that does not pay.
None of these changes the rows.

#### D813. A pool's test reading a page fails first if a frame is left latched exclusively

A read waits for its frame's latch, and a thread that still holds the
page for writing holds that latch, so it would wait for ever. A test of
the pool's stamps that took one while it held a page for writing hung
for a day instead of failing. The thread was the only one left, and its
own write guard held the latch. The stamps' tests now count the frames
latched exclusively, with a try that never waits, before each read, and
fail if any is. The pool itself is unchanged. The hang came from the
test's own order of holding and reading, not from an order in which the
pool takes its latches, and the test as it is now on main never held
and read at once.
#### D814. A leaf a delete leaves sparse merges into its right neighbour when the two fit in three quarters of a page

A table's rows take new ids at the right edge of its tree, so a row
deleted and inserted again never returns to its leaf. When only the
leaves that deletes emptied were taken out, the rest stayed sparse for
good. Under a steady
mix of deletes and inserts, the live rows spread over about three times
the pages, and every checkpoint wrote all of them.

A delete that leaves its leaf at most three eighths full now tries to
merge it into its right neighbour (`engine/tree/merge.rs`). If the
entries of both fit in three quarters of a page, the neighbour is
written with all of them, and the leaf is taken out as an emptied one
is (D31, `reclaim.rs`), its range given to the neighbour. The leaf on
its left, the leaf, the neighbour and their parent are locked in that
order, bottom to top and left to right, as every writer locks, so no
writer changes either leaf between the neighbour written and the leaf
marked deleted. Keys move only right, as in a split, so a scan or read
that reaches the leaf afterwards follows its link to where its keys
went, and a scan returns no key twice. A leaf first or last under its
parent stays, as an empty one does.

Three quarters is derived from the node layout, not swept. The longest
entry takes a quarter of a page less two headers, so a leaf merged to
three quarters takes any entry next without splitting, and two halves
of a split together fill more than three quarters, so a split is not
undone. A larger share could leave a merged leaf to split at the next
insert, and a smaller one only leaves more pages. A leaf is tried at
half that share, three eighths, because one fuller can only merge with
a smaller neighbour, which tries its own right one.

A tree's pages reach the file through the shadowed data file, as a
split's do (D25), so a merge is in a checkpoint whole or not at all, and
the log redoes the deletes after it.

Freeing a leaf's page is not part of the delete that took it out. Once
no operation may hold the page, the next unlink frees it, which writes
it zeroed. If its file fails that write, as a checkpoint's failed sync
leaves writes failing, the page is kept to free at a later unlink, and
the delete stands: the tree no longer reaches the page, so until then it
is only space. Failing the delete would fail the undo of an insert,
which deletes, and so damage its table.

The pages taken out and not yet freed are noted in the tree's meta page
too (`engine/tree/retired.rs`), not only in memory, so a crash loses
none for good. A tree opened takes the pages its meta page notes as its
own to free, as no operation of the run before can hold them. A page is
noted after the tree stops reaching it and unnoted before it is freed,
so a checkpoint's image never notes a page its tree reaches, nor one
freed and given again; a checkpoint in between costs a page of space.

#### D822. An update's log record writes the columns it changed in place, and a scan's batch has room for its rows before it gathers them

An update's log record (D475) wrote each column of the row before into a
vector of its own to compare it with the row after, and the columns that
changed into a second vector, copied into the record at its end. A scan's
batch gathered from records in place (D31) began each batch's vectors
empty, as the last batch took them, and grew them by doubling to the
rows asked for.

So the row before's columns are written straight into the record after
the count, each taken back again if its bytes are those it has after,
and the count is written last into its place (`log/record/images.rs`).
A batch reserves room in each column's vector for the rows it is asked
for before it gathers them (`Gathering::reserve`). A batch is at most
`BATCH_ROWS` rows, so the room is bounded, and a scan that stops short
of it leaves only that room unused. In a TPC-C profile at 2 users they
were among the allocation sites outside planning, with the log's
update images the largest.

#### D835. A write decodes the row it replaced once, for its caller and the zone it widens alike

The row store's write gives the row it replaced, decoded from the
version it found (D417), and widens the row's zone over that version's
values of the columns kept. Each decoded the version on its own,
so an UPDATE decoded the row it replaced twice. The write now decodes
it once (`RowTable::replaced`) and widens the zone over that row
(`RowTable::widen_over`). A deletion's version, or one the write could
not decode, widens the zone as one not known, as before. Decoding the
whole row reads every column the kept ones are among, so the zone holds
the same values. A procedure's keyed UPDATE of one row, profiled, spent
about a twentieth of its time in the second decode.

#### D836. A routine's variable in a subquery of a change is the subquery's slot, not an outer reference, so the subquery probes a key

A routine's SQL variable or parameter is bound as a slot of its frame.
In a subquery it is bound as an outer reference whose outer expression
is that slot, as a column of the query around the subquery is. So a
subquery of a procedure's UPDATE or DELETE that reads a variable, an IN
of the UNNEST of array variables or a lateral's MIN of a parameter, was
correlated. The change's plan decorrelated it over every row of the
object table, a scan of it in place of a probe of its key (D775). A
CALL whose UPDATE named ten keys of a table of 300000 rows read the
table twice.

The value of such a reference is the same for every row the subquery
is applied to. So before a change's object rows are planned
(`db/compiled.rs`), each outer reference whose outer expression is a
constant or a slot is replaced by it, at any depth, and a subquery left
with no outer reference has none (`logical::fixed_outer`). Its plan
then reads the slot as a `?` there does, the IN is a semi join, and its
few rows probe the key (D774, D777). A subquery whose identity a kept
program keeps its plans by is left alone unless a reference is
replaced.

A collection constant, as a filled array slot is, had no declared type,
so a probe took no value from its elements (D779). Its type is now the
collection type of its elements' type, when each element that is not
null is of one kind (`physical/indexed/typed.rs`).

#### D837. A scan takes back the index entries of rows gone for every reader as it meets them

A queue's rows are inserted at the high end of its key's range and
deleted from the low end, and the search for its first row begins at
the low end. A deleted row's index entries stay until collection takes
them back (D29), and every search before then passes them, each a read
of a row it does not see. Collection waits for the horizon and runs a
batch of commits at a time (D451), one collector a table (D445), so
under many writers the deletions pile up at the low end, the search for
the head of the queue passes more of them each time, and its
transaction holds its row locks longer while others queue behind it.

A read by row id that finds no row now tells, in its `Near`, the commit
of the deletion that the row's newest version is, if it is a committed
one (`RowTable::deletion_of`). A scan of an index that meets such an
entry, the deletion at or before the horizon, takes the entry back on
the spot by the call collection would make, `Index::remove`
(`exec/entries/pruning.rs`). The searches of an index scan, a point
read, a data change's object rows and an index join do so. The horizon
is read once and again only for a deletion past it, as it only moves
on.

The semantics hold for these reasons.

- No snapshot open or to come is before the horizon, and a deletion at
  or before it is seen by all of them, so none reads any version of the
  row. Row ids are never given again, so every entry of the row is
  garbage, whatever its count.
- A deletion not committed, or committed after an open snapshot, is
  never taken back, so undo and every older reader find what they did.
- The removal is collection's own, made earlier. Collection, finding an
  entry gone, has nothing to take back (an ordered index and a hash
  index count only what they remove), and a checkpoint's stale entries
  are taken back at recovery the same way. Like collection, it logs
  nothing: the row store's files are shadowed (D25), so a crash leaves
  the last checkpoint's entries, and recovery's replay of the deletion
  and its collection take them back again.
- An index whose entries are projections of their keys, and a global
  index over partitions (D157), whose rows are read through their
  partitions, are left to collection.

Collecting the table at the first such meeting was rejected. It would
move a batch of commits' collection onto one reader's statement, and
the one collector a table (D445) would make every other reader pass the
same entries meanwhile.

#### D838. A scan priced by a sample of its zones reads at least one zone of the sample

A scan of a row store table is priced by the share of the rows its
conditions may match, by its zones (`TableStorage::scan_share`), and of
a table of more than `SAMPLED` zones the planner looks at that many,
evenly apart, so planning costs no more as the table grows. A delivery's
update of an order's lines asks for one order, whose lines lie in one
zone, and once the table held twice as many zones the sample passed
over every other one. Of an order in a zone passed over, no zone of the
sample held it, so the scan was priced at nothing, below the index that
finds the lines, and the procedure kept that plan, reading every line of
the table at each call. So a share of a sample is never less than one
zone of the sample (`rows/zones.rs`): the zones passed over may hold
the rows asked for, as many as one zone looked at. Nor is the share of
a table whose every zone is looked at, though none may hold them now,
as rows written later may (D839).

#### D839. No estimate makes a scan of a whole unique key, nor of a key's range a scan reads past, and a plan kept is learned again with statistics

Three plans of the TPC-C procedures were made from estimates that no
estimate should decide. A probe fixing every column of a unique key was
taken unpriced only of a table of a thousand rows or more and with no
order asked (D45, D408). DISTRICT and WAREHOUSE are smaller, so every
payment and order entry scanned them for their one row, as did a plan
kept while its table was still empty. Such a probe now is the path
whatever the table's size and whatever order is asked, as it finds one
row at most, which is in any order (`physical/access.rs`).

A range of an index whose first key columns its probe holds equal, of a
primary or unique key or of an index holding every column read, finds
only rows a scan told the same conjuncts reads too, in the zones they
may lie in. Its cost by its estimated rows, each fetched by row id,
could still pass that scan's. A stock level's lines of its district's
last twenty orders were estimated at several times their rows by the
index's share of its tree, while the scan was priced by the zones of a
sample, those of the newest orders, which hold every district's. The
scan then cost the less, so the plan made with the values scanned,
reading thousands of lines at each run, and the plan made with slots,
the range, never kept its shape, so it was planned twice at every call.
Such a range is now never priced above the scan of the conjuncts it
answers, and so never above a scan of the whole table. Where the two
are then priced alike, it is taken if it is estimated to read fewer
rows than the scan, and fewer than the table's rows over
PLANNER.ESTIMATE_MARGIN, as the joins weigh their estimates (D386). A
range that reads a share of the scan's rows fetches no more than that
share. One that reads most of them finds them together, as the zones
the scan reads hold little else, so its fetches by row id come in
order and each starts at the leaf of the last. A range of most of the
table, whose zones may not tell, is left to the costs
(`physical/access/bounded.rs`).

A stock level's join of its lines to the stock of their items hashed a
scan of STOCK, of every zone, priced at nothing, as no zone yet held a
quantity below the threshold asked. A new order's update of a stock
row writes it again, where zones gain low quantities, and STOCK gains
no rows, so the plan kept it and read more of the table at each call,
tens of thousands of rows where its probes by key read a few hundred.
A scan's share is now never less than one zone of those looked at,
sampled or not (D838): a zone holding no row asked for now may hold
rows written later, and a plan kept reads them.

A plan kept by a prepared statement or a procedure's body (D45, D414)
was learned again when a table it reads gained or lost rows as its
statistics would be gathered again for. A plan of index probes alone
was learned again also once a table without statistics got them (D613),
but a plan with a scan kept the defaults it was made with until its
table drifted, and a warehouse's tables seldom drift. Every plan kept
now notes which of its tables had statistics when it was learned, and
is learned again once one of those without them has them
(`db/prepared/plans/grown.rs`). Statistics gathered again of a table
that drifted already have it learn again by its drift.

#### D840. A probe of a B-link tree searches slots without building errors, reads inner copies parsed once, finds a writer's leaf from its parent and writes it through the frame it owns, and allocates no path or scan buffer

The storage engine is the floor of a transaction once its procedures
skip SQL, and the B-link tree was the largest part of it, about a third
of the time of a TPROC-C transaction. Each probe of a table or index
paid for work the tree's design does not need. The node format of D500
already searches the page's bytes over a slot array of key heads, but
every step of the search read a slot through a field reader returning a
`Result` whose error is a `SqlError` of many words. So each head and
each tail was a call that returned that large value through memory, and
none was inlined. Parsing a node read each header field the same way.

A node parsed now borrows its slots as an array of four-byte slots,
checked once to fill the end of the page in whole slots, and its bytes
before them (`engine/tree/node.rs`). Its header is read as one array of
fixed size, so no field read can fail. The search runs over the slots
with each step an `Option`, and an error is built once, only if a slot
leads past the heap. The bytes searched and the order found are those of
D500.

A descent read each inner node from the thread's copy of D502 and parsed
the copy again at every visit. Each copy now keeps its node's header as
parsed beside it, as a leaf's copy does (D808), and a descent rebuilds
the node from it with no header read and no check made again
(`engine/tree/inner.rs`). The copy is current exactly while its frame's
version holds, so its header parsed is too.

A writer went down to the leaf, read it under its latch only to learn
its page, owned it, read it again, then held it for writing. Each of the
owning, the second read and the write found the frame in the page table
again, a shard locked, a map searched and a pin taken. A writer now
stops at the node above the leaves and takes the leaf's page from it
(`engine/tree/write.rs`), as the leaf is read once it is owned. A leaf
split or taken out in between is moved right from once owned, as before,
since Lehman and Yao's move right (§5) needs only a page the key was once
reachable from, and the writer's epoch keeps a page taken out from being
freed (D814). The owner then reads and writes the page through the frame
it owns (`disk/buffer/owned.rs`). The frame is pinned to the page while
owned, so no page table is looked in, and the write marks the page dirty
and gives a checkpoint's capture its copy exactly as a write through the
page table does (D30). A frame owned of another pool is written through
its page table.

A descent kept its path in a vector, allocated at its first level, and
every scan copied the key below each node on the way down, though only a
backward scan uses it. An index probe built its range's bounds, and the
scan copied them, and each scan allocated its buffers of D809. The path
is now kept in place, at most 24 levels, a taller one giving up its top,
which only makes a writer find a parent again from the root
(`engine/tree/levels.rs`). Only a backward scan copies the key below. A
scan takes its bounds as built (`scan_owned`), and gives its buffers back
to its thread when done, so the thread's next scan takes them
(`engine/tree/scan/ready.rs`). So a probe that finds one entry allocates
nothing in the tree.

#### D841. A procedure's body runs as the program it is compiled to, its point reads and point changes straight on their tables

A CALL of a procedure whose body its session keeps (D406) ran the body's
program through the interpreter, and each statement of it through the
session's general path: the statement looked up in the plans the program
keeps, bound or taken bound, wrapped as a statement the session runs,
and of a SELECT ... INTO of a delta table, the delta table's query run
by the executor over the rows the change gave. An order's entry spent
more than half its time there, and not in its reads and writes. So the
program is compiled as a CALL first runs it, to a tree of code kept with
the program (`db/routines/program/compiled.rs`), made again whenever the
program is: once a definition, privilege, role, schema, time zone or
setting it was bound with no longer holds (D45, D414).

The tree runs as the interpreter runs a program. Each statement empties
the diagnostics area as it begins and places its condition there as it
ends; a condition is offered to the handlers in scope where it is raised;
each atomic statement is undone alone if it fails; an ATOMIC compound
statement runs at a savepoint level of its own. Its values are found as
it was compiled. A row of values that reads nothing is evaluated where
it is, over the frame's slots. A variable or parameter assigned as a
whole is its slot, its value cast by store assignment there. A SELECT
... INTO whose query plans to one point read of a whole unique key
(D752) reads its row by that point read, its tables locked, its snapshot
taken and its reads recorded as a leaf's are.

A change runs the general path first, which keeps its plans. Once they
are kept, a searched UPDATE or DELETE, alone or as a SELECT ... INTO's
FINAL, NEW or OLD TABLE, and an INSERT of one row of values, run with
them past the statement's binding and wrapping: its object rows by its
plan kept as that plan stands, learning or learned (D422), a point read
once it is one (D752), and its rows by the write functions the general path
writes with, so its row locks, rechecks, escrow (D452), BEFORE triggers,
defaults, identity, generated columns, constraints and the unique check
at its end are the general path's own, as are its ROW_COUNT and its
errors. The delta table's rows are gathered by the collector the general
path gathers them with, and the select list is evaluated over them.

A searched UPDATE or DELETE whose plan is a point read as the execution
runs it is written straight on its table (`db/write/direct.rs`), past
the notes the write functions keep of each row for the statement's end.
Its row is found by the point read, locked, rechecked and written by the
same calls, its candidate row made with its casts and generated columns
as theirs is. Its end checks its reads as any statement's end checks
them, and between, each constraint of the row it wrote that the end
would check of it, which are the NOT NULL, foreign key and CHECK
constraints on the columns it gives values to and each CHECK without a
subquery, and then its UNIQUE constraints on those columns. An INSERT of
one row of values is written as the write functions write a row, its end
checking every constraint of that row so. The delta
table's one row is the row it wrote, or of OLD TABLE the row it deleted,
and its ROW_COUNT is the one row or none. The change runs the write
functions instead wherever its end would check more than its row, or the
rows it notes would be read by more than its delta table, as of a
constraint that may be deferred, a foreign key referencing a column it
gives a value to or a row it deletes, a CHECK that reads tables, an
assertion, a delta table's statement running around it, or increments
escrow would reserve.

A change of a view, of a typed or partitioned table, of a table some
trigger is on that the change may write, or with XML options in scope,
runs the general path always, as does every other statement, cursor and
FOR. EXECUTOR.COMPILED_PROCEDURES OFF runs each body by the interpreter.

#### D842. A home waits on its client for a second, its permit given up after a millisecond

A worker waited for a client's next request only `lent::WAITED`, a
millisecond (D42). A client slower than that, as one that thinks between
its requests or one whose threads outnumber its processors, had its next
request read by the connection's task: the socket handed back to the
runtime and registered with it again, the task woken by the runtime, the
request handed to the home under its lock and the home woken, and the
loan given back to the task as the reply went out. Two moves between
threads and two of the socket at every request, and a client near the
millisecond moved between the two paths request by request.

Now a connection's home waits on, after `WAITED`, as long as
`waiting::HOME_WAITED`, a second, in slices of `lent::LOOKED`
(`native/waiting.rs`). Between slices it looks whether the operator
ended the connection or the server stopped, and if so gives the client
back to the task, which ends the connection as before. Its wait ends
sooner than SERVER.IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS, and SERVER.IDLE_IN_TRANSACTION_TIMEOUT_MS
while a transaction is active, and the task counts the client's idle time
from when the home began to wait (`Lent::idle_since`), so a client is
closed as idle at the time it was. A home waits whether or not its client
was fast, so a client once slow is not read by the task from then on. A
worker that is not the connection's home still waits only `WAITED`.

Past `WAITED` the worker gives its permit to run statements up, whether
or not another waits for one, so a statement waiting for a permit waits
for a home's client no longer than D815 allows. A home whose client's last
request came later than `WAITED` waits in slices of `LOOKED` from the
first, its permit given up at once, so a client that thinks is not woken
for in vain after a millisecond at every request; once a request comes
within `WAITED` again the client counts as fast. A client slower than a
millisecond then takes the limit's lock again at its next request, as
every request of a client did before D815, but no longer moves between
threads. A client that thinks longer than a second pays the two moves
once a second at most, under a ten-thousandth of its time, and a waiting
home is woken fifty times a second, so a longer wait gains nothing
measurable and keeps a thread from the pool longer.

#### D843. A commit stamps each row in place from the leaf its write left it in, with no descent

A commit's stamp of each row it wrote (D440) read the row's entry by a
descent of the table's tree and wrote it back by another, a version
encoded anew each time. In an order entry that was most of the commit's
cost, two walks from the root for every row, though the write that made
the entry had held its leaf.

Now a write of a row's version tells where it left the entry, its leaf
and the tree's stamp read before the write (`engine/tree/placed.rs`), and
the transaction keeps that with the change. Its stamp locks that leaf,
moves right past the splits since, finds the entry, and writes the
commit timestamp and its flag over the version in place, under the
leaf's lock (`RowTable::stamp_placed`). The stamp's bytes are as long as
the transaction id they replace, so nothing in the leaf moves.

The leaf is trusted only while the tree's stamp is unchanged. A leaf
leaves the tree only by being retired, which moves the stamp first, so
an unchanged stamp means the leaf is still a leaf of this tree and the
entry is in it or to its right (D446, D500). A moved stamp, or an entry
not found from the leaf, sends the stamp down from the root as before.
Under the leaf's lock the version is stamped only if the transaction
still made it, as a stamp replaced an entry only as it read it, so a
writer that wrote over it meanwhile keeps its own.

Nothing else changes. The stamping runs when it did, after the locks are
released and inside the checkpoint gate, so visibility, validation,
recovery, checkpoints and the collection of old versions read the same
versions as before.

#### D844. A transaction begins from its session's kept origin, its id on its thread's stripe

A transaction's begin wrote lines every core shares. It took a reference
to the coordinator, the log, the work areas and the type registry, each
an object every session shares, and dropped them again at its end, so
each count's line moved between cores at every begin and end. It added
one to a count of open transactions that every begin wrote. Its id came
from one counter, and its snapshot's stripe, its end (D442) and its stop
(D44) were placed by that id, so consecutive transactions of one session
landed on stripes another core had written last. In point selects and
deletes on many threads the begin was the largest function of the
server, its cost in those atomic writes and the cache misses after them.

A session now keeps what its transactions begin from, an `Origin`
holding the coordinator, the log and the space its undo entries spill
in (`txn/begin.rs`). A begin takes one reference to the session's own
origin, whose count only its thread writes. The session keeps it while
the snapshot it begins against has the same coordinator, log, work
areas, type registry and work memory, which a look tells without
taking a reference to any of them. Else it makes a new one, so a
session that sets MEMORY.WORK_BYTES spills its next transaction's undo
by its own setting. The undo log holds the origin's space shared, not a
copy.

An id is still later than every one given before, so ids keep the order
transactions begin in, but ids are 64 apart, and each id's last six bits
are its thread's stripe (`sync::thread_stripe`). The stripes of the
snapshots and the shards of the ends, stops and held records, whose
counts divide 64, are then its thread's, and stay on its core. The
count of open transactions is kept in each snapshot stripe and summed
when read, which only a close and a status ask. An id stride of 64
leaves 2^58 transactions, which cannot run out in practice. Ids order
nothing against timestamps, as before. So nothing compared with a commit
timestamp may be taken from an id: an index filled with the table's
writers kept out is filled through the latest commit timestamp
(`Transactions::latest_commit`), not the highest id or timestamp a
