The bound is 64 commits past a table's earliest garbage, the bound D451
chose for a busy table. A sweep of it on the in-repo order entry bench
at one session, over 1, 4, 16, 64, 256 and 1024 commits, counted the
allocations a commit makes, which no load on the machine moves. They
fall from 1 to 4 to 16 to 64 and are level from there, and a commit's
time follows them within the spread of the runs. A larger batch saves
nothing more and holds more versions, so the bound stays the one rule
for quiet and busy tables. The sweep's figures are in the commit that
made the change.

The semantics hold for these reasons.

- The horizon rule is unchanged. A collection removes only what commits
  at or before the horizon superseded, so no reader, at any isolation
  level, meets a version collected too early. A batch only comes later.
- The garbage a table holds is bounded by a batch, 64 commits or 4096
  versions, whichever comes first, beyond what a lagging horizon keeps
  as before. Its lists are counted against the memory budget and spill
  as before (D38, D870).
- A table no transaction writes again is collected by the pass, within
  a second of the end that left it, so its zones become visible to all
  and its undo store is truncated without another commit.
- Maintenance is noted as before. An end notes a table whose engine has
  some due whether or not it collected it.
- A checkpoint and a close collect every table, waiting, as before.

#### D921. The log holds a segment's records in a buffer, and a commit that does not wait for its sync makes no write of its own

A commit wrote its records to the log's segment with one positional
write (D470, D882), whether or not it then waited for a sync. With
LOG.COMMIT_SYNC OFF that write was the one call into the system a commit
made, and many sessions' writes took the file's lock in turn.

The database's file log now writes its segments through a buffer
(`log/file/buffered.rs`, `FileLogOptions::buffer`, 64 KiB). An append
copies its records into the buffer and returns. The buffer is written to
the segment, in one write for the records of many commits, when it
fills, when a sync, a rotation or a cut of the segment needs the file
whole, when the log is dropped, when the log sync job runs
(`Log::write_buffered`), and with the first append made a second after
the oldest record it holds. Records are read back from the buffer from
the moment they are appended, so the undo of a statement, a reader of the
log and recovery's replay find them as before. A position is given as
before, by the block file, so the order of records is unchanged.

A commit that waits (LOG.COMMIT_SYNC ON) appends and then syncs. Its
sync writes the buffer, its own records and those of the commits before
it together, and syncs the segment, so a lone committer still makes one
write and one sync, and a group commit one write and one sync for the
group. A log that syncs nothing (LOG.DURABILITY NONE) still writes the
buffer at each sync asked of it. Under LOG.SYNC_AFTER_MS 0 the log sync
job is asked for a second after a commit left unsynced and only has the
log write its buffer.

What a failure may lose is what LOG.COMMIT_SYNC OFF promised before. A
commit that did not wait is lost by a failure before the log's next
sync, with every commit after it, so recovery finds a prefix of the
commits (D25). The log's next sync comes within LOG.SYNC_AFTER_MS as
before. One case changes inside that promise. A failure of the process
alone, the system going on, used to keep such a commit once its record
was written, and now loses it while the record is still in the buffer,
which is at most a second while commits come, or until the log sync job
runs, a second after the commit by default. A failure of the system
loses the same commits as before, those not synced. A commit that waits
is durable when it returns, as before, under either failure.

A write of the buffer that fails is kept by the file, and every later
append, sync and cut of the segment fails with it. The log then fails
its next sync, and the database takes no change until it is opened
again, as after any failed write of the log (D25).

A segment keeps zeros written past its records so that a commit's sync
carries no growth of the file (`disk/block/fill.rs`). While no commit
waits for a sync those zeros bought nothing, and every byte of the log
was written twice, the zeros being most of the time a commit spent in
the system. A buffered log's segments are now refilled only once the
segment has been synced since its last refill
(`BlockOptions::ahead_once_synced`). A database whose commits wait keeps
its zeros as before, one whose commits do not writes them once after
each sync of the log sync job, and a block past the zeros is written
past the file's end, as in a file given none.

The undo stores, the replicated journal and a log a program opens for
itself are not buffered. Their options leave the buffer at 0.

The buffer is 64 KiB. A sweep on the in-repo order entry bench at one
session, of none, 4, 16, 64 and 256 KiB, showed no difference between
the sizes beyond the spread of the runs, and little against none. At one
session a commit's write of its own is a small write over zeros already
there. What the buffer takes away is that write from each commit, and
with it the file's lock each session's commit took in turn. 64 KiB
holds the records of some tens of order entry commits, and stays under
half of the zeros a segment keeps written ahead (`DEFAULT_FILL_AHEAD`),
so a refill of those never passes through it. The sweep's figures are
in the commit that made the change.

#### D922. A commit takes its participants without copying them, and names the tables it wrote only for the embedders

A commit of a transaction that wrote copied its list of participants, to
keep the list for a rollback should the commit fail, and its session
named every table it wrote, a copy of each name, for the queue of
embeddings after commit, which reads the names only while a column
waits for an embedder. An order entry's new order writes five tables,
so each of its commits made eleven allocations for names nothing read.

The commit now takes the list, and gives it back to the transaction
before the rollback of a commit that fails (`txn/end.rs`). The session
names the tables written only while the embedders watch (`db.rs`), read
once the commit has ended, as the queue's mark was. Nothing else changes:
a failed commit rolls back in the same participants, and a commit while
a column waits for an embedder marks the same tables.

#### D923. Increments reserved are applied by a write told the columns they add to

A transaction's increments reserved are applied as it commits, each
row's as one write of the row (D452). That write went the general way.
The table's storage, lock, seal and indexes were found again for each
row, the column types were copied for each table, the row replaced was
read whole a second time by the write, each index's key was compared
between the two versions, and the log record was made from both rows
whole.

The application now finds what a table's writes need once
(`State::writing`), tells it the columns the increments add to
(`Writing::setting`), and makes each row's write as a point UPDATE
written straight makes its own (D875, `db/escrow.rs`). Of the row
replaced the write reads those columns alone, it looks at no index,
since no key or index names a column an increment is reserved on, and
its log record is made of those columns, the bytes a record of the rows
whole holds. The increments are added using the column types of the
table's description, which is not copied. A table whose column reserved
on lies past the last a mask tells apart is written whole, as before.

The semantics hold for these reasons.

- The row written is the row the general write wrote: the newest version
  with the sums in its columns, recomputed over a version another
  transaction committed first.
- The write still passes the reservations of others, waits for a row
  another transaction is writing, and is undone with its statement, as
  the same `change_row` makes it.
- The log holds the same record, so recovery replays it to the same row.

#### D924. A commit's rows that one leaf holds are stamped with the leaf latched once

A commit stamps each row it wrote first, from the leaf its write left
the entry in (D440, D843). Each stamp latched its leaf, searched it and
wrote. A transaction that inserts a run of rows, as an order's lines,
leaves them in one leaf, and latched and searched that leaf once a row.

The rows of a commit are now sorted by the leaf their writes named, and
those of one leaf are stamped under one hold of it
(`BLinkTree::change_placed_run`, `mvcc/stamps.rs`). A row the node no
longer holds, as after a split moved it right, ends the run, and it and
the rows after it are stamped one at a time as before, by the leaf or
by a descent.

Leaving the stamps to the first reader or to collection was weighed and
not done. The statuses of a store's transactions (D440) already let a
reader resolve a version left unstamped, and a slot is taken again only
once every table of its commit is stamped, so readers would be safe. A
checkpoint is not. Its image must hold stamps, since recovery resolves
an unstamped version by the log, and redoes only commits whose records
lie after the checkpoint (`db/recovery.rs`). Stamps left to collection
would have every checkpoint stamp each table's backlog with the gate
shut, and a stamp made long after its write goes down from the root
whenever a leaf of its tree was retired meanwhile (D843). The stamp of a version a later writer
replaces first is saved either way, as that writer appends it stamped.

The semantics are unchanged. Each row is stamped as it was, a version
another writer replaced meanwhile left alone, a deletion filed as
garbage, and a row that cannot be stamped queued for collection.

#### D925. A batch due is collected by the maintenance job's pass, and by a commit only once it is long due

A commit that found a table's batch due collected it (D451, D920). The
fixed costs of a collection were then paid once a batch, but the work a
version takes, its undo slot released, its values freed, its index
entries and its deleted row taken out of their trees, was still the
committer's, before its reply.

The end of a transaction that finds a batch due now leaves the table
noted and asks for the maintenance job at once, whose pass collects
every table awaiting (`txn/collect.rs`, `db/maintenance.rs`). The end
collects a table itself only once its batch has been due for 256 commits
of the horizon, four batches, or 4096 versions wait, or a rollback's
versions do. So the versions a table holds are bounded as before when
the job does not run, as under JOBS.POLICY PAUSED, or falls behind many
sessions' commits, and the committers then take the work back. A
session that collects once its reply is sent collects its tables' batches
itself, after the reply, as before (D450, D453).

Four batches is a derivation, not a sweep. A pass that keeps up takes a
batch within the one after it, so the bound is not met while it does,
and four leaves the job's thread time to be woken and to run while
bounding the versions held to five batches.

The work is not less. It is the job's thread's, not the committer's, so
a commit is shorter and the database uses more of a second processor
while commits come. The semantics hold as D920's do. The horizon rule
is unchanged, and a collection only comes at another moment.

#### D926. A database following takes back the entries its image's checkpoint saw awaiting collection as it replays them, and notes what a replay leaves

A checkpoint logs the index entries of the versions awaiting collection
after its position (`Change::Stale`), and recovery from it takes them
back (D25). An export carries the records recovery reads through the
checkpoint's position, not those after it (D57), so a database
following that installed one held the image's stale entries and met
their records only as it replayed what came after, which it passed
over. Its tables then kept an entry more for each such version for
good. Before D920 a checkpoint seldom found a version awaiting
collection; with commits leaving a batch for later, most do, and the
replication simulation's replicas held an entry more than their
primaries.

A database following now replays the log knowing the checkpoint its
image came from (`Definitions::Following`, `recovery/stale.rs`). A
stale entry that names it is mended as `State::mend_indexes` mends a
row a change touched: every entry of the row under the key taken back,
then the entry of its version now made again if that version has the
key. A change of the row replayed in an earlier call may have mended
its entries under that key already, so taking back one entry, as
recovery does before it redoes the changes after, could take the
row's own. Every other reading of the log passes such an entry over as
before.

A replay ends no transaction, so no end leaves the tables it changed
noted as awaiting collection (D920). Its end now notes each table
whose versions await collection (`State::note_replayed`), and a
standby's asks for the maintenance job, so a replica collects what its
replays leave as its primary does.

#### D930. A kept plan of one index range is run where it is kept, its rows handed up through its filters, projections, sort, limit and set functions with no operator built

A kept plan that was no point read (D752) was opened for each run. The
plan was copied, an operator was built for each of its nodes, each boxed
as a stream of rows, and the rows were pulled through them. A query of a
procedure's body that counts a dozen rows of an index range spent more
on opening its plan than on reading them.

A kept plan may now be a direct range read (`exec/range.rs`,
`Kept::range`). It is one index scan under any of a filter, a
projection, OFFSET and FETCH FIRST of a count, a sort and a grouping,
with expressions that read their row alone. A subquery, a routine
invoked or a sequence generator leaves the plan to the executor, as do
a percentage and WITH TIES. What it needs of the plan is taken once, as
the plan is first asked for it, and each run reads the statement's
values where they are.

The range is read as the index scan reads it in place (D821). Its probe
is placed with the run's values, the index is searched for its entries
as the tree holds them, and each row is read of the columns listed alone
(D862) into a row kept with the plan, through what the table keeps from
read to read. The row is checked against its entry's key as bytes. Its
values are put in a row as wide as the table, kept with the plan too and
lent upward, so the expressions of the plan read their columns where the
plan numbered them. A covering read of a row every reader sees is made
of its entry's key, as before (D34). The read is told to the table by
the condition of the key's columns and the probe, entries are counted
for the statement and the index, a cancel is looked for at each entry,
and the entry of a row gone for every reader is taken back (D837), all
as the scan does. An index by a sort key, an expression or a projection
of its keys, a global index, a probe whose keys must each be checked, a
scan that decides a conjunct and a located scan are not read so.

Each row is handed to what the plan puts over the range, by a call and
not through a stream. A filter judges it, a projection makes its row of
it, and FETCH FIRST stops the read once its rows are given, but for an
input that can raise, which is read to its end as before. A grouping by
no column folds each row into its set functions and gives its one row
at the end, a DISTINCT function's values kept in a bag of the
statement's work area as the grouping keeps them (`range/fold.rs`). A
sort gives each row to the executor's sorter as it is read, so rows
past the work area are written as sorted runs (D38). A grouping by a
column, and a sort that keeps its first rows alone, take the rows read
and then group or sort them by the executor's own functions, so their
order and their groups are the executor's. They hold 1024 rows at most.
A range of more reads nothing direct and is run by the executor, whose
operators hold their rows in work areas, and so is every run of that
plan after it.

A leaf of a kept program whose plan is kept and is such a read runs it
(`kept/leaves.rs`), compiled or interpreted. A compiled SELECT INTO
asks its leaf's plan for it with no plan opened, its tables locked and
its snapshot taken as the session takes them (`compiled/evaluated.rs`).
A plan still learning, or one whose tables moved, runs as before and
learns as before (D414). A read that finds it is not read direct with
its values gives nothing, and the plan is opened and run.

EXECUTOR.POINT_OPERATIONS OFF runs every kept plan through the
executor, a direct range read as a point read.

#### D931. A cursor of a kept plan that is a direct range read holds its rows as it opens, a range that gives rows as fetched only while it is short

A cursor's rows are read from its plan as it is fetched from, but a plan
that can raise an exception is read in full at OPEN, and a cursor is
settled, its rows read, before its transaction changes a table it reads
(`db/stream.rs`).

A cursor whose plan kept is a direct range read (D930) now reads it as
it opens and holds the rows for its fetches (`db/stream/ranged.rs`). A
plan that can raise was read at OPEN already. A plan that sorts or
groups read its whole range before its first row. Any other gave its
rows as they were fetched, so a cursor closed early read few. Its range
is read direct only while it has no more than 128 rows, about the rows
of a few leaves of an index. A longer one is left to the executor, its
first rows read twice that once, and so is every range of that plan
from then on. A plan that cannot raise fails only by its
reading, at the first fetch, so one whose direct read fails is left to
the executor, which fails there as before.

The rows a cursor holds from OPEN are those a settled cursor holds, so
it sees no change its transaction makes after, as before. They are held
up to the bytes a cursor may hold and spilled past them (D38).

#### D932. An index join whose probe is a whole unique key is run, in a direct read, as nested point reads

An index join built an operator that bound a probe for each row of its
left operand, searched its index through a boxed iterator of decoded
keys, read each entry's row whole of the columns used, and made each
pair by copying the left row (`exec/join/indexed.rs`). A join of a
range's rows each with the one row of a unique key spent most of its
time there.

A direct read (D930) now takes an inner index join whose probe fixes
every column of a unique index by columns of its left operand
(`join/indexed/direct.rs`). Its left operand is the range, filtered or
projected to columns, constants and the statement's values. The probe
of each left row is read as a point read reads (D881), made once with
the plan. The row's values of the key are its values, its index is
probed by the whole key with nothing boxed, and the row found is read of the columns
the statement reads alone into a row kept with the plan. The pair is
made in a row kept for the run. The left row's values are moved into
it, as a unique key pairs a left row once, and the rest of the join's
condition is judged of the pair as the join judges it.

A point read casts each value to its key column's type, where the join
places it as it is, so the probe is not a point read itself. So the join is taken only if each key column takes
what its left column gives unchanged, which is a value of the column's
own type or a constant the cast leaves as it was. A left row with a null
for a key column pairs with nothing and reads nothing, as in the join.
Each probe is told to its table, counted for its index and looked to
for a cancel as a probe of the join is. Its rows are not counted among
the rows the statement read, as the join's are not, so a procedure's
ROWS_READ is the same on both paths. An outer, semi or anti join, a probe
of part of a key, of a range or by a function, a spatial join and a
located one are the executor's.

#### D933. A compiled SELECT INTO of set functions over the delta table of a change run straight folds them over the rows it wrote

A change of a compiled program ran straight on its table only if the
query over its delta table was a select list over the table's row
(D841). A query of set functions, as a sum over the rows an UPDATE
wrote, ran the general path. That path binds the rows as a table, opens
the query's kept plan over them and builds its grouping.

Such a query now runs with the change (`compiled/folded.rs`). It is a
grouping by no column of the delta table's rows alone, under a select
list that reads its row alone. The change's rows are collected as its
write functions write them, as before, and each set function is fed
each row as a direct read's are (D930, `exec/range/fold.rs`). The
select list is then evaluated over the one row of their values, which
there is even of no rows, and assigned. A change by a whole unique key
that is written straight (D880) folds its one row the same way. The
columns the functions' arguments read are those the delta table shows,
so an increment of another column may still be reserved (D849).

A grouping by a column, a set function with a filter or an inverse
distribution, and an argument or a select list that reads a subquery,
a routine or a sequence generator leave the statement to the general
path, as does every case that left a change to it before.

A point UPDATE written as a patch reads of its row only the columns
its statement needs (D917), and the rest of the row it holds after is
null. Under a fold, the select list reads the row of the functions'
values, so its columns say nothing of the delta table's row. What the
point UPDATE reads for its delta table is then the columns the
functions' arguments read at that execution, their CASEs judged as
D918 judges a select list's. So a COUNT or a MAX of a column the
UPDATE neither sets nor keys an index by sees that column's value, as
it does on the general path.

#### D940. A prepared CALL found kept runs its procedure's compiled program over a frame the session keeps, its arguments assigned to their slots

A prepared CALL kept its binding (D793), its procedure's text was read
once (D406) and its body ran compiled (D841). Each execution still did
around the body what a first execution does. It filled a VALUES plan
with its arguments and evaluated it as a row. It built the procedure's
scope from the catalog's description, parameter by parameter, and
copied it to look for the program. It looked the procedure up by its
specific name and compared its text. It made a frame of the arguments,
copied that into a second frame with the variables, and copied the
parameters back after. The body's own statements aside, that was most
of what a short procedure cost.

Now the binding holds the procedure's scope, made as the CALL is bound,
and how each parameter takes its value where every argument is a `?` of
the parameter's type or a constant (`routines/call.rs`, `Given`). Once
an execution has run the CALL as any is run, the session keeps beside
that binding the body's program as it keeps it, whether the body is
ATOMIC and runs at a savepoint level of its own, the owner its context
runs as, and a frame (`routines/direct.rs`). An execution that finds the
same binding kept takes them and runs the compiled program over the
frame. Each `?` is cast to its parameter's type, as a kept plan's slot
is filled, and assigned to the parameter's slot. Each variable's slot is
set to the null value. The output parameters are read from the frame.
No plan is filled, no row is evaluated, no scope is built, and the frame
is neither made nor copied.

The binding found kept was kept with the definitions, authorization,
schema, time zone and settings that hold now (D45). The program was kept
with those that held when the session took it beside the binding, and
the binding was kept with them too. So the program is the one a lookup
would find now. A CALL bound again is another binding and finds nothing
beside it, and runs as any CALL until it is kept in turn. The session
keeps this for a fixed number of bindings and forgets the oldest.

A value cast to its parameter's type with no warning is assigned to that
type unchanged where the type is an exact number, a character string, a
truth value, a date, or an array of one of these. The cast gave it the
type's scale, length or cardinality already. Such a value is not
assigned again, so an array is copied once. A value of another type is
assigned after its cast as before.

Everything else runs as any CALL does and gives what it gave. That is an
argument that is an expression or reads a table, an output parameter
whose target is no `?`, a body that is one statement, a program not
compiled or not kept, and an execution whose argument's cast raises a
warning or an exception. Such an execution has run nothing when it turns
warning or an exception. A binding found kept is of a procedure with an
SQL routine body, so a procedure written in Rust is looked for only
where none is found. Such an execution has run nothing when it turns
to the general path, so the condition raised is that path's own. The
general path itself now takes the scope from the binding and builds a
program's frame of scopes only when it binds the program.

#### D941. An execution's values that hold no large object are taken as given, not read for locators

Each execution of a prepared statement read its values for large objects
sent by their locators (`db/lobs.rs`), which made a copy of every value,
arrays element by element. It then made a second copy of them all only
to count them.

Now the values are looked at first (`prepared/locators.rs`). A large
object, a structured value, and an array, multiset or row that holds one
at any depth are read for locators as before. Where there is none, the
values are copied once into the execution's parameters. The count is
checked without a copy. The values an execution runs with are the same.

#### D942. A point change whose increments may be reserved reserves them where it reads its row

A compiled program's UPDATE by a whole unique key runs straight on its
table (D841), but one whose increments may be reserved (D452, D849) was
handed to the general path, which alone took reservations. TPROC-C's
Payment adds to the warehouse's and the district's year to date this
way, so its two cheapest changes were its dearest. The general path
collected the row, noted it for the statement's end and gave it to the
delta table's collector to be read back.

Now the point change reserves the increments itself
(`write/direct.rs`, `escrowed`). It takes the locks the general path
takes, reads the row by its point read, makes the candidate row,
derives the increments from it and reserves them by the same
`State::reserve_row`, guarding the same columns. The statement ends as
a point change that wrote no row ends. The delta table's row is the
candidate row, which shows the columns read and the sums not yet
applied, as the general path's collector held it. Nothing is written
until the transaction commits.

What is reserved, what is guarded, what waits for it and when it is
applied are those of D452 and D849 unchanged. A reservation that is not
taken hands the change to the general path as before. That is a row
changed since it was read, a sum that would leave the column's type, or
an increment that is not what made the candidate row. The general path
then reserves or writes it as it always did.

#### D943. A compiled body nothing of which reads the diagnostics area places no statement's condition there

A compiled program emptied the diagnostics area as each statement began
and placed the statement's condition there as it ended (D841), as the
interpreter does. That was done for every assignment, every IF, and
every turn of a loop, and was a good part of what such a statement cost.
In most bodies nothing reads what was placed.

The area a procedure's statements write is the procedure's own. Its
context takes a new one as it is pushed and gives the caller's back as
it returns (`db/nested.rs`), so nothing after the CALL reads it. Within
the body it is read by GET DIAGNOSTICS, and kept on the stack as a
handler is activated. A triggered action and a function invoked have
areas of their own.

So a compiled program is looked at once, as it is compiled
(`compiled/run.rs`, `unread`). If none of its statements is GET
DIAGNOSTICS, no compound statement of it has a handler, and each
statement the session runs for it is an INSERT, MERGE, UPDATE, DELETE,
SELECT, OPEN, FETCH or CLOSE, its statements leave the area as it is.
Each still empties the warnings heard as it begins, as emptying the area
does, and the run empties them once more as it ends, as its last
statement's condition would. Any other program runs as before. The
values, rows, exceptions and completions of the CALL are the same, since
none of them is read from the area.

#### D950. A read by key finds its entry in a leaf's bytes with no node made of them, and trusts a leaf of its tree that holds the key

A fetch of a row by id from an index's entry read the leaf noted for the
row (D500), parsed every field of its header (`Node::parse`), compared
the key with the leaf's first key and its high key to learn the leaf
answers for it, and then searched its slots. The first key and the high
key are each a cache line the fetch has no other use for.

A read by key now looks for its key in the leaf's bytes as they are
(`engine/tree/node/lean.rs`). It reads the header's level, flags, tree,
prefix and count, bounds the slots by the header's hints (D847), and
compares heads before tails, as `Node::search` does, with no node
built. A key found in a leaf of its tree that is in the tree, not
marked taken out, is the key's entry, with no check of the leaf's
range.

A split and a merge move keys only right (D814), and write the leaf
they move them to before they take them from the first, under the
first's latch, so a key in two leaves at once has one value in both,
and a key found in any leaf of the tree is found where a descent would
find it. A key not found in a leaf noted or remembered says nothing, as
it may lie right of the leaf or left of it, and the read goes on as
before, checking the leaf's range. A read from the leaf it last read,
or from the copy of it its `Near` keeps (D806), tries the slot after
the last one found first, with one comparison, and the copy keeps no
header parsed for it (D808).

#### D951. A page read hashes its page once, for the thread's leaf copies and the pool's hint alike

A read of a leaf hashed its page with XXH3 to find the thread's copy of
it (D858), again to find the pool's hint slot for it, and a third time
to note it among the thread's leaves. The three hashes are of the same
two words. The pool now gives the hash it places a page by
(`BufferPool::page_hash`), and takes it back in `read_resident_at` and
`read_stamped_at`, so a leaf read hashes its page once. A hint found
through the hash is still checked against the frame's page, as a stale
hint always was.

#### D954. A transaction whose reads are not checked reads its snapshot with no lock of its bookkeeping

Every read of a row by a transaction took the lock of its bookkeeping
in the table (`Mutex<Open>`, D871) to read its snapshot and to record
the read where its reads are checked for serializability. A transaction
whose reads are not checked, at READ COMMITTED or preserving, records
nothing, and needs of its bookkeeping only the snapshot. The
bookkeeping now carries that snapshot in an atomic word beside its lock
(`Opened::unchecked`), a value no clock gives while its reads are
checked. The word is set under the lock as the snapshot and the mode
are, after them, and read with no lock. A read not checked takes the
snapshot from the word and records nothing. One checked takes the lock
as before. A snapshot only moves forward, so a read that finds the word
just before a change of mode reads at a snapshot the transaction held a
moment before, as it would had it read a moment earlier.

#### D955. A read by key finds its leaf through the thread's copies of the inner nodes, with no node made of them

A descent read each inner node from the thread's copy of it (D807), but
parsed the copy's header into a node, searched it through fallible
steps, and counted its holders, at each level of each fetch. A read
by key and a probe from a key now first walk the copies alone
(`BLinkTree::leaf_by_copies`). Each level's copy must be current, be an
inner node of the tree not taken out whose range holds the key, and be
at the level its parent says. The child is found in the copy's bytes as
D950 finds an entry. The leaf reached is the one a descent that latched
each node at that moment would reach, so its range begins before the
key. A key it does not hold, within its high key, is not in the tree.
Where a copy is missing or changed, as past a split not yet posted, the
walk gives up and the read descends as before. The walk goes down at
most 16 levels, more than a tree of 4 KiB pages has.

#### D956. An integer of an integer column is written as its key with no anchor made of it

A probe of a whole key (D881) made each value's anchor (`anchor_into`),
a value rounded down at the column's scale and checked for exactness,
and then encoded the anchor, building a value and comparing scales for
each integer of the key. An exact number at its column's scale, of a
column whose values 64 bits hold, and within 64 bits, is its own
anchor, exactly. Its key is now written straight from its units
(`value/types/exact.rs`, `narrow_key`), the bytes `encode_key` writes.
Every other value is anchored as before.

#### D960. A character string of at most 32 octets is held in its value, a longer one in a buffer its clones share

`Value::Char` held a `String`, so every character column of every row
read, cloned, cast, padded or assigned took an allocation and gave it
back. A row of STOCK has eleven character columns. On the order entry
path the padding of a CHARACTER read from its record alone was over a
third of all allocations, and the clones of values a seventh.

A character string is now a `CharString` (`value/chars.rs`). One of at
most 32 octets of UTF-8 is held in the value itself, an array and a
length. A longer one is an `Arc<str>`, never changed, so a clone of it
adds to a count and copies nothing. A `Value` is 48 octets, as it was.
Its tag takes the first octet, and the 40 past its alignment hold the
widest values, a large object and an XML value. A character string
takes those 40 and no more.

The crate has no unsafe code (R-SAFE-1), so the text of a string held
in the value can only be handed out as a `str` through
`str::from_utf8`, each time. That check reads sixteen octets at a time
only from an aligned address. So the array is aligned as a word is, and
the check reads the whole of it, the string and the zeros past it. The
zeros are UTF-8, so the array is UTF-8 exactly when the string is, and
the string is then cut at its length, which ends a character. Aligning
the array leaves it 32 octets of the 40, where an unaligned one would
have 38. Measured over strings of 2 to 38 ASCII octets, an aligned
array of 32 checked whole costs the same whatever the length, and less
than either array checked to its length. Characters of two octets cost
the same in each form, and the octets of either form read with no check
cost least. The aligned array of 32 was chosen. In the order entry
load every string fits it but the data of customers and about seven in
ten of the data of stock and of items.

So a string is shown to be UTF-8 once, where it is made, and the paths
taken for every row read its octets, not its text. A record is decoded
and encoded, a key encoded, two strings compared, trailing spaces left
out and characters counted over the octets. A CHARACTER padded to its
length is built in the value where it fits. A longer one of at most 256
octets is built on the stack and copied to its buffer, the one
allocation. Two strings concatenated are joined in the value where both
fit. `CharString` lends its text by `Deref`, compares and orders by its
octets, and hashes as its text does, so equal text is equal and hashes
equal in either form and a table keyed by strings is asked by a `str`.

What a statement returns is unchanged. Comparison, collation, padding,
truncation, the limits of length, the errors and the encodings on the
wire and in a record are those of the text, whatever holds it.

#### D961. A binary string of at most 22 octets is held in its value, a longer one in a buffer its clones share

A binary string held its octets in a box, so each one read from a
record, cloned or cut took an allocation, as a character string did
before D960. A reference value holds a binary string too.

`Binary` now holds at most 22 octets in the value itself and a longer
string in an `Arc<[u8]>` its clones share (`value/binary.rs`). It needs
no check to lend its octets, so the array is not aligned and the
capacity is what leaves a `Binary` three words. That is the width of
the `String` a normalized key and a bucket hold, so nothing that holds
a binary string grows. A UUID's sixteen octets and a reference's fit.
`Binary::of` makes one of a slice, with no vector between, where a
record, a key or a message is read. It compares, orders and hashes by
its octets, whatever holds them.

The other values that a row of an order entry table holds allocate
nothing. An exact number is its units and its scale, a decimal
floating-point number its coefficient and exponent, a datetime its
instant, zone and precision, an interval its units and qualifier, a
truth value itself. A large object, a value of the JSON type, an
array, a multiset, a row, a structured value and an XML value were
already shared by count.

### Conditions

#### D970. A numeric literal no number type holds breaks a Syntax Rule, and text of such a number cast or given is out of range

An exact numeric literal of more than 38 digits, and an approximate one
beyond the range of DOUBLE PRECISION, were refused as valid SQL beyond a
limit (D18), SQLCODE -900 and SQLSTATE 0A000. The same number given as
a parameter or computed was 22003, and text of it cast was 22018, as
though it were no number at all.

SQL:2023 settles each case. "There shall be an exact numeric type
capable of representing the value" of an exact literal [ISO/IEC
9075-2:2023 §5.3 SR29], and an approximate one shall be within the
range of the approximate types [SR30], whose NOTE 130 calls overflow its
one syntax error. The maximum precision is implementation-defined, but
the rule a literal past it breaks is a Syntax Rule, so the literal is
SQLCODE -103 and syntax error or access rule violation, 42000 (D971),
whether the statement is run directly, prepared or sent by a client.
Underflow, a literal too near zero for its type, is no error [NOTE 130]
and is read as zero.

A value is another matter. A cast of text reads the `<signed numeric
literal>` it holds and casts that [§6.13 GR8b ii, GR9b ii], as a value
of the target type, so text of more whole digits than 38 is a value an
exact type does not fit, 22003 [GR8a ii], as a parameter or a result
out of range is, and cast to DOUBLE PRECISION is the nearest number
[GR9a i]. It is read as an approximate number, as no exact one holds
it, and text past every approximate number's range is 22003 cast to
any type [GR9a ii]. Text that is no literal stays 22018 [GR8b i]. A
fraction's digits past those its whole digits leave of 38 are
truncated as the text is read, as every exact target truncates them,
so a long fraction is no error.

A numeric literal of the SQL/JSON path language has the value of the
`<signed numeric literal>` of its characters [§9.45 GR1a], so one no
number holds breaks a Syntax Rule as that literal would, SQLCODE -103.

#### D971. A statement that breaks a Format, Syntax Rule or Access Rule is SQLSTATE 42000, prepared or run directly

SQL-92 gives the condition three classes: 42, and 2A when a statement
is invoked directly [ISO/IEC 9075:1992 §3.3.4.3, §20.1 GR5] and 37 when
it is prepared [§17.6 GR4]. Turborel raised 2A000 of a statement run
and 37000 of one prepared, so a query naming a missing table was 2A000
run and 37000 prepared.

SQL:2023 has the one class. A `<direct SQL statement>` that breaks a
Format, Syntax Rule or Access Rule raises syntax error or access rule
violation, 42000 [ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §22.1 GR6a], and so does a
`<preparable statement>` that does [§20.7 GR6c]. Its table of
SQLSTATE values has no class 2A or 37 [§24.1, Table 39], and classes
beginning with 2 or 3 are the standard's to define, so turborel may not
keep them as its own. Turborel reads the standards as one language, the
newer prevailing (doc/README.md), so every such error is 42000:
of PREPARE, EXECUTE IMMEDIATE, `Session::prepare`, a client's prepared
statement and a statement run directly alike.

The SQLCODE still tells which rule is broken, -101 a token, -102 a
Format, -103 a Syntax Rule and -104 a privilege. GET DIAGNOSTICS fills the names
of what was referenced of a condition of class 42 [§23.1 GR4h].

#### D972. The check of threads finds scoped threads, imports of what starts them, and passes over the files of modules of tests

`cargo xtask verify` checks R-SAFE-5 by reading production sources for
what starts a thread (`xtask/src/threads.rs`). It knew `thread::spawn`,
`thread::Builder` and a runtime's builders, so a scoped thread,
`std::thread::scope` and `spawn_scoped`, or a starter imported and
called by its bare name, passed unseen. It told tests apart by a file's
path and by an inline `#[cfg(test)]` module, so a module of tests in a
file of its own, as `src/engine/rows/zones/costs.rs`, read as
production code.

The check now finds scoped threads and any `use std::thread::` that
names `spawn`, `Builder` or `scope`. It reads each production file's
`#[cfg(test)]` declarations of `mod name;` and passes over the file each
names and that file's submodules, as tests may start their own threads.
A module whose body is inline is passed over to its closing brace as
before, and the line after a declaration of a file's module is read, as
it was not.

### The client

#### D975. An export writes each large object as its value, read by its locator a chunk at a time between a cursor's fetches

An export wrote a large object by its text, which for one the server
sent by its locator is a description of it, not its value. A large
object longer than SERVER.LOB_INLINE_BYTES comes by its locator, which
names it until the transaction it was sent in ends, and is read by Lob
requests. No request can go out while a statement's replies are coming,
so an export read all at once could not read them before holding every
row.

`Connection::export_with` writes rows by a `Layout`: `Delimited` for CSV
and tab-separated text, `Native` for the protocol's frames, or the
program's own. It prepares the query. A query whose columns may hold a
large object, one of a large object type or of a composite type of one,
a structured type or an extension's, opens its cursor and fetches 256
rows at a time within the transaction. That is a reply's longest body
over the longest value sent whole, so a batch held while its large
objects are read is at most a reply's body for each such column. Each
batch is written before the next is fetched.

A large object a column holds is read a chunk at a time as it is
written, its locator freed once read, so the server holds no more than a
batch's. One within a row, an array, a multiset or a structured value is
read whole, as its value's text needs it all. A query whose columns hold
none is executed once and its Rows replies written as they come, as
before. Under autocommit, a transaction the export began is committed
once its last large object is read, or rolled back if the export failed.
A failed write closes the cursor and leaves the connection of use.

In delimited text a CLOB or NCLOB is written as its text, and a BLOB, as
every binary string, as its octets in upper case hexits, two to each,
as a `<binary string literal>` writes them between its quotes
[ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §5.3]. One streamed is quoted in CSV whatever it
holds, as what it holds is not known ahead, and each chunk is cut where
a character ends. Text refuses a chunk that holds the delimiter or a
line break. The command-line client's `\export` writes by `Delimited`
too, its lines ended by LF.

Native rows keep every value. A Rows frame holds at most a reply's
longest body. A large object sent by a locator is written in it as a
locator numbered within that frame from 1, depth first, and its octets
follow the frame in Lob Data frames of at most a chunk each, as many as
its length takes. `read_native` checks the numbers and holds each value
whole. The protocol is unchanged.

#### D976. An import reads a binary string column's field as its octets' hexits, as an export writes them

A delimited file's field is a character string, which the server casts
to its column's type, and a character string is not cast to a binary
string [ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §6.13 SR7]. So no BINARY, VARBINARY or BLOB
column could be imported, nor what an export wrote of one read back.
An import now reads a field for a binary string column as the octets
its hexits write, two to each, of either case, spaces passed over, as a
`<binary string literal>` reads them [§5.3 SR4], before it is sent.
Anything else, or an odd number of hexits, fails the row with SQLSTATE
22018. A BLOB longer than a value sent whole then goes by a locator, a
piece at a time, as a CLOB's field does, and the bulk copy takes a
BINARY or VARBINARY column's value as a binary string.

#### D977. Each `?` of a prepared CALL is described with its parameter's mode and ordinal position and the procedure's specific name

`Prepared::parameters` gave the types of the input `?`s alone, so a
program could not tell which `?` of a CALL was an OUT parameter's, nor
which parameter any was of. It now gives every `?` in the order
written, a `DynamicParameter` of its type, its mode and its ordinal
position, and `inputs` gives the types of those an execution takes
values for, which callers that pass values use. Of a CALL of an
SQL-invoked procedure each `?` an argument simply contains has the mode
and the position of that argument's parameter, and `procedure` gives
the procedure's specific name [ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §20.10 GR7e].

The parser keeps, of each argument, the numbers of the `?`s read within
it, so several of an IN argument's expression each take that
parameter's, and named arguments keep the order they are written in. A
`?` of any other statement is IN, of no position, and so is one of a
procedure written in Rust, which has no specific name. DESCRIBE INPUT
and DESCRIBE OUTPUT set PARAMETER_MODE to Table 33's code, 1 IN, 2
INOUT and 4 OUT, PARAMETER_ORDINAL_POSITION, and the three
PARAMETER_SPECIFIC items, of each top-level item of a CALL, and SET
DESCRIPTOR sets none of them [§20.5 SR3a]. A parameter left to its
default value holds no `?` (D979).

#### D978. With `parameter-modes`, a Prepared of a CALL carries its procedure and each `?` with its parameter's mode, tag 20

A Prepared's head lists the input `?`s alone, those an Execute gives
values for, and its columns the output ones, so a client could not tell
a `?`'s mode nor match the two lists. A client that asks for
`parameter-modes` and is granted it is sent, in a Prepared of a CALL of
an SQL-invoked procedure, tail tag 20 after tag 19: the procedure's
specific name, then every `?` of the statement in the order written,
its mode's code, its parameter's ordinal position from 1, and its type.
A mode of no code of Table 33, a position of 0, or the tag before tag
19 fails the connection. The head is unchanged, so a client not granted
it reads what it always read, and the protocol's version stays 1. The
OUT and INOUT values still come back as the one row of the statement's
columns, which `Statement::parameters` now matches by mode. The
client's `parameters` gives the modes told, else the inputs, each IN.

#### D979. A procedure's IN and INOUT parameters take their defaults by DEFAULT, by an argument left out, or by a name not named

A `<parameter default>` of a procedure's IN or INOUT parameter (Features
T522 and T523) is read, a value expression or NULL, with no host or
dynamic parameter [ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §11.60 SR19], and an OUT
parameter's is refused [SR16e ii]. The routine descriptor keeps its text
as written [GR3c vi], logged and checkpointed with the rest, and
PARAMETERS shows it as PARAMETER_DEFAULT, a last column, as the 2006
draft's view has none. It is bound as the body is, under the owner of
the procedure's schema, in a scope of the routine's path and horizon and
of no parameter, its type one the parameter's takes by store assignment
[SR16e i]. The tables, columns and routines it names join the body's,
after the body's SQL-data access is checked, so a drop of one is refused
without CASCADE [§11.23 SR7d, §11.31 SR7f, §11.62 SR4c ii].

A CALL's candidates are the procedures of the name with at least as many
parameters as arguments, each parameter past those written, or named by
none, of a default [§9.18 SR9b, SR9d], and of those of the schema first
in the path the one of fewest parameters is invoked [SR9e to SR9g]. Such
a parameter, and one given DEFAULT, takes its default, bound again from
the kept text as at definition and evaluated in the row of the CALL's
arguments, so the compiled and the direct paths take it as any argument;
with no default it is null [GR3b ii]. An INOUT parameter given DEFAULT
has no target, so its value out goes nowhere [SR9h iii 2]. NULL of an IN
parameter is the null value, as it is of a procedure written in Rust,
whose parameters have no default. A function's default stays refused,
SQLCODE -900 (T525).

### Plans

#### D980. EXPLAIN without ANALYZE shows a data change's plan as EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows it, running nothing

`EXPLAIN` alone now takes INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE, searched
or positioned, read so when INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE, or MERGE followed
by INTO or WITH, follows EXPLAIN. No query begins with a table named
EXPLAIN followed by those words, so nothing read before is read
otherwise. The statement is parsed and bound as running it would bind
it, and the plan of the rows it reads is made by the planner that runs
it, then described as EXPLAIN ANALYZE describes it (D622,
`db/explain/unrun.rs`). The text is that of EXPLAIN ANALYZE without
what ran: a line naming the statement and its table, the plan below
it, and lines that say what the change would do beside (D983, D984).

A row of values that reads nothing has no plan, as it is evaluated
(D419), so its INSERT shows the head line alone. A positioned change
shows its cursor's row in place of a plan, its cursor declared, open
or not, as preparing it needs it declared. A change an INSTEAD OF
trigger takes in place shows the trigger. A program reaches the same
text by `Session::explain`, its parameters given values as a module's
procedure gives them. Only the physical stage is shown, as EXPLAIN
ANALYZE shows only it.

#### D981. EXPLAIN of a data change needs the privileges preparing it needs

[ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §20.7 GR6] has preparing a statement check its
Format, Syntax Rules and Access Rules, and nothing more. EXPLAIN of a
change binds it as preparing binds it, through the same binder, so it
is refused by the code preparing gives without a privilege its access
rules need, and shown with them. Its General Rules are not applied, so
it is shown in a READ ONLY transaction, where the change itself is
refused, and a trigger's or a referential action's privileges, which
are their owners', are not looked at.

#### D982. EXPLAIN of a data change reads, locks and writes nothing, so no trigger fires

EXPLAIN of a change takes none of the locks running it takes, of its
table to be written or of the tables it reads, and runs none of its
plan, its triggers, its actions or its checks. It opens a transaction
as EXPLAIN of a query does, which reads no row. So a second session
writes the rows the change would write while the first's transaction
is open, waiting for none, the files of the database are byte for byte
as they were, its rows, indexes and log alike, and no trigger fires.

#### D983. EXPLAIN of a data change names the indexes it maintains, the actions that cascade and the triggers that fire

After the plan, `-- maintains:` names each index of the table whose
entries the change would write (`db/explain/unrun/effects.rs`): every
one of an INSERT or a DELETE; of an UPDATE, each whose key reads a
column it sets or a generated column computed from one, every global
index over a partition, and every index where a BEFORE row trigger may
set any column (D875). An index of no column set keeps its entries. A
`-- cascades:` line names each referential action that writes the rows
referencing the table [ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §15.18]: CASCADE, SET NULL
or SET DEFAULT of a DELETE, and of an UPDATE of a referenced column.
The tables they write are followed in turn, each table and event once,
so the list ends. A `-- trigger:` line names each trigger, but INSTEAD
OF ones, that a change of the table or of a table the actions write
would activate [§4.46.2], its column list read as the state change's
columns, once each, in the order the definitions list them. A NO
ACTION or RESTRICT rule writes nothing and is not named.

#### D984. EXPLAIN of a data change says whether a point path runs it when prepared or in a procedure

A last line, `-- point path:`, says how a path past the executor's
operators would run the change. A searched UPDATE or DELETE whose plan
is one read of a whole unique key runs as that read when its plan is
kept, by a prepared statement or a procedure's body (D752), unless
EXECUTOR.POINT_OPERATIONS is OFF, and the line names the index. One
whose table no trigger or referential action reaches, whose
constraints its end may check of the row alone, writes that row
straight when a procedure's body runs compiled (D841), and an INSERT
of VALUES or of a query specification does too (D901), unless
EXECUTOR.COMPILED_PROCEDURES is OFF. The judgement is that of the
compiled program's own, from the statement's shape and its table
(`routines/program/compiled/change.rs`). A row of values evaluated
says so (D419). None of these is `none`. A statement run directly
plans its rows each time, so the line tells what its prepared or
procedure's form gains.

### Statistics views

#### D990. COLUMN_STATISTICS shows what the planner's statistics hold of each column, its values as text, to those holding a privilege on the column

The standard has no view of the statistics a planner keeps, and it lets an
implementation add objects to INFORMATION_SCHEMA [ISO/IEC 9075:1992 §21.1].
A tool tuning queries needs them, so INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMN_STATISTICS
has a row of each column of each base table (`system/column_stats.rs`).
The row shows the rows the last pass found and when it was made (D991),
the share NULL, the distinct values, the average width of a row read for
the column, the least and greatest values, the most common values with
the share of the rows each holds, and the histogram's bounds. Each figure
is read through `State::statistics`, so it is what the planner reads. The
distinct values of a column an index keys alone are the index's count
(D383), and the width is what the engine answers for the column, of a row
store the whole row's. A table's engine knowing none shows NULL in each.
No correlation of a column with its rows' order is kept, so none is shown.

A view's column has one declared type in every row, and a table's columns
have many. So a value is shown as a character string, its text as the
client shows it, from which a CAST to the column's own type reads it back
[ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §6.13]. Its `<literal>` was tried first, but an
array of literals quotes each string twice over, which no reader wants.
The most common values and the bounds are arrays of these texts, and the
shares an array of DECIMAL(18, 4). A text is cut at 4,096 characters, as
a statement's text in STATEMENT_STATISTICS is.

Reading the view reads the statistics as a plan does. Ones not gathered
become due, and the database's maintenance gathers them, so a tool that
opens the view sees them soon after (D473).

The owner and a user granted MONITOR (D520) see every column, as in
TABLE_STATISTICS (D522). Any other user sees the columns on which it
holds a column privilege, SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE or REFERENCES [ISO/IEC
9075-2:2023 §4.42.2], SELECT on the table counting for each column. That
is how COLUMNS shows the columns accessible to a user [ISO/IEC 9075:1992
§21.2.9]. DELETE alone is on no column and shows none. A table none of
whose columns is shown is not asked for its statistics.

#### D991. A table's lock stamps when its statistics were last gathered, as a pass the engine counts is seen

An engine has no clock of the database's, so it cannot stamp its own
passes with the instant CURRENT_TIMESTAMP would read. It counts them
instead (`TableStorage::statistics_passes`, none by default). The row
store adds one as each pass stores its statistics. The database reads the
count before and after it has the engine gather, by ANALYZE
(`Database::analyze`) or by its maintenance, and stores its clock's
instant in the table's lock if the count moved. The stamp sits beside
the commit and compaction stamps of D522, which every snapshot shares.
TRUNCATE TABLE gives a table a new storage and a new lock, so its
statistics and their stamp both begin again from none.

#### D992. INDEX_STATISTICS shows the distinct keys an index counts, as the planner reads them

The planner estimates an equality on all of an index's columns by the
distinct keys the index counts (D35, D383). INDEX_STATISTICS shows them
in DISTINCT_KEYS, through `State::distinct_keys`, rounded to a whole
number, NULL while the index has not counted them. Asking makes a count
due as a plan's asking does.

### The routine debugger

#### D1000. DEBUG is a routine's privilege of its own, granted and revoked as EXECUTE is

The routine debugger lets one session stop another's routine and read
its parameters and variables. That reads the data the routine was given,
so it needs a privilege, and none of the standard's says it. EXECUTE
lets its holder run a routine, not watch another's run of it.

DEBUG is an `<action>` of GRANT and REVOKE *(extension)*, written beside
EXECUTE or alone, on a routine named as ROUTINE, FUNCTION or PROCEDURE,
by its name, its parameters' types or its specific name. It is read as
a word, not a reserved key word, so no name written before it is lost.
A routine's descriptor keeps it in a list of its own beside EXECUTE's
(`SqlRoutineDesc.debug`), written in the catalog's bytes after EXECUTE's
and so in a checkpoint's snapshot; the log holds the statement's text,
as of any GRANT. Granting needs it held with grant option, else the
warning 01007; a revoke takes the grants named and, by the rule of
§12.7 GR9, those made by a grant option it takes, refused with RESTRICT
(2B000). It abandons no definition, as none needs DEBUG to bind.
ROUTINE_PRIVILEGES shows each grant with PRIVILEGE_TYPE DEBUG, and
dropping a role or a user takes its grants as it takes EXECUTE's. Of a
table, a module or another object it is refused (SQLCODE -103).

#### D1001. The owner of a routine holds DEBUG on it by owning it, as the owner of a domain holds USAGE

The owner's EXECUTE is a grant from `_SYSTEM`, made as the routine is
defined, grantable only if its body needs nothing it holds without
grant option [ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §11.60 GR1]. DEBUG needs no such rule.
A grant from `_SYSTEM` would also put a row in ROUTINE_PRIVILEGES for
every routine, changing what the view shows of every database. So the
owner holds DEBUG with grant option by owning the routine's schema
(`catalog::usage_held`), the list keeps only grants, and the view shows
only what was granted.

#### D1002. ALL PRIVILEGES on a routine stays EXECUTE alone

ALL PRIVILEGES is every privilege its grantor may grant on the object
[§12.3]. Were DEBUG among them, a statement of the standard would grant
and revoke what the standard does not define, and ROUTINE_PRIVILEGES
would show rows a database of the standard's privileges never had. So
ALL PRIVILEGES on a routine grants and revokes EXECUTE, and DEBUG is
granted and revoked only by name.

#### D1003. A program notes where each of its statements begins, in the order its steps are walked

A debugger names a place by a character of the routine's text, as an
error does (`SqlError::at`). The parser keeps, beside each statement of
an `<SQL statement list>` and each handler's action, where it begins
(`ast::StatementList`), and the binder pushes each place as it binds the
statement, in the very order `Step::steps` walks a program's steps, the
body first (`Program::places`). A frame pushed while a debugger is
attached walks the steps once and gives each step's address its place,
as a program kept finds its statements' plans by address. No program
with no debugger attached reads the list, and binding pays a push per
statement.

#### D1004. A program knows the routine or trigger it is the body of

A frame shows what routine it runs, and a breakpoint names one, so a
program carries its origin (`debugger::Origin`): of a procedure, from
the routine kept (`KeptRoutine::origin`); of a function or a procedure a
function invokes, from its descriptor as its body is bound inline; of a
triggered action, the trigger the session pushed last. A control
statement run directly has none, and no debugger sees into it.

#### D1005. A debugger's link hangs on its target's Stop, looked at by one flag

A `Session` is of one thread; another may hold only its `Stop`, as a
server does to cancel its statements. So a debugger and its target share
a link (`debugger::Link`) hung on the target's Stop (`stop/debugged.rs`):
an atomic flag, and behind a lock the link itself. Each statement a
program runs looks at the flag first (`Run::debugged`). With none
attached that is one relaxed load and one branch, and nothing else is
made. Attached, the run pushes a frame on the link's stack as its first
statement is looked at, and pops it as it ends.

#### D1006. A debugged session runs its procedures interpreted

Compiled procedures (D841) and the straight CALL of a prepared one run
their bodies with no step to pause at. A session with a debugger
attached runs them interpreted. `compiled_procedures` and `call_direct`
each look at the same flag first, and the interpreted path gives the
same results (D841), so only the time differs. Detached, the next call
runs compiled again.

#### D1007. Breakpoints are by line of a routine's text; steps by the depth of the frame

A debugger sets a breakpoint where a user reads one, a line of the
routine's text as its definition holds it; the line is kept as the span
of characters it holds, and a statement that begins in it pauses there.
A compound statement does not, as its first statement does. A step is
kept as the depth it pauses at: into, at the next statement of any
frame; over, of a frame no deeper; out, of a frame shallower; continue,
at a breakpoint. The interrupt asks for a pause at the next statement,
as into does.

#### D1008. A debugger sees into, and pauses in, only what its user may debug

DEBUG shows the values of a routine's variables, which its owner may
not want shown (D1000). The debugger runs as the user its session was
when it attached; of a routine its frames are seen into only if that
user holds DEBUG on it, owner included (D1001); of a trigger only if it
owns the trigger's schema, as no privilege is granted on a trigger. A
frame not seen into shows its name alone and never pauses, and a step
into it pauses at the next statement that may.

#### D1009. A breakpoint's condition is evaluated by the debugger's session over the paused frame's values

The target, paused, should run nothing for the debugger, as it may be
inside a statement. So the debugger's own session evaluates a
breakpoint's condition, as the search condition of a query of one row
whose columns are the paused frame's parameters and variables, named as
they are and cast to their types, given their values as dynamic
parameters. Where it is not true the debugger tells the target to go on
and the wait goes on, so the pause is never an event.

#### D1010. Detaching, dropping the debugger and the target's end let the target go on; a cancel ends the pause

Nothing a debugger does may leave its target stuck. Detaching, which
dropping the debugger does, as a server does when its connection drops,
clears its breakpoints and lets a pause go on as if nothing had paused
it; the target's next debugger may attach. The target session's end
tells its debugger (`Event::Ended`), whose waits then return at once. A
paused statement cancelled fails as cancelled (SQLCODE -920), as a lock
wait does, the pause looking at its Stop as a lock wait does, every 20
ms, and the debugger is told (`Event::Cancelled`).

#### D1011. A pause ends by itself after DEBUGGER.PAUSE_TIMEOUT_MS, a database setting

A paused session holds its locks, and a debugger may go quiet. The
pause waits at most DEBUGGER.PAUSE_TIMEOUT_MS, then goes on to its next
breakpoint and tells the debugger (`Event::TimedOut`). Its default, five
minutes, is long enough to read a frame and short enough that no lock is
held for long. It is the database's setting, not a session's, so the
session paused cannot lengthen it; 0 goes on at once.

#### D1012. The stack is one thread's, and a function run on another thread is not debugged

A function a parallel query evaluates may run on a worker thread of its
own, with no frame beneath it and no way to stop its siblings. The link
holds the thread whose frames its stack holds, while it holds any; a
frame of another thread is not pushed, and its run is not debugged. So
the stack is always one thread's calls, from the outermost down.

#### D1013. A debugger's request its target's state refuses fails with SQLSTATE TBD01

Attaching to oneself, to a session with a debugger attached, resuming
what is not paused, and clearing a breakpoint there is none of are
misuses of the interface, not errors of an SQL statement. Each fails
with SQLCODE -910 and SQLSTATE TBD01 of class TB, the implementation's
own; a breakpoint in no routine, or past its last line, is -103, as a
name of no object is, and in one its user may not debug, -104.

#### D1014. Each statement of a plain triggered action pauses as a frame of its trigger of its own

A triggered action of statements alone, BEGIN ATOMIC with no
declaration, runs its statements one by one, each as a statement runs
directly [ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §11.49], not as a program, so no step of a
program begins them. Compiling it as one program instead would change
how it runs with no debugger attached. So the parser keeps where each
statement begins (`TriggerDefinition::action`, a `StatementList`), and
as each begins with a debugger attached the trigger's run pushes a frame
of the trigger for it alone (`Tracked::alone`), showing that place, its
line and the transition variables, and pausing there as a program's
statement would; the frame is popped as the statement ends, so a routine
it invokes is a frame above it. A control statement among them is a
program, whose own frame does that. With none attached each statement
costs the one look at the flag (D1005).

#### D1015. A statement first looks at how many debuggers the process has attached, a static

The session's flag (D1005) is reached through its host: of a function a
query evaluates, through the query's runner, whose `Stop` it finds by
its transaction, under a lock, the first time it is asked. Asked as each
statement of a function begins, that lookup would cost a function's
invocation what it never paid before. So the process counts the
debuggers attached (`stop/debugged.rs`, `ATTACHED`), raised as one
attaches and lowered as it detaches or its target ends, and a statement,
a CALL and a triggered action's statement look at that static first, one
relaxed load. With none attached, no host is asked, no session's state
is reached and nothing is made. Only while one is anywhere does a
statement look at its own session's flag.

#### D1030. The routine debugger's messages are one request and one reply behind the capability `debugger`, and an Event sent unasked

Studio drives a routine running in one session from another connection,
so the debugger needs messages of the native protocol, and the protocol
stays at version 1 (D185). The capability `debugger` grants them, and a
client that does not ask sees none of them.

Each call the database's debugger offers (`turborel::debugger`) is a
kind of one request, Debug, which carries its kind as its first octet,
as Lob does (D79). What a call gives back is a kind of one reply,
Debugged, or a Complete where it gives nothing. A third message, Event,
is what the debugger hears of its target. Three frame kinds, not one a
call, keep the protocol's list of kinds short, and a client that has
the capability reads every one of them.

The messages carry the database's own types (`Kind`, `Action`,
`Paused`, `Frame`, `Event`), so what the client reads is what the
database's debugger gave, with no copy of its own to keep in step. A
breakpoint is the protocol's `DebugBreakpoint`, since the database's
keeps the span of its line to itself. Values go as a Rows reply's do.

#### D1031. A debugger attaches by a connection's ID to a session of its own user, or of any if its user sees every session, and is told of no other

A debugger names its target by the connection's ID that
INFORMATION_SCHEMA.CONNECTIONS shows, which CANCEL CONNECTION and END
CONNECTION name it by too (D42). Attach finds that connection's session
through the `Stop` the server keeps of it (`Present::session_of`), the
handle another thread may hold of a session.

A user attaches to the sessions of its own connections. The database's
owner, and a user granted MONITOR, attach to any, as they see every
connection in CONNECTIONS (D520, `Session::may_monitor`). An ID of
another user's connection is refused as an ID of none (08003), so a
user learns nothing of connections it cannot see. Attaching shows
nothing by itself. What a debugger sees of the routines its target runs
is what its user owns or holds DEBUG on (D1000, D1008).

#### D1032. An Event is sent only while the debugger's connection waits for a request, and a client takes it wherever it reads a reply

A request's replies come in a fixed order (D393), and an Event within
them would break it. The server sends an Event only from the
connection's task as it waits for the client's next request
(`native/debugging.rs`). A request that comes first is read, and the
event waits until the request is answered.

The client may have sent a request as the Event went, so it reads one
wherever it reads a reply. It keeps the Event, as it keeps a Notice
(D187), and reads on. `Reply::ends_request` says an Event ends no
request, so a reader that drains a request's replies (D393) reads past
it. A debugger's requests are short, so an event waits at most for one
of them.

#### D1033. The server waits on its debugger a slice at a time apart from the workers, the wait under way kept until its event is sent

The database's debugger is waited on by blocking (`Debugger::wait`). A
worker held for the wait would take a worker from the statements of
every connection while a debugger is attached, so the wait runs on a
thread of the runtime's for blocking work, as the watch of a client
gone does (D335).

Each wait lasts at most a slice of 100 milliseconds, the time a
connection whose request runs is looked at again. A request that comes
first drops the read of it, but not the wait, which is kept and looked
at again once the connection next waits, so an event a wait took is
never lost. The debugger is dropped once a Detach or the connection's
end lets go of it and the wait under way ends, so its target hears of
the detach within a slice.

A wait judges a breakpoint's condition in a session (D1009), and the
connection's own session is lent to workers for its requests, so it
cannot be lent to the wait as well. The server opens a second session
of the debugger's user as it attaches, and the wait holds it while it
runs. A condition reads the frame's values, which are the same in
either session.

#### D1034. A connection learns its own ID by a Debug request, so Ready keeps its first form

A program that debugs its own other connection must know that
connection's ID. CONNECTIONS shows the IDs, but two connections of one
user look alike there. Ready could carry the ID in a tail, but Ready has
no tail in the first form, and every client reads it. A Debug request,
Identify, answers with the connection's ID instead, under the same
capability.

#### D1035. The client's debugger is methods of its connection, the events kept in it until read

The client's `Connection` gains `debug_id`, `debug_attach`,
`debug_detach`, `debug_break`, `debug_clear`, `debug_breakpoints`,
`debug_resume`, `debug_interrupt`, `debug_stack` and `debug_wait`
(`client/src/debug.rs`). Each is one request and its reply, as the
other calls are. A connection is blocking, so the events the server
sends wait in it (`Told::events`). `debug_wait` gives the first kept,
or waits for the next frame for at most the time it is given. Waiting
looks for the first octet of a frame with the stream's timeout set to
that time, and reads nothing of it, so a timeout loses no frame and
the connection goes on.

#### D1036. The command-line client drives the debugger by `\debug` and a word, one call each

The client's commands that act on its connection, as `\conninfo` and
`\password`, are backslash commands (D210). The debugger is one command,
`\debug`, and a word after it for each call. `\debug wait` waits for the
next event, so a script reads the target's pauses in order. A
breakpoint's condition is the rest of its line, taken as typed, so its
quotes are SQL's, not the command's. A pause is written as its call
stack, the innermost frame first, as a debugger shows it. The routine's
name is read as SQL reads an identifier, folded to upper case unless
quoted. A breakpoint is shown by the specific name of the routine it
is in, as the engine keeps it, so an overloaded name's breakpoints
are told apart.

### Defects a review of comments found

#### D1040. An index join is read direct as nested point reads only by a unique index

A direct read takes an inner index join whose probe fixes every column
of an index (D932), and reads each left row's probe as a point read
does. The read stops at the first row it finds with the key, as a
unique key has one row at most. The join was taken of any index whose
every column the probe fixed, and `Direct::of` never asked whether the
index was unique. A kept query joining a range's rows with a table by
an index that is not unique, on all its columns, gave each left row its
key's first row alone. Of three rows a key, the executor gave twelve
pairs of four left rows and the direct read four.

The join is now taken only of an index that is unique
(`join/indexed/direct.rs`). Any other is the executor's, whose probe
gives every row of the key.

#### D1041. A filter goes below a projection only if each of its expressions is deterministic

`PushFilterThroughProject` moves a filter below a projection with each
column of its condition replaced by the projection's expression for it
(D35). The expression is then evaluated once for the condition and again
for the projection's row. The rule asked only that neither the condition
nor an expression could raise an error (D15). A function call was taken
as able to raise, so none was replaced. Since then a function may say
that no call of it raises (`ScalarFunction::raise_free`), and a call of
one is replaced. One that is also not deterministic gave the condition
one value and the row another. A filter of a derived table's column
equal to 2, the column a call counting its calls, gave a row whose
column was 4.

The rule now also asks that every expression of the projection is
deterministic and changes nothing (`unnesting::expr_pure`), as
unnesting asks of what it evaluates again (D317). It asks it of all of
them, read by the condition or not, as each is evaluated of fewer rows
once the filter is below.

#### D1042. COPY DESCRIPTOR with TYPE copies a reference type's SCOPE components, each a character string

COPY DESCRIPTOR with TYPE sets the target item's type components to the
source's, SCOPE_CATALOG, SCOPE_SCHEMA and SCOPE_NAME among them
[ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §20.6 GR7h iii 2]. The list of components copied
(`dynamic/ptf.rs`) was written when there were no reference types and
left the three out, so an item copied from one describing REF(PERSON)
SCOPE PEOPLE named its referenced type and no scope.

The three are also character strings [§20.1 Table 29]. They were not
among the fields `is_text` names, so GET DESCRIPTOR took only an exact
numeric target for one and then failed to assign it its name, and one
not set read as 0. They are now copied with the other type components,
read into a character string, and read as an empty string where not
set, as a type's other names are.

#### D1043. A slow statement's text is withheld only while an encryption is in use, not for a compression of the spill areas

A slow statement is told without its text while anything of the
database is encrypted, so no value meant for an encrypted table reaches
a log in the clear (D40, D48). The test was whether the spill areas'
pipeline had any stage (`db/slow.rs`). SPILL.ENCODINGS naming a
compression alone gave it one, so a database with nothing encrypted lost
the text of every slow statement.

The test is now whether that pipeline holds an encryption
(`Pipeline::confidential`). It does while the database's files or a
table are encrypted, whose encryption the spill areas take (D48), or
while SPILL.ENCODINGS names one itself.

#### D1044. An IVF directory whose write fails frees the pages it made

`lists::write_directory` makes the directory's pages and then writes
each. It freed the pages made when making one failed, and not when a
write of one failed, as its page could not be held or read back. Its
callers free only the pages it returns, so those pages stayed in use
with nothing referring to them.

Both steps now fail through one place that frees every page made
(`engine/ivf/lists.rs`). A free that fails still leaks its page alone,
as before.

#### D1045. A range join is costed as a plan of no order

Join enumeration keeps the cheapest plan of each order of a set's rows
(D303). A range join was offered with its left operand's order
(`enumerate/methods.rs`), and its plan gives rows in no order
(`physical/range/planned.rs`), as the plan made of it says
(`ranged.rs`). The rows were right, as a sort is added by the order of
the plan made. The costs were not. A range join stood as the plan of an
order it does not give, in place of the nested loop or the join that
does, and was chosen for an ORDER BY or a merge join at a cost without
the sort it then needed.

A range join is now offered as a plan of no order.

#### D1046. A correlated subquery stays probed past its runs only if its kept plan is one probe of a whole unique key

D790 keeps a subquery probed past EXECUTOR.DECORRELATE_AFTER_RUNS while
