its probes, each weighed as `PROBE_ROWS` rows, come to fewer than its
build's rows, if its run is one probe of a whole unique key. The test
was that its plan was kept (`subquery/probed.rs`). A plan is kept at
once if it is such a probe, and also once it is learned over its runs
(D675), which any plan may be when the setting is `MOST_LEARNING_RUNS`
or more. A learned plan that reads many rows a run, a range of an index
or a whole table, was weighed as one descent and stayed probed for
many times the runs it should have.

The runner now asks the kept plan whether it is one probe of a whole
unique key (`physical::keepable`), found once and kept with the plan.
A subquery whose kept plan is any other is decorrelated after the
setting's runs, as D790 says.

#### D1047. A read, a write, an accept or a connect a signal interrupts is made again, and is no failure of a connection

A call that waits in the system under a timeout returns
`ErrorKind::Interrupted` when a signal reaches its thread, or when its
process is frozen and thawed, with nothing read, written or lost. The
standard library's `read_exact`, `write_all` and `read_to_end` make the
call again. A single `read`, `fill_buf`, `flush` or connect does not.
The client's Terminate waits for the server's close by one `fill_buf`
under its read timeout, and reported "cannot receive: Interrupted
system call" (SQLSTATE 08006) for a server that had answered nothing
wrong.

Every such call is now made again while it is interrupted. In the
client that is `timeouts::uninterrupted`, around Terminate's wait for
the close, the debugger's wait for an event, the flush after a
request's bytes and after a Cancel's, the TLS handshake's steps, and a
connect by TCP or by a local socket, which makes its socket anew. In
the server the thread that reads and writes a connection itself already
made an interrupted read or write again (`native/wire.rs`), and now its
flush too, which over TLS writes the session's last records. An accept
that is interrupted is asked again at once, with no failure told and no
backoff, for clients (`server.rs`) and for the members of a cluster
(`replication/net.rs`).

The reads and writes through the runtime are of sockets that do not
block, which wait nowhere a signal could interrupt, and the replication
crate reads and writes no socket itself. A wait made again begins its
timeout again, so a call interrupted waits at most its timeout after
the last signal.

### Parallel joins

#### D1050. A hash join of a part builds an operand that gives batches of its vectors, not of rows made one by one

A hash join probed by a part run in parallel builds its right operand
before the probing side is split (D292). An operand that was itself a
part was read by its morsels. Any other was read through the row
executor, one row of values at a time, and its rows pushed into vectors
of values. Over the column store that undid everything its scan by
batch does. No condition was judged on the encoded column, no column
was decoded late, and every value of every row the scan read was made,
kept or not. Such an operand is the usual one, as D291 keeps a filtered
scan of the column store off the workers. So a join whose built operand
was a filtered scan of a large table ran slower in a part
than alone, where the serial join reads the operand by batch.

Now an operand that gives batches (`stream::layout`) and whose tables
read by batch is read by `stream::whole_batches`, as the serial join
reads it. Each batch's kept rows are held as vectors of their kinds and
charged to the part's grant, and the operand gives way past it as
before. The table then hashes typed vectors, so keys of whole numbers
dense in their span get a direct table (D601), which vectors of values
never did. An operand that gives no batches, as a grouping or VALUES,
and any operand while EXECUTOR.BATCHES is off, is read row by row as
before.

#### D1051. A hash join's built operand reading the column store is a part of its own

D291 keeps a scan, filter or projection of a column store table off the
workers, since a part's rows are made one by one where it hands them to
the statement's thread. That reason does not hold of the operand a hash
join of a part builds. Its morsels are read by batch on the workers and
each morsel's kept rows are gathered into a batch of vectors
(`exec/parallel/probe.rs`), with no row made. So the planner marks such
an operand, if it is a pipeline, by its rows alone, whatever store its
tables are of (`physical/parallel.rs`, `built`). An operand below
EXECUTOR.PARALLEL_MIN_ROWS is no part and is read by batch on the
statement's thread (D1050). An operand that is not a pipeline is walked
for its parts as before.

#### D1052. A column store's split judges its table's zones once for all its morsels

A morsel of a column store table reads its groups, then the rows of its
tree within its row ids, of the zones the scan's condition may match
(D354). Each morsel asked the table's zones for those ranges itself, a
pass over every zone of the table under each zone's lock, though it
keeps only the few within its own ids. A scan of a large table in
thousands of morsels so made thousands of passes over all its zones,
and its threads spent a large share of their time there and on those
locks. A split of the row store judged the zones once, as it was made
(`engine/rows/split.rs`).

Now a split of either store does. It holds the ranges the condition
may match as they were when it was split, and hands each morsel those
within its ids. A zone that would pass only later holds no row the
split's reader sees, as its rows were written after the reader's
snapshot, so each morsel still reads every row it would have.

#### D1053. A join's built operand keeps datetimes and truth values as vectors, and is joined of its parts' words

A hash join holds its built operand as one batch joined of the batches
read (`Batch::joined`, D38). Integers of one scale, approximate numbers
and character strings stayed vectors of their kind. A column of dates,
times, timestamps or truth values became a vector of values, one made
for each built row, so every row a probe gathered of it cloned a value
and every expression over it above the join left the vectors. And each
vector was put together a row at a time through the kind of its part,
its nulls looked for in every row.

Now datetimes of one type and truth values stay vectors of their kind
(`storage/batch/joined.rs`). A vector of integers, approximate numbers
or datetimes is made of its parts' words, a part all of whose rows are
kept, in order, copied whole, and truth values a word of bits at a
time. Nulls are looked for only if some part holds a mask of them or
lacks the column. Datetimes of two types, or with displacements in
some parts alone, are joined as values, as before.
### Subquery plans

#### D1060. SUM and AVG of exact values whose sum the declared types keep within 38 digits raise nothing, so their subqueries are unnested as COUNT's are

Unnesting asks of each subquery whether running it can raise an error
(D15, D311, D314). Its answer took every arithmetic operator and every
set function but COUNT, MAX and MIN as able to. A correlated subquery of
SUM or AVG was therefore never pulled up by its equalities (D314). It
took the general case (D312), which reads the outer rows a second time
for the domain of bindings and joins the subquery's table with it before
grouping. IN and EXISTS of a subquery that held such a subquery were
not made semi joins (D541).

The answer is now typed (`optimizer/unnesting/pure.rs`,
`logical/raises.rs`). A condition or expression of a plan is judged by
the declared types of the columns it reads, as filter pushdown judges
one (D373). A set function is judged so too
(`logical/raises/totals.rs`). SUM judges its sum once, finished, against
38 digits, and keeps it on the way in 128 bits (D15). A statement reads
fewer than 2^63 rows, the bound COUNT already rests on (D552), and 2^63
has 19 digits. The sum of exact values of precision p therefore has at
most p + 19 digits at their scale. While p + 19 is at most 38 the sum
fits finished, and fits the 128 bits on the way, as 10^38 is less than
2^127. AVG keeps the same sum, and its mean has its values' digits
before the point and two more after it, so it fits as well. SUM and AVG
of such an argument raise nothing. Of an approximate argument, an
interval, a wider exact one, or a column whose type is not known, they
are taken as raising, as before.

A column a grouping computes has a type for this judgment. A grouping
column has its input column's type. A SUM has p + 19 digits, an AVG
p + 2 digits at scale s + 2, MAX and MIN their argument's type and COUNT
its result's. So `0.2 * AVG(Q)` over a column of 15 digits is known to
fit, and the projection over the grouping raises nothing.

A scalar subquery inside the plan judged was taken as raising, for the
cardinality error of a second row. It is now judged by its own plan. One
whose shape gives one row at most, an ungrouped set function's, raises
what that plan raises, judged the same way. Any other still counts as
raising.

The effect is on plans alone. A subquery such as
`(SELECT 0.2 * AVG(Q) FROM L WHERE L.K = P.K)` is grouped once by K and
joined to the outer rows on K. A subquery whose sum could pass 38 digits
keeps the general case, and is computed for the outer rows' bindings
and no others, so a key no outer row has raises nothing (D15).

#### D1061. A WHERE conjunct over both operands of an outer join that is never true of a null operand makes the join the join it is

`push_filter_into_outer_join` made an outer join inner when a WHERE
conjunct over the columns of the operand given nulls alone was not true
of nulls. It evaluated that conjunct once on a row of nulls. A conjunct
over both operands' columns, as `T.A < U.B` is, was left, since the
preserved operand's values are not known. A LEFT join filtered by such
a comparison stayed an outer join, which no join order moves and no
parallel pipeline probes. The join an unnested scalar subquery makes
(D313) is the common case, as its comparison reads the outer row and the
subquery's value.

Such a conjunct is now bounded instead of evaluated
(`optimizer/outer/rejecting.rs`). The rules that make a value null and a
condition unknown whatever else it reads give the truth values it may
have while one operand's columns are all null. A column of that operand
is null. Monadic minus, arithmetic and CAST of a null are null. A
comparison or LIKE of a null is unknown, and IS NULL of one is true.
AND, OR, NOT and IS follow their truth tables over the sets of values
their operands may have. A CASE is the result of its first WHEN that can
only be true, passing over a WHEN that cannot be true, and is null if
every result it may still give is null. Anything else may be any value.
A conjunct that cannot be true is never true of the rows the join gives
nulls, so the join gives none that the WHERE keeps, and it is made the
inner join, or of a FULL join the join preserving the other operand.

A rule that moves an outer join onto the one operand of a product its
condition reads leaves the WHERE clause over the product. The join
unnesting makes is moved so, onto the table its keys come from. The same
bound is therefore applied to an outer join that is an operand of the
product a WHERE filters (`optimizer/outer/within.rs`). Each row of the
product holds one row of the join, so a conjunct never true of the
join's null rows keeps none of them there either.

The bound is sound and not complete. A function call is not looked
into, so `COALESCE(U.B, 0)` keeps the outer join, as it must. The value
an unnested COUNT has of no row is 0, given by a CASE, and that CASE is
seen to give a value, so its join stays outer as well. As before, the
rule applies only to a WHERE condition that cannot raise (D15). That is
now judged by the declared types of the join's columns, as a filter
pushed into a product is (D373), so `T.A < U.B + 1` over INTEGER columns
moves as well.

#### D1062. A runtime filter goes below a projection and into a grouping that the declared types prove raise nothing, and to the grouping's scan when its arguments hold no null

A hash join's runtime filter goes down its probe side through each
operator that passes the column on and raises no error (D369, D600). A
row the filter drops below an operator is never evaluated there, so the
operator must be one that cannot raise (D15). The executor judged that
by `Expr::can_raise`, which takes every arithmetic operator as able to
raise, and it took a grouping of SUM or AVG as able to overflow. The
join that unnesting makes of a subquery of SUM or AVG (D1060) has a
grouping of the whole inner table on one side, under a projection such
as `0.2 * AVG(Q)`. No filter reached that grouping, so it grouped every
row of the table to keep the few groups the other side has keys for.

The executor now judges both by the declared types
(`exec/batch/typed.rs`). The type of a column of a physical plan is
found through scans, filters, projections of columns, inner hash joins
and groupings, as D1060 types a logical plan's. A projection passes a
filter of a column it moves when none of its expressions can raise by
those types. A grouping takes a filter of a grouping column when each of
its set functions is COUNT, MIN or MAX, or a SUM or AVG whose sum the
types keep within 38 digits. Any other SUM or AVG keeps every row, as
before.

A set function of a column warns of a null it eliminates [ISO/IEC
9075-2:2023 §10.9 GR4b], so a grouping of one judged the filter itself,
above its scan, to warn of a null in a row the filter dropped (D600).
The scan then read and decoded every row. A column declared NOT NULL has
no null to eliminate and no warning to keep. When every column the set
functions take is such a column, the filter is told to the grouping's
scans, which judge it before they decode the other columns.

#### D1063. A grouping run in parallel takes the runtime filters of its grouping columns, judged of each morsel's batches

A grouping read by batches took a runtime filter of a grouping column
to its input (D600, D1062), but only run alone. A grouping over a large
table is run in parallel (D293), and a part run in parallel took no
filter from a join above it. The join read the part's groups row by row
and dropped the groups its other operand has no key for after every one
was made. A join of a few keys with a grouping of a whole table, as
unnesting makes of a correlated subquery of a set function (D1060), paid
for every group.

A hash join now reads such a part by batch, as it reads the grouping run
alone, and tells it its filters (`exec/batch/parted.rs`). The part's
pipeline is told the filters of the grouping's input columns
(`Pipeline::told`). Their ranges go down to the scans, as the ranges of
the pipeline's own joins do (D389), so a morsel outside them is skipped.
A step right after each scan they reach judges the filters of each
morsel's batches, their key sets and Bloom filters too. D389 left those out of a
morsel's scan because the probe of the filter's join follows in the same
morsel and drops the rows anyway. Here no probe follows. The grouping
follows, so each row the step drops is one the grouping does not hash.
The columns no step reads before that one are decoded of the rows it
keeps alone (D361).

The filters are told only when no set function takes a column that may
hold a null. One that does warns of a null it eliminates, and a morsel
has no one place to raise the warning of a row it dropped, so that
grouping is told none and groups every row, as before. A part that gives
way is grouped alone with the filters, as D600 has it. The groups come
in the order of their first rows either way.

#### D1064. A conjunct of a correlated subquery that cannot raise is judged of the rows a semi join keeps

When a conjunct of WHERE or HAVING is made a semi join or an antijoin
(D541), the node's other conjuncts filter the join's left operand, below
the join, so each is judged of every row as it was (D15). A conjunct
that compares with a correlated subquery was placed there too. Its
subquery was then unnested over every row of the operand, grouping the
whole inner table and joining it with the whole operand, before the semi
join dropped most of the rows.

Such a conjunct now filters the rows the semi join keeps, above the
join, if it cannot raise, by the typed judgment of D1060. A conjunct
that cannot raise may be judged of any rows. Its subquery is then
unnested over the rows the semi join keeps alone, so the join with its
grouping has those few rows on one side, and their keys reach the
grouping as a runtime filter (D1062, D1063).

Three cases stay as they were. A conjunct that can raise stays below,
judged of every row. A conjunct of no subquery, or of an uncorrelated
one, stays below, where it is cheap and may be told to a scan. Beside an
antijoin every conjunct stays below, as an antijoin often keeps most of
its rows and the conjunct may keep few.

#### D1065. An uncorrelated NOT IN or ALL that is a conjunct is an antijoin

The semi join rule took every correlated subquery of existence, and of
the uncorrelated ones the IN and SOME conjuncts alone (D541). An
uncorrelated `x NOT IN (SELECT ...)` or `x <> ALL (SELECT ...)` stayed a
nested subquery. The executor reads such a subquery once, but then
judges the comparison of every outer row against the rows it holds, on
one thread.

The rule is now offered those conjuncts too (`found::negated`). NOT of a
comparison with SOME is the antijoin on `(x op y) IS NOT FALSE`, a
comparison with ALL the antijoin on `(x op y) IS NOT TRUE`, and NOT of
one with ALL a semi join, as D541 makes them of a correlated subquery,
so a null on either side still decides as the standard's truth tables
say. The join is made only of a subquery that is pure and cannot raise,
as before. One that is refused is offered to no other rule and stays
nested, read once, since the general unnesting of an uncorrelated
subquery would gain nothing over that.

#### D1066. A DISTINCT by hash under a join is read by batch as the grouping by every column it is

A stream gathered the rows of a grouping that takes filters, so a hash
join read it by batch and told it its runtime filters (D600). A DISTINCT
had no such reading. An operand that held one, run alone or in
parallel, gave a join no batches, and an index join over a DISTINCT gave
none either, as it needs its left operand's width. The join above then
ran row by row with every operand of it, and told no filter to any of
them. The semi join a planner makes of `x IN (SELECT ...)` by probing
an index from the subquery's distinct rows is such an operand, so the
join beside it lost the filters D1062 and D1063 give a grouping.

A DISTINCT by hash is now read as the grouping of its rows by every
column, no set function, which the executor already makes of it
(`batch::distinct_grouping`). A join reads it by batch and tells its
input the filters of any of its columns, run alone
(`told::grouped_batches`) or in parallel (`parted.rs`). A row the
filter drops would give a distinct row the join keeps no row of. Its
rows come in no order the plan relies on, as a grouping's by hash, so a
join's left operand takes them as they come. A DISTINCT whose input
comes in order, compared row by row (D550), is read as before.
#### D1067. An IN list of a computed expression is judged by its set from two constants on, the expression computed once

An `<in predicate>` of constants is bound as an OR of equalities, and an
OR of eight or more of one column is judged by a set (D31). Of fewer the
OR stays, as comparing a column with each constant costs no more than
finding its bucket. Of an expression that is no column the OR stayed
whatever its length. An OR evaluates every operand (D15), so
`SUBSTRING(C FROM 1 FOR 2) IN ('13', '31', '23', '29', '30', '18', '17')`
computed the substring seven times for each row, each a string made and
dropped.

Such an OR is now judged by its set from two constants on
(`logical/sets.rs`). The set computes the expression once and compares
its value with each constant, or finds its bucket of eight or more. The
count needs no measurement, as one computation is less than two of the
same. The expression is of columns and constants by deterministic
functions, arithmetic and casts alone, and the same in every equality,
function for function and constant for constant. It then has one value
for a row and raises one error, however often it is computed, so the
condition's value and its error are those of the OR.

#### D1070. A semi join planned to build its left builds it by batch too, its right read by morsels that mark the held rows

The planner builds the left operand of a semi join or an antijoin when
it has fewer rows than the right (D540). Read by batch, the join built
its right whatever the plan said. So EXISTS of an order's line items
held every line item, on the statement's thread, and past the work area
as rows in a table of the spill area. A join planned to build its left
now does so by batch (`exec/batch/joined/semi/marked.rs`). The left is
held as one batch in a join's table (D368), a mark beside each row. The
right is read once, each of its rows marking the held rows it matches.
The held rows are then given in their order, those marked, or of an
antijoin those not. A held row of a null key is in no table, so no row
marks it, as the join that builds its right finds no match for it.

The right operand is told a runtime filter of each key (D369), of an
antijoin too. A right row whose key no held row has marks none, so
leaving it out changes no mark. It is told one only of a left of no more
rows than a filter lists the keys of (D600). The scan then reads little
but those keys' rows. Of a larger left the filter is a range and a few
spans. Judging them costs each row read a comparison, and spares it only
a look into the held rows' table, which costs as little. Measured on the
EXISTS of line items, the filter of a larger left made the query slower.

The right operand of such a join is a part run in parallel when it is a
stream of rows enough (`physical/parallel.rs`), though a serial scan by
batch serves a reader of rows better (D291). Its morsels' batches mark
on the threads that read them (`exec/parallel/each.rs`), and no row is
made of them. A mark is only ever set, and the held rows are read after
every morsel ended, so the rows given do not depend on the threads. The
first morsel that fails, in the order of their numbers, is the error
raised (D15).

A left operand asked for in an order is read, held and given in it. One
past the work area gives way to the join that builds its right, the
batches read of it given first (D38). A semi join's rows are asked for
in an order only if its left operand's are, so a join over a semi join
reads it by batch.

#### D1071. A hashed semi join of streams read row by row is made of its batches

An operator that reads its input a row at a time, as a sort of rows not
held whole does, ran a semi join under it by the row path. Its operands
were then read a row at a time, of the column store too, each value
decoded alone, on one thread. A hashed semi join or antijoin of streams
every table of which reads by batch is now made of its batches whoever
reads it (`exec/join/semi.rs`), while EXECUTOR.BATCHES is on, and its
rows made of them. Its operands are read by batch, and by morsels where
D1070 says so. The rows are the row path's, in the left's order where
one is asked.

#### D1072. A join reads a grouping by batch whatever its set functions, and a grouping run in parallel too

A stream gathered a grouping's rows into batches only if the grouping
took runtime filters, one of COUNT, MIN and MAX (D600). A join over any
other grouping, as one of SUM, had an operand that gave no batches, so
the whole join ran a row at a time, its other operand's table read row
by row and told no filter. A grouping not streamed is now gathered
whatever its set functions (`exec/batch/told.rs`), and so is a grouping
that is a part run in parallel, alone or under its HAVING condition
(D1073), its rows made by the part's threads. A grouping of SUM or AVG
still takes no filter to its input (D15, D600). A filter told it is
judged of the batches it gives.

#### D1073. A HAVING condition that cannot raise is judged by its grouping's part

A grouping run in parallel gave every group to the statement's thread,
which merged the partitions' groups in the order of their first rows
(D293) and then judged the HAVING condition of each. Of a grouping of
many groups few of which the condition keeps, that thread did most of
the work. A filter over a grouping not streamed is now a part with it
(`physical/parallel.rs`) if its condition cannot raise and a worker can
evaluate it alone. The thread that finishes a partition's groups judges
the condition of each (`exec/parallel/grouped.rs`), and only the groups
kept are ordered and merged. The condition raises nothing, so the order
it is judged in shows nowhere (D15). One that can raise stays above the
part, judged in the groups' order. The part gives way as the grouping
alone does (D298), to the filter over the grouping run alone. EXPLAIN
ANALYZE counts the part by its filter (D378).

#### D1074. A LIKE pattern of no `_` is matched by its pieces, each searched for as a substring

A pattern was matched a specifier at a time, and at each character
where it failed after a `%` it was begun again one character on. Of a
pattern as `'%special%requests%'` over long strings that is a comparison
or more for every character of every string. A pattern of no `_` is now
split once into its pieces, the strings between its `%`s
(`value/like/pieces.rs`). A value matches if it begins with the first
piece, ends with the last past the first, and holds the pieces between
in order and apart in what lies between the two. Each is looked for by
the library's substring search from where the piece before it ended,
and the first place found is taken, which leaves the most to the pieces
after it. A piece is whole characters, so it is searched for among the
value's bytes. A pattern with `_` is matched as before. The rows are
those the standard's rule gives [X3.135-1986 §5.14 GR5], as a test
compares the two matchers over patterns and values.

#### D1075. A hashed semi join's or antijoin's probe is a step of its left operand's pipeline

A pipeline run in parallel ended at every join but an inner hash join
(D292). So a semi join or an antijoin that builds its right, the smaller
operand, was probed on the statement's thread, and so ran the grouping
over it. Its probe is now a step of its left operand's pipeline
(`exec/parallel/pipeline.rs`), as an inner join's is. The right operand
is built once for every morsel (`exec/batch/joined/shared.rs`). Each
batch of a morsel keeps the rows a built row matches, or of an antijoin
those none matches, selected (`exec/batch/joined/semi/step.rs`), and a
pipeline read a row at a time judges each row so.

The first built row that matches decides. A left row of a null key
matches nothing. A semi join tells its left's scans its keys' runtime
filters, an antijoin none (D369). The rows a morsel keeps and their
order are the serial join's, so the part gives the plan's rows in its
order (D290). A join whose condition beyond its keys a worker cannot
evaluate alone ends its pipeline as before. One planned to build its
left is no step. Its right is the part (D1070).

#### D1076. A LEFT outer join's probe on its keys alone is a step of its left operand's pipeline

A LEFT outer join ended every pipeline (D292), so the join and the
grouping over it ran on the statement's thread, as the count of each
customer's orders did. A LEFT join that matches on its keys alone, with
no condition beyond them and none of an operand's own (D15), is now a
step of its left operand's pipeline (`exec/parallel/pipeline.rs`). Its
right operand is built once for every morsel, and each left row is
joined with the built rows of its key, or with nulls if none has it
(`exec/batch/joined/shared/outer.rs`), which depends on no other morsel.

A morsel gives the rows the serial join gives of its rows, in their
order, so the part gives the plan's rows in its order (D290). The join
tells its left no runtime filter, as it gives every left row. Its built
operand, and that of a semi join that is a step (D1075), is a part run
in parallel by its rows alone, its morsels gathered by batch into the
join's table, so a condition of its own, as a LIKE, is judged on the
part's threads. A LEFT join with a condition beyond its keys, and a
RIGHT or FULL join, whose unmatched right rows no one morsel knows, end
their pipelines as before.

#### D1077. NOT IN of columns that hold no null is an antijoin hashed on their equality

NOT IN is the antijoin on `(x = y) IS NOT FALSE`, which a null on either
side satisfies (D541). That condition is no equality of columns, so the
join was a nested loop, every outer row read against every row of the
subquery, and an uncorrelated NOT IN made an antijoin (D1065) ran far
longer than its subquery run once. Of a column of each operand declared
to hold no null, `x = y` is never unknown, so the condition is `x = y`,
and the rule that makes the antijoin writes it so
(`optimizer/unnesting/filled.rs`). The join is then hashed on it, and a
step of its left operand's pipeline (D1075). A column that may hold a
null on either side keeps the condition as it was, so NOT IN keeps its
exact meaning.
#### D1080. A hash join's operand read by its morsels is put together by those threads, its table in parts of the hashes' high bits

A hash join probed by a part run in parallel reads an operand that is
itself a part by its morsels, on the workers (D292, D1051). What
followed ran on the statement's thread alone while the workers waited.
The morsels' batches were joined into one batch, a copy of every vector.
Every key was hashed. The table was made in three passes over the
hashes, the second a write at random for each row (D368). Each key was
hashed again for its runtime filter (D369). Of an operand of millions
of rows this was the longest stretch of the join that one thread ran,
and a chain of joins ran one such stretch after another.

Now an operand read by its morsels that holds more rows than a morsel
is put together by the threads that read it, in four runs of morsels
(`exec/parallel/build.rs`). A vector of the batch is joined by one
thread (`Batch::joined_at`), so as many threads copy as the batch has
vectors. The keys are hashed a run of EXECUTOR.MORSEL_ROWS rows at a
time, a run to a thread. Each run's rows are then sorted by part. Last
each part of the table is made by one thread, and each key's runtime
filter by another beside them.

The table is in 64 parts (`exec/table/join/parted.rs`), as many as a
parallel grouping has partitions (D357). A hashed table's slot is the
high bits of a hash, so the rows whose hashes share their 6 highest
bits own a run of slots that no other row is placed in. Each part is
then a table of its own, with its directory, its rows and their hashes,
and a probe finds its part by those bits before its slot. A direct
table (D601) is parted the same way by the high bits of a key's place
in the span. Whether the keys are dense is known only once every run
has given its least and greatest key, so such keys are first asked as
numbers and, if they prove not dense, hashed from those numbers with no
vector read again. No thread writes what another reads, so nothing is
placed atomically and the core needs no `unsafe` (R-SAFE-1).

A run's rows are sorted by part by a counting sort that keeps their
order, and a part takes the runs in order. So a slot's rows and a key's
rows are in the order the operand gave them, as in the table one
thread makes, and a probe finds the same rows in the same order of
either. The table one thread makes is the same structure of one part.

An operand of no more rows than a morsel, a part of degree 1, and an
operand that is not read by its morsels (D1050) are built by the
statement's thread as before. The first took one thread's work to
read, and the others have no threads of their own. No setting turns
this on or off, as the result is the same and the threads are those
the part already has.

#### D1081. A pipeline run in parallel carries the probing table's unread columns late across a hash join's probe

The serial stream carries the columns of an inner hash join's left
operand that no operator reads as the places of their rows, through
the join, and decodes them of the rows the join kept (D361). A pipeline
run in parallel did so only up to its first probe (D366). At a probe it
counted every column as read, so a morsel decoded every column the
pipeline carries, of every row its filters kept, before the first join
dropped any. A scan of a large table probing a selective operand so
decoded, gathered and copied its other columns for rows the join then
dropped, and again at each join after it.

Now a probe step counts as read the columns of its keys alone
(`Deferred::left_of`), as the serial join does, and as dropping rows.
The other columns of the probing table that no later step reads go
through each probe as places, which a probe's gather composes with its
pairs (`Late::gathered`), and are decoded at the pipeline's end of the
rows every join kept (`morsel_kept`). The built operand's columns are
held as vectors as before. A column a later filter, projection or
probe reads is decoded at the scan as before.

#### D1082. A grouping by a deterministic expression has no more groups than the columns it reads take values together

The distinct values of a column are counted by its table's statistics,
found through the nodes that pass columns on (D370). A column that is
an expression of a projection has no table, so it was counted as one
value for every row of the plan. A grouping by such a key, as by the
year of a date or by a sum of two columns, was then estimated at as
many groups as rows. With that many groups a sort of the rows and a
streamed grouping costs less than a hashed one (D550), so a grouping of
millions of joined rows into a few hundred groups was planned as a
sort of every row, and its hash table would have been sized for a
group a row.

Now a grouping or DISTINCT counts an expression that is deterministic
and changes nothing (`expr_pure`, D1041) by the columns it reads
(`cardinality/lineage.rs`, `computed_of`, `grouped_distinct`). It is a function of them, so
it takes at most as many values as they take together: the product of
their distinct values, and no more than the plan's rows. An expression
that reads no column takes one value. The bound goes through
expressions of expressions, to the depth estimates walk (D370). An
expression that is not deterministic may give a value of its own for
every row and is counted as before.

The bound is not tight. A year takes far fewer values than its date
does. It is still the plan's rows or fewer, which is what it was, so no
estimate of groups grows by it. What the expression does to the values
is read of its table's sample (D1279).

The distinct values a join's equality is estimated by are counted as
before, an expression's as its plan's rows. Join orders rest on those
counts, and what bounding them would do to the orders chosen was not
measured, so the bound is the grouping's alone.

#### D1083. A parallel probe holds its pairs as row numbers gathered on the kernels, and pairs a key of one column of integers in its units

A morsel's batch probing a shared table (D292) made its pairs as two
lists of optional places, 16 bytes each, and gathered every vector of
the joined batch through them one option at a time. The serial join
holds its pairs as row numbers of 32 bits and gathers integers on the
vector kernels (D570). Each pair was also compared through
`keys_equal`, which asks both vectors' kinds again for every pair and
every key column, and each probing key was made a double and hashed
even for a direct table, which finds a key by its place alone (D601).

Now the shared table's pairs are row numbers too, gathered by
`Column::gathered_by` on the statement's kernels. A key of one column
of integers, of one scale in the batch and in the built operand, on
which a null matches nothing, is paired in its units
(`exec/batch/joined/shared/paired.rs`). Equal units of one scale are
equal numbers, so a probing row's units are compared with a built
row's as they stand. Of a direct table of whole numbers a probing row
finds its key's rows by its units less the least key
(`JoinTable::rows_of`), with no double made and no hash. Every row at a
place holds that key, so nothing is compared. A null probing row pairs
with none.

Every other key is paired as before: keys of several columns, of
texts, of integers of scales apart, which match when rescaled, and a
key whose nulls match. The pairs, and their order, are the same of
either.

#### D1084. Integers known as runs are judged by walking their runs and the rows asked of together

A column store's scan and a filter judge a conjunct of integers known as
runs once a run (D31, D360). Each judgment made the list of every row
asked of first, even of all of a run's rows, then found each run's rows
in it by a binary search, and gave the rows kept one at a time. A key
of a fact table read in its order, as an order's number in its lines,
is runs of a few rows each. A join's runtime filter tells its scan the
key's least and greatest built values (D600), so every row of such a
key was judged that way, and the judging took more of a query than the
probe did.

Now the runs and the rows asked of are walked together, both ascending
(`storage/batch/runs.rs`). Each run is met once and each row once. No
list of every row is made when all are asked of, since a kept run is
given on as the span of its places. A run that holds no row asked of
is not judged. The rows kept, and their order, are what judging each
row gives. A comparison of integers known as runs is still judged once
a run, not by the kernel over every row, which was measured the slower
of the two.

#### D1086. An equality of an expression of each operand's columns is a hash join on the keys computed once a row

A hash join's keys are columns (D35). A condition equating sort keys of
a collation of a column of each operand had them made columns of its
operands, computed by a projection under the join, which another takes
away above it (D60). Any other equality of expressions, as
`Q.K = X.TAG + X.K`, found no key, and the join was a nested loop that
computed both sides for every pair, even at degree 1.

Now any equality, or IS NOT DISTINCT FROM, of an expression of the left
operand's columns alone with one of the right's alone is lifted so
(`physical/collated.rs`), unless both are columns alone, which the join
keys as they are. Each key is computed once a row of its operand, the
join is planned as any, by either store and in parallel, and its rows
are the nested loop's. A null key matches none, or a null if the
condition is IS NOT DISTINCT FROM. An expression lifted is
deterministic and holds no subquery, so a row's key is the value the
condition compares of it with every row of the other operand. A
condition that can raise an exception condition by its columns'
declared types is not hashed at all (D776), so computing the key of a
row that no pair holds raises nothing the nested loop would not. An
outer join keeps such a condition whole too, as its keys would be
computed of every row of an operand even when the other has none.

#### D1087. A probe of a join table past a thread's share of the cache is screened by its key's Bloom filter, and a semi join of many held keys filters its right

A probe of a hash join's table reads one word of its directory at a
random place for every probing row. A table past the last level of
cache makes that read a trip to memory, and most of a probe's time
waits on it, even for the rows no built row matches. Laying out the
table another way (located a batch at a time, a slot of one row
holding its row and key) left that read where it was and gained
nothing when measured.

A parallel build of one key sums its keys in a Bloom filter as it is
built (D1080). A probe of such a table (`batch/joined/shared/probing.rs`)
now first asks that filter of its batch's hashes, on the kernels, and
reads the directory only at the places it passes. The filter takes a
byte a key and stays in a core's cache, so a probing row of no match
costs a read from cache instead of one from memory. A table that fits
in a thread's share of the last level, 4 MiB (36 MiB shared by 8
threads on the reference machine, rounded down), is not screened, as
its directory read is a cache read already. The filter judges itself
as a runtime filter does (D369). After its first batches, if it kept
most rows, it stops being asked. The pairs a probe gives are those it
gives unscreened, as the filter keeps every row whose key the table
may hold, and a LEFT join's row it drops is paired with nulls as one
that matched no built row.

The kernels screen hashes by the filter's blocks with one vector of
blocks at a time on x86 (`simd/src/x86/bloom.rs`), with AVX2 or
AVX-512 as the machine has, and the portable code elsewhere; a hash
passes the same filter on every kernel.

A semi join that builds its left (D1070) gave its right's scan no
runtime filter when it held more keys than a filter lists, on the
reasoning that the scan's comparison costs as much as the probe it
spares. Past the cache that probe is a read from memory, so it now
tells the scan its filter of a range and a Bloom filter whatever the
number of its keys.

### Planning statistics

#### D1089. A statement's planning reads each table's statistics, rows and index keys once, and every step of it reads them so

The maintenance thread gathers a table's statistics whenever they are
due (D35), so they may appear between two readings of one statement.
One planning's estimator asked each table's once (D370), but other
steps of the same statement asked the state afresh. The optimizer's
rule that groups an outer join's right operand first (D1112) made an
estimator for each of the three estimates it weighs. The marking of
parallel parts asked whether a grouping's columns are counted (D355),
predicate transfer asked the distinct values of each step's column
(D667), and a prepared statement's plan learned recorded which of its
tables had statistics only after it was planned (D839). A table
gathered in between was weighed with statistics by one step and without
by another, and a plan made with the defaults was kept as if made with
the statistics, so it was not learned again once they were known.

Each statement now plans through one snapshot
(`physical/cardinality/seen.rs`). It asks a table's statistics and rows,
and an index's distinct keys, the first time a step wants them and keeps
them for every step after. The optimizer's rules read them through their
context, and the physical planner's estimator, the marking of parallel
parts, predicate transfer and the measure of a plan learned read them
too. An execution of a prepared statement that plans with its values and
with its slots plans both through one snapshot, so the two plans it
compares are made of one state, and the plan it keeps is measured from
what they saw. Statistics gathered after the snapshot asked are seen by
the statement's next planning, and a plan kept without them is learned
again then (D839). A subquery planned as the statement runs plans
through a snapshot of its own.

### Column store reads

#### D1090. A group's header is held by its entry of the directory and read with no lock of the cache, whose bound is a share of the memory budget

The headers of frozen row groups were held in one map behind one mutex,
ordered by when each was last read (D31). Every read of a header held
took the mutex and moved the header in an ordered tree, so the scans of
a parallel query, a group each, met on it once a group. Its bound was
16 MiB whatever the database's memory. A header of a table of sixteen
columns takes about 180 KiB, so the cache held some ninety of the 915
groups of a table of sixty million rows. A scan of the table then read
and parsed every header again on every query, and a join that fetched
rows by id from groups all over the table parsed a header for most of
its fetches.

A header held is now kept in a slot of its group's entry of the
directory. A read of it takes the slot's own lock shared and looks
nothing up, so readers of different groups share no word. The cache
keeps the bytes and a queue of the headers in the order they were put.
When it must give one up it takes the first of the queue, but passes
over once each header read since it was last passed over, so the
headers read lately stay. The order is no longer exactly by last read,
which cost the shared ordered tree.

COLUMNSTORE.HEADER_CACHE_BYTES is -1 by default, which bounds the cache
at a 64th of MEMORY.BUDGET_BYTES. That is the share the old 16 MiB was
of the default budget of 1 GiB, so a database of the default settings
holds what it held, and one given more memory holds the headers of as
much more data. A value of 0 or more is the bound in bytes as before.
What the cache holds is still reserved of the budget (D38).

#### D1091. A frozen row read by its id reads the one chunk of each column asked for, and is priced as measured

A read of a frozen row by its id found the chunk of each column by
looking at the column's chunks one after another, made a row of the
table's width for a read of a few listed columns, and listed every
column's place for each read. It now finds the chunk by halving, as a
column's chunks are in the order of their rows, and a read of listed
columns appends their values alone (`TableStorage::get_listed`, D862).

The planner priced a frozen fetch a tenth more than a fetch of the
tree's, a figure never measured. `bench/fetch.rs` now reads the same
table from the tree and from two groups of the column store with every
header held. FROZEN_FETCH is set from its case of four columns read by
scattered ids against the tree's case of scattered ids, as a join or an
index scan fetches a few columns, each a page of its own
(`engine/rows/frozen.rs`). A fetch of one column costs less than that,
and one of every column more.

#### D1092. A table opened gathers its first statistics on the thread of the plan that asks, and a sampled pass costs its sample

A table opened has no statistics, and they were left to the maintenance
thread once a plan had asked for them (D35, D473). The first plans
after a start were therefore made without them, on the fixed
selectivities. A grouping of a table of sixty million rows was planned
as a sort and a streamed grouping on one thread, where the plan made
with statistics groups it in parts, and joins planned so were worse.

The plan that first asks for the statistics of a table opened now
gathers them itself, and plans asking meanwhile wait for that pass, so
it is made once and no plan is made without them. The pass is bounded
whatever the table holds, as a table of more than twice the sample's
rows is sampled (D31). If it fails, the statistics are due for the
maintenance thread as before. A table made in this run, and every later
pass, are as they were, so D473 still keeps a table no plan reads from
being gathered.

For the bound to hold of the column store a sampled pass had to cost
its sample. It read the header of every group and listed and hashed
every row id of every group to find those sampled. It now takes the
runs of row ids chosen, passes over a group none of them lies in with
its header unread, and of a group whose rows are every id of its range
in order reckons a run's places from its ids
(`engine/rows/frozen/sampled.rs`).

#### D1093. A table's statistics are saved with its pages at each checkpoint, sealed as its rows are, and are a table opened's from the first

A table's statistics were kept in memory alone, so a database opened
had none, and the first plan of each table read a sample of it before
it could be made (D1092). A server started therefore paid a pass of
every table its first statements named, and what a pass had learned of
a column growing with insertion (D381) was lost at each start.

The row store now saves them. A table's meta page names a page of its
own for them, of any length, written at the checkpoint after each pass
that gathered them (`engine/rows/stats/saved.rs`), and read as the
table is opened. It holds every number the pass found, and each value,
a bound, a histogram's bound, a common value or a sampled row's, as a
record of the table's own format (`engine/rows/stats/image.rs`), so
nothing new describes a value. A table opened with statistics saved
plans by them at once and makes no first pass. The rows it holds more
or fewer than they found count as changes since, so a table that
changed much after its last pass is due as it would have been. A table
with none saved gathers its first as D1092 says. An index's count of
its keys was already kept, with its locator (D35).

The page holds a sample of the table's rows, so it follows the table's
protections. It is sealed by the table's encodings (D30, D48), its
page number the context, with a bit of its own, and passes through
the file's encodings as every page does. Statistics that cannot be
sealed, their encodings not registered, are saved empty. The page is
freed with the table's other pages when the table is dropped, and a
table truncated is a new table with no such page.

Statistics are advice, so no failure of them fails a table. A page
that is empty, that cannot be opened, or that is not what was saved is
read as no statistics, and the table gathers them again.

The meta page gains one word, the statistics page. A meta page written
before, which ends at the large objects' tree, is read as naming none,
so a database written before this decision opens as it is and has its
statistics saved at its next checkpoint. A build from before this
decision refuses a meta page of the new length as not a table's of its
format (SQLCODE -916), and does not misread it. Formats stay 1.

#### D1094. A chunk whose page passed through no encoding is read in the pool by each run, and is not copied out of it

A scan opened each chunk once for all its runs (D352) by copying the
chunk's bytes out of the buffer pool into a buffer of its own, since
the page was not held between runs. On a scan of a few narrow columns
that copy was the largest cost after decoding, a page copied for every
page decoded.

A chunk whose page passed through no encoding is now read where it
lies. What D352 keeps of a chunk, its table of symbols and its
dictionary's entries, is still made once and kept. Its bytes are not.
Each run finds the page in the pool again, holds it while it decodes
its rows of it, and lets it go (`engine/columns/prepared.rs`). Finding
a page the pool holds is a hash and a latch, which costs less
than copying the page, and a run of a vector of rows touches a chunk
once or twice. A group's pages are not written again while a reader
holds the group, and a run never reads a second page while it holds
one, so the page is held for one decode and by nothing that waits.

A chunk whose page its table's encodings open is read as before, its
opened bytes kept for its runs, as opening it once is what D352 saves.
Which a page is is known as it is read, page by page, so a table whose
encodings changed reads each page as it was written. No format
changes.

#### D1097. A fetch of a frozen row is priced by the number of columns it reads

The planner priced a fetch of a frozen row as one of four columns
(D1091), whatever it read. A frozen row read by its id reads one chunk
of each column asked for, each on a page of its own, so a fetch of one
column costs less than a fetch of the tree's row and one of every
column of a wide table more. One figure could not be
right for both, and a join that fetched one column of a frozen table
was priced as if it read four.

`TableStorage::fetch_cost` is now given the number of columns read,
and every planner's and executor's caller passes the columns its plan
reads. A frozen row costs `FROZEN_FETCH` to find its group and place
and `FROZEN_FETCH_COLUMN` for each column read, against a fetch of the
tree's row costing 1 (`engine/rows/frozen.rs`). The two are the line
through the cases of `bench/fetch.rs` that read one and four columns of
a frozen table by scattered ids, against its case of the tree's row
read by scattered ids. Its cases of eight and of all seventeen columns
lie near that line, the seventeen, wide texts among them, a little
above it, so a column's cost is taken as one whatever its type. A
table whose rows are
in its tree reads them whole, and its fetch costs the same whatever is
read. So does that of an engine that does not keep its columns apart,
the default.

#### D1098. A join hashes a vector of integers of scale 0 by a loop with no branch, the kernels' hash of words, as their buckets hash

A join hashed each integer of a key's vector one at a time (D368). It
checked the row for a null, widened the units to 128 bits, looked up the
power of 10 of the scale, made the nearest `f64` by `MAGIC` and divided
it by that power, then hashed the bits as a word. A profile of TPC-H's
ninth query put about a twelfth of its cycles on hashing keys, almost
all of them integers of scale 0.

A vector of scale 0 is now hashed in two loops with no branch
(`table/join/keys.rs`, `integers_hashed`). The first makes each row's
`f64` by `MAGIC`, which is exact below 2^51 in magnitude and is the
nearest `f64` the bucket gives, and notes whether any row is that wide.
The second hashes the bits as words on the statement's kernels
(`Kernels::hash_i64`), the XXH3-64 of 8 bytes that `Seed::word` gives,
seeded alike (`Seed::word_seed`). Without kernels it hashes each by
`Seed::word`, and for a direct table (D601) it gives the bits. A null is
then given a null's hash and marked a miss unless nulls match
(`nulls_marked`). A vector holding a value of 2^51 or more is hashed as
before, as is one of another scale.

Every hash is the one the bucket gives, so a table built one way and
probed the other, a runtime filter and a Bloom filter (D369, D1087) all
agree. A key of integers need not be one on both sides. The probe and
build of a shared table pass the statement's kernels. Every other
hashing passes none and takes the loop of words.

#### D1099. A join keeps a vector of texts as codes of a dictionary: a built operand's parts of one, and a built operand's texts of no more rows than a batch

A join gathered a vector of texts at its pairs by reading each row's
text and copying it. It put the parts of its built operand together the
same way, so a store's dictionary codes became texts at the first join.
Every join above then read a row's end and its bytes at random from a
vector that could hold millions of rows. A profile of TPC-H's ninth
query put about a sixth of its last-level cache misses on those reads.
They gathered a nation's name, of 25 values, from a built operand of
three million rows.

A vector of texts of a dictionary now keeps it (`storage/batch/coded.rs`).
The parts of a built operand whose vectors are codes of one dictionary,
the same entries for all, make a vector of their codes (`of_codes`), and
parts of two dictionaries or of texts are put together as texts as
before. A built operand of no more rows than a batch holds, 2,048, makes
each vector of texts that is not coded a dictionary once as the table is
made, each row an entry (`dictionaries`). A join gathers that
vector as codes of it, a built row's code its row, a pick of none, past
the end or of a null a null (`Column::gathered_coded`). Both the probe of
a held operand (`batch/joined/pairs.rs`) and a shared table's
(`batch/joined/shared.rs`) do so. A join above gathers four bytes a row
of it, and puts its parts together as codes.

Coded vectors were already given by a store's scan, and every reader of a
batch's vectors reads them. Conditions, hashes, comparisons, groupings
and sorts take each entry once, and none takes two codes for unequal
texts. So entries that repeat a text, as a built operand's rows may, are
read as a store's are, and a grouping by a name finds one group for each
text (D1161).

The bound is derived from the batch, not tuned. A reader of codes takes
each entry once per batch, so entries no more than a batch's rows cost
it no more than reading the batch's rows as texts would. A batch of codes
is charged its entries as well as its codes, so entries no more than a
full batch of the same texts keep the charge at that batch's plus four
bytes a row. The dictionary a table makes is a copy of at most a batch of
its texts, charged to no grant.

A built operand of a row more is gathered as texts, as it was before, so
past the bound a join costs what it did and never more. The step at the
bound is the gain, not a loss.

#### D1100. A group's shadow bits are trusted only once the entries the tree held as it was published are marked

A group is put in the directory first, and the entries the tree holds in
its range of row ids are marked in its shadow bits after, so that a
writer either finds the group or is found by the mark (D510). Between
the two a reader could take the group with no bit set, and a scan by
batch then read nothing of the tree over the group's range, and left
that range out of the tree's rows it reads last
(`engine/rows/frozen/batches.rs`). It missed every row of the range the
group does not hold. A freeze leaves such rows out when their commit is
not yet stamped on their entries as it reads them (D440), which a commit
does a leaf at a time, so a freeze racing a commit made a group whose
range held some of the commit's rows in the tree alone. The scan also
read the frozen value of a row updated, and the row of one deleted, just
before the group was published. A count read this way was of no state
ever committed.

A group's bits are now settled only when its mark has read the tree
(`engine/rows/frozen/shadow_bits.rs`). Until then every bit is taken as
set, so a scan reads the tree over the group's range whole, as it did
before there were bits, and a group is not said to have no bit. A reader
reads that the bits are settled before it reads any of them, so the bits
it trusts hold every mark made by then. A table opened settles its
groups' bits once it has marked them. Publishing is two steps, the group
put in the directory and its bits marked (`engine/rows/frozen/freeze.rs`),
so a test reads between them.

Rejected was marking the bits before the group is in the directory,
which misses the writer that writes between the mark and the directory.
Rejected too was holding the directory's lock while the tree is read,
which would stop every reader and writer of the table for as long as the
mark takes. A scan in row id order, a morsel's by row and a scan in the
groups' order merge the tree's entries with the groups' rows by row id
and never read the bits, so they were not at fault.

#### D1110. A grouping run in parallel merges each morsel's groups a column at a time, into tables made with room

A grouping run in parallel groups each morsel in a table of its own and
merges the morsels' groups by partition (D293, D356). Each group was
merged alone. Its key was read as a cell and compared and appended by
its kind, and each set function's state was merged by its kind, group
after group. Each morsel's table and each partition's grew a vector a
group at a time, and a morsel's groups were split among the partitions
into a vector a partition. Of a grouping of many groups, as one by an
order's key over its line items, the merge and the allocator took more
time than grouping the rows did.

A partition now merges a morsel's groups a column at a time
(`exec/table/made.rs`). Each group is looked up by the hash it came
with. A morsel's groups are of distinct keys, so those not found are
all new, and they are appended lane by lane, integers in one loop, and
then placed. Each set function's states are then merged in one loop,
the kind of the two columns and their scale compared once
(`exec/table/states/typed/merged.rs`). Columns of different kinds, and
accumulators, merge group by group as before. A table placed by keyed
hashes (D357) makes its new groups one by one, and one whose probe
grows long as new groups are placed turns keyed with every group
placed.

A morsel's table is made with room for the groups the morsel last
grouped made, so its vectors and slots are made once. A partition's
table is given room for every group of the wave it merges. The places
of a morsel's groups are kept partition after partition in one vector,
counted and then placed, in place of a vector a partition. None of
this changes a group, its number or the order the groups are given in.

#### D1111. A HAVING condition judged by its grouping's part is judged of a group before the group takes a row

A part that judges its grouping's HAVING condition (D1073) finished
every group into a row of its own and then dropped the rows the
condition was not true of. Of many groups few of which are kept, the
rows made and freed cost more than judging them. Each group's row is
now made in the room of one row, the condition is judged of it there,
and only a group kept takes a row of its own (`exec/table.rs`). The
groups kept, their rows and their order are as before.

#### D1112. A grouping over a LEFT outer join groups the join's right operand first by its keys

A grouping by the left operand's columns over a LEFT outer join, as the
count of each customer's orders, read every pair the join made, and the
join held every row of its right operand. The rule
`group_before_outer_join` (`optimizer/pregrouped.rs`) now groups the
right operand first, by its columns of the join's equalities, and
computes each set function of each of those groups. The join then
holds a row a key, a left row matches one group at most, and the
grouping above merges what the groups below computed: MAX and MIN
their greatest and least, COUNT their sum. A projection above gives a
count of 0 where the sum is null, of a left row no group matched, in
COUNT's type.

The rule takes a join whose condition is equalities of a column of
each operand alone, and set functions that are COUNT, MAX or MIN of a
column of the right operand declared to hold no null, neither DISTINCT
nor filtered. The right operand is a table's rows, as they are or
filtered by a condition that cannot raise. So the grouping below warns
of no null, and the grouping above warns of the null of a left row no
group matched, as the function did of that row before. Nothing that
could raise is evaluated of a row it was not before (D15). MAX and MIN
are taken of exact numbers alone. COUNT(*), which counts a left row
nothing matched, SUM and AVG, whose sums of parts could pass a bound
their whole does not, and every other shape are left as they were.

Grouping the right operand first costs a row grouped for each of its
rows. It spares the join every row beyond one a key, and the grouping
above every row beyond one a left row. So the rule rewrites only where
the right operand's estimated rows less its estimated keys outnumber
the left operand's rows. Without statistics a column's distinct values
are taken as its table's rows (D370), so the rule then leaves the plan.

#### D1113. A grouping over another whose grouping columns hold its own runs in one part, each partition's thread making both

DISTINCT_AGGREGATES (D340) makes a query of DISTINCT set functions two
groupings, the first by the grouping columns and each argument, the
second by the grouping columns alone. Only the first was a part run in
parallel (D293). Its groups, as many as the query's rows nearly, were
merged in order on the statement's thread, which then grouped them
again a row at a time while the workers waited.

A grouping over another is now one part when the second groups by some
of the first's grouping columns and no others, neither by a collation
nor with groups of empty grouping sets, its set functions none DISTINCT
nor an inverse distribution function and each evaluated by a worker
alone, and the first's states merge (`physical::first_level`). The
first's groups are split among the partitions by the hash of their
values of the second's columns alone (`GroupTable::made`), the same of
a value in every morsel, so each partition holds every group of the
first that a group of the second takes.

The thread finishing a partition orders its groups by their first rows
and groups them again (`exec/parallel/grouped/regrouped.rs`), each set
function taking its values in that order, as the serial plan feeds
them. A group of the second is numbered by its first group of the
first, so the statement's thread merges only the second's groups, in
the order the plan run alone gives them. A HAVING condition over the
pair is judged of the second's groups by the same thread. A join's
runtime filters (D1063) are of the second's columns, so the part's
pipeline is told none. The results, their order and the warnings are as
before. EXPLAIN shows both groupings under one `Parallel`, and EXPLAIN
ANALYZE counts the first's groups as its partitions finish them.

A grouping by no column is left as it was, as its one group would be
one partition's and one thread's.

#### D1114. An index nested-loop join over a part run in parallel probes its index on the part's threads

An index nested-loop join probed its index for each row of its left
operand on the statement's thread, though that operand held a part run
in parallel and so many rows. A semi join by an index over an inner one
over such a part, as of a correlated EXISTS, made every probe and every
joined row there while the workers waited.

Such a join now probes on the part's threads (`exec/parallel/looped.rs`).
The statement's thread reads the left operand's rows, a wave of
morsels at a time, four for each thread, and each morsel is joined by a
thread through the join and every index join below it of the chain, as
one thread joins them. A morsel of probes takes a sixteenth of
EXECUTOR.MORSEL_ROWS of left rows, a probe costing a walk of the index
and a read of its row. A sweep of 1, 4, 16 and 64 measured 16 the
fastest. The morsels' rows are given in the order of their numbers, so
each left row's matches come where they would alone, and the first
error in that order is the one raised, after the rows before it.

A join takes part if it gives each left row's rows as it reads that
row, an inner, LEFT, semi or antijoin, and a worker evaluates its
condition alone, as of a part's pipeline (D291). A FULL join, which
gives the table's unmatched rows at the end, a spatial join and a probe
by a function's predicate, which a statement's prepared budget bounds,
stay on the statement's thread, as does a join over a left operand that
holds no part. The degree is the greatest of the parts the left operand
holds.

#### D1115. A semi join that builds its left holds a left run in parallel by the threads that read it

A semi join or an antijoin that builds its left (D1070) read its left
operand's batches on the statement's thread, though that operand was a
part run in parallel. Each batch's kept rows were gathered into a
batch of their own, then all of them joined into one, hashed and put
in the join's table there, while the workers that read the part waited.
Of a wide left of many rows, as the lines and suppliers of an order
waiting on its suppliers are, that thread ran a stretch of the join
alone between the left's reading and the right's.

Such a left is now held by the threads that read it
(`exec/parallel/held.rs`). Each morsel's kept rows are gathered into
one batch by the thread that read them, and the statement's thread
takes the morsels' batches in the order of their numbers, so the rows
are held in the order the part alone gives them. They are put in their
table by those threads too, as a hash join's built operand is (D1080).

Each morsel's rows are charged to the join's work grant as its thread
gathers them (D1150). Once a morsel outgrows the grant, or the rows
taken are on course to, the batches taken so far are given on, then the
rest in order, to the join that builds its right, a morsel past the
grant read again by the statement's thread a batch at a time, so every
left row is read once and in order. The
first morsel that fails, in the order of their numbers, is the error
raised, after the rows before it are taken (D15). A pipeline whose
morsels are not read by batch, or whose batches hold other columns
than the plan's, and a left asked for in an order are read as before.

#### D1116. An analyzed grouping over another that crosses its partitions passes the counts of the projections between them

EXPLAIN ANALYZE wraps each operator in a count (D378). Of a grouping
crossing another's partitions (D1133), as a query groups customers by
their count of orders, a projection between the two was wrapped too.
The pair was found by the projections down from the second grouping,
and a count is no projection, so the part no longer saw a pair. It took
the rows for a pipeline, met the first grouping, which is no step of
one, and failed with "a part run in parallel is not a pipeline". The
query ran, and its analysis failed.

The projections between the two are now found under their counts
(`physical::between`), so an analyzed plan runs the part the plan run
alone runs. A partition's thread takes each group of the first through
the projections, so each projection's count is given a row for each
group of the first, as the first grouping's own count is, and is shown
with no time of its own, as a step of a pipeline is.

#### D1117. A grouping over a LEFT outer join by a key of its left table, its right grouped first, is a projection of the joined rows

D1112 groups the right operand of a LEFT join first, by its columns of
the join's equalities, and merges what those groups computed in the
grouping above, by the left operand's columns. Of a query that groups
its customers by their key, each group above held one joined row, and
the grouping hashed and merged every row into a group of its own to
give them back as they were.

The grouping above is now a projection of the joined rows
(`optimizer/pregrouped.rs`) when each of its groups holds exactly one
of them. That holds when all of the following hold:

1. The left operand is a table's rows, filtered or not.
2. The grouping columns hold every column of a unique key of that
   table, by a constraint not deferrable and of no period. Each key
   column is NOT NULL by a constraint not deferrable and has no
   collation of its own, and the grouping is by no collation. No two
   left rows are then alike in the grouping columns, as grouping
   compares them [ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §11.7 GR2, §8.9].
3. Each column the join equates, of either operand, is an exact number.
   Two exact numbers equal by the join's comparison are one value, so
   the groups of the right operand's keys, which differ in that value,
   differ by the join's comparison too. A left row matches at most one
   of them, and the LEFT join gives it once: joined with that group, or
   with nulls if it matches none [§7.10 GR1].

A group of one row computes each set function over that one row. MAX
and MIN of one value are that value. The grouping above computed MAX
and MIN of the group's MAX and MIN, and the sum of its counts for
COUNT, so each is the value the group below computed. A left row no
group matched has null in each, as the grouping above found it. COUNT
gives that row 0, as D1112 has it, and MAX and MIN give null. The
grouping above raised the warning that a null value was eliminated
(01003) of that null [§10.9 GR4b]. The projection raises it of the same
row, by an expression that warns as it gives the null, so the
statement's warning is the one it was.

COUNT of a column that may hold a null is left as it was, by D1112's
own condition. A right row whose column is null counts nothing below,
and its warning would differ. The projection changes nothing below.
Every other shape keeps the grouping above: grouping columns that hold
no key, a key that may hold a null, a deferrable key, a key or a
grouping of a collation, a left operand that is a join, and a join
equating strings, whose equal strings may differ as values.

#### D1118. A LIKE pattern's pieces are each made once into a finder that marks eight places at a time

A pattern of no `_` is matched by its pieces (D1074), each piece between
its first and its last searched for by the library's substring search.
That search made its searcher again for each value it searched, so of
a pattern as `'%special%requests%'` over many short comments the making
took a large part of the matching's time.

Each piece between is now made once, as its pattern is, into a finder
(`value/like/finder.rs`). The finder reads the eight bytes from a place
of the value and the eight bytes the piece's length less one further on
as two words. It marks each of the eight places whose byte is the
piece's first and whose byte that far on is its last, by the test of a
word for zero bytes. That test marks every zero byte and at times a
byte above one, so a mark is a candidate, which is compared with the
whole piece. No place that holds the piece goes unmarked. The places
past the last whole word are compared one at a time. The first place
that holds the piece is taken, as the substring search took it, so the
rows are those D1074 gives, as a test compares the finder with that
search over pieces and values.

#### D1119. A LIKE of a piece between two `%`s searches a batch's whole text at once, on vector instructions where the processor has them

A batch keeps its strings one after another in one arena, each row's end
noted. A pattern of a piece between two `%`s, as
`'%special%requests%'`, was matched a value at a time, each value's
pieces searched for alone (D1074, D1118). A comment is a few dozen
bytes, so the search spent much of itself starting, finishing a word
and comparing the bytes past its last whole word one at a time.

The longest piece between is now searched for in the batch's whole
arena by a kernel, `Kernels::find_bytes` (`value/like/arena.rs`). A
place found is in the row whose end is the first past it. If the piece
ends past that row's end, the row does not hold it there. Otherwise the
row is matched whole by its pieces, as a value alone is, and the search
goes on from the row's end. A row the search never stops in lacks the
piece, and any value that matches holds every piece, so no such row
matches. The rows are those a match of each value alone gives, as a
test compares the two over rows that hold the piece across their ends,
twice, out of order and not at all.

The kernel's portable body is the search of D1118, moved to the
kernels (`kernels/portable/find.rs`), and a value alone is still
searched by it. On AVX2 and AVX-512 the kernel loads the 32 or 64 bytes
from a place and as many from the needle's length less one further on,
compares them with the needle's first and last bytes, and compares each
place where both are equal with the whole needle, in order
(`simd/src/x86/find.rs`). The places past the last whole step are left
to the portable body. NEON has no instruction that gathers a compare's
lanes into a mask of bits, so it runs the portable body. The contract
and differential tests hold each set to the portable body, of needles
of every length to past a step and haystacks of few letters.

The arena is searched of a filter's conjunct when it judges at least
half the batch's rows, and of a program's LIKE, which NOT LIKE is
judged by. Neither searches a store's dictionaries, whose entries are
each matched once (D31). A pattern of no piece between, as `'PROMO%'`,
compares only a value's ends, and a pattern with `_` has no pieces, so
each is matched a value at a time as before. A scan that decodes each
value into its own buffer matches it by its bytes (`BytesLike`), the
pieces made once for its conjunct.

#### D1120. The sums and counts of a grouping of few groups are fed by lanes, and a batch's dictionary places made a column at a time

A grouping of few groups, as one of a table's lines into four, gives
each group many rows in turn. A typed SUM, AVG or COUNT state added
each row's value to its group's total, and the add of one row waited on
the store of the row before it of the same group. Each row also matched
the set function's kind, and COUNT(*) asked a boxed closure whether the
row was null.

A sum of at most 64 groups, of a vector with no null, is now fed in
lanes. Rows go in turn to four partial totals and counts of each group,
so the adds of a lane do not wait on the others, and the partials are
added to the groups' states once the batch is fed
(`exec/table/states/typed/few.rs`). COUNT(*) of at most 64 groups
counts its rows the same way. A sum of at most 2^63 numbers below 2^63
each stays below 2^126, so no partial or total reaches the 128 bits the
states sum in; the overflow is still checked, and the totals are those
the rows fed one at a time give. A vector with a null, or more groups,
is fed a row at a time as before.

Grouping by dictionary codes (D1161) made each row's place by asking
each key column for its vector and code, row by row. The places of a
batch's rows are now made a column at a time, each column's codes read
in one loop into a vector of places, and the rows then look their
places up in the memo (`exec/batch/groups/coded.rs`).

#### D1122. The pager's free list finds the smallest free run that holds a request by its runs kept by size, and counts its free pages as they change

A spill area keeps its pages in a pager file of its own (D38), and a
grouping or sort that spills takes and frees pages there a page at a
time, so its free list holds many runs. The list found the smallest
free run that held a request by a pass over every run, and counted its
free pages by another, at each page taken.

The free runs are now kept by size and first page beside the map by
first page, and their pages counted as runs are added and removed
(`disk/pager/free.rs`). The smallest run that holds a request is the
first of those by size at least the request's, the first by page of
runs of one size, which is the run the pass found. A request no run
holds is made as before (D30). The runs by size and the count are
those of the runs after every change, which a unit test checks through
merges, splits and the run that ends the file taken and released.

#### D1123. The second grouping of a pair is made in the executor's table, of the first's groups given as a batch

A pair of groupings run as one part (D1113) finished each partition in
three steps. The first grouping's table gave each of its groups as a row
of values, the rows were put in the order of their first rows, and the
second grouping keyed each row by the bytes of its grouping values in a
map of accumulators, one a group. Of a DISTINCT set function the first
grouping holds nearly a group a row of the query, so the part made a
row, a key and a probe of the map for each, where the first grouping
itself had made none.

A table now gives its groups as one batch, a group a row in the order
the groups were made (`exec/table/given.rs`). The lanes of its keys are
the columns as they are, integers, approximate numbers and texts in
vectors of their types with their nulls a mask, any other lane its
values. Each set function's results are a column after them, COUNT's
counts as integers and every other function's as its accumulator
finishes each group, so each value is the one the group's row held. A
