set function that fails raises what the rows raised, the error of the
first group that fails.

The second grouping reads that batch as a grouping by batch reads a
scan's (`exec/parallel/grouped/second.rs`). Its keys are hashed a vector
at a time, each row's group is found or made by its key in the vectors,
and each set function's states are fed the rows in one loop, in columns
where a column holds them (D356). A group of the second is numbered by
its first group of the first, as before, so the statement's thread
merges the partitions' groups in the plan's order.

It does so when three things hold. The second crosses no partition
(D1133). Each of its set functions is one a grouping by batch reads
(D354), which a filtered one is not. And the first's groups lie in the
order of their first rows, which the table tells of its numbers
(`GroupTable::in_order`) and which holds when its morsels were merged in
order. That is the order the plan run alone feeds each set function in,
so a set function whose result depends on that order gives the plan's
result. Any other pair, and a
pipeline read a row at a time, is grouped again of rows as before
(`regrouped.rs`). The batch is made only as the last wave finishes a
partition, so what the part holds and when it gives way are unchanged.

#### D1124. The first rows of a sort over a grouping run in parallel are taken from its partitions' tables

A sort of which only the first rows are asked for (D379), over a
grouping run in parallel, read every group back. Each partition's thread
made a row of values of each of its groups, the statement's thread
merged the partitions' rows in the order of their first rows, and the
sort kept its few. Of a grouping of many groups nearly all of that work,
and all of the memory the rows took, which no grant was charged, was for
rows the sort dropped.

Each partition's thread now takes the first rows from its own table
(`exec/parallel/grouped/top.rs`). The table gives its groups as a batch
(D1123), the columns the projection over the grouping names in its
order, and each group's first row's number as a column after them. The
thread keeps that batch's first rows under the sort's keys and then the
number, as a sort run in parallel keeps a morsel's
(`sort::first_of_morsel`), so only those are made rows. The statement's
thread sorts the partitions' rows the same way, gives the first asked
for, and leaves the number out.

The plan run alone sorts the groups stably, in the order of their first
rows, so of two groups of equal keys the one whose first row came
earlier comes first. The number as the last key orders any two groups
so, in whatever partitions they are. The rows given and their order are
therefore the plan's.

It does so of a grouping by hash, alone at the top of its part, whose
groups are made by batch, under a projection of its columns and of
constants alone, or none. A sort that asks the peers of its last row (WITH TIES) is not
taken so, as the number would part groups that are peers. Neither is one
over a HAVING condition, a projection that computes a value or DISTINCT;
the sort reads those groups as before. A pair of groupings (D1113) gives
them from the second's tables (D1281). A
grouping whose groups are made of rows gives its groups in order, which
are projected and sorted. A part that gives way is grouped alone and its
rows projected and sorted, the part not tried again.

#### D1125. A partition of a grouping run in parallel gives its table's groups as a batch, a row made of a group as it is given

Each partition of a grouping run in parallel finished its table into a
row of values a group, every row made before the first was read. The
rows were held beside the tables they were made of, in memory charged to
no grant (D38), so a grouping of very many groups held several times its
grant, and its threads spent their time growing the vectors of rows.

A partition of a grouping with no HAVING condition and no second
grouping over it now gives its table's groups as one batch (D1123) and
their first rows' numbers (`exec/parallel/grouped/runs.rs`). The batch
is the table's own vectors, which the grant was charged as the table was
made, so the part holds nothing more to give its groups. The statement's
thread still takes the partitions' groups in the order of their first
rows, as a merge of sorted runs takes them, and makes a row of a group
only as that group is given. A run read to its end gives back what it
held.

A grouping under a HAVING condition, a pair of groupings (D1113), a
grouping whose groups are made of rows, and a table whose groups are not
in the order of their first rows give rows as before. So does a
partition asked a sort's first rows (D1124), which are few, and one
whose groups go to the grouping's spill (D1226), which writes them there
as rows.

#### D1126. SUBSTRING of a constant start and length, and IN a list of strings, are evaluated of a vector's text

A function with no body over vectors is called for each row of a batch
with the row's values (D363). SUBSTRING had none, so a filter such as
`SUBSTRING(C FROM 1 FOR 2) IN ('13', '31')` made a value of every string
of the column, a vector of characters and a string for each call, and a
value of each result to look for in the list (D1067).

SUBSTRING now has a body over vectors (`functions/strings/slices.rs`). Of
a vector of character strings and a start and a length that are
constants, each string's slice is copied from the vector's text into the
result's. The slice is the one the call gives [ISO/IEC 9075:1992 §6.7
GR1], placed by the same rule, the octets of a string of one octet a
character and the characters of any other. The entries of a dictionary
are sliced once each and the rows keep their codes, while the entries
are no more than the rows. Of more entries each row is sliced, as most
entries would be sliced for no row.

The body gives none wherever a row's call could differ from a slice,
and the rows are then called one by one as before. That is a start or a
length that is no constant or is null, a negative length, which raises
an error of every string not null [§6.7 GR1d], and a count in octets of
a string that holds a character of several, whose cut characters the
call leaves out.

IN a list whose constants are character strings, nulls aside, is judged
of a vector's text too (`exec/batch/expr/compare.rs`). A string is
looked for without its trailing spaces among the constants without
theirs, as two strings are equal if they are equal so [X3.135-1986 §5.11
GR5], which a long list already did for a column (D31). A list of any
length keeps that set. A dictionary's entries are each judged once.

#### D1127. A filter's scalar subquery with no outer reference is run as its first row is judged, and the filter judged with its value a constant

A scalar subquery that reads nothing of the rows around it has one value
for the statement [ISO/IEC 9075:1992 §7.11 GR1], and its runner runs it
once (`exec/subquery.rs`). A filter that held one was still judged a row
at a time whole. No vector holds a subquery, and a filter that can raise
is judged over vectors only if all of it can be (D15, D362). So
`C > (SELECT AVG(C) FROM T)` beside any other conjunct made a row of
every row of every batch.

A filter read by batch now runs such subqueries as its first row is
judged, and judges every row with their values in their places
(`exec/batch/judge/bound.rs`). The condition is then of columns and
constants, judged by the kernels and programs that judge any other.

The errors are those the filter raised before. A filter evaluates both
operands of every AND and OR of each row it judges (D15), so its first
row runs each subquery that is an operand of a comparison, of IS NULL or
of IS DISTINCT FROM, or of arithmetic, a monadic minus or a cast under
one. Those alone are made constants. A subquery under CASE, a function,
LIKE, IN or a quantified predicate is left where it is, as a row may not
reach it. A batch of which no row is judged runs none. If a subquery
raises an error, the batch is judged a row at a time by the condition as
it was written, so the first row raises what it raised, after the error
of any operand before the subquery.

#### D1128. A subquery run once for its statement is planned as a statement is, its parts in parallel

A statement's plan has its parts marked to run in parallel (D291) and
its chains of joins given predicate transfer (D665) as it is compiled
(`db/compiled.rs`). A subquery's plan is made as it is first run, by its
runner (`exec/subquery.rs`), which marked nothing. So a subquery with no
outer reference read its tables on the statement's thread alone, however
many rows they held, while the same tables in the statement around it
were read by every worker. A view read in a statement and again in such
a subquery of it was computed the second time on one thread.

The runner now marks the plan of a subquery it runs once for the
statement as a statement's is marked (`physical::parallel_run`). That is
a subquery with no outer reference, and one decorrelated, which is run
once without its equalities (D35). The statement's thread runs it, as
no part's worker evaluates a subquery (D291), so its parts take workers
as a statement's parts do and give way as they do.

A run asked for its first rows alone, as EXISTS and a scalar subquery
ask, stops as it has them, and parts read morsels ahead of the rows
taken. Such a run is marked only if its plan reads its input whole
before its first row, under a grouping or DISTINCT not streamed or a
sort, where stopping early saves nothing. A run that reads every row, as
IN and a quantified comparison ask, is always marked. A subquery run
again for each set of outer values is planned as before.

#### D1129. A grouping that a filter's input and a subquery of its condition compute alike is computed once

A view or a WITH query is bound in each place it is read, and each place
is planned and run. A statement that compares a view's rows with a set
function of the same view, as
`... FROM V WHERE V.TOTAL = (SELECT MAX(TOTAL) FROM V)` does, grouped the
view's tables twice, once for the statement and once for the subquery.

As a filter is opened, the subqueries of its condition that have no
outer reference are planned, as their run would plan them
(`exec/shared.rs`). The groupings by hash of the filter's input and of
those plans are written out, operator by operator, with their tables,
the columns read of each, their conditions, expressions, join keys,
grouping columns and set functions (`exec/shared/written.rs`). Costs,
estimates, labels and the marks of parts run in parallel are left out.
Two groupings written alike are the same operators over the same tables,
and one statement reads them, so they give the same rows. Each place
such a grouping stands becomes a reader of one cell (`Plan::Shared`).
The reader that opens first runs the grouping and keeps its rows, in
memory within its work area and in a run of the spill area past it
(D38). Each reader reads them from there. The plans made of the
subqueries go to the runner, which runs them and plans nothing again.

Only a plan that gives the same rows each time it runs is written. That
is one of scans of whole tables in no order, filters, projections, hash
joins and groupings by hash of COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX and MIN, with
expressions of columns and constants by deterministic functions that
raise no warning, and no subquery, outer reference, parameter, sequence
or routine. The same grouping under another filter, or reading other
columns, is written otherwise and is another grouping.

Nothing runs that did not run before, and nothing runs sooner. A reader
runs the grouping as it is opened, where its own plan ran it, and a
place never opened runs nothing, so the errors and warnings are those of
the plans run apart (D15). A grouping that raises an error keeps no
rows, and each reader that runs it raises the error. The executor makes
the readers of copies of the plans it runs. The planner makes none, so
no kept plan, no plan shown and no part run in parallel holds one, and
no cell outlives its execution.

A reader is told no runtime filter (D1062, D1063), as each reader is
given every row. A grouping read once is not made a reader and takes
its filters as before. A join computed alike in two places under
different groupings is still run in each.

#### D1130. A LIKE of a prefix and `%` is estimated by the sampled strings with the prefix when the sample holds enough of them

A LIKE whose pattern is a prefix and `%` was estimated by the share of
the range of strings beginning with the prefix, by the column's common
values and histogram (D381), and at least an equality's. A histogram's
bucket of strings places a value within it by the characters where its
bounds part. A prefix of a word, whose strings fill part of a bucket
whose bounds part at its first characters, was placed in almost no
share of it. So `P_NAME LIKE 'forest%'`, a ninety-second of a table of
words drawn from a list, was estimated at one row. The plan made with
that estimate read the rows it joins by an index, one probe for each of
thousands of rows, where a hash join had read them in a part of the
time.

The share is now that of the table's sample of rows whose string begins
with the prefix, as the sample holds at least `SAMPLE_HITS` of them or
is the whole table (`physical/estimate/like.rs`). That is the share a
conjunction the sample can tell is given (D382). Of fewer, the range is
estimated as before. A pattern with more than `%` after its prefix takes
this share times what the sample says the rest keeps of it, as before.

#### D1131. A chunk's varying texts are judged UTF-8 once for the range read, and IN a list of strings looks for a string by halving them

A chunk of the column store holds its strings as octets, and a batch
holds them as text (D361). Of a chunk of varying fields, each field read
was judged UTF-8 by itself before it was copied into the batch's text.
The octets from the start of the first field read to the end of the last
are now judged once, and each field is a slice of them
(`engine/columns/encoded.rs`). Strings that are each UTF-8 are UTF-8
together, and a field that begins or ends within a character gives no
text as before, so the batch is the one each judgment gave.

D1252 took this to the run. The octets of every chunk a run reads are
judged once together (`engine/columns/texts.rs`), and a run of varying
fields is copied there at once.

IN a list of strings judged of a vector's text (D1126) compared a
string of a short list with each constant, each made unpadded again for
each row, and hashed it for a longer one. The constants are now unpadded
once as the set is made, sorted and each kept once
(`logical/sets.rs`), and a string is looked for by halving them, which
compares it with as many as that takes. A string is found if it equals
one without trailing spaces [X3.135-1986 §5.11 GR5], as before.

#### D1132. A filter whose scalar subqueries raise nothing and warn of nothing runs in parallel, each bound once before the morsels

A filter holding a subquery stayed on the statement's thread, as a
worker runs no subquery, so the part below it was its scan alone and the
filter judged every row it gave by itself. A scalar subquery that reads
nothing of the filter's rows has one value for the statement [ISO/IEC
9075:1992 §7.11 GR1], and of those a filter's first row runs (D1127) it
is now judged whether running it is seen by anything but its value
(`optimizer/unnesting/quiet.rs`). It raises no error if it gives one
row at most and the typed judgment of D1060 finds nothing in its plan
that raises, of the declared types of the columns it reads. It raises
no warning if its plan holds no subquery, invocation or carried
warning, no parameter, no window and no join but a product, and each set function
takes no argument or a column that holds no null, so no null is
eliminated [ISO/IEC 9075:1992 §6.5 GR1b]: one declared so, or one a
filter below the set function compares or judges IS NOT NULL, which
keeps no row of a null there.

A filter whose every subquery is such a one, and that is calm with them
made constants, is a step of the part below it (`physical/parallel.rs`).
As the part's pipeline is made, on the statement's thread before any
morsel starts, each is run and made its constant
(`exec/parallel/pipeline.rs`), and the workers judge the filter of each
morsel. A filter that judges no row ran no subquery before, and runs
one now, which nothing sees. The rows are those the filter kept, and a
subquery the judgment cannot clear leaves its filter as it was, so the
errors and warnings are the serial run's (D15).

SUBSTRING of a column of a character string type, of a constant start
and of no length or a constant one not negative, is now judged to raise
nothing (`functions/strings.rs`), as only a substring of negative length
raises [ISO/IEC 9075:1992 §6.7 GR1d]. A comparison with a quiet
subquery, which reads no parameter, is not made a semi join (D773). Run
once and compared as a constant it costs no join, and the filter
holding it runs in the part below it. One compared with a column an
index of its table holds, or one that reads a parameter, as a
transaction's bound of keys does, is joined as before, so the index may
be probed from its row (`optimizer/unnesting/scalar.rs`).

The left of a semi join that builds its left is now marked as a hash
join's built operand is. It is held by batch whatever its store, so a
table kept by column is read in parallel there too.

#### D1133. A count over another grouping's groups crosses its partitions, each partition's counts merged by the statement's thread

A grouping over another runs as one part when it groups by some of the
first's grouping columns (D1113). A grouping that groups by a set
function's result of the first, or by an expression a projection
between the two computes, as a query groups customers by their count
of orders, stayed above the part. Each of the first's groups came to
the statement's thread as a row, went through the projections and was
grouped again there, a row at a time.

Such a grouping whose set functions are COUNT alone now runs in the
part too (`physical::crosses`). Its partitions are the first's, by the
whole key. The thread that finishes a partition takes its groups of the
first, in the order of their first rows, through the projections and
groups them again, and writes each group's states
(`exec/parallel/grouped/regrouped.rs`). The statement's thread merges
the states of each group of the partitions and numbers it by the least
of their numbers, the first row of the group of all, so the groups come
in the order the serial grouping gives them.

Its HAVING condition is judged after the merge. A count is the same
whatever order its rows are counted in. Another set function's state,
as a sum of approximate numbers or an extreme of values a collation
holds equal, could differ by the order its partitions are merged in, so
a grouping of one stays above the part. A projection that fails in a
partition gives the part way to the serial plan, which meets the rows
in their order and raises what it raises (D15).

#### D1134. A partition looks up every morsel's groups, as its morsels come to it out of their keys' order

A grouping run in parallel merges each partition's groups of the
morsels, each group looked up in the partition's table before it is
made. A grouping by one integer column of a table kept in the order of
that column, as a query groups lines by their order, has morsels of
keys apart from one another, so a morsel's lookups mostly miss. A
partition's table was made to keep the least and greatest of its keys,
and a morsel's groups lying wholly below or above them were made with
no lookup.

That cannot work. A partition merges its morsels in the order they
are handed over, which is the order the threads finish them, not the
order of their keys. So a morsel mostly lands in a gap between the
morsels merged before it, inside their least and greatest keys though
apart from every key there, and one pair of keys cannot see the gaps.
It was taken out. Every morsel's groups are looked up, as before.

#### D1135. A HAVING condition comparing a grouping's one set function with a constant is judged of that value alone

A HAVING condition judged by a grouping's part (D1073) finished every
group's row, its keys and each set function's value, and judged the
condition of it. A condition that compares the grouping's one set
function with a constant, as `HAVING SUM(L_QUANTITY) > 300`, needs only
that value. Such a condition is now judged of the value as it is
finished, by the comparison the condition makes, and the row is made
only of a group kept (`GroupTable::finished_above`). Every group's
value is still finished, so a set function that raises as it finishes
raises as it did.

#### D1136. A file the process has no descriptor left for closes one of the database's, and FILES.MAX_OPEN is 512

A load of a wide table failed past a few million rows with "too many
open files". Its log kept a segment for each 64 MiB written since the
last checkpoint, each open through the file manager (D56), and the
manager let 1024 be open, which is all a process gets by default. The
manager stayed under its limit while the process ran out, and the spill
file an execution then needed could not be opened.

Two changes keep a database within what the system allows. The default
of FILES.MAX_OPEN is 512, half the usual limit, leaving the other half
for connections and the server's own files. And an open the system
refuses for want of a descriptor (EMFILE or ENFILE on Unix,
ERROR_TOO_MANY_OPEN_FILES on Windows) is SQLCODE -918 from
`OsFileSystem`, which the manager answers as it answers its own limit.
It closes a file of the database's not in use and tries again, or waits
for one to be done (`files/spent.rs`). Only when the database holds no
other descriptor is the error returned. A limit lower than FILES.MAX_OPEN
then slows the work, through files closed and opened again, but no
statement fails for it. The server does not raise its own limit. The
engine has to live within whatever the operator gives it.

#### D1137. CHECKPOINT.AFTER_BYTES counts the bytes written to the log too

A checkpoint came due after CHECKPOINT.AFTER_CHANGES row changes, or
CHECKPOINT.AFTER_BYTES written to the tables file's side file. A load
into a large pool writes almost nothing to the side file, and wide rows
make each change many bytes, so the log grew by tens of gigabytes, its
segments all kept, before the changes came due. Recovery after a crash
then replayed all of it.

The log's bytes now count as well (`Transactions::bytes_since_checkpoint`),
and a checkpoint is due once either the side file or the log has grown by
CHECKPOINT.AFTER_BYTES since the last. The log's position is noted as a
checkpoint captures what it holds, as the row changes are, so a checkpoint
that fails counts them still. The log tells its bytes from that position
on (D1231). The log a checkpoint lets go of, and the recovery after it,
are then bounded by the setting whatever the shape of the rows.

#### D1138. The rows an execution of a load is given are held, never spilled

An execution of a prepared INSERT given many rows, as the client's
import sends them, held them in a list that spills past 4 MiB (D298). A
batch of 65,536 rows of a wide table is tens of megabytes, so each
execution made a spill area, wrote the batch to it and read it straight
back. A load made thousands of spill files that way, one descriptor
each while it lasted.

Those rows are already in memory, in the request that gave them, so the
list that holds them as candidates is never more than as many again. It
is held whole (`db/write/given.rs`). No spill area is made for it, and
the batch size a client chooses bounds what it holds. Rows a statement
reads itself, as an INSERT from a query, are held as before.

#### D1139. A checkpoint's captures go to its sealed batch's side file, not memory

A checkpoint marks each dirty page of the pool owed and captures it
after writers go on (D590). Each capture was put into the sealed batch
in memory, held until the batch was committed. During a load nearly
every frame of the pool is dirty, so one checkpoint held a copy of most
of the pool beside the pool, outside MEMORY.BUDGET_BYTES. With a pool of
48 GiB that copy took tens of gigabytes, and the server was killed for
memory.

A capture is now appended as a block to the sealed batch's side file
(`Side::append_captured`, `disk/shadow/side.rs`), where the granules of
its other blocks already are. It is newer than every block before it,
as a capture is, and the commit copies it into the file as it copies
the others. A crash before the commit block finds a side file with no
commit, which recovery throws away, as before. A capture the side file
refuses, as one whose sync failed, is held in memory as before, so the
failure is met by the commit, which a later checkpoint takes again,
rather than stopping checkpoints until the database is reopened, as a
capture lost does (D590). The checkpoint's memory
is then the copies writers and frees make while it walks, and the walk
writes each capture to disk as it goes.

#### D1140. A value out of line of an entry a freeze takes out is freed only once no read may still fetch it

A freeze takes the tree's entries of the rows it froze out once no
reader holds a directory from before their group (D31), and it freed
each entry's values kept out of line at once. A read does not fetch
such a value under the leaf's latch (D869). It copies the entry out and
fetches the value after. A scan that took the new directory before the
group's shadow bits were settled reads the tree over the group's range
whole (D1100), and a read by row id reads the tree before any group,
holding no directory at all. Either could copy an entry, the freeze
then take it out and free its value's page, and the read fetch a page
freed, or one a later row had taken. A scan by batch after a large load
then failed with a page not allocated.

The pages of the values of the entries taken out are now held, with the
directory that stood as they were taken out, and freed once no reader
holds it (`free_unread`, `rows/frozen/freeze.rs`), in the order they
were held. The directory is then put again as another of the same
groups (`Directory::again`), so a read that begins after, which cannot
find the entries, holds up no free. A scan holds its directory as it is
made. A read by row id, and the newest version UNIQUE reads, take the
directory first and hold it until the values are fetched
(`Frozen::pinned`). A table that has never frozen rows takes nothing,
so its reads still share no word.

#### D1141. A log record as long as the buffer reaches its segment after the bytes the buffer holds

A segment's file is written through a buffer (D921), and a write as long
as the buffer went to the file at once, leaving what the buffer held.
That suits the zeros written ahead (D796), but a record so long went to
the file past bytes the buffer still held. Under LOG.DURABILITY NONE
nothing syncs the buffer, so a new segment's header could stay held while
megabytes of long records reached the file behind it. A server killed for
memory in a load into a column store left such a segment, its header
zeros, and the database could not be opened again.

A write as long as the buffer now has what is held written first, unless
it is all zeros, which may still go to the file alone
(`log/file/buffered.rs`). The file then never holds a record past bytes
held, so a failure of the process loses only the log's tail, which
recovery cuts as it cuts a torn end.

#### D1142. Loads into a column store table at once each write their own groups, no lock taken alone

A load into groups (D533) took the table's lock alone, and the table
noted one transaction as its loader. A second load at once waited for
the lock, or, if it began while the first was noted, wrote its rows
through the tree. The first load's next batch then found rows past the
last group and went to the tree as well. A client importing with six
streams so wrote nearly every row through the tree, and the freeze then
had them all to do.

The table now notes every transaction loading it, and each writes its
own groups (`frozen/stamped.rs`). A group takes its row ids as one run
(`RowTable::next_ids`), so the groups of loads at once never share a
range. A load that holds back no index takes no lock beyond its
insert's (`db/write/bulk/load.rs`). A load that holds back an index still
takes the lock alone, since others' readers would miss its entries
(D532). Each group is stamped with its transaction, undone with it and
recovered as before. A row another transaction writes through the tree
meanwhile lies between groups and is read as any row of the tree. The
freeze takes rows past the last group only, so it stays in the tree.
#### D1143. A clean close keeps the groups of every load committed, settled or not

A group a load writes (D533) is stamped with its transaction, and keeps
that stamp after the commit until the maintenance thread finds the
commit before every snapshot. A directory stored meanwhile names the
transaction as open, and opened again the table holds such a group
apart for recovery to keep or drop. A database closed cleanly is
reopened with no recovery, so nothing kept those groups, and a load's
rows since its groups last settled were lost. A load whose groups had
settled lost only its last batch, the group written after the last
commit the maintenance thread saw.

Reopened after a clean close to serve, each table now keeps every group
held apart as committed (`db/recovery.rs`, `settle_closed_loads`). A
clean close is taken with no transaction open, and a load rolled back
takes its groups out of the directory, so each group stored is of a load
that committed. A crash still leaves recovery to judge each group by
the transactions it redoes, as before. A replica opened to follow keeps
its groups apart, its loads being the primary's.

#### D1144. A chunk of a column is sized once, in the plan found as its values were fitted

A group's column was cut into chunks one at a time (D31). Each chunk's
values were added to a sizer until the next passed the page, the sizer
asked after every value which encoding took fewest bytes. A new sizer
then took the same values again to choose that encoding for the chunk.
The width the column's values share was found again over the whole
column for each chunk, and each value was copied twice before it was
written. A load of wide rows spent most of its time there.

The plan found as the last value that fits was added is the plan a
sizer of those values chooses, so it is kept and the chunk is written
in it (`Fields::chunks`). The width is found once, as the fields are
made. The sizer weighs each encoding as it finds it, keeping the first
of the fewest bytes as before, with no list made, and keeps its
dictionary's entries by XXH3. The fields are made of the values as they
are, not of copies. Each chunk is the same, byte for byte.

#### D1145. A load sorts its group's rows by reference, none copied

A load written straight to groups (D533) sorts each group's rows by
COLUMNSTORE.ORDER before it writes them. It sorted copies of them, every
value of every row copied, since the rows given are still logged and
indexed after. Writing a group reads each row's values only, so the
group is now written of the rows where they are, sorted by reference
(`frozen/stamped.rs`); the freeze, which owns the rows it freezes,
sorts them as before. The group written is the same.

#### D1146. A load writes its groups to segments of its own, never through the buffer pool

A load straight to groups (D533) wrote each group's pages through the
buffer pool as dirty frames of the data file, and each checkpoint wrote
them again by way of its shadow file. Several loads at once held most
of the pool as dirty frames, the server's memory grew with them, and
every byte was written three times. A load into a table of the column
store of no index now writes each group it makes as an extent of a
segment (`rows/frozen/extents.rs`). A segment is a block file of the
database's `groups` directory, `g<table>-<n>`, and each loading stream
takes one no other stream appends to, so its groups follow one another.
The group is framed in memory as it is written, each page a block
numbered by its offset within the extent, after a head block that names
its rows, its length and a digest of the rest (`group/sink.rs`). The
directory names a group by its segment, its offset and its length.
The pool reads an extent's blocks as it reads any block file's, clean,
and a scan reads ahead of it a megabyte at a time.

A segment takes no more extents past 1 GiB. Below, it should hold some
fifty of the largest groups, some 20 MB each; above, a segment is given
back only whole, once no group stored names it, so its size bounds the
space a table's dropped groups can hold.

The group is logged as one record, its extent the record's last field
(GROUP_LOADED), in place of a record of its rows. So its bytes are
written twice, to its segment and to the log. The log must carry them,
since a standby and a recovery to a point in time from the archive have
only the log to make the group from. The record is written from the
extent's own buffer, which went to the segment, its head apart, so the
group is copied for neither (`Txn::log_parts`). Recovery redoes a
committed load's group by appending its extent to a segment of the
table again, wherever it lands, as its pages are numbered within it; a
table of no segments, of a database in memory following one on disk,
writes the group again on pages. A group too large for one block of
the log, past half its longest, goes to pages and is logged as rows.

A checkpoint syncs each segment appended to since the last before its
batch is committed, then removes each segment no stored directory
names, no stream holds and no reader still reads. Opened, a table cuts
each segment it names to the end of the last group named in it, so a
crash's torn extent and the groups no checkpoint named are gone, and
removes its other segments; recovery appends the committed ones again
from the log. A dropped table's segments go once a checkpoint after the
drop is committed. An export and a backup carry the segments as files
of the database.

A table with an index keeps its groups on pages and logs its rows, so
recovery takes back its index entries from the rows' images as before.
The row store and a write of a single row are untouched. The store's
format is new and its versions stay 1, so data loaded before must be
loaded again.

#### D1147. A load into a table that qualifies for extents goes to groups unless told otherwise

COLUMNSTORE.LOAD was TREE unless set, so a load into the column store
went through the table's tree and was written again as it froze, and
then by the checkpoints, unless the table asked for GROUPS. It is now
DEFAULT unless set. A load (D532) under DEFAULT goes straight to groups
(D533), as extents of segments (D1146), if its table qualifies for
them: no index, no constraint but NOT NULL (and, since D1148, CHECKs
that read no other table), and no column of a large object; a table a trigger, a foreign key or an assertion reads loads
none at all, as before. Any other table, and every write that is no
load, a single row's INSERT or a few rows', goes to the tree. TREE and
GROUPS set stay what they were, either way. Where a load's rows land
changes no result of any statement, only how often they are written.

#### D1148. A load given by column is parsed into each column's type and written as a group with no row of values

A bulk copy sent each row as values of text, which the server cast one
cell at a time, gathered as rows, and then took apart again by column
to write the group. Most of a load's time went to making, casting,
copying and freeing values that the group never keeps. A copy may now
send its rows by column as text (the `columns` capability). The server
parses each column straight into its type, writing each value as its
type writes it in a record, end to end, and the group is written from
those columns, its chunks from their records as they are, its zones,
filters and sketches read from them, and its rows sorted by position.
No row of values is made.

The rows go so only where nothing they need is given a row alone. That
is an INSERT into a base table, through no view WITH CHECK OPTION, of no
identity, generated or self-referencing column; rows checked as they go
in, so no trigger, deferred constraint or assertion reads the table; a
table that qualifies for extents (D1147), or since D1235 one of keys and
indexes, whose load writes groups; and columns of numbers, character strings, datetimes and truth values. A
column the copy does not name takes its default, the same for each
row. A NOT NULL constraint is checked by its column's nulls, and a
CHECK by the columns it reads alone. A CHECK that reads no other table
no longer keeps a table from qualifying for extents, since it is
checked as the rows go in either way.

A cell is parsed straight to its record only where the result is sure
to be the record of the value the cast of its text gives; any other
cell (one with spaces, an exponent, more digits than the scale or a
form not plainly its type's) is cast as a value given is. A cast that
warns, a cell that is no value of its type, or a row that breaks a
constraint fails the execution, and the copy then inserts those rows
as rows, one at a time, which names the row and the rule as before.
Where a load's rows go by column changes no result of any statement.

With `columns`, granted with `copy`, CopyColumns sends a batch of a
copy's rows by column as text. It holds the count of rows, then of each
column a bit for each row set where its cell is null, where each cell's
text ends, and the cells' UTF-8 end to end. A cell is a field's text as
the file holds it, its quotes taken off, so it is what CopyData would
carry as a character string, and a null what it would carry as null. A
frame is checked whole before anything takes it, with a byte of null
bits for each eight rows and no bit past the last, an end for each row,
ends that never fall, a null's end where the cell before it ends, the
last end the text's length, and a column for a frame of rows, so a
false count cannot make the server hold more than it was sent.

The client library's import goes by column where `columns` is granted,
no bad row is to be skipped, no column is a large object's or a binary
string's, and its source splits its records itself. Each field is
appended to its column's buffers as the record is split, and the
buffers are kept from batch to batch. A record wrong in any way is
split again by the row path's splitter, so its failure reads the same.
Binary string columns stay on the row path, which reads their hexits
into octets before it sends them (D976).

`--jobs N` imports one file over N connections at once. The file is
split into N contiguous ranges of bytes of about equal size, each
beginning just after a line break, the first after the header, and each
job imports its range on a connection of its own. Contiguous ranges
keep each job's records a run of the file's, so its groups hold
neighbouring rows, as rows striped across jobs would not. Splitting
reads only the header and, from each range's share of the bytes, up to
the next line break, so the jobs begin at once: a pass over the file
before them, even on a thread a range, made the built-in import slower
than as many split streams. Of CSV, each range's quotes are counted
side by side, on a thread a range, beside the jobs; a range begins
within a quoted field just when the quotes before it are odd in number
[RFC 4180 §2 rules 5-7]. A batch commits as its last record is read, so
each job reads that record of its first batch, or the end of a batch of
all, only once the count is told: a range found to begin within a
quoted field is found before any row is committed, and the import is
refused saying to use one job, its jobs' failures not told. The lines
and records before a range are counted only when a job tells a record,
so it is told by its place in the whole file. Standard input and any
file that is not a regular one cannot be read in ranges, and are
refused. The rows said are every job's, and a job that fails stops the
others at their next record. Each job's connection is proved by the
password typed for the first, not asked for again. Ctrl-C cancels each
job's statement and stops each at its next record, and the import is
told once.

#### D1149. A load's group held in memory is charged to the budget until it is logged

A group a load writes to a segment (D1146) is framed whole in memory,
some 20 MB of a wide table's 65,536 rows, and held until its record is
in the log. Its bytes are charged to the budget of the work areas from
when it is framed until its record is written, and the load fails with
SQLCODE -918 if the budget cannot hold them, as a work area's grant
does (D38). So the memory of loads at once is bounded by one group in
flight a stream, and is seen by the budget. The rows of the batch each
group is made of are held as the statement's held rows, which spill
within their own grant as before.

#### D1150. A morsel's rows are made as they are read and charged to the part's grant as they are gathered

A morsel's rows were taken through its pipeline's steps and gathered
whole before the first was read, by every thread and for every morsel
running ahead of the reader, three times the degree, and none of it was
charged to the part's work grant (D38, D298). A join whose keys each
match thousands of rows makes millions of rows of one morsel of 16,384,
so a plan that joined two tables on a key of few values, as a plan made
before any statistics may, grew the server past its memory budget until
the kernel killed it. A morsel read row by row is now made a row at a
time as it is asked for (`exec/parallel/rows.rs`). A probe's matches of
a row are held as their built rows' numbers, each joined as it is read.

What a thread gathers of a morsel is charged to the grant a batch's
worth at a time, and stays charged until the reader has taken it, so the
morsels running ahead are held within the grant too
(`exec/parallel/charged.rs`). A morsel that outgrows the grant is given
up and its charge given back. A stream's reader then reads the rest of
that morsel's read as its thread left it, after the rows the thread
gathered, a row or a batch at a time, holding none, while the threads go
on with those after it. It never reads the morsel again, since a split's
part is read once.

An index scan's entries are taken by the morsel that reads them. A sort
writes the rows its thread gathered and then the rest of that read to
its runs, or the morsel's run if it outgrew the grant only once sorted;
a window's or a set operation's partitions put its rows in their lists,
which spill; a join's build gives way to the serial join, which
partitions. A grouping's morsel is fed its rows as they are made and
holds its groups alone. Every answer, and its order, is the one the plan
gives alone.

#### D1151. A probe of a table built for a pipeline's morsels makes its pairs a batch at a time

A probe by batch of a table a pipeline's morsels share (D368) gave every
pair of a left batch at once, its rows times their keys' rows, a list
of batches held before the first was read. It now makes them as they
are asked for (`exec/batch/joined/shared/probing.rs`), a batch of at
most `BATCH_ROWS` pairs at a time, and keeps where it stopped, the left
row and how many of its key's built rows it looked at, a run of a key's
rows taken up again in one step. The pairs come in the order they did,
those before an error first, then the error. A LEFT join's probe (D1076)
is made so too, a row no built row matches paired with nulls, and a key
of one column of integers is paired in its units (D1083), of a direct
table taken up at its place among its key's rows.

#### D1153. A stream's morsels ahead of its reader hold no more rows than they scan

The morsels a stream's threads gathered and its reader had not taken
were charged to the part's work grant (D1150), so a result read at a
client's pace held up to MEMORY.WORK_BYTES of rows it had not sent, 32
GiB where the grant is set so, and each statement so read took as much
of the budget. A grant is for what must hold its input, a build, a sort
or a grouping, and a stream holds its rows only to keep its threads
busy while its reader takes them.

The rows a stream's morsels hold ahead of its reader are now counted
too, shared by its threads (`exec/parallel/charged.rs`): at most the
rows the morsels a run takes past the one its reader waits for scan,
two a thread (D290), each of EXECUTOR.MORSEL_ROWS. A morsel that gives
no more rows than it scans is gathered whole, as before. One whose
joins multiply its rows past what is left is given up and read by the
reader as it is given, as a morsel past the grant is (D1150), so a
result of billions of rows holds a few morsels' rows whatever the
grant. A thread never waits for the reader. A worker so held would hold
its thread from every other statement while a client is slow.

#### D1154. A hash join of streams probed by batch stops at each batch of pairs it makes

A hash join of streams run by batch (D31) probed its right operand with
every row of a left batch before it gave a pair, its pairs made into
batches held until read. A left batch of 2,048 rows whose keys each
match thousands of right rows so held millions of pairs at once, and
one whose keys each match a million held billions, past any grant.

The probe now stops at the left row after which a batch of pairs is
made, and takes the batch up there again once that batch is read
(`exec/batch/joined/probe.rs`); its keys are hashed once, as its first
row is probed. A batch so holds the pairs of one left row at most past
the batch made, and those of a row are no more than the right rows,
held within the work area. A FULL or RIGHT join's probe, and a LEFT
join's the simple probe does not take, stop so too
(`exec/batch/joined/outer.rs`). The pairs come in the order they did,
those before an error first, then the error, as before. A probe of a
table its morsels share stops so already (D1151).

#### D1155. Whether a part run in parallel will pass its grant is told by the morsels its reader has taken

A join's build, a sort, a grouping and a held join operand each look,
as a morsel is taken, at whether the morsels left would pass the work
grant if each held as much as those so far, so a part that will give way
does so after its first morsels. What the part holds was divided by the
morsels taken, which was right while only the reader charged them. Since
D1150 a build's and a sort's threads charge a morsel as they gather it,
so the part holds the morsels gathered ahead of the reader too, up to two
a thread, and a first morsel taken while sixteen more were gathered was
counted as seventeen. A part that fit its grant then gave way or not by
how fast each thread was, and the plan ran again alone. Each caller now
gives the bytes of the morsels taken (`Limit::on_course`), and what the
part held before its morsels is read before a thread starts on one.

#### D1157. A column no statistics count is of no more values than a key NOT NULL its class equates, declared alone

A column whose table has no statistics is taken as a key, of its rows'
distinct values (D302). A class of equalities keeps one row in as many
as each of its columns but the least distinct has values, so a column
of 1.5 million rows equated with a key of 25 was counted as 1.5 million
values. Customers and suppliers of one nation, joined through the
nations, were estimated at the suppliers' rows where each customer
meets 4,000 of them, and a plan made before the first statistics joined
them first, 6 billion rows. D1152 bounded such a column by the least
counted or keyed column of its class. A count of statistics then moved
the bound, a sketch a little under a key's rows lowered the other
column to it, and a join order followed which tables the background job
had reached. It was taken back.

Each column of a class whose distinct values neither statistics count
nor a key of its relation proves is now counted of no more values than
the least key the class equates that is declared alone on a column NOT
NULL, by a PRIMARY KEY, a UNIQUE constraint or a unique index
(`physical/cardinality/composite.rs`), for the estimates and the
enumeration alike. Such a key's values are its table's rows, whatever
filters read it, known of the catalog and the engine's count before any
statistics. So the bound is the same whichever tables statistics have
counted. The bound rests on containment, the assumption the module
already makes of a guess joined with a key. The columns a class equates
are taken to hold values of one domain, the key's. A referential constraint makes
it exact. A UNIQUE of a column that may be null bounds nothing, nor does
a statistics count, and a class of no such key is left as it was.

#### D1158. A plan asking for a table's first statistics while the maintenance thread gathers them waits for that pass

D1092 has the plan that first asks for the statistics of a table opened
gather them, and plans asking meanwhile wait on the lock that pass
holds. The maintenance thread's pass of the same table did not take
that lock. A plan asking while it ran saw the pass under way, noted its
own as tried and was made without statistics, on the fixed
selectivities, so the first plans after a start could differ by
whether the maintenance thread happened to be gathering.

A pass of a table opened, by the maintenance thread too, now holds the
lock the asking plan's holds, taken before the flag that says a pass
runs. A plan asking for the first statistics during it waits for the
pass and is given what it gathered. Plans that find statistics never
take the lock, so later passes do not hold them up
(`engine/rows/stats.rs`).

#### D1159. A plan costs its spills at the grant of a statement running alone

The planner costs what an operator spills past its grant (D651), and took
the grant as the executor would give it at that moment (D683). That is
half of what the grants' share has free, after the grants other
statements hold and after the standing reservations. Two things moved it
that have nothing to do with the statement. Every grant held beside it
halved it, so a grouping of sixty thousand rows was hashed over a scan
when planned alone and streamed over its key's index in order when
planned beside two others. The kept undo is a standing reservation that
grows and shrinks with the writes (D746), so the same statement on an
idle database was costed at a grant that depended on what had run
before. One query was planned two ways, and a benchmark run and its
rerun could time different plans.

The planner now costs at the grant a statement running alone would be
given. No grant is taken as held, and each standing reservation is taken
at the bound it may grow to, a buffer pool at its bytes and the kept
undo at its share of the budget (`Reservation::stand_up_to`,
`MemoryBudget::planned`). The plan then depends on the settings alone,
and EXPLAIN shows the plan the statement runs. The executor still takes
what is free when an operator starts (`spill/grant.rs`), and spills or
gives way as it must. So beside other statements an operator may spill
more than it was costed for. That was chosen over a plan that changes
with its neighbours.

#### D1160. A prepared cursor's values are cast to their types as it opens, whether its plan is kept or made with them

A value given for a `?` is cast to the parameter's type [ISO/IEC
9075:1992 §17.9 GR5f]. A plan made with the values casts each as it is
made, so a value that does not cast raised at OPEN. A plan kept reads
its values where they are and casts one as it reads it (D610). That is
at OPEN for a plan that can raise, which is read whole then (D931), and
at the first FETCH for another. So the moment a cursor raised followed
whether its plan was kept yet, and a plan learned before its table had
statistics is learned again once they are known (D839), which the
maintenance thread decides as it runs. The same cursor raised at OPEN
in one run and at FETCH in another.

Each value is now cast as the cursor opens (`db/prepared.rs`), and the
first that does not cast raises CAST's error there, before any plan is
looked for. A value already of its type is not cast again. The plans
still cast each value as they read it, which then raises nothing.

#### D1161. Rows whose grouping columns are all codes of dictionaries are grouped by their codes

The column store gives a character string column's rows as codes of a
dictionary its batches share (`storage::Coded`). A grouping of a morsel
read each row's text of its code to hash it, read it again for each
group it was compared with, and compared the texts. A grouping by two
such columns of a few values each spent most of its time there.

A morsel's rows whose grouping columns are all coded are now grouped by
their codes (`exec/batch/groups/coded.rs`). Each row's codes, a null's a
place after its dictionary's codes, are its place in a memo of the
groups its codes have gone to. A row whose place has a group goes to it,
no key hashed, read or compared. The first row of a place is hashed and
its group found or made by its key as before. So two codes whose texts
are equal as keys, a text and the same with trailing spaces, find one
group, and a group's text is copied once, as it is made. The memo holds
while the batches come of the same dictionaries and is made anew when
one differs.

A grouping by a column that is not coded, as a mix of a coded column
and one of integers, is grouped as before, and so is one whose places
pass 65,536. That memo is 256 KiB of group numbers, an eighth of the
2 MiB a performance core of the benchmark machine caches next to it, and the
groupings it is for, by a column or two of few values, take a small
part of it.

A grouping on one thread groups so too (`exec/batch/groups.rs`). Its
memo holds only groups it holds, as a row of a group written past the
work area is found by its key, and it forgets them as the work area is
split and the groups held after the split are moved.

#### D1162. A late column of rows kept in order is decoded of their places, none searched for

A late column (D361) resolved of the rows a filter kept listed their
places, sorted them if they were not in order, took out those given
twice, and then searched the places decoded for each row's, to gather
the values to the rows. Of a column no join gathered, the rows a filter
keeps are ascending, each once, and so are their places, so the search
found the `k`th row's value at the `k`th place every time. Of a scan of
a large table filtered by a comparison of two of its columns, that
search was the most of the samples outside the join.

Such a column is now resolved of its rows' places as they come, and the
`k`th row kept takes the `k`th value decoded (`storage/batch/late.rs`).
Rows given out of order or more than once, and a column a join
gathered, are resolved as before.

#### D1163. A zone settled visible to every reader is saved so, and opens settled

A row store table's zones are saved at each checkpoint with its pages
(D31), but whether a zone's rows were visible to every reader (D34) was
kept in memory alone. A table opened had every zone unsettled, and the
maintenance thread read each zone's rows again to settle it, at every
start. Of a large table that is a pass over all its rows, which the
read-ahead thread fed from disk while queries ran, pushing their pages
out of the cache.

A zone settled visible is now saved with a flag of its own
(`zones/saved.rs`), and the table opened has it settled visible. Its
rows were committed at or before the horizon when it was settled, none
a deletion, no version left to collect, and every reader after the
table opens sees what was committed before it closed. A write after
the save clears the flag before its index entries are written and
marks the zone's segment to be saved again, and a row recovery writes
does so too. A zone saved unsettled, or not visible, opens unsettled
as before, and is summed up or settled once a zone of its table is
asked for (D1212). So a table reaches its steady state once, after the
first checkpoint that follows its zones' settling, and keeps it from
start to start.

#### D1164. A start that changes nothing records no catalog image

Each start recorded two catalog images: one, not clean, as the
database opened, so a crash from then on was recovered, and one, clean,
as it closed, after logging a checkpoint record. With nothing changed
the catalog file grew by two images a start until it compacted.

A database reopened clean now records nothing as it opens. It makes the
file `opened` in its directory, durably, before anything else runs, and
its clean close takes it out once its image is durable
(`db/files/running.rs`). Opened while the file is there, its last image
is taken as not clean, and it is recovered from it as from the image
the open recorded before. The log alone cannot tell a crash. A
transaction open at the crash may have logged nothing yet. A database
recovered, or made, records its image again, not clean, as before.

A close that finds the log where the last clean image left it logs no
checkpoint record, and a checkpoint or close whose image is the one
recorded last, but for a higher id given, records none
(`db/checkpoint.rs`, `db/image.rs`). The ids given since are held by
nothing kept, as no record was logged. An image now lists its tables
and indexes by name, not in the order a map held them, so the same
database is the same bytes. A catalog in other formats than its
settings say is recorded again, so it moves on to them.

The settings a database is started with, as a server's configuration
gives them, are set again at each start, and each was logged, so the log
moved on and the close recorded an image. A setting set to the value it
already has is no longer logged (`db/settings.rs`).

The mark is a kind of file the database knows (`FileKind::Opened`,
`files/classes.rs`), so an export of a running database is not refused.
No copy carries it. An export, and the backup and the state transfer
taken from it, records its image not clean, so the database restored or
installed from it recovers as from any copy of one running
(`db/export.rs`). A database following that installs an export takes
out the mark of the state it replaces (`standby/import.rs`).

#### D1165. What each column takes, by the encoding of its chunks, is shown, and a tree's bytes are counted

TABLE_STATISTICS showed a table's bytes as its frozen groups' pages plus
its tree's rows times their mean width, so a table never analyzed, of
either store, showed none. Nothing showed what a column takes, or how
its chunks were encoded, so a table taking ten times the bytes it might
could not be told apart by column.

A tree's bytes are now its pages, counted (`BLinkTree::pages`). Its
nodes above the leaves are read, each level by its right links, and its
leaves counted as the level above names them, none read. The view
INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMN_STORAGE (`system/column_storage.rs`) has a row
of each column and each way its values are kept. Of a column store's
groups, it is the chunks of one encoding, with their count, rows, bytes
encoded and the bytes of the pages they take. Each chunk's kind and
length are read from the chunk itself (`rows/sizes.rs`), so groups any
build wrote show them, and no group's format changes; reading the view
reads every group's pages. Of a tree's rows, of either store, it is ROW.
TABLE_STATISTICS reads no chunk
(`TableStorage::sizes`, asked without the columns).

A tree keeps each row whole, so of its rows COLUMN_STORAGE shows their
number and no bytes; the tree's bytes are the table's. Every sum of
bytes is checked. A size past what a column of counts holds (`BIGINT`)
is the null value, never a bound reached and shown.

#### D1166. A count past 2^32 is itself, as an estimate and as a sum of bytes

A count of things as an `f64` (`stats::parts::count`) stopped at the most
a `u32` holds, and the ceiling of an estimate as a count
(`linearize::count`, `parallel::rows_of`) took that same bound as its
cap. A table's bytes past 4 GB were then 4 GB, so its mean width, its
bytes over its rows, was short by as many times, and the planner priced
its sorts and hashes (`cost/spill.rs`) as if far smaller. An estimate of
more than 2^32 rows or bytes was counted as the most a count holds, and
a table's bytes so estimated were shown as that bound plus its frozen
pages.

A count is now exact to 2^53 and the nearest `f64` past it, its high and
low words each converted. The ceiling of an estimate is the most a
count holds only of one reaching it.

#### D1167. Each operator carries only the columns read above it

A scan reads the columns its statement uses, and each operator carried
every column its input gave. A column a filter alone reads, or a join's
key, was copied into each row of every join above it, though nothing
read it again. A query that matches the names of its parts with LIKE
copied each name once for every line item joined to the part, at
every join, and each join's keys at every join above.

A plan is now walked from the top, once it is planned, with the columns
of each operator's rows read above it (`physical/blind/pruned.rs`). The
plan's own columns are all read. A scan reads those and the ones it is
ordered by. A filter reads its condition's columns, a sort its keys', a
grouping its groups' and its set functions', and a join its keys' and
its conditions'. A projection's column moved is read only if one above
reads it. Any other expression reads its columns whether or not it is
read, so no error it raises is lost. An operator with a subquery reads
every column of its input, as the subquery may read the row, and so
does one of any other kind; the inputs below it are walked as plans of
their own. A located scan, whose row's id follows its columns, reads
them all.

An operand of a join, built or probing, or the input of a sort, that
gives a column neither it nor one above reads is put under a projection
of its columns giving that column null, or, if it is a projection of
columns, gives the null itself. An operand whose columns holding a
value are not known here, as an index's scan, is left as it is, and the
join over it is the one put under the projection. The join or the sort
carries a vector of nulls in its place, which costs nothing to copy.

Such a vector is charged to a work area only once its values are made
(`storage/batch/held.rs`). It was charged a value a row, so an operand
mostly of nulls outgrew its work area and was joined row by row. A filter's
column or a join's key drops out after its operator. Every column keeps its
place, so nothing above is renumbered and the plan's columns and their
order are as they were. EXPLAIN shows each such projection, the columns
kept by name and the others as NULL. A projection of columns and the
null value moves its vectors and makes a vector of nulls
(`exec/batch/picks.rs`), so it costs a pipeline no more than a move.
The plan is pruned in place, so the walk of a deep plan holds little
on the stack. The texts gathered of a vector are found once and copied
into a buffer made at their length (`storage/batch/gathered.rs`), not
one grown as they are copied.

#### D1170. A morsel of set functions of no grouping feeds one set of states by vectors, no row hashed

Set functions of no grouping run in parallel were grouped as any
grouping by batch is (D293, D356). Each morsel's table hashed every row
on a key of no columns, found the one group by it, compared the key and
took the row for the group, and then fed the group's states. So each
row cost a hash, a probe, a compare and three pushes, and a sum of a
column on eight threads took longer than it did on one.

A morsel of no grouping columns now feeds one set of accumulators each
batch's vectors, as a set function of no grouping run alone is fed
(`exec/batch.rs`, `exec/batch/groups/morsel.rs`). The vector kernels
that sum a column, the null lane that counts it and the extremes taken
a vector at a time all apply. Once the morsel's batches are fed, each
state is written into the morsel's one group, which is made of its
first row, numbered as before. The morsels' groups are then merged in
morsel order as before, so a function keeping its first value keeps the
first row's, and a grant refused gives way as before.

A morsel of no rows makes no group, and the set functions of no rows
are one row as before. A set function whose accumulator writes no
state, as a sum or an average of approximate or DECFLOAT numbers, is
not run in parallel at all (D53, `physical/parallel.rs`). Its total
depends on the order its values are added in, so partial totals merged
would differ from the plan run alone. It keeps its serial plan, fed in
the input's order, and a morsel that met one anyway would be grouped as
before. DISTINCT and filtered set functions are not read by batch, so
they never come here.

#### D1171. A chunk of runs gives its values and its runs' ends of one reading, unpacked a block at a time

A column whose chunks keep their values as runs (D31), as a table's
sorted key does, was read for a batch twice over. Its values were
written out run by run, each run's value and end read alone, and then
each run's end was found again for the batch's runs (D1084). A value or
an end read alone takes its bytes into a window of its own, so each run
cost four such reads and the copies they make, and the vector of ends
grew an entry at a time.

A chunk of runs now gives both of one reading (`engine/columns/runs.rs`,
`engine/columns/scan.rs`). The runs from the one of the range's first
position to the one of its last are found by two searches. Their values
and ends are unpacked a block at a time, as a frame of reference is
(D352). Each run's value then fills its rows among the range, and its
end is pushed beside them, the vectors made room for once. A chunk of
one value gives one run, as before. A chunk of another encoding gives
its values as before, and the batch then holds no runs. The values,
their nulls and the runs' ends are those read apart before.
#### D1172. COUNT of a column known not null, or of a literal not null, counts rows and reads no value

COUNT of a column read every value of the column, decoded a chunk at a
time, though of a column declared NOT NULL its count is the count of the
rows. So a COUNT, not DISTINCT, of a column known to hold no null, or of
a literal that is not the null value, is rewritten to COUNT(*) (rule
`count_rows_of_values`, `optimizer/counted_rows.rs`), its filter clause,
type and label kept. A column is known so as `unnesting::never_null`
traces it, declared NOT NULL through the operators that pass it on as it
is and add no row of nulls, never through an outer join. Taking out the
nulls of such a value takes out none and raises no warning
[X3.135-1986 §5.8 GR1], so the count and the warnings are as they were
[GR4]. The rows are then counted with no value read. A bare count of a
table is answered by what its storage counts (D351, D1180), and of
batches each batch adds its rows. The column, read by nothing else,
drops out of the scan (D1167). A column that may hold a null is left, as
its nulls are not counted and their taking out warns.

#### D1173. A group's header is read for the columns its reader asks for, the others passed over undecoded

A group's header holds each column's chunks, each chunk with its count
of nulls, its least and greatest values, and the same of each of its
parts of 1,024 rows. A header was read whole: every column's bounds
decoded as values, its texts made strings, whatever the query read. A
table of a hundred columns and wide strings takes about 1.6 MB a group
so decoded, and of a table of a hundred million rows its headers take
more than the cache holds by default (D1090). Each scan then read and
decoded every header again, and a header read for one query was given up
before the next.

A header is now read for the columns its reader asks for (`group::read`,
`group/wanted.rs`). A scan asks for the columns it reads and those its
condition reads, a fetch by row id for the columns it fetches, and a
count for none. Every other column's chunks are passed over by their
lengths, none of their bounds decoded, and the group holds none of
them. A header held that lacks a column asked for is read again for it
and the columns it held, and held in its place, so the cache counts
what each holds as it is. A group asked for a column its header was not
read for fails with SQLCODE -910, never taking it for a column with no
chunks, which is one added after the group was written and reads as
nulls. The pages of a group, its summary and its rewriting read every
column, and ask for all. The format is unchanged, so no table is loaded
again.

#### D1175. A column's texts are judged UTF-8 by the database's kernels, on AVX2 32 bytes a step

A batch holds a column's strings as text (D361), and text read of the
store is judged UTF-8 before it is given as a `str`: the varying fields
read, once for their range (D1131), and the texts an FSST chunk decodes,
once for the run of them. The core forbids `unsafe` (R-SAFE-1), so it
cannot take octets for text without judging them, though only text was
written. The standard library judges a byte at a time past the first
octet above 127, so text of other scripts than Latin, as of the titles
and phrases of a web log, took the judging longer than the reading.

The judging is now a kernel (`Kernels::utf8`, D354), its portable body
`str::from_utf8`. `turborel-simd` judges 32 bytes a step on AVX2 and on
AVX-512's level, as Keiser and Lemire, "Validating UTF-8 In Less Than
One Instruction Per Byte" (2021), §5, judge them. Each byte's high
nibble and the byte before's high and low nibbles each look up the
errors their pair may make, the errors all three allow are the pair's,
and the bytes two and three back say where a continuation must be. A
step of no octet above 127 looks nothing up. A step whose last bytes
begin a character the next must end, and the text's end must end every
character (`simd/src/x86/utf8.rs`).

The text so judged is given as a `str` only where `str::from_utf8`
gives one. The contract tests (`turborel-test-support`, `kernels.rs`)
hold every set to it, of every pair of octets and every lead of three
and four with every second octet at each place on and across a lane's
and a step's edges, of text cut within its characters, and of octets of
no structure. A column's texts read by the varying fields, an FSST
chunk, a constant or a dictionary are judged by the set the table
opened with (D570). A dictionary's entries, made text as its chunk is
opened, are judged once from the first entry's start to the last's end,
each entry then a slice of them, as the varying fields are (D1131).

#### D1180. A bare COUNT(*) of a table that holds groups adds its groups' rows from its directory and reads only the tree

A table that froze rows or held groups was counted by its scan. A count
of all its rows then read every group's header and every chunk's run
of row positions, on every core, as a scan of no column does. D351's
zone counts do not apply to it. A freeze takes out the tree's entries
of rows it froze without a change of their zones, so a zone's rows are
not the table's.

Such a table now answers `TableStorage::count` from its directory
(`rows/frozen/counts.rs`). The directory is taken first, of the groups
the reader sees (D533's stamps), as a scan by batch takes it before it
reads the tree. Each group adds the rows its summary holds. The tree is
read over the group's shadow bits alone (D1100), the same ids the scan
reads there. Each entry the reader sees adds a row, and each of the
group's own rows such an entry stands for takes one away, found by the
group's row ids, which are read only then. Then the tree's entries
outside every group's range are read, each the reader sees adding one.
So a count is the scan's at every isolation level, of frozen rows
updated and deleted, of rows frozen while it counts and of rows not yet
frozen, and a group no entry shadows costs an addition. Under
SERIALIZABLE the read is noted as the whole table's, as D351's is.

The plan, EXPLAIN's line and the planner's choice not to split the
count are D351's, now of the column store too. Rejected: summing the
summaries' rows alone, which counts rows deleted or changed since the
freeze; a count kept per group of its rows still live, which every
delete of a frozen row would have to write and which is no snapshot's.

#### D1181. MIN and MAX of a table that holds groups take each group no entry shadows from its summary

`SELECT MIN(EventDate), MAX(EventDate) FROM hits` read every value of
the column, on every core. Yet a group's summary, held in memory, keeps
each column's nulls and its least and greatest values that are not null
(D31), exact as the group was written.

`TableStorage::summarized` gives the rows a scan of some columns with no
condition gives, in pieces (`rows/frozen/summarized.rs`). The directory
is taken first, as D1180's is. A group whose shadow bits are all clear
has no entry of the tree over its rows, so the reader sees each of them
as frozen, and it is given whole: its rows, and of each column asked
for its nulls and bounds, none of its values read. The other groups and
the tree's rows past them are given by batch, by the scan itself
(`Batched` over those groups alone, its tree's rows those outside every
group), so each row the scan gives is given once. Under SERIALIZABLE the
read is noted as the scan's of those columns is. The row store gives
none, its zones' bounds being kept as rows change, not exact.

The executor feeds an aggregation of one group, over a bare scan, whose
set functions are each COUNT(*), MIN or MAX, at least one of a column,
the pieces in place of the scan's batches (`exec/batch/count.rs`). A
piece given whole adds its rows to each COUNT(*), its least to each MIN
and its greatest to each MAX, and its nulls raise the warning of a null
taken out [X3.135-1986 §5.8 GR1]. A batch is fed as the scan's is. MIN
and MAX are fed so only of a column of exact numbers or a datetime.

A summary's bounds are compared as values are, and a text's MIN and MAX
are taken by its collation (§9.15), while an approximate number's
bounds would also need NaN and signed zero ordered as the set functions
order them. A bare COUNT(*) stays D1180's. EXPLAIN adds the line `--
summarized by storage: <table>`, and the planner keeps the aggregation
whole, as D351 keeps a count. Rejected: COUNT of a column from a
group's rows less its nulls, whose accumulator takes values, not
counts; keeping bounds of a group exact as its rows are deleted, which
every delete of a frozen row would have to write.

#### D1183. A collation of NO PAD that orders strings as their octets do is compared in place, no sort key made

A comparison under any collation but the default made a sort key of each
operand (D60), a binary string, and every operator that reads vectors
gave way to rows for it. Under UCS_BASIC or SQL_TEXT with NO PAD the key
is the text's own octets, so a key was built of each row to say what the
row already said. A table whose character columns were all of such a
collation ran its text queries slower than under the default.

The two pad characteristics differ in two cases alone [ISO/IEC
9075-2:2023 §4.3.2, §8.2 GR3b]. Strings that differ only in trailing
spaces are equal padded and apart unpadded, the shorter the less. And
where one string is a prefix of the other, the rest beginning, after any
spaces, with a character below a space, the longer is the less padded
and the greater unpadded. Everything else orders alike.

The plan keeps its marks (`Expr::SortKey`, `Aggregate.collations`), so
every rule of the optimizer reads it as before, and an index on such a
column still holds sort keys, which are the strings' octets, so no index
and no format changes. What changed is how the marks are carried out
where `CollationRef::is_octets` holds.

- A comparison of a marked column with a constant is judged over the
  column's vector in place (`Judged::Unpadded`) and told to the scan
  (`Conjunct::Unpadded`, `logical::compared_unpadded`), which judges it of
  texts, of a dictionary's entries and of texts coded by symbols
  (`Symbols::compare_unpadded`). IN is an OR of them, NOT IN and BETWEEN
  ANDs of them.
- A zone's least and greatest are in the padded order. Equal octets are
  equal padded too, so an equality passes over a zone the constant is
  outside. No other comparison passes over a zone, as `'a'` alone in a
  zone is below `'a'` and a tab unpadded and above it padded. A sorted
  dictionary's order, a sketch and a Bloom filter take no such constant.
- GROUP BY, and DISTINCT bound as a grouping, read by batches and in
  parallel. The grouping's seed says which key columns are unpadded
  (`Seed::unpadded`), and a table made by it hashes those strings whole
  (`Kernels::hash_texts_unpadded`) and compares their octets
  (`Lane::equal`).
- MAX and MIN compare the strings' octets (`CollatedAcc`), a vector of
  them where it lies since D1290.
- ORDER BY, a join's keys and COUNT(DISTINCT) still take a key, made of a
  vector of texts in one pass as the text's octets (`calls::octets`), which
  sort, join and compare as binary strings do. A sort by a column reads
  the column in place since D1185.
- LIKE never pads [§8.5 SR3d], so under UCS_BASIC or SQL_TEXT of either
  pad characteristic its operands are no longer folded
  (`binder::collation::like_under`), and a constant pattern stays one.

Which collation a comparison takes is §9.15's, unchanged. Two columns of
different collations are refused [SR4e], and an explicit COLLATE on one
side wins, so a join's keys are of one pad characteristic.

These still compare sort keys, made a row at a time, and so are correct
and no faster than before. Each is tested by
`unpadded_collations::the_rest_compare_sort_keys_unpadded`. They are a
window's partition and order, UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT, IN and a
quantified comparison of a subquery, a comparison of rows, NULLIF and a
simple CASE, GREATEST and LEAST, a grouping streamed in an index's order,
and a range read of an index. A second grouping over a first run in
parallel was among them until D1184. A join's condition under a collation is not
moved by the join order's search (`enumerate/extract.rs`), as before.

#### D1184. A DISTINCT set function's pair of groupings under a collation of octets runs as one part

A DISTINCT set function is computed by two groupings, one over the other
(D340), and a part runs the pair whole, each partition's thread making
both (D1113, D1123). `first_level` refused the pair if either grouping
named a collation, so a query grouping by a column of a collation of NO
PAD that orders strings as their octets do (D1183) ran its first grouping
in parallel and its second above the part, a row at a time on the
statement's thread, keyed by bytes made of each group.

The pair is now a part's if each column of either grouping is by no
collation or by one whose key is the text itself, and each column the
second groups by is by the same in the first (`keyed_alike`). The rewrite
gives the first the second's collations, so its pairs always agree. One
written by hand whose second groups a column padded and whose first
groups it unpadded, or the other way round, stays above the part, as does
