a pair under any other collation. The agreement is what keeps the
partitions right. A partition's groups of the first are split by the
first's own hashes of the second's columns (`Keys::hash_of`, by the
seed's flags), so two groups that one group of the second takes are in
one partition only if the first holds equal every string the second
holds equal.

The second grouping groups as its own collations say. Made in a table
(D1123), it is handed the seed flagged by its own key's columns
(`Seed::unpadded`), so its keys are hashed whole and compared by their
octets. Made of rows, and of one that crosses the partitions (D1133),
merged on the statement's thread, a group's key is `group_key`'s under
its collations, the strings' octets, where it was the padded bytes
before. A second that crosses the partitions takes any mix of the two
kinds, since its groups are merged by its own keys whatever the
partitions were split by.

Nothing a query answers changes. `'a'` and `'a '` under such a collation
were two groups before and are two groups now, counted by more threads.
#### D1185. A sort by a column under a collation of NO PAD by octets reads the column in place, its key marked to order by octets

ORDER BY under a collation sorts by a column the projection under the
sort makes, each row's sort key [ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §10.10]. D1183 left
that key in place where the collation's key is the text itself
(`CollationRef::is_octets`), made of a vector of texts in one pass. It
was still a binary string made of every row, held as a value beside its
row, and a projection that computes reads every column of its input, so
none was read late and each row's other columns were decoded before the
sort chose its first rows.

A sort key now says whether it orders its column's character strings by
their octets (`SortKey::octets`, `logical/sort_key.rs`). Only the
physical plan's pruning sets it (`physical/blind/pruned/octets.rs`), so
no rule of the optimizer and no choice of the planner sees a key that
has it. Walking the plan from the top (D1167), a sort over a projection
whose key column is the sort key of a column under such a collation,
read by none above the sort, is keyed by the column instead, by octets.
The key reads the first column of the projection that moves the column,
and the place the key was made in, now read by none, is given null. With
no such column the key's own place moves it. The projection is then one
of columns, so it makes no value, the columns the keys do not read are
read late, and EXPLAIN shows NULL where the key was.

Every way a sort runs honours the mark, as all compare through the same
two functions and one layout.

- The normal key (D364) of a string of such a key is a binary string's
  field, its first octets padded with zeros and then its length
  (`normal::seen_as`, `encode::value`), so the bytes order as the octets
  do, a prefix the less.
- Strings alike in the octets a field holds are compared whole by their
  octets, where they lie in their vectors (`vectors::compare_cells`) or
  as values (`SortKey::cmp`, which `compare_rows` calls). A sort of
  batches held or spilled, the merge of its runs, a top-N of batches or
  of rows, a sort run in parallel and its splitters, a merge of ordered
  inputs and a SCROLL cursor's sort of its rows' keys order through
  these.
- A string's 8-byte prefix (`sort/prefix.rs`) is of the padded order, so
  a key by octets has none. Where the keys have no normal form, a key of
  a DECFLOAT beside it, the rows are compared whole.
- The bound a top-N tells its scan (D379) held exact numbers and
  datetimes alone, so none was told of a key by octets. D1187 tells one
  that holds a string.

A key stays made, and the sort as it was, where the mark would be
wrong or is not known to be right. A key column read above the sort is
kept, as its rows would hold strings where binary strings are read.
FETCH FIRST WITH TIES reads its sort's keys of the rows it is given to
find the last row's peers [§7.17 GR7d i], so the pruning now counts
those columns as read above the sort, and its key stays made. A key of
an expression that is no column, a collation that pads or orders by
anything but scalar values, and a sort whose input is no projection are
left alone. Each refusal is tested
(`pruned::octets::tests::a_key_read_above_or_not_of_octets_stays_made`,
`octets_sorts::ties_and_expressions_sort_by_octets_7_17`).
#### D1186. A part of a built-in set function is kept in that function's column of states, and gives its part of each group

A query with a DISTINCT set function is computed by two groupings
(D340), and its set functions without DISTINCT are computed in parts
(D341). The first grouping computes PARTIAL of each, whose value of a
group is the function's state as bytes, and the second merges them. The
first grouping has a group for every distinct value of every group of
the second, by far the more groups of the two. D356 keeps COUNT, SUM,
AVG, MAX and MIN in columns of states, a slot a group, fed a batch's
rows in one loop. PARTIAL told the table nothing of what it is a part
of (`AggregateFunction::columnar` gives none of it), so each group of
the first grouping held an accumulator of each part on the heap, and a
batch's rows were sorted by group and fed to each group's accumulator in
turn.

A part now tells the built-in function it is a part of and that
function's result type (`AggregateFunction::part_of`, none by default),
and the table keeps its states in that function's column
(`States::Part`, `exec/table/states/parts.rs`). A part's accumulator
forwards everything it is fed, merged and asked to write to its
function's, so the column is fed, grown, merged with another table's,
written past a work area and sent to another thread as the function's
own column is, by the same code. Two things differ.

- What a group gives is its part, the function's state after the tag of
  a state, or its result after the tag of a result where the function
  writes no state, as a sum of approximate numbers does. The part's
  accumulator and the column both make it by `functions::part_value`, so
  the bytes are the same whichever held the group.
- A column fed values it does not hold, integers of another scale, turns
  into the part's accumulators, each holding the function's accumulator
  the group would have had (`functions::part_acc`). A column that comes
  back from another thread is a part's again (`States::thawed`). One read
  back from a spill (D1226) is read as the column of the function the
  part is of (`Typed::read`).

A group's state was written by making the accumulator the group would
have had and asking it. A grouping of parts writes every group's state
as it gives its groups, so that made an accumulator of each on the heap
after all. A count's, a sum's and a mean's state are now written by the
accumulator's own code of the slot the column holds, with none made on
the heap (`typed/stated.rs`, `functions::count_written`,
`sum_written`, `avg_written`). An extreme's still goes through its
accumulator.

The second grouping is as it was. It reads each part as a binary string
and merges it into its own accumulator, of which there are few.

#### D1187. A top-N by a key that orders strings by their octets tells its scan a bound that holds a string, judged of each row by octets

D379's bound holds the first key of the last row a sort of its first
rows keeps, and D1241 has the scan judge it of each row. It held exact
numbers and datetimes. A sort by a column under a collation of NO PAD
by octets (D1185) was told none, so a FETCH FIRST by such a column
gave its sort every row its filter kept, and the sort made a key of
each to drop nearly all of them.

- A bound of a key marked `octets` holds a character string
  (`Threshold::by_octets`, made by `sort::topped_of`). It narrows by
  the strings' octets, a prefix the less, as the sort compares them
  (`SortKey::cmp`), and a bound shared by the morsels of a sort run in
  parallel counts the first keys offered in that order
  (`Threshold::among`, `Threshold::offer`). A value that is no string
  neither sets nor counts.
- The test it is of a row (`Threshold::row_test`) is a comparison of
  octets with the string it holds (`Conjunct::Unpadded`), at most it of
  an ascending key and at least it of a descending one. The scan judges
  it as it judges any such comparison (D1183), once an entry of a
  dictionary and then by the rows' codes, of texts coded by symbols in
  place with no text decoded, and of plain texts where they lie. A null
  is left out, as D1241 says of every bound.
- It passes over a group or a part only where that is proved right
  (`Threshold::may_match`, `threshold/octets.rs`). Their least and
  greatest are kept in the padded order, which differs from the order
  of octets in two cases alone (D1183). A string and the same with
  spaces after it are one value padded and apart by octets, the shorter
  the less. And a string that goes on past another with an octet below
  a space, after any spaces, is the less padded and the greater by
  octets. So a range whose ends look past the bound may hold a row at
  or before it by octets, and comparing the ends with the bound as
  values would lose rows. Each rule reads the first octet at which the
  range's end and the bound differ, both having one there. Of a
  descending key the range is past the bound if its greatest has the
  lesser octet there. Of an ascending key it is past the bound if its
  least has the greater octet there, that octet is above a space, and
  no octet of the least before it is below a space. A range whose end
  is a prefix of the bound, or the bound of it, is never passed over.
  `octets.rs` gives the proof, and a test tries both rules over every
  string of at most four octets of a tab, a space and two letters, as
  a zone's contents and as the bound
  (`a_zone_passed_over_holds_no_string_at_or_before_the_bound`).

The zones of a column of such a collation are not rebuilt in the order
of octets. A zone's least and greatest are written once, when a group
is frozen, as values of the column's type, and every other reader of
them compares values padded, a comparison of the column under the
default collation among them, which a column of any collation may
still be asked. Keeping a second pair of ends by octets for such a
column is a change of the store's format and is not made here. The
rules above take from the ends that exist what they can prove.

What D1241 says of when a bound is read holds here unchanged. The
bound only narrows, a run judged by a bound read before the sort last
narrowed it keeps more rows and never fewer, and the sort judges every
row it is given. So the rows given, their order and the errors are as
before, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE counts fewer rows of the scan.

#### D1188. A regular expression with no back-reference is matched by an automaton for where it ends and by a matcher that marks for what it captured

D61's matcher of a program with no back-reference keeps a list of
threads at each position, each with a copy of what it has captured, and
follows every thread at every character (`regex/pike.rs`). A copy of the
captures was made on the heap for each thread at each position, a string
was turned into a vector of characters before it was searched, and a
function called for each row began all of it again. TRANSLATE_REGEX of a
column spent nearly all its time there.

Three things replace that path. None changes what matches. Each is held
to the matcher of threads by tests over patterns of every instruction
and texts from every starting position, with captures and without.

- `regex/bounded.rs` follows one way at a time, going back to the last
  fork on failing, with one set of captures put back as it goes back. It
  marks each instruction at each position it meets and gives up a way
  that meets a mark. That is right because whether a match is found from
  an instruction at a position depends on those two alone, on nothing
  captured and not on where the search began. The way that met them
  first is preferred to every later one and found no match from there,
  or the search would have ended. So the marks are kept from one
  starting position to the next, and a search of every start takes time
  within the product of the text's length and the program's. A
  back-reference breaks this, as what it matches depends on what was
  captured, so a program with one never runs here
  (`Regex::matcher`, tested by
  `it_is_given_programs_of_no_back_reference_and_texts_within_its_marks`).
  The marks are a bit each, `MARKS_MOST` of them at most. A sweep of
  `bench/regex.rs` at five budgets found no length of text at which the
  matcher of threads ran a text faster, to the largest budget swept, so
  the budget is of what a search holds and is derived from that. It is
  the octets the matcher of threads takes for its two lists of threads
  of the longest program, what they captured not counted, so a search
  here never holds more than a search there may. Past it the matcher of
  threads runs. A program whose first instruction is `^` of the whole
  string is tried from the string's start alone, as a way from any
  later start fails at that instruction.
- `regex/dfa.rs` is an automaton made as texts are read (Thompson, 1968).
  A state is the ordered list of threads at a position, cut after the
  first that matches, and whether a match was found before it. The state
  a character leads to is kept once found. It gives where the preferred
  match ends, not where it begins nor what it captured. `^` and `$` of
  the whole string are judged at the first state and after the last. The
  wildcard of the flag `s`, any character but a CR before an LF [ISO/IEC
  9075-2:2023 §9.28 GR9a i], reads a CR before an LF as a character of
  its own. A program with `^` or `$` of each line, or a back-reference,
  has no automaton. Its states' steps, keys and threads are counted in
  octets, and past `OCTETS_MOST`, as many as a search's marks may take,
  it gives up and the search goes on without it. An automaton that still
  meets new states there follows its texts no faster than the matchers.
- `regex/searcher.rs` puts them together for text after text. A search
  that asks only whether there is a match asks the automaton. A search
  for captures runs the matcher that marks, which reads no further than
  the end the automaton gave if it was asked. The automaton before such a
  search is a pass more over a text that matches and the whole search of
  one that does not. On the bench those balance where about half the
  texts have no match, so the searcher counts what a window of its
  searches found and asks the automaton first only while at least half
  found none. The window is 64 searches. A share is known from n
  searches to within 1/(2√n) near one half, one sixteenth of 64, so a
  share two such errors from the half is taken for the other side about
  once in forty windows, and nearer the half the two ways cost nearly
  the same. It is one thirty-second of a vector's rows, so the first
  window of a vector, which asks unasked, is a few hundredths of its
  searches.

The automaton's states are worth keeping only across texts, and a scalar
function's call is given one row and nothing to keep them in. So they
live in a searcher, which a call over a vector makes for the vector
(D363), with the marks, the captures and the forks left to try of the
matcher that marks, which a search clears and uses again. TRANSLATE_REGEX
has such a call, taken when its subject is a vector of texts and its
other operands are constants, and LIKE_REGEX has one, taken when its
value is a vector of texts and its pattern and flag are constants. Each
compiles the pattern and makes the searcher once for the vector, and
TRANSLATE_REGEX reads the replacement once. No state is kept in the
function, in the thread or in the session. A search of one text alone
makes no automaton, which would be made only to be dropped. A call over
a vector that fails gives way to the calls of each row, which raise what
a row raises (D363).

TRANSLATE_REGEX replaces a match as fn:replace replaces the match as a
string of its own [ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §9.29], which was a second search
of every match. That search finds the same groups where the match is the
whole subject, which is that string, and where no instruction of the
program reads beside the character it matches, no `^`, no `$`, no
wildcard that looks for an LF after a CR and no back-reference. The way
that matched then reads the same characters in both, and every way
preferred to it failed on characters the string has too. So
`Regex::matches_alone` says which matches are replaced from their own
groups, and only the others are searched again. `(^a)|(a)` after a `b`
is one of the others. It matches `a` by its second group and that `a`
alone by its first.

Once a match of a subject is replaced the pattern is known to match no
zero-length string, which `Regex::replacement` refuses, so no match
begins at the subject's end and TRANSLATE_REGEX searches for none there.
That search of each subject found nothing every time, which told the
searcher that half its searches find nothing and kept it asking its
automaton before every search of subjects that all match.

A subject whose characters are all ASCII's is matched where it lies, its
octets its characters (`regex::Ascii`), so no vector of characters is
made of it.

A pattern that ends `.*$` under the flag `s` takes the rest of any text.
Its program ends with a greedy loop of the wildcard that matches every
character, CRLF as one, and then asks only that the string ends
(`regex/compile/rest.rs`). From the loop's first instruction the way
preferred takes every character to the string's end, where `$` holds,
whatever the characters are, and no way preferred to it matches, since
the loop's fork takes its other branch only where the first fails. So
the matcher that marks goes from that instruction to the string's end
and walks no character between. The loop is found in the instructions,
by its shape, and only where nothing but closing groups and the match
follows `$`. A reluctant loop, a loop of a class, `$` of each line and a
loop in a branch are walked as before, and so is every loop on the first
matchers, which the corpus holds this one to.

OCCURRENCES_REGEX, POSITION_REGEX and SUBSTRING_REGEX take the matcher
that marks and the text in place through the same `Regex` methods, each
call of a row a search of one text alone.

The first matchers stay, and a search falls to them where the new ones
do not hold. A program with a back-reference runs on the matcher that
counts its steps and has no automaton. One with `^` or `$` of each line
has no automaton. A text whose marks would pass `MARKS_MOST` runs on the
matcher of threads. A corpus of several hundred patterns made of atoms,
quantifiers, alternation, groups, anchors and back-references under the
flags, in every text of at most three characters of two letters, CR, LF
and a letter of two octets, from every position, holds a searcher kept
across the texts to the first matchers
(`over_a_corpus_a_searcher_finds_what_the_first_matchers_find`).

#### D1189. A character string of any characters is matched where it lies, by the octets its characters begin at, and a match over a vector takes no memory of its own

D1188 matched a string of ASCII where it lay. Of any other string it
made a vector of characters first, four octets for each character,
allotted, filled and freed for every subject. And each match found gave
its captures as a copy of the searcher's slots and its match vector as
a vector made anew, two more pieces of memory a match.

A text's positions are now its own to step (`Text::after`,
`Text::before`). Of a vector of characters and of a large object they
count characters, as before. Of a string read where it lies (`Utf8`)
a position is the octet a character begins at. The character there is
decoded as it is read, one of ASCII by a single test of its octet, and
the position after it is past its octets. No matcher adds one to a
position to pass a character. The matcher that marks, the matcher of
threads, the automaton and the matcher that counts its steps all step
by the text, and so does a search of one match after another past a
match of no characters. Where a match is known to end is a position of
the same text, so the marks, which are of positions, need no change.

A back-reference under the flag `i` is matched by case variants, and a
variant may take other octets than the character captured, as the
Kelvin sign takes three where `k` takes one. So the matcher that counts
reads what was captured and what is matched against it a character of
each in turn, each by its own positions, and what it matched is as long
as the positions it passed (`backtrack.rs`, `again`).

A regular expression function's subject that is a character string is
read where it lies, whatever its characters (`subject.rs`,
`Body::Utf8`). Its positions are octets, so a start position given in
octets is the octet itself, moved to the next character if it falls
within one, and one given in characters is found by passing that many
characters. A position found is counted back into the units asked for.
The first position, which most calls ask for, is the first character's
in either units and needs no count. What lies between two positions is
cut out of the string as it is. TRANSLATE_REGEX copies the spans
between its matches that way, where it wrote each character of a vector
again.

A search leaves where its match's groups are in the searcher's own
memory (`bounded::Scratch`). `Searcher::find_into` reads them into a
match vector the caller keeps from one match to the next, and
TRANSLATE_REGEX over a vector of subjects keeps one for the vector. A
match found there takes no memory of its own. `find_in`, which gives a
match vector of its own, is that with a vector made for it.

A value that is no character string, a number given as a subject, is
still made a vector of characters, and a large object is read a chunk
at a time as before. Nothing any function gives changes. The corpus of
D1188 holds every search of a text read where it lies, from every
position, on each matcher and through the searcher, to the matchers
over the text's characters, with each match after another and what
replaces it (`over_a_corpus_a_searcher_finds_what_the_first_matchers_find`,
`a_text_of_longer_characters_read_where_it_lies_matches_as_its_characters`).

#### D1190. A greedy loop of one class before a character outside it is run through by the matcher that marks, no fork kept

The matcher that marks (D1188) follows a loop as it follows any fork.
At each character it marks the fork, keeps the way out of the loop to
try later, and marks and follows the loop's instructions, five of them
for a loop of one class. A pattern that takes a part of a text up to a
delimiter, as `[^/]+/` takes a host name, spent most of its search
there, and nearly every way out it kept failed at its first
instruction.

A program now knows the loops it runs through (`compile/runs.rs`,
`Program::runs`). Such a loop is greedy and of one instruction that
matches a character by what the character is alone, and the next
character asked for after the loop, positions kept for groups between
them or not, is one that instruction never matches. `[^/]+/`, `a*b` and
`(\d+)\.` each have one. At a position where the loop's instruction
matches the character, the way out comes to that next instruction with
the same character and fails. Where the loop's instruction fails, the
way out is the only way. So the first way that can match leaves the
loop at the first character it does not take, and every way out before
that fails at once and changes nothing, no group's position either, as
a way that fails puts back what it kept.

The matcher that marks follows such a loop to that character with no
fork kept (`bounded.rs`, `through`). It marks the loop's fork at each
position it passes, as following the forks did, so a way that comes to
the loop at a position passed before stops there and a search still
takes time within the product of the text's length and the program's.
It reads no further than where a match is known to end.

A loop stays a loop of forks where the proof does not hold. That is a
reluctant loop, a loop of more than one instruction, a loop of the
wildcard that looks for an LF after a CR, and a loop followed by an
assertion, a fork, a back-reference or the match before any character
is asked for. The other matchers follow every loop as before, and the
corpus of D1188 holds the matcher that marks to them over patterns
with such loops and without
(`a_loop_of_a_class_before_a_character_outside_it_is_run_through`).

#### D1200. The groups of far more values than rows are the rows, the formula computed without its power

The groups n rows fall into by columns of D distinct combinations are
D(1 - (1 - 1/D)^n) (D370). The power was computed by its logarithm and
taken from 1. Once D passes 2^53 times n the power is nearer 1 than a
number tells, the difference is nothing, and the groups were clamped to
one. A grouping by seven columns of a customer, their distinct counts
multiplied to about 10^30, was estimated at one group where it made
381,105, and every choice above it was made for one row.

The difference is now computed whole, as -expm1(n ln(1 - 1/D)), which
keeps the digits of a value near nothing (`cardinality/groups.rs`). Its
limits are the formula's. One value gives one group, since the logarithm
is then negative infinity and the difference 1. As many values as rows
give 1 - 1/e of them. Far more values than rows give the rows, each
meeting a value of its own. A product of distinct counts past every
number is taken as the greatest one, so the formula never multiplies
nothing by infinity. The result stays within one group and n.

#### D1201. A grouping column functionally dependent on the others is carried, not grouped by

A grouping by a table's key and other columns of that table, as a
report by customer that shows the customer's name and address, hashed
and compared every column written, the wide ones too, though the key
alone tells the groups apart. The rule `reduce_grouping_keys`
(`optimizer/dependent_keys.rs`) now leaves out of the grouping columns
each one the others determine, and carries its value as the set function
that keeps a group's first row's value of a column
(`functions/any_value.rs`), which is what a query that references such a
column without grouping by it gets [ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §6.7 GR1e]. A
projection above puts the columns where they were.

It is sound by the standard's own definition. A dependency A ↦ B holds
if two rows not distinct in A are not distinct in B [§4.26.1], and two
rows are of one group if they are not distinct in every grouping column
[§9.12]. So rows grouped by A alone fall into the groups A and B
together made, each group has the rows it had, in the same number, and
every set function, DISTINCT, filtered or ordered, is given what it was
given. Nothing is evaluated of a row or a group it was not before (D15).
HAVING, ORDER BY and the select list read the carried column at the
place the grouping column had.

The dependencies are the known functional dependencies of the grouping's
input, found by the rules the binder already follows for column
references (`binder/dependencies.rs`), with these conditions.

- A key is a PRIMARY KEY, or a UNIQUE constraint of columns known not
  null or NULLS NOT DISTINCT, not deferrable [§4.26.3]. A UNIQUE column
  that may be null determines nothing, as two rows null in it are not
  distinct and may differ elsewhere.
- An equality AND-component of a WHERE or an inner join's ON makes each
  of two columns determine the other [§4.26.12], so a key reaches the
  columns of a table joined on its key, and theirs in turn.
- Of an outer join, a dependency of the operand extended with nulls
  holds only where a column of its determinant is known not null, and
  the condition adds what §4.26.7 gives of the preserved operand's
  columns. A FULL join's condition adds nothing.
- Only the strict dependencies are used (`dependencies/strict.rs`).
  Character strings equal but for trailing spaces or by a collation,
  two approximate zeros and datetimes of one instant in two zones are
  not distinct, yet an expression tells them apart. A dependency on the
  columns an expression or a generation expression reads is kept only
  of exact numbers, truth values and datetimes of no zone. An equality
  counts only where it compares both columns by their own values under
  one relation, so not an approximate number with an exact one. An
  outer join's condition counts only if each AND-component that reads
  the preserved operand is such an equality or reads such types alone.
  An ordinality column determines nothing, and nothing is known of a
  grouping made by a collation.
- A column takes part only if the grouping groups by it as its own
  values are told apart, by its base column's collation or by none of
  none. A column grouped by another collation stays a grouping column
  and determines nothing. A column left out is compared by nothing, so
  its collation drops out of the grouping.
- A grouping that makes groups before any row, of an empty grouping set
  [§7.13 GR2a], is left. Grouping sets otherwise read rows whose masked
  columns are new columns, of which nothing is known. One grouping
  column at least is kept, as a grouping by none is one group even of
  no rows.
- A column whose declared type is not known is kept.

Of two columns that determine each other the first written is kept.

The rule is a late one. The optimizer applies the late rules once the
others have reached their fixpoint, and does not apply the others again
(`Optimizer::add_late`). The rules that move a HAVING condition of
grouping columns into WHERE (D15), turn a join under a grouping into a
semi join (D542) or group below an outer join (D1112) read the grouping
as it was written first, and a column carried is none of theirs.

A grouping read by batches keeps the values it carries in a column of
them, a value a group, its first row's, read of the batch's column in
place (`exec/table/states/carried.rs`). An accumulator a group was given
a row made of the value of every row, and had each batch's rows sorted
by group to be fed them. A group written, merged or finished is as its
accumulator writes, merges and finishes it, and a column given what is
no column read in place turns into accumulators.

#### D1202. Columns a grouping carries of a table joined on its key are fetched after FETCH FIRST

A report of the twenty customers of the greatest revenue, showing each
one's name, address and comment, carried those wide columns through
every row of its joins and every group, and kept twenty of them. The
rule `fetch_dependents_late` (`optimizer/late_fetch.rs`) now reads them
after the FETCH FIRST. Where a table below the grouping has a key the
grouping columns determine, by the strict dependencies of D1201, every
row of a group is of one row of that table, so the group's value of any
column of the table is that row's. The grouping then carries the key's
columns in place of the others, unless it groups by them already, and
above the FETCH FIRST the rows kept are joined to the table again on
the key, which gives the columns left out.

The table stays joined below, reading its key and what the joins
compare, for the rows it leaves out. The grouping, its groups and what
each set function is given are as they were, so nothing is evaluated of
a row or a group it was not before (D15). A group has one value of the
key, and it is not null, as the key's columns are NOT NULL, of a PRIMARY
KEY or UNIQUE constraint not deferrable, and the table's row reached
the group through filters and inner joins alone. So the join above finds
exactly one row for each row kept, the one its group's rows were of. It
neither adds nor loses a row, and the value it gives is the one the
grouping would have carried. A join may give its rows in another order,
so the rows are sorted again above it by the same keys.

The rule takes a FETCH FIRST of a constant count of ROWS ONLY, with or
without OFFSET, over a sort or none, over select lists and HAVING
conditions, over a grouping by its columns' own values that makes no
group before any row. A column is fetched late only if nothing between
the grouping and the FETCH FIRST reads it but to hand it on. A sort key,
a HAVING condition or an expression of the select list that reads it
needs it of every group, and it stays carried while the others are
fetched. WITH TIES and PERCENT keep a number of rows no constant gives,
and are left. A table an outer join extends with nulls has no row for
some groups, and is left. A table whose key the grouping columns do not
determine may give a group rows of several of its own, and is left.

Fetching n rows of a table of r rows by its key reads n log2(r) keys of
a tree of them, or the r rows once more, whichever is fewer, and
carrying a column reads it once for each row the grouping groups. A
column is fetched where the fetch so counted reads fewer rows than the
grouping is estimated to group.

The grouping itself is not moved below the joins that only add such
columns, though grouping first would spare those joins most of their
rows. A join that may leave a row out, having no NOT NULL foreign key
onto the key or having a filter on its table, would then have the
grouping compute its set functions of groups the query never formed,
and one that may raise, as a SUM whose total is not bounded within the
digits an exact number has (D1060), would raise where the query does
not (D15). Grouping first is sound only where every such join keeps
every row, or no set function and no argument can raise. Fetching late
needs neither.

#### D1203. A set function compared with a constant keeps the groups its column's statistics give

A HAVING condition that compares a set function with a constant kept a
third of the groups, the default of an order comparison of which nothing
is known (D31), whatever was compared. The orders whose quantities sum
past 300, 624 of 15 million, were taken for 5 million, and the table
joined to them was read into the hash table those few rows then probed.

The share is now estimated from the statistics of the column the
function is of (`cardinality/having.rs`). A grouping of n rows into G
groups has m = n / G rows a group. A group has one row at least, and
the rows past it are taken as a Poisson number of mean m - 1, each row's
value of the column drawn alike and apart from the others, the
independence the estimator assumes of rows everywhere. With F the
column's distribution, as its statistics give the share of its values a
comparison keeps, and mu and s2 its mean and variance:

- MAX is at most c in F(c)^m of the groups and MIN above c in
  (1 - F(c))^m, each being of m values, and the other comparisons are
  their complements.
- COUNT(*) has mean m and variance m - 1.
- SUM is a sum of a number of values that has mean m and variance
  m - 1, so it has mean m mu and variance m s2 + (m - 1) mu^2.
- AVG has mean mu and variance s2 / m.

The share of COUNT, SUM and AVG past c is the normal tail of those two
moments, Q((c - mean) / deviation), which the central limit theorem gives
a sum of values drawn alike. Q is half the complementary error function,
computed by the rational approximation of Abramowitz and Stegun's
formula 7.1.26. Of a column with nulls, m counts the values not null,
and COUNT of the column has variance m. The mean and variance are those
of the column's most common values, each at its share, and of its
histogram, whose buckets hold equal shares, each spread evenly between
its bounds; of no histogram, of values spread evenly between the least
and the greatest. No constant is tuned.

It is given only of a set function of a column alone, neither DISTINCT
nor filtered, whose table's statistics were gathered, with bounds of the
column among them. A set function of an expression, a comparison of two
set functions or with a parameter not yet a value, and an equality keep
the defaults. One group at least is kept.

The estimate may be low, as of a column whose values are far from a
normal sum's. It decides which operand of a hash join is built, the one
estimated to give fewer rows (`physical/join.rs`), and whether an index
join is weighed, and nothing reads it as a bound. The upper bound of the
rows stays the grouping's, so an index join is weighed at the estimate
times PLANNER.ESTIMATE_MARGIN, at most that bound, and taken only if it
is the lesser regret there too (D386). A hash join's table is sized by
the rows it is given, never by the estimate, and one that outgrows its
work area is partitioned (D38). So an estimate a hundred times low builds
the larger operand and costs a slower join, with no memory granted on
its word and no wrong result. An index join weighed at the margin's
times the estimate is exposed past it. Of rows a hundred times the
estimate it makes a hundred times the probes, where the margin weighed
eight.

#### D1204. A relation whose column of a class of equalities is a key of it is joined to the class's other relations by the implied key, within the enumeration's budget

The enumeration joins two sets only where an edge of the graph joins
them, and the graph had an edge only for a conjunct or an operator. So
of `p.k = l.k AND ps.k = l.k` it never joined `p` to `ps` alone, though
the class of the three columns (D302) makes `p.k = ps.k` true of every
row the query keeps and D387 joins two such sets by that key. Where `p`
is filtered and `l` is the largest table, joining `p` to `ps` first and
`l` to their few rows is the cheaper plan, and no order of the stated
conjuncts gives it.

A relation whose column of a class is a key of it now has an edge to
each other relation of the class (`enumerate/graph/implied.rs`). A key
is what the estimates take for one (`cardinality/keys.rs`, D384). That
is a PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint of the one column, not deferrable
and of no period, a grouping by the column alone, or DISTINCT of it
alone. A key matches at most one row of its relation to a row of the
other, so the join gives no more rows than the other relation has, and
fewer where the keyed one is filtered. A column that is no key gets no
edge, as its join may multiply rows and its edges are what made D387's
clique. A UNIQUE column that may be null is a key here. A null equals
nothing [X3.135-1986 §5.11 GR2], so its rows of a null join no row, by
the implied key as by the stated ones, and its other rows are each of a
value of their own. A deferrable constraint is none, as it may be
broken until it is checked [ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §4.25.2].

The edge is of no operator and no conjunct. A join made over it alone
judges the equality the class implies of a column of each side
(`Model::implied_keys`), by a hash, merge or index join as cost
chooses, and is an inner join like any other. The rows are those of the
query as written [X3.135-1986 §5.20 GR2b]. The implied equality holds of
every row the stated ones keep, since the stated ones are equalities of
bare columns under one comparison, which is transitive, numbers of
exact and approximate types comparing by algebraic value [§5.11 GR4].
An equality by a collation is no bare column's and enters no class.
Each stated conjunct is still judged where its relations first meet,
so the join of `p` and `ps` to `l` judges both stated equalities. The
rows do not rest on the key. Were it broken, the join would only give
more rows than estimated, the same ones any other order gives. A chain
with an outer join, a semi join or an antijoin has no class (D387), so
no such edge.

The edges of a relation are a star, and a class each relation of which
is keyed, as tables split one to one on a shared key are, would have a
star from each, a clique. Twelve such relations chained by their keys
have 286 pairs of sets to join as written and 261,625 as a clique. So a
star is taken only while the work exact dynamic programming does of the
graph with it stays within PLANNER.DP_BUDGET (`Graph::work`). The work
is the connected subgraphs the enumeration meets and the pairs it
joins, counted by its own traversal with no table and stopped past the
budget. The connected subgraphs alone would not do, as a clique of
twelve has 4,095 of them and passes no budget of 10,000. The stars are
offered from the relation of fewest estimated rows, whose join reduces
most, and one that passes the budget is undone and the next offered. A
graph past the budget with no star takes none. So a chain with stars
does at most the budget's work, the adaptive switch (D304) never leaves
exact dynamic programming for a star, and a chain no star fits is
planned as it was. A rule taking a star only from a filtered relation
was not taken. It bounds nothing, as twelve filtered relations are a
clique still, and a relation with no filter of its own may be reduced
by a join below, as a nation is by its region.

#### D1205. The unique index of a deferrable constraint is no key to the estimates

The estimates take a table's keys from the catalog (D384): the columns
of each UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY constraint not deferrable, and of each
unique index. But every such constraint has a unique index, a
deferrable one too, and that index holds two rows of one key from the
statement that breaks the constraint until its check [ISO/IEC
9075-2:2023 §4.25.2]. So a deferrable key was taken for a key through
its index, against D384's own words. A column of it was counted as of
one row a value, and its join as giving no more rows than its other
side.

The index of a deferrable constraint is now left out of a table's keys
(`cardinality/keys.rs`), told by its columns, which are the
constraint's, with its period's if it has one. Only estimates read
these keys, a row bound, a class's distinct values, the choice of a
hash or an index join, and the implied edges (D1204), so no query gave
wrong rows. The rules that rewrite a query by a key read the
constraints themselves and pass a deferrable one by (D1117, D1201,
D1202).

#### D1206. An inner hash join hashes one equality a column, the others of that column judged of the matched rows or, where the operand's joins imply them, not at all

A hash join took every equality of a column of each operand for a key.
Of `l.a = s.x AND l.a = ps.y`, as a join over an implied edge judges
(D1204), both were keys, though they are of one column of `l`. Each row
of either operand then hashed and compared `a` twice, and the scan of
`l` was told two runtime filters of the one column (D369).

An inner hash join now hashes at most one key of each left column and
one of each right column (`physical/join/single.rs`). The equalities are
taken in the order of the distinct values of their more distinct column,
most first, which is how the estimates count the pairs an equality
keeps (D302), so the key kept is the one that leaves the fewest pairs to
judge. Equalities of equal counts are taken in the order stated, so a
plan does not change with nothing. One is a key unless a key already
taken is of its left column or of its right column. So an equality that
shares no column with a key is always a key, and of
`l.a = r.x AND l.b = r.y AND l.a = r.y` the first two are hashed where
they rank first. The keys keep the order stated.

An equality that is not a key is judged of the matched rows, in the
filter over the join, which of an inner join is its condition and is
judged a batch at a time. Nothing is dropped by this, so the rows are
those of the query as written [X3.135-1986 §5.20 GR2b]. An equality is
true of no null [§5.11 GR2], the same as a key, which matches no null.
A key on which a null matches a null is judged as NOT (a IS DISTINCT
FROM b) [ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §8.15 SR6].

Such an equality is not judged at all where it is implied. Take the key
`l.a = s.x` and the equality `l.a = ps.y`, the right operand a join that
judged `ps.y = s.x`. That equality is true of every row of the right
operand, and the key is true of every matched pair, so `l.a = ps.y` is
true of every matched pair too. Both are true, so no value of the three
is null, and equality of bare columns is transitive, numbers of exact
and approximate types comparing by algebraic value [§5.11 GR4], as D1204
relies on. The mirror holds of two left columns and one right. The
planner knows what an operand's joins judged by construction. Each
realized subtree carries the equalities of columns its inner joins
judged (`Realized::equated`, `enumerate/realize.rs`), a LEFT join, a
semi join and an antijoin passing their left's and a FULL join none,
and an equality is implied only by a chain of those. An equality still
to be judged above, or one a relation's own filter holds, implies
nothing here, and the equality stays in the filter.

The join planned without the enumeration (`physical/join.rs`) has no
such record, and reads the same from the logical plans of its operands
(`equated_in`). A conjunct of a filter is true of every row the filter
gives, whatever plan runs it, so the equalities of columns in the
filters over an operand, and through each product in those over its
left operand, whose columns are the product's first, hold of each of
its rows. An equality these do not imply goes to the filter over the
join. One they imply stays a hash key of this join, and is not dropped
as the enumerated join drops it. A chain of tables each joined to the
first by one value shows why. Predicate transitivity (D404) adds the
equality of each pair, so join `i` of the chain has `i` equalities of
one column of its right operand, each implied by the filters below.
Filtered, they would put each join under a filter that keeps every row,
a pass over its rows and two more calls a level as the chain is read.
Dropped, they would leave each key column unread above its join, and
the join's operand would be put under a projection that gives it null
(D1167), two more calls a level too. Either way the deepest chain the
parser accepts took more than the stack it is read within, measured by
its test (`pruned_columns.rs`). Kept as keys they cost a hash and a
comparison of a column a level and no call, as before this decision.

Outer joins, semi joins, antijoins and mark joins keep every equality
as a key. They judge a condition beyond their keys of each pair inside
the match, a row at a time, and a semi join with such a condition no
longer keeps only the first row of each key (D540), so a key moved
there would trade a hashed column for a condition judged pair by pair.
A filter above an outer join would be wrong besides, as it would drop
the rows the join preserves. Index and merge joins hash nothing and are
as they were.

A runtime filter is made of each key, from the values of its built
column, and told of its left column (D369). Fewer keys make fewer
filters, each still holding every built value of its column, so each
keeps every row that matches. Predicate transfer steps along the same
keys (D665) and takes fewer steps, each sound alone. The cost model
needs no change. It prices each row hashed once whatever its keys
(`HASH_ROW`), and counts a join's runtime filter once a class of
equalities (D653), which is now what runs.

#### D1208. Sorting a grouping's input first is weighed by the rows of the input as built

A grouping under an ORDER BY of its keys whose input is in no such
order is streamed over a sort of its rows where that costs less than
hashing them and sorting the groups (D550). The rows weighed were the
estimator's count of the grouping's logical input, the statement as
written. The plan built for that input is another matter. Its joins
were enumerated and chosen by the model's count of each set of them
(D303), and that count is the one its operators carry. The two can be
far apart. Of a join of a table to two readings of another under an OR
of two pairs of their values, the count as written came out far under
the plan's, and the plan's was the nearer to the rows the statement
gave. By the lower count every row was thought a group of its own, a
sort of the rows looked the cheaper, and the grouping sorted every
joined row where, by the same weights and the plan's count, hashing
them into their few groups costs less.

The comparison now takes the rows the built input is estimated to give
(`Plan::est`, `physical/streamed.rs`), and the logical count only of a
plan that carries none. The rule of the choice and its weights are as
they were. The grouping's own estimate of its groups was left made of
the logical count, which D1278 changes. Why the two counts part is the
estimator's matter, a condition and the conditions derived from it
counted as independent, and is not settled here.

#### D1212. A table opened has its zones summed up only once one is asked for

A table opened with zones not known, stale or unsettled was noted for
maintenance as the database opened (D31, D1163), whether or not
anything read it. A table warmed once (D868) and closed before its
zones were summed up was then summed up at every start, by a pass that
decodes every row of each zone not known, on the cores the sessions run
on and through the buffer pool they read through, until some start
lasted long enough to finish it. A session that read other tables alone
paid for it. Its queries shared their cores with the pass, and the pool
filled with pages none of them read.

A table now notes whether a zone of it was asked for since it was made
or opened (`rows/zones/cold.rs`). The asks are those that warm a cold
table (D868), which are a scan told a condition of a column kept, a
read asking whether a row is visible to every reader, a count of its
rows, and a plan weighing an index-only read. The zones of a table opened are wanted by the
maintenance thread only once one was asked for (`rows/zones/summed.rs`),
as its statistics are gathered only once a plan read them (D473). The
table opened tells its database of its first ask (`spill/asks.rs`), through
the work areas its store is attached to. A note is set and the
maintenance job asked for, and the job, finding the note, notes each
table with maintenance due. A transaction that wrote notes its tables
as it ends, as before, but one that read alone collects nothing and
notes none, and its commit is the path of every read by key, so nothing
is asked there. The telling stands in for the noting the database's
opening did, so a table opened is summed up as it was before, only
later. The thread sums the zones up from then on, 64 a
call, with the rests of D771. What it summed up is saved by each checkpoint as
before, so a table closed part summed up goes on from there once asked
again. A zone saved settled visible opens so (D1163), asked or not.

A table made in this session is as before. One of the row store is
cold until asked, and one of the column store is warm and asked from
its first row. Its
first ask tells nothing. A read that warms it leaves its zones for the
commit of the next write to it, as before, so the maintenance thread
does not start beside the statements of a session that only read a
table it made, and the plans made of such a table do not change with
when the thread ran. With the telling, a join was planned by an index
or not, and read direct or not, from one run to the next. A write
to a table opened and not asked keeps its zones, as a warm table's
writes do, and leaves them due until one is asked for.
`Database::maintain` sums up every table's zones now, asked or not, so
a program that wants a database settled before it is used, or copied,
calls it. An ask after the first reads one flag and writes nothing, so
a read by an index, which asks of each row, costs what it did, and the
commit of a transaction that read alone is as it was.

A load into an empty table of the row store does not begin warm, though
its zones would then be known as its rows are written and no pass
would be owed later. Every write after the load would keep its zone,
the cost D868 took from tables written and read by key alone, and an
order entry's tables are loaded in bulk too. The pass is paid once, by
the table whose zones are asked for.

#### D1215. A FETCH FIRST with no ORDER BY over a grouping asks it for that many groups, and the grouping makes no more

Without ORDER BY the order of a query expression's rows is
implementation-dependent [ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §7.17 GR5a] (US036), and
OFFSET and FETCH FIRST remove and keep rows by that order [GR6, GR7d
ii]. So of a grouping under them any of its rows answer, as long as each
is a row of the grouped table, a whole group with its set functions of
every row of it [§7.13 GR2b]. A grouping by hash made every group of
its input all the same, and the limit over it took the first few and
dropped the rest, so a statement asking ten groups of a table of many
millions of them built and merged a table of them all.

The limit already tells a sort or an ordered scan how many of its first
rows are asked for, through projections that raise nothing and through
a part run in parallel (`exec/limit/bounded.rs`). It now asks a
grouping it reaches the same way for that many groups, OFFSET's count
added to FETCH FIRST's (`Plan::Aggregate`'s `first`). A sort between
them is told instead, and a filter, as a HAVING condition is, stops the
count, since the condition is judged of whole groups and the first
groups met may not be the ones it keeps. The count is a permission. A
grouping that ignores it gives every group and the limit keeps the
first, so each path that is not taught it stays right.

A row passed over is one no General Rule judges of the answer given,
yet evaluating it could have raised an exception or a warning, which
D15 does not let a plan lose. So a grouping is asked only if it is read
by batch, groups by some column, makes no group before its rows as
grouping sets do, is not streamed, and each set function counts rows or
takes a column and raises nothing whatever rows it is given, as D1063
asks of a grouping a join's runtime filter is told
(`exec/batch/first.rs`). A set function of a column that may hold a null
is refused too, as a null eliminated is a warning [§10.9 GR7a]. A
DISTINCT or filtered set function is not read by batch, and an
expression as argument is evaluated of every row, so neither is asked.

What a physical plan says it can raise (`Plan::can_raise`, D552) is left
as it is, every SUM and AVG taken as raising, since it reads no declared
type. The test above reads them (`exec/batch/typed.rs`, D1060), so a
grouping whose SUM is of exact values that cannot pass its range is
asked all the same, and the limit over it, which reads on for an
exception, finds no group more to read.

Run alone (`exec/batch/groups.rs`), the grouping makes groups until it
holds as many as asked for, then finds each row's group among them or
passes the row over. Every row of a group it holds reaches it, so each
group is whole. If a group is written past the work area before that
many are held, nothing is passed over from then on, as a row passed over
could be of a group already written.

Run in parallel (`exec/parallel/grouped/first.rs`), no morsel may keep
the first keys it meets, as another morsel would keep others and a
group would lack the rows of the morsels that dropped it. The
statement's thread first groups the first morsel by its keys alone and
keeps the first groups made, as many as asked for. Of each grouping
column it makes a runtime filter of the kept groups' values, as a hash
join makes of its built keys (D369), a null among them matching a null,
and the grouping's input is told them as D1063 tells a join's. The
scans skip what the filters' ranges exclude, and each morsel drops the
rows a filter excludes before the grouping reads them. A filter drops
no row whose value it was made of, so every row of a kept group is
grouped. A row every column of which passes, though no kept group has
its key, makes one group more, whole as well, which the limit drops.

The kept groups are the ones the part gives first when nothing is
fixed. A group is numbered by its first row, morsel then place, and
groups are given in that order (D293). The kept groups' first rows are
in the first morsel, before the first row of any other group there and
before every row of a later morsel. The first morsel is the first
morsel of the first scan the pipeline reads, whatever filter is over
it. That these are also the groups the plan run alone gives is true
where the scan run alone reads its rows in the morsels' order, which
this decision does not rely on. Any groups are an answer.

Nothing is fixed, and the part runs as before, when the first morsel
makes fewer groups than asked for, when the input is not scans under
filters and projections, whose pipeline is made twice at no cost, or
when EXECUTOR.RUNTIME_FILTERS is off. The first morsel is read twice.
Telling a part over a join, and choosing the groups from later morsels
when a filter empties the first, are left out.

Tests in `test/integration/first_groups.rs`: the groups given are whole
groups of the grouping, of each count, alone and in parallel, of both
stores; a part gives the groups of its first rows, the null group whole;
HAVING, grouping sets, a DISTINCT set function and a sort give whole
groups; a null eliminated, a sum past its range and a division by zero
in a later group are raised still; and groups past the work area are
whole. Mutations in `xtask/src/mutate/list/areas/first_groups.rs`.
#### D1216. SUM of a value and a constant is computed from the value's sum and count, shared among such sums

A statement of many sums of one column, each with a constant of its
own added, evaluated each sum's argument a row, one vector of the
column and its constant a batch for each. Repeats of one call were
shared already, by their label, as the binder registers them. Calls
whose arguments differ by a constant shared nothing.

The sum of x + c over the rows where x is not null is the sum of x and
c times the number of those rows. The rule `share_shifted_sums`
(`optimizer/shifted.rs`) rewrites SUM(x + c) and SUM(c + x) as SUM(x) +
c * COUNT(x), SUM(x - c) as SUM(x) - c * COUNT(x) and SUM(c - x) as
c * COUNT(x) - SUM(x), in a projection over the grouping, which then
computes one SUM(x) and one COUNT(x) for all of them, found by their
labels among the calls the statement wrote. Both are fed the column as
it is.

The rewrite holds only where the two forms cannot differ, in value, in
null or in what they raise (D15).

It takes exact numbers, x of an exact type and c an exact literal.
Exact arithmetic is exact, and both forms have the scale of x + c, the
greater of the two scales. An approximate or DECFLOAT x or c is left, as
their sums round and the two forms round apart.

c is a literal that is not null, so x + c is null exactly where x is.
COUNT(x) is then the number of values summed [ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §10.9
GR7a, GR7c], the nulls eliminated raise the same warning, and of no
value SUM(x) is null [GR7d ii], so the value computed of it is null and
not c times 0.

SUM raises once its result is past the range of its type [GR7d vi], 38
digits at the argument's scale, summed on the way in 128 bits and judged
once (D15). D1060's `total_fits` shows that a SUM cannot raise when its
argument's declared digits and the 19 digits that count a statement's
rows are within 38. The rule takes a SUM only if that holds of x + c and
of x. Then SUM(x + c), SUM(x), c * COUNT(x) and their sum or difference
are all within 38 digits, and x + c is within its own, so neither form
raises, and no appeal to an order of evaluation is made. A SUM of a
wider value is left.

A filter clause goes to both shared calls, which are shared among the
sums of one value under one filter. DISTINCT is left. So is AVG, which
truncates its quotient toward zero at two digits past its argument's
scale [X3.135-1986 §5.8 SR9c], so AVG(x + c) is not AVG(x) + c where the
mean is below zero. Of -1, -1 and 1 with c of 1 the first is 0.66 and
the second 0.67.

x is columns and constants under arithmetic, negation and casts, so one
evaluation of it for a row stands for each the sums made. A call or a
subquery in it leaves the SUM as written. A grouping that makes groups
before its rows, as grouping sets do, is left.

Tests in `test/integration/rewrites/shifted.rs`: each form gives what it
gives with the rule off, of both stores, by batches and row by row, with
nulls and their warning, scales, a filter clause, groups, a group of
nulls alone and no rows, and the plan shows one sum and one count; each
case left is left and gives the same; and the mean's counterexample.
Mutations `shifted-sum-minus-added`, `shifted-sum-unbounded`,
`shifted-sum-distinct` and `shifted-sum-unshared`.
#### D1218. A sort that reads its input whole passes it no row goal

A FETCH FIRST tells the plan under it how many of its first rows are
read (D552), and a node that gives its rows as it reads them passes the
count to its input, which is then priced by the share of it read. A
sort passed it on as it was, on the ground that an input read in the
sort's order gives the sort's first rows as its own. That holds of such
an input alone. When the input did not give the order, the planner put
a sort over it and kept the plan it had made of the input under the
goal, though the sort reads every row of it before it gives one.

So a statement that sorts a grouping's results and keeps the first few,
ORDER BY a set function with FETCH FIRST, planned its grouping for a
few rows. Of a table kept in the order of the grouping column that
picked the grouping streamed over the ordered read, priced at the rows
of the few groups asked, over the grouping by hash run in parallel, and
then read the whole table on one thread, a row at a time.

The planner now builds a sort's input under the goal as before, and if
that plan does not give the sort's order, builds it again with no goal
(`physical/ordered.rs` `read_for_sort`). A grouping asked an order by
every one of its columns did the same one level down, its input built
under the goal and then hashed, or sorted and streamed, when it did not
give the order. That input too is built again with no goal
(`physical/streamed.rs` `grouped`). An input that gives the order keeps
the goal, and a streamed grouping under FETCH FIRST with no sort between
stops its read as before (D551).

Each node `goals::passes` lets a goal through was read against what its
executor does. A scan, a projection and a filter give rows as they read
them. A product and a hash join probe by their left operand and build
their right, which is planned whole. UNION ALL reads its operands in
turn. A grouping or DISTINCT passes a goal only to an input read in its
keys' order, and plans a hashed one's input whole. A window, a set
operation other than UNION ALL, an outer, semi or mark join stop it.
The sort was the one that passed a goal to an input it reads whole. The
other places that put a sort over a plan, a window's, a row pattern's, a
merge join's operand and a partitioned table's part, are under nodes
that stop the goal or over a read of one table, whose plan a goal
changes only when it is read in an order asked.

Tests in `test/integration/streamed_grouping.rs`: the grouping under a
sort and FETCH FIRST is the plan of the same statement without FETCH
FIRST, a part run in parallel, under HAVING too, and a grouping whose
own order is asked stays streamed with no sort. Mutation
`row-goal-under-sort`. The second site, the grouping's input built again
in `grouped`, has no test that tells it from the code before and no
mutation. Its input under a goal differs from its input with none only
when something below the grouping plans otherwise for a few rows, as a
join's left operand may, and no statement was found whose plan shows
that difference there. It was changed by reading, as the same defect.

#### D1219. COUNT(DISTINCT) of no GROUP BY runs as one part, a string argument under a collation of octets grouped as it is

A DISTINCT set function is computed by two groupings (D340), and a part
runs the pair whole where the second groups by some of the first's
columns (D1113) or counts across its partitions (D1133). A second
grouping by no column was left above the part. So of COUNT(DISTINCT x)
with no GROUP BY, every group of the first, one a distinct value, was
made a row by its partition's thread, the partitions' rows were merged
in the order of their first rows, and the statement's thread counted
them one at a time while the workers waited.

Such a second grouping whose set functions are COUNT alone now crosses
the partitions as D1133's does (`physical::crosses`). Its one group
takes groups of every partition. Each partition's thread counts its
own, and the statement's thread merges the counts
(`exec/parallel/grouped/regrouped.rs`). A count is the same whatever
order its values are taken in. Of no rows the merge still gives one
group, COUNT of it 0. A HAVING condition is judged of the merged group.
Another set function there, as SUM(DISTINCT), takes its values in the
order of their first rows, so its second grouping stays above the part,
as does one with groups of empty grouping sets.

A second grouping that crosses the partitions with no projection
between the two now reads each partition's groups of the first as a
batch from their table (D1123, `grouped/second.rs`) and writes each of
its groups' states for the merge. No row is made of a group of the
first. One over a projection makes rows as before, as the projection is
evaluated of each.

The binder gives a DISTINCT function of a string under a collation the
string's sort key for its argument, so the rewrite's projection made a
binary string of every row and the first grouping keyed its groups by
those values. Where the collation's key is the text itself (D1183), the
rewrite now groups by the string under that collation
(`optimizer/distinct_aggregates.rs`, `Slot::of`), which a table hashes
and compares in place. Two strings are in one group exactly when their
keys are equal, so the groups are the same. COUNT then counts the
strings, as a key is null exactly when its string is. Any other
function takes the key, made of each group in the second grouping, as
it took it before. An argument under any other collation is grouped by
its key as before.

Results, their warnings and the row of no rows are as before. EXPLAIN
shows both groupings under one `Parallel`.
#### D1220. A parent that reads by batch takes a parallel grouping's groups as batches made of its partitions' own

A join that builds or probes over a grouping run in parallel, and a
pipeline whose source is one, read the grouping by batch (D1063, D1072).
They were given its rows gathered: each group made a row of values, the
partitions' rows merged in the order of their first rows, and the rows
put back into batches, every column a vector of values whatever its
type.

Where every partition gives its table's groups as a batch (D1125), the
parent is now given batches made of those
(`exec/parallel/grouped/runs.rs`, `Merged`). The statement's thread
takes the partitions' groups in the order of their first rows, as before,
and puts each group's values straight into the next batch's vectors, in
lanes of the columns' types as a table keeps its keys (D356). No row is
made of a group, and what reads the batches finds integers and texts in
vectors of their types.

The groups and their order are those the rows gave, so the parent's
result is unchanged. A grouping any of whose partitions gives rows, one
under a HAVING condition or a pair among them (D1125), or reads a run
back from the spill (D1226), gives its rows gathered as before. A part
that gives way is grouped alone and its rows gathered.

#### D1221. A join that builds of a grouping on keys holding every grouping column is handed its partitions' groups in any order

A grouping run in parallel gives its groups in the order of their first
rows, as the plan run alone does, whatever partition made each. A parent
that reads by batch was given them so too (D1220). The statement's
thread took the partitions' groups one at a time, the earliest first row
next, and put each into a new batch. Of a grouping of very many groups
that was one thread's work on every group, done after the part's threads
had finished.

A join did not read the grouping it builds of by batch at all. It asked
whether the operand's tables read by batch, which a grouping by hash
answers only as the operand of a join inside it, so the join took the
groups a row at a time, each made by the statement's thread (D1125), and
put the rows back into a batch for its table. A join now reads such an
operand by batch (`exec/batch/parted.rs`, `built_by_batch`), a grouping
by hash run in parallel alone or under projections, whatever its tables
are read by, as its partitions give batches either way.

A hash join that builds of the grouping keeps no order of what it
builds. It finds the built rows by their keys. Where the join's keys
hold every grouping column, no two groups share a key, so a probing row
finds one group at most, and the order the groups were built in shows in
no row the join gives. Such a join now asks the grouping for its groups
in any order (`exec/batch/parted.rs`, `keyed_whole`), and the grouping
hands it each partition's batch as it is, one after another
(`exec/parallel/grouped/runs.rs`, `Handed`). No group is compared with
another's first row and none is copied to a batch between.

The joins that ask are those that give a built row only when a key
found it. They are an inner join, a LEFT join that probes, and a semi
join, read alone (`exec/batch/joined/held.rs`, `read_keyed`) or as a
step of a pipeline run in parallel (`exec/parallel/probe.rs`). A RIGHT
or FULL join gives its unmatched built rows in the order built, and a
product pairs them in it, so they read the groups in order as before.

The request is kept narrow, so that no result's order can differ from
the plan's run alone.

- Every grouping column must be a key's right column. A join on some of
  them finds several groups of a key and gives them in the order built.
- Every grouping column must be grouped by the default collation. Two
  strings are then one group exactly where the join finds them equal
  [X3.135-1986 §5.11 GR5]. A column grouped by another collation may
  make two groups of strings one key matches.
- The operand must be the grouping itself, or projections of columns
  over it, which give a row of each group in the order they are given
  it. A key's column is then the grouping's column the projection
  names. What a filter, a projection that computes a value or another
  join asks of its own input is in order again (`exec/batch/late.rs`,
  `Deferred`).
- A DISTINCT, a grouping under a HAVING condition, a pair of groupings,
  and one any of whose partitions gives rows or reads a run back from
  the spill (D1125, D1226) give their groups in order as before.

#### D1225. A node stopped waits for its driver's turn in flight before its database is deposed

A node stops before its database closes (D57). Its transport ends, its
driver is halted, and its database is deposed, so it closes as a
replica's does and logs nothing. The driver's turns run on its job's
thread (D55), and a halt only made the next thing the driver took fail.
A turn already carrying out what the database was asked went on, and
what it ended after the stop undid the stop. A promotion ended left the
database serving, and a replay or an opening again left it following.
The close then took a checkpoint of a database serving or following,
asked the halted log to log it or to let records go, and failed with the
halt's own error (SQLCODE -910, "the node stopped"). This happened on a
node stopped just as its group changed view, as when the primary beside
it had stopped a moment before.

`Driver::settle` halts the driver and then waits until no other thread
is carrying out what the database is asked (`driver/effects.rs`). Each
thing a turn asks begins by reading the driver's failure, so after the
halt a turn asks nothing new, and the one in flight ends soon, since a
sync it waits for fails with the halt too. `Replication::stop` settles
the driver before it deposes the database, and nothing of the driver's
changes the database after. Called from within a turn, `settle` does not
wait for its own thread.

A stop that returns an error, or a close refused after it, is therefore
a defect and never the node's ordinary end, and a caller has no reason
to pass over either.

#### D1226. A grouping run in parallel whose partitions outgrow its grant holds them in the spill and merges them back a partition at a time

A grouping run in parallel by batch merges its morsels in waves into 64
partitions, each partition's table frozen between waves and held of the
statement's grant (D355, D356). Once the tables held passed the grant,
the grouping gave way. The threads' work was dropped and the plan run
again on the statement's thread alone, as a grouping a row at a time
that spills its rows (D38). Of a grouping of tens of millions of groups
at a grant of a few GiB, that rerun was most of the statement's time.

A partition's groups frozen already hold every state in a form that
goes to another thread: columns of states, and the states of other
accumulators written (D293). They now go to the spill as well
(`exec/table/made/written.rs`, `keys/written.rs`,
`states/written.rs`): a lane's or a column's values by their bits, a
null's place and the unpadded flag of D1183 too, so groups read back are
the groups written. A partition is written in pieces of at most `PIECE`
groups, one record a piece, so neither writing nor reading it holds its
groups twice.

Once the partitions' tables after a wave pass the grant, or a morsel's
groups or the statement thread's table (D355) do not fit beside them,
each partition's thread writes the table it holds to a run of the
grouping's spill area (`exec/parallel/grouped/waves/spilled.rs`), and
the grant gives back what they held. Each wave after merges each
partition's morsels into a table of that wave alone, which its thread
writes to a run of its own. A morsel's groups, or the statement
thread's table, that do not fit the grant even with nothing else held
are written to the partitions' runs as they are, after the waves before
them. The area is reserved of the budget as any
operator's, of the grouping's own grant (`Work::of_grant`), and nothing
of a partition in the spill is held of the grant.

At the end the last wave goes to the spill too, and each partition's
runs are read back a piece at a time and merged, in the order of the
waves, into one table, which is finished as a partition held in memory
is. A partition is weighed by what its groups held as they were
written, and the partitions are merged on as many threads at once as
half the grant holds the largest of. A partition that holds more than
half the grant is split, a piece at a time, into 64 parts again by the
next six bits of the hash it was found by (of a pair, the hash of the
second grouping's columns, D1113), each part to a run of its own and
finished alone, up to SPILL.PARTITION_DEPTH levels.

The rows come in the order a grouping held in memory gives them. Waves
take the morsels in order, so a group new to a later wave has a later
first row than every group of the waves before. A group of several
waves keeps the earliest first row of its pieces, as any merge of two
tables keeps the earlier, so its first wave's. A partition read back in
the order of its runs therefore holds its groups in the order of their
first rows, and a part split from it holds its share in that order too.

What still gives way: a value no run holds by its bytes alone, a large
object, an XML value, a value of a type beyond the standard, or one
that holds others, as a key or a value carried (D1201); a partition
still past half the grant at
SPILL.PARTITION_DEPTH levels; and the spill area refused (SQLCODE
-918). A grouping of a set function that writes no state is not run
in parallel by batch, as before. SELECT DISTINCT and the first grouping
of a pair (D1113), as DISTINCT set functions are run (D340, D342), wave
and are held in the spill the same way. A pair's second grouping that
crosses the first's partitions still merges its groups on the
statement's thread, all in memory (D1133). DISTINCT set functions and
that second grouping are the next to be held in the spill, as
COUNT(DISTINCT) groupings of many groups meet them at a small grant.

The groups a part finishes go to a run of the same area, each numbered
by its first row, and the statement's thread reads the runs back as it
merges them in that order. No more groups are held at once than the
threads finish together, so a grouping of nearly as many groups as rows
holds no more than the grant at the end, where holding its finished rows
until the statement read them outgrew the memory the server was given.
Of a grouping that keeps the first rows a sort asks of its tables
(D1124), a part's run holds those rows alone.

#### D1227. A window or set operation run in parallel holds each partition's result in a list that spills and merges the lists as they are read

A window function split by row, EXCEPT and INTERSECT run in parallel
split their rows into 64 partitions by key, each held in a list of its
share of the grant that spills, and run the serial operator over each
partition on a thread, in a share of the grant too (D295). The
partitions' results, though, were each gathered whole as rows and
merged into one more vector of every row before the statement read the
first, none of it charged to the grant. A window over a table of a
hundred million rows held them all twice at the end, past the memory
the server was given, at any grant.

Each partition's thread now pushes its result into a list of its own
share of the grant, which spills past it as the partition's input does
(`exec/parallel/partitioned.rs`), and the statement's thread merges the
lists as it reads them (`partitioned/merged.rs`). Of each list's next
row it takes the least by the window's sort keys, or, of a set
operation, by the place of the first operand's row carried after its
columns, a tie taken from the earlier partition. A window's partitions are never tied, as
its sort keys begin with its partitioning, and the place is a number
each row has alone, so the rows come in the order the plan alone gives
them. No more of the result is held at once than the lists hold in
memory, one grant in all, and a row of each.

A window computed over batches (D560) computes its partitions in
pieces up to its work area and gives them as they are done; it gathers
no partition's result, and is as it was.
#### D1228. A second grouping crossing the first's partitions holds its groups of a grant of its own and spills them by key past it

A second grouping over a first that crosses its partitions, by a set
function's result of the first or an expression of one (D1133), has
each partition's thread group its own groups of the first again and
write their states, and the statement's thread merges the states of each
group of all. Every partition's groups were gathered in one list, then
merged into a table of every group, neither charged to any grant. Of a
second grouping of many groups, each of them came from up to 64
partitions, and the list held them all before the merge began.

The groups the partitions give are now held of a work grant of the
second grouping's own, made of the budget when the first are given, as
a second operator's would be (`exec/parallel/grouped/regrouped/
crossing.rs`). Once they pass it, those held and every partition's
