after are written to the spill, each to one of 64 runs by the hash of
its key as the grouping compares keys, so all of a key's groups share a
run: its grouping values, then each state as a binary string. At the end
each run is read back and merged alone, its groups finished, numbered by
their least firsts and kept as the HAVING condition keeps them, and
written to a run of their own in that order, which the statement's
thread merges with the others as it reads them, as a spilled first
grouping's are (D1226). No more is held at once than one run's groups.

A run whose groups alone pass the grant is still merged whole: the
groups of one key cannot be parted, and a run holds a 64th of the keys.
#### D1229. A sort that asks for its last row's peers is run in parallel, each morsel sorted whole

FETCH FIRST n ROWS WITH TIES asks for the first n rows of a sort and
every row after them that is a peer of the n-th under the sort's keys
[ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §7.17 GR5, GR6]. The planner kept such a sort out
of a part run in parallel, and the part gave way had it met one, so the
sort read and sorted every row on the statement's thread alone.

It is now run in parallel as a whole sort is (D294): each morsel sorted
whole by a thread, since which of a morsel's rows are peers of the n-th
is known only once every run is merged, and the runs merged in memory
or, past the grant, from the spill (`exec/parallel/sorted.rs`). The
first n rows of the merge are given, then each row after them while it
is a peer of the n-th, which ends at the first that is not. Each sort is
stable and the runs are merged in the order of their morsels, so the
peers given are those the plan run alone gives, in its order.

#### D1230. A structure's tally counts a miss only when the pool evicted a page for it

The planner prices a fetch, and an index's probe, by the share of its
lookups that missed the pool, counted by each table and index once it has
had LEAST_LOOKUPS lookups (D35). Before that, the share is reckoned from
how much of the table the pool's frames could hold. Every miss was
counted, the first read of a page into a pool still filling as well. The
sampled statistics pass that follows a start begins each run of rows it
reads with a lookup, into a pool that holds nothing yet, so nearly every
one missed. A table of a few megabytes that a pool of 64 MiB holds three
times over was priced as two thirds missed, and a range read through its
index before the pass was planned as a scan of the whole table after it.
It went back to the index only a few thousand lookups later, and paid for
those first misses until the tally's window halved them. One query was
planned two ways by what had touched the table first since the start.

A miss is now counted only when the pool had no empty frame and evicted
a page for it (`Claim::evicted`, `BufferPool::hold`). A page read into an
empty frame says nothing about whether the pool holds the structure, and
is not counted. A table the pool holds is then priced as held, cold and
warm alike, as the reckoning before LEAST_LOOKUPS prices it. Once the
pool is full, every miss evicts and is counted. That covers a table
larger than the pool, and a table first read into a pool full of other
tables' pages, which does not fit beside what the pool holds. The
lookups are counted as before, so LEAST_LOOKUPS and the window are
unchanged. A hit costs nothing more, and a miss only notes which way the
pool found its frame (`disk/buffer/tally.rs`).

#### D1231. The log's bytes since a checkpoint are told by the log from its positions, no counter shared by the appends

D1137 counted the log's bytes in a counter that every append of every
session added to, beside the count of row changes. Each commit that
wrote paid a second write to a line all the committing threads share,
for a figure the log already holds in its positions.

Each log now tells the bytes between two positions as its own layout
says (`Log::bytes_between`). The file log's positions are its segment and
the offset in it, so it answers from them alone, each segment between
taken as the segment size (`log/file/segments.rs`). A segment ends a
record past that size, or further when the next could not be begun, so
the count is near, not exact, which a threshold allows. A log whose
positions number its records, the memory log, a log a plug-in keeps
(the hosted log and any given through `LogStorage`) and the replicated
logs, keeps the bytes appended before each record it holds, set under
the lock its append already takes (`log/marks.rs`), and answers by the
difference of two of them. A log that wraps another asks the one it
wraps. The method has no default, so every log answers it.

The checkpoint notes the position it holds through, not a count of bytes
(`Transactions::captured`). A commit that wrote asks for the log's bytes
up to its own commit record, whose position its session already holds
(`Served::last_committed`), so the log's end is not read and the file
log takes no lock. Before the first checkpoint the count runs from the
first position asked, as it ran from the open before. A rollback, a
replica's replay and the checkpoint job ask up to the log's end. The
appends write nothing for the count, and the commit reads only the
position of the last checkpoint.
#### D1232. A merge join is priced by the pairs its key matches

A join added to its cost the rows it gives (D303). A merge join pairs
each left row with the run of right rows of its key, and judges the rest
of its condition of each pair. Where its key holds few values, the pairs
are many more than the rows it gives, and none of them was priced. A
stock level procedure joining a district to its order lines on the
warehouse, a key of one value on both sides, was merged on it while the
statistics of the order lines were still being gathered. It paired a
thousand rows with each of thirty thousand, and read the right run back
from the spill area for every left row, for a few hundred rows.

A merge join now adds the pairs its key matches, the product of its
operands' rows over the larger count of distinct values of its key
(`Space::merge_pairs`), where that is more than the rows it gives. The
distinct values are those the class of the key's equality counts of each
operand's relation, bounded by the operand's rows (`Model::key_distinct`).
A key of one value on both sides is priced as the whole product. The
merge join matches on one key and judges the other equalities of its
condition of each pair (`exec/join/merge.rs`), so it is priced as it
runs. Matching on several key columns at once would let it judge fewer
pairs, by comparing the keys as one tuple and holding runs of the whole
tuple; it is not built.

A hash join hashes every equality of its condition, so its keys match
only pairs of every equality's value, and an index nested-loop join pays,
for each probe, the rows the probe finds (D35). A nested loop pays the
product of its operands. None of them changes. The statistics pass and
its window are unchanged, and nothing waits for them.

#### D1235. A load by column into a table of keys and indexes adds each group's entries at once, a leaf's run at a time

A load by column (D1148) went only into a table of no index and no key,
so a table of a primary key or a foreign key, which most are, loaded
row by row. Such a table now loads by column too, where its UNIQUE
constraints have no period and each foreign key references another
table, of no subtable, through an index of exactly its referenced
columns, with no period. Its group is written and logged as its extent,
as a table of no index's is, and then each index takes the group's
entries at once through `Index::insert_sorted`. A B-link tree sorts
them and writes them a leaf's run at a time: each leaf a run falls in is
reached and locked once for the keys it covers, each key searched,
written and found alone or not under the leaf's latch as one key's
insert does, and a leaf that fills splits as it would for one key, the
keys after it going down again. A reader sees each entry as it is
written, as it does one written alone. Any other method keeps the
default, `insert_from` of each entry in turn. The checkpoint gate is
held from the group to its last entry, so a checkpoint holds both or
neither. An entry's undo is logged even when its insert fails, as an
entry absent is removed as nothing.

A row whose key was not alone in a unique index is noted for the
statement's end, which checks it as a row inserted alone is checked.
A key of a row in a group of a load still open in another transaction
is that transaction's change pending (D1236), so the check fails the
whole statement as another transaction's row of the key does (SQLCODE
-911, SQLSTATE TB911), exactly as it fails a multi-row INSERT of the
row path today, whether the other row is a version in the tree or a row
of an open load's group; it never rests on a row that may yet be rolled
back. A foreign key's distinct
keys among the group's rows are each looked up once in its referenced
table before the group is written, and a key that matches no row sends
the rows to the row path, which names it; nothing of the group is
written before that. A load into a table of foreign keys holds back no
index (D532), as a write to a table it references reads its rows by
them.

Recovery mends the entries of an index reopened as its checkpoint left
it a group at a time: the entries of the rows the group's extent holds
are taken back, as a row's are under its images, and then the entries
of the rows it holds now that an index lacks are added at once.

#### D1236. A key of a row in another transaction's open load is pending to a UNIQUE check

A UNIQUE check at a statement's end reads the newest state of each other
row its key's entries name. A row a load wrote straight into a frozen
group (D533) has no version in the tree, and its state was read from its
group as if it stood, whoever made the group. So a row of another
transaction's open load was taken as a committed holder of its key, and
an insert of that key failed as a duplicate (SQLSTATE 23000) though the
load might yet roll back. The newest state of a frozen row now tells
the group's maker: a row of a group of another transaction still open
is that transaction's change pending, as a version in the tree made by
it is, so the check fails the statement as a key another transaction is
changing does (SQLCODE -911), and an insert of the key after the load
rolls back goes in.

#### D1240. A hash join run in parallel whose built operand outgrows its grant is built in parts and probed in passes

A hash join's operand read by its morsels was held whole in its grant,
and once its rows passed it the join gave way. The part was dropped and
the plan run again on the statement's thread alone, as the serial join
that partitions both operands (D38). At a grant of a few GiB a build of
tens of millions of rows was that rerun, on one thread.

The build now goes on in parts (`exec/parallel/probe/spilled.rs`). Each
built row goes to one of 64 parts by the low six bits of its key's hash,
seeded and not direct (D601). A pass's table places its rows by the high
bits of the hash, so a table made of a few parts still spreads them over
all its slots and its own parts (D1080). A part's rows are held in a list
of its share of a pass and written to the join's spill area past it, in
the order the operand gave them, so a probing row meets its matches in
the order one table gives them. A row whose key matches nothing is left
out, as the table leaves it out. The key columns of every row are kept
beside the parts, and the runtime filters the probing side's scans are
told are made of them once the operand is read, the filters of the
whole operand (D369).

The parts are then put in passes, in order, each of no more than a third
of what the grant has free once the keys are let go, as the first pass's
table is held to the end beside the pass probed and the next. A part
past a pass is split into its 64 cells by the hash's next six bits. A
built row weighs in a pass what its batch was charged a row and its
place in the table, as the planner weighs a built row by its width and
an entry, not what it takes held as values, which its list spills past
its share. The
first pass's table is made at once and its join is a step of the
pipeline, with a step before its probe that keeps the rows whose keys
fall in its cells. The pipeline's morsels are those of each pass in
turn (`exec/parallel/passes.rs`), each pass's numbered on after the
pass before, so a grouping or a gathering over it reads the passes as
more morsels. A pass past the first reads the pipeline's scans again,
with the same conditions, zones and runtime filters. Its table is made
of its parts by the operand's threads when its first morsel is asked
for, and let go once its last is. A probing row's key falls in one pass
alone. A row of a key that matches nothing is kept by the first pass
alone, so a LEFT join pads it once and an antijoin keeps it once.

Rescanning the probing side costs a pass. The most passes a join may
take come from the planner's constants (`cost/spill.rs`, `pass_limit`).
Partitioning instead writes and reads each probing row once more,
PARTITIONED_ROW and SPILLED_BYTE a byte in rows of a scan, and the built
rows are written once either way. So passes win while the passes past
the first, times what making a probing row again costs, stay within
that. The cost of a probing row is the probing side's plan cost over its
estimated rows (`rescanned`), at least a scanned row's, and its bytes
are taken at an entry's, the least a row holds, so the limit errs low,
in the plan as at the run, which knows no estimate of its width.
The planner costs a join run in parallel past its grant the least of
both operands partitioned and the build written once and the probing
side read again for each pass (`passed_spilled`). Only an inner join
and a LEFT one whose left probes are weighed so, as only those are steps
of a pipeline that builds its operand in parts. A semi join, an antijoin
or a join whose preserved rows are built is weighed partitioned, which
is how it runs, so it is not chosen over the probes of an index for
passes it never takes. The same limit is
checked as the operand is read, of its passes as its morsels so far
project them, and a build past it gives way at once, its lists dropped
with the spill areas they hold.

These still give way. A probing side that is not scans in no order,
filters, projections and the probes of hash joins, as an index scan's or
an ordered scan's rows come in an order a plan above may rely on and
passes would lose; a second join of the same pipeline built past its
grant, as passes would multiply; a cell past a pass; keys that do not
fit the grant beside what it held before; and more passes than the
limit. A pass drops a probing row once it has hashed its keys itself, a
second hash of the probe's own; the probe hands its hash to such a step
once the shared table exposes it (D1242).

#### D1241. A scan judges a top-N's bound of each row, and a top-N of the column store runs in parallel on one shared bound

A sort under FETCH FIRST tells the scan under it the bound of its first
key (D379), and the scan passed over groups and parts whose zone maps
lie past it. Within a part it read every row. A filter of a wide column
over such a scan, as LIKE of a text, then decoded that column of every
row of every part read, though the sort would drop nearly all of them
by their key. And D291 kept such a sort of a column store table on the
statement's thread, from when a worker made each row of its morsel.
Since D380 a morsel is read and sorted as batches, so that reason no
longer held.

The scan now judges the bound of each row (`engine/columns/judged.rs`).
A bound that holds a value is a comparison of its column with that
value, at or before it as the key is ordered, read as each run of a
group is judged and judged by the kernel over the column's vector. A
bound that holds none yet is not judged, and its column is not decoded
for it. The rows a run keeps are decoded of the filter's other columns
at their places alone (D366). A row left out is past the first key of
the greatest row the sort holds, so the sort would drop it whatever its
other keys. A null is left out too, as a bound is told only of a key
whose nulls sort last, and it holds no null. A row equal to the bound
is kept, as the sort's other keys or its peers decide of it. The bound
is told only where no filter or projection on the way can raise (D379),
so no error of a row left out is lost. A scan may still give a run
whole where most of its rows are kept, as the sort judges every row it
is given.

A sort over a column store table that FETCH FIRST asks for a count of
rows, ONLY, is now a part (`physical/parallel.rs`, `Asked::under`), as
it is over the row store. The planner knows it by the limit above it,
through what the limit tells a sort through, a projection that raises
nothing. A whole sort of one, one under OFFSET alone, WITH TIES or of a
percentage stays on the statement's thread as before. A part's pipeline
read by such a sort of few rows, whose batches hold every column, is
told what the serial stream is told (`Pipeline::topped`,
`parallel/sorted.rs`). Each branch's scan is told the bound through its
steps as `Deferred` carries it, by a split told one conjunct more
(`Split::told`). The columns neither a step nor a key reads are left
late past the pipeline's end, and each morsel's sort decodes them of
the rows it gives alone, where a morsel decoded them of every row its
filter kept.

One bound is shared by every morsel (`Threshold::shared`). A filter
that keeps few rows leaves most morsels with fewer rows than are asked,
so a morsel's own rows seldom prove a bound. Each morsel's sort
therefore offers the bound the first key of every row it takes, and the
bound keeps the first so many keys offered by them all. Once as many
are offered as rows are asked, the bound is the last of those. That
many rows of the sort's input are then at or before it, so no row past
it is among the first of all. The bound only narrows, under a lock, and
a scan that reads it before another thread narrowed it only reads more
rows. Each morsel keeps its rows equal to the bound, and the runs are
merged in morsel order as before, so rows of equal keys come in the
order the serial sort gives them.

No result and no plan depends on the order the threads narrow the
bound in, nor on when a scan reads it. The plan is chosen before any
morsel is read and reads no bound. A row among the first of all is
never past the bound, whatever it holds when the row is judged, as the
bound is never before the last of those rows, so every morsel's run
holds each such row of its morsel. A morsel's run is its own first rows
in the order of its rows, and the runs are merged in morsel order, so
the rows given and the order of peers are those of the keys and the
rows' places alone. What does vary from run to run is how many rows a
scan reads before the bound narrows, which EXPLAIN ANALYZE counts of a
part, and no more than that.

The scan judges the bound as the test the bound gives of a row
(`Threshold::row_test`, `Pred::now` in `engine/columns/judged.rs`), a
conjunct judged as any other the scan is told. The bound chooses the
kind of test by the kind of value it holds, so a bound of another kind
of key is judged by the same loop.

A run the scan judged and kept one row in eight or more of is given
whole, and its late columns were then decoded with it (D366), as those
rows were taken to be the ones kept. Under a sort's bound the sort
keeps few of them, so such a run now leaves its late columns late
(`frozen/batches/run.rs`).

The rows given, their order and the errors are as before. EXPLAIN shows
`Parallel` over such a sort, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE counts fewer rows of
its scan.

#### D1242. A probe of a table built for a pipeline pairs the rows a pass keeps alone, told each row's seeded key hash, and drops the rest before it looks any up

A join whose built operand passes its grant builds and probes it in
passes, each pass holding some parts of it. A pass pairs the probing
rows whose keys fall in its parts, and leaves the rest to the pass that
holds theirs. The probe of a shared table (`batch/joined/shared/kept.rs`)
and its whole batch's match (`matched_kept`) take what a pass keeps, a
test of a row's key hash. The hash they are told is the one a hashed
table's probe makes, seeded as the table's. A direct table's probe finds
its rows by a key's number (D601), so its rows are hashed a second time
for the test, and a row falls in the same pass whatever kind of table a
pass makes. A key that matches no row, a null's where a null matches
nothing, has no hash, and the test is told so. The pass that takes the
rows of no part, the first, keeps it.

A row a pass does not keep is dropped once the batch is hashed, before
it is screened by a Bloom filter (D1087), looked up or paired. So
no slot is read for it, and a LEFT join pairs it with nulls only in the
pass that keeps it, never twice. A probe told nothing to keep makes its
hashes once and drops no row, its loop over the rows unchanged, at the
cost of one test of the batch.

#### D1245. A window carries only the columns it and those above read, its rows narrowed to them, and merges its partitions in order only where an order is asked

The pruning of the columns no one reads (D1167) left a window as it
was, with all it read. So every window over a wide table read every
column of it, and a window run a row at a time on its threads (D295,
D1227) held, sorted, split and spilled each row whole. Over a table of
a hundred columns the rows its partitions held were mostly text no one
read, and the statement's thread spent its time sizing and spilling
them.

A window now reads its partitioning's columns, its ordering's, and its
calls' arguments, filters and frames' offsets, and passes on those of
its input's columns read above it (`physical/blind/pruned/windowed.rs`).
Every call is computed whether or not one above reads it, so no error a
call raises is lost, as a projection's expressions are. Its input is
pruned as a sort's is, so the scan under it reads those columns alone.
A window that searches for a row pattern, or whose call holds a
subquery, is left as it is.

Pruned, a window's input still gives a row a place for each column,
null where nothing reads it, and so does a scan that reads some of its
table's columns. A window under a projection is then narrowed
(`pruned/narrowed.rs`). The projection under it keeps the columns that
hold a value, or a projection of them is put over the scan, and the
window's partitioning, its ordering, its calls, its sort's keys and the
projection above it are numbered anew. A column a nested window function
gives (ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §6.11) moves with the calls'. The projection
above gives what it gave, so nothing above it changes. A window under
any other operator keeps its nulls, which cost nothing in a batch's
vectors.

A window run in parallel a row at a time merged its partitions' lists
back by its sort keys on the statement's thread (D1227). A window
planned for no order asked of it now says so (`ordered`, set in
`physical/ordered.rs`), and its lists are read one after another
instead. Every other window, and any made elsewhere, is ordered, so the
merge is left out only where the planner knows nothing above reads its
rows in an order.

A window split by row stops at a cancel in each of its phases as a scan
does. Its rows are split as the scans' morsels are read, which look for
a cancel, and each partition's thread reads its rows through the
statement's stop and looks again at each chunk of a run its sort
writes (D44). Cancelled wherever it lands, it leaves nothing of its
lists held.

A run of morsels whose reader dropped it (D290) took no more morsels
and woke the idle workers, but its work and the results not read went
only with the pool's last hold on the run, as a worker next looked at
it. So a statement could return, cancelled or ended early, with its
partitions' lists and their spill areas still held, seen by the next
statement's grant and by MEMORY_RESERVATIONS. The drop now waits for
the morsels running, which a cancelled statement's do at their next
row, as each reads through the statement's stop. It then lets go of the
work and of the unread results on the reader's thread before it
returns (`exec/parallel/run.rs`). A statement that ends early with no
cancel, as a FETCH FIRST met does, waits for at most a morsel's work on
each thread, which no stop bounds, as the statement has not stopped.

#### D1246. A run's workers number one fewer than its degree, the statement's thread the last, and a thread's runs keep their workers

A run of morsels let no more morsels run at once than its degree (D290),
but it was offered to every worker of the pool, and its reader, the
statement's thread, took morsels too while it waited. With as many
workers as the degree, one thread more than the degree took turns at
the run's morsels, and where the reader worked on a result between two
morsels, merging a morsel's groups or making rows, it worked beside a
full degree of workers. One thread more than the processors a statement
was given is no harm by itself. The harm is the order of the results. A
run gives its results in the order of its morsels and takes no morsel
more than its window past the one its reader waits for, so a morsel on
a thread that shares its processor holds back every thread that has one
to itself, once they have taken the window's morsels.

The workers of the pool now run one morsel fewer of a run at once than
its degree, and the reader's thread is the last of the degree's
(`exec/parallel/run.rs`). It takes a morsel itself whenever it has to
wait for one, as before, so a reader with nothing to do between results
works as a worker does, and one that works on its results does so
beside one worker fewer. No measure of the reader's work is taken and
no threshold decides. A reader that waits has just found no morsel to
take, so no worker could have taken one in its place, and nothing is
lost by counting it always. A run of degree 1 is offered to no worker
and is its reader's alone, as before, and one of degree 2 has one
worker beside its reader.

Which workers serve a run is fixed as it is offered
(`threads/pool.rs`). A job is served by as many workers as it asks,
numbered on from its first and round past the pool's last. The jobs one
thread offers are served by the same workers, the lowest numbers of a
thread offering alone, so the threads busy for a statement are the same
from one of its runs to the next and from one statement of a session's
thread to the next. Jobs of other threads offered meanwhile are
numbered on past them, so statements running at once spread over the
pool before they share a worker. Whatever places threads on processors,
the system's scheduler or a tool that pins them, then meets as many
busy threads as the degree, the same ones, where it met one more, a
different set each run.

The rows a statement gives, their order and its errors are as before,
as each morsel's result is still given in the order of the morsels.
EXECUTOR.DEGREE keeps its meaning, the most threads a statement's query
runs on at once, its own among them, which the executor now keeps.

#### D1247. A grouping stops handing morsels whole once the statement thread's table holds more groups than a morsel has rows

A morsel whose groups are few beside its rows is handed whole to the
statement's thread, which merges it into one table of its own (D356),
on the reckoning that merging a group costs what grouping a row or two
does, so that thread keeps up. The test was of the morsel alone. A
grouping by a column most of whose rows hold one value, the others many
values, passed it with every morsel, a few hundred groups of some
thousands of rows, and the statement's thread merged every group of the
grouping into one table by itself. That table is not a morsel's. It
holds every group there is, so each merge looks a key up outside the
processor's cache, each new key is added to lanes that grow by copying,
and the groups are finished by that one thread at the end. The rows
cost less than reckoned too, as a run of one value is taken with no
lookup. The statement's thread was busy without pause and the workers
waited on it.

What makes the merge cheap is that the grouping has few groups in all,
which no morsel can tell and the statement thread's table can. So the
morsel's test stands and the grouping's is added
(`exec/parallel/grouped/waves.rs`). Morsels are handed whole while that
table holds no more groups than a morsel has rows, EXECUTOR.MORSEL_ROWS.
No table a thread makes of a morsel holds more, so up to there the
reckoning compares like with like. Once the table holds more, the
statement's thread takes it to the partitions, as a morsel of many
groups after it always did, and from then on no morsel is handed whole.
The grouping then runs as one of many groups does, its morsels split
among the partitions and merged by the threads, each partition's table
given its room once.

The threads group morsels ahead of the one the statement's thread
reads, so as the table passes the bound some morsels have already been
handed whole and others not, by how fast each thread was. That much
depends on timing, and nothing a statement can see does. A morsel
handed whole after the bound is merged into a new table of the
statement's thread, in its order, and that table is taken to the
partitions before the next morsel that was split, so each partition
still merges its morsels in the order of their numbers. The groups,
their order, each set function's value, the warnings and the errors are
those of the plan run alone, whichever morsels were handed whole. The plan is chosen before
any morsel is read and does not change. What a grouping holds of its
grant at a moment may differ by a few morsels' groups, as it already
did by the morsels grouped ahead.

#### D1250. A record of a transaction reaches the log only while it may still commit, or with its abort record after it

A transaction holds its records until its commit, and a checkpoint, its
gate shut, writes what every open transaction holds, finding each by its
buffer noted among the database's (D470). A rollback undid its changes
under the gate and wrote its abort record there, if a record of it had
reached the log. It left the records it still held in its buffer, which
stayed noted until the transaction was dropped, after the gate was left.
A checkpoint taking the gate in between wrote them. They then stood in
the log, before the checkpoint's position, with no commit record and no
abort record after them. Recovery reads such records as those of a
transaction a crash interrupted and puts each row back as its record
found it (D25). When another transaction had since updated the row and
committed before the position of the image recovered from, its change
was in the image and not redone, and the row was put back over it. The
commit lost that row and kept its others.

Recovery read that far back when a transaction open at the image's
checkpoint had written its first record before them. It also did
through a second fault. The write of held records noted the
transaction's first record, from which the log is kept and recovery
reads, once it had let the buffer's lock go. A transaction dropped
meanwhile had already looked for a first to forget and found none. That
first then stayed noted while the database ran, every later image
started at it, and the log was never truncated past it.

A record of a transaction now reaches the log only while the
transaction may still commit, or with its abort record after it. A
rollback drops the records it holds under the gate, in the step that
decides its abort record (`Txn::log_abort`, `Txn::drop_held`), so a
checkpoint finds none of a transaction rolled back, however long the
transaction is kept after. A statement, mark or savepoint undone drops
its held records, or logs those written as undone, under the gate too
(D470). A database deposed writes no abort record, its log being its
replica's, and writes no held record either. The primary promoted
aborts each transaction that log leaves open (D57).

A write notes a first record with the buffer locked. A transaction's end
marks the buffer over and reads whether a first was noted, under that
lock (`TxLog::write`, `Txn::forget_held`). So the end finds the first
and forgets it, or the write finds the transaction over and notes none.

Recovery is unchanged. Nothing in the log tells a transaction rolled
back in memory from one a crash stopped, so the rule is kept where
records are written.

#### D1251. A column store's scan judges a LIKE of a constant pattern of each chunk's texts where they lie, those coded by symbols by the pattern's machine stepped a code at a time

A filter's LIKE of a column and a constant pattern reached the scan
only as the bounds of the pattern's prefix (D31), and a pattern that
begins with `%` has none. So the scan gave every row with the LIKE's
column decoded, and the filter searched the text (D1074, D1118, D1119).
Each text was read out of its chunk, checked to be UTF-8 and copied, to
be searched once and, of nearly every row, dropped, and of a chunk
coded by a table of symbols (D31) it was decoded from its codes first.

The scan is now told the LIKE itself, beside the bounds of its prefix,
and NOT LIKE as the same with its answer turned (`Conjunct::Like`,
`logical/pushed.rs`). It is told a LIKE of a column as it is, whose
pattern and escape character are constants, not null, that raise no
error, the pattern with no arbitrary character specifier `_`. A pattern
with `_` matches a character, which a machine over octets does not
count. A LIKE under a collation that folds case or contracts characters
is not of the column as it is, as the binder folds both sides or calls
the collation (`binder/collation.rs`), so it is not told. LIKE pads no
string (ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §8.5 SR3d), so under the default collation
and under one of NO PAD that compares each character as itself (D1183)
it matches the same octets, and both are told. An ESCAPE character only
makes `%`, `_` or itself a character of a piece, so a pattern with one
is told like any other.

The pattern is made one machine over octets, once for the statement
(`value/like/machine.rs`). Its pieces are those of D1074. The states
are, in this order, the octets of the first piece matched so far, where
any other octet leaves no match, then of each piece between the octets
of it matched so far, and then the same of the last piece. A piece is
searched for as Knuth, Morris and Pratt, "Fast Pattern Matching in
Strings" (SIAM Journal on Computing, 1977), search for a string. An
octet that does not go on falls back to the longest start of the piece
that the octets read end with, so no octet is read twice. The last
piece is searched for to the value's end, and the value matches if it
ends in the state of the whole piece. A pattern that ends in `%` has in
its place an accepting state that no octet leaves, and a pattern of no
`%` a state that any further octet leaves for no match. A piece is
found where it first ends, which leaves the most of the value to the
pieces after it, so the machine matches what the pieces match. A test
compares the two over every string of three octets up to seven long,
for patterns of each shape.

A state is held in one octet, so that a table of states is an octet a
place. The states are the octets of the pieces and two more, and one
value of the octet is left for a code of no symbol. So a pattern whose
pieces are 253 octets together at most has a machine, and a longer one
is not told to the scan.

Searching a text's codes for the codes of a piece would be wrong. The
encoder takes the longest symbol at each place, so a piece is coded in
as many ways as there are octets before it. The scan steps the machine
over the codes instead (`engine/columns/fsst/stepped.rs`). For each
state and each symbol it steps the machine over the symbol's octets
once and keeps the state after in a table, and a text is then matched
by one place of the table for each code. A piece that ends inside a
symbol is found there, since the symbol's octets after it step the
machine on from the piece's end, into the states of the next piece or
into the accepting state. The escape code quotes the octet after it,
which steps the machine by itself. A state's row therefore has 256
places for codes and 256 for quoted octets, and a pattern's table is at
most 255 rows of 512 octets. The table is made once for a pattern and a
table of symbols. A group's chunks of a column are coded by one table,
written in each (D31), so the scan keeps the steps beside the table
they were made of and makes them again only when a chunk's table
differs, which is once a group (`Stepped`, held by `Prepared`).

A text's codes are read in runs that leave the machine in the state it
is in. Most of a text leaves it at the start of a piece, as few symbols
end with a start of the piece. The loop of a run asks only whether the
place it reads holds the state it is in, and carries from one code to
the next only whether an octet is quoted, so no read waits for the one
before it. A step that changes the state ends the run, and the next run
reads the new state's row. Reading stops at a state no octet leaves.

A column's chunks are each in the encoding that takes fewest bytes
(D31), so one run of a scan reads chunks coded by symbols beside chunks
kept as dictionaries, plain or as one value. The scan therefore judges
the LIKE a chunk at a time, of a VARCHAR column, and never decodes the
column to judge it (`engine/columns/judged/coded.rs`). A chunk coded by
symbols is judged by the steps above. Any other chunk of texts keeps
each text's octets as they were written, each alone, once for the chunk
or as a dictionary's entries, and the pattern's pieces are searched for
in those octets where they lie (D1074), with no text copied and none
checked to be UTF-8.

That search is exact because the octets are text. The field of a
character string in a record is the octets of the string its value
holds (`value/types/character.rs`), and a value holds a string of the
language, which is UTF-8 by its type, so every string written to a
chunk was UTF-8 when written and no check at reading adds to that. A
piece is whole characters, and in UTF-8 no character's octets begin
inside another's, so a piece found among a text's octets is found at a
character of it. A chunk that fails its own structure, with codes of no
symbol, codes that end in an escape, or a field or an entry that lies
outside the octets the chunk holds, is not judged. Every row asked of
it is kept, once, in the place of any judged before the fault was met,
and the filter's decoding of the chunk raises what is malformed as it
did before. A chunk whose structure holds but whose octets are damaged
is searched as it is, as a comparison judged in place reads it (D360),
and the rows it keeps are checked as they are decoded.

The scan judges the LIKE of a run after its other conjuncts (D360), of
the rows they kept, since it reads every octet or code of a text where
a comparison reads a few. A null is left out, as LIKE of a null is
unknown (X3.135-1986 §5.14 GR4). Of a CHARACTER column the scan judges
nothing and gives the run's rows, since its strings are padded as they
are read, which no chunk holds. The filter still judges every row the
scan gives (D15). So a row the scan leaves out is one the filter would
leave out, and the rows of the delta tree, which the scan does not
judge, are judged there.

A run of which one row in eight or more is kept is given whole, and the
filter judges every row of it again (D360), so judging the LIKE of such
a run to its end is work done twice. The scan judges a chunk at a time,
so it stops (`whole_by`). Once at least one in eight of the rows asked
of the run are judged, if the rate kept of them, carried to all the
rows asked, comes to one row in eight of the run, the chunks left are
not judged and their rows are kept. The share is the one the run is
given whole by (`KEPT_SHARE`), so no constant is added. Before one in
eight of the rows asked are judged nothing is told, as even every one of
them kept would leave the run short of the share. A LIKE that keeps
every row is so judged of an eighth of each run, and one that keeps few
is judged of every row. A run wrongly taken for whole costs what it cost
before the scan was told the LIKE, and one wrongly judged to its end
costs the judging.

Where a conjunct is asked of a row's values (`Conjunct::matches_key`),
the LIKE is true of a string the pattern matches, never of a null, and
taken as true of any other value, as a large object's, which the filter
reads. Zone maps, Bloom filters and imprints pass over nothing by it, as
the prefix's bounds do that, so the share of a table the planner prices
a scan by (`scan_share`) is what it was.

#### D1252. A run's texts are gathered into one vector of octets and judged UTF-8 once, texts coded by symbols decoded straight into it

A scan gives a character string column of a run of rows as text (D361),
one string of every row's text and where each ends. A run is at most a
vector of rows (D31). The chunks of a column of long strings hold a
hundred or two rows each, as a chunk is what a page holds, so a run
reads a dozen chunks or more.

The string was begun empty and grew as rows were pushed to it, so a run
allocated it again and copied it many times. A dictionary's rows were
pushed one at a time, each read by its own code and judged UTF-8 by
itself. Texts coded by symbols were decoded into a vector of their
chunk's own, judged there and copied to the string. And a run was first
tried as dictionary codes, which copied each dictionary's entries until
a chunk that was no dictionary was met, and all of it was then dropped.

A run's texts are now gathered into one vector of octets
(`engine/columns/texts.rs`). Room is made for it once, of as many octets
as the chunks the run reads take stored, which a dictionary's entries,
varying fields and one value never pass. Texts coded by symbols may pass
it, and the vector then grows as any vector does. Each chunk adds its
octets and where each text ends, and nothing is judged as it is added. A
dictionary's entries and a run of varying fields are added by one copy,
as each field begins where the one before it ends (D1131). Texts coded
by symbols are decoded straight after the octets held
(`engine/columns/fsst.rs`), and copied nowhere else.

The vector is then made the run's text by one judgement of all its
octets, `Kernels::text`, which gives the vector itself as the string
where the octets are UTF-8 as `str::from_utf8` judges them. The core
forbids `unsafe` (R-SAFE-1), so its body is `String::from_utf8`.
`turborel-simd` judges on AVX2 as D1175 does and then takes the vector
for the string, which is sound because every octet of it was just
judged. Each text's end must then lie on a character's boundary, so each
text is UTF-8 alone. Strings that are each UTF-8 are UTF-8 together, and
a text that begins or ends within a character fails that test, so a run
gives text exactly where judging each value by itself would.

Octets that are no text, a position past a chunk's end and a chunk whose
offsets or codes are malformed give no column. The rows are then read as
values, which raises what is malformed, as before.

A CHARACTER string is padded as it is read [X3.135-1986 §8.7 GR7b]. The
spaces are added to the octets by the count of the field's characters,
which are its octets that go on with no character. That is the count of
the text once the octets are judged, and octets that are not text give
no column whatever was counted.

Nothing is made of a dictionary of texts when its chunk is opened, and
nothing of it is kept for the chunk's other runs, which withdraws the
cell of D1298. A run copies the entries it reads from the chunk's own
octets, which costs no more than copying them from a text kept, and
judges them with the rest of the run. A reader that asks for no text
still pays for none.

#### D1253. A LIKE judged of a dictionary's chunk matches each entry once, the entries searched as one arena, and each row by its code

A chunk kept as a dictionary holds each distinct text once, its entries'
octets one after another, and a code a row (D31). The scan's LIKE
(D1251) matched the entry of each row asked for, so an entry many rows
share was searched once for each of them. A filter over a batch did the
same of the texts it was given (`exec/batch/judge/texts.rs`).

The scan now judges the entries (`engine/columns/judged/entries.rs`).
The entries are one arena whose values end where the entries do, so the
pattern's longest piece between two `%`s is searched for in all of it
at once by the database's kernels (`BytesLike::matches_each`, D1119),
which compare a vector of places at a time. An entry the search never
stops in does not match, and one it stops in is matched whole by its
pieces. A pattern of no piece between, as `abc%` is, is matched an
entry at a time. A row is then kept by its code alone, and a null is
left out.

The entries are judged where the rows asked of the chunk are no fewer
than its entries. Judging the entries searches each entry once, and a
row at a time searches the entry of each row asked for, both by the same
pieces over the same octets. So with as many rows as entries or more the
entries are no more octets to search than the rows' entries, whatever
kernels search them, and the arena search only makes them cheaper. With
fewer rows, as an earlier conjunct leaves of a dictionary of many
entries, each row's entry is matched alone and the entries no row asks
for are never read. The bound is that comparison of two counts, so it
has no constant to tune.

A dictionary whose entries do not lie one after another within the
octets the chunk holds, or one of whose codes is of no entry, is not
judged by its entries nor a row at a time, and its rows are kept for the
filter, whose decoding raises what is malformed (D1251).

#### D1254. The first rows of a sort are taken from a grouping's tables under an analyzed plan's counts as under none

EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the statement's plan with a count over each
operator (D376, D378). The top-N that takes its rows from a grouping's
partitions (D1124) looked for the projection, the part and the grouping
by their own shapes, and a count over the projection or the grouping hid
them from it. So the statement analyzed read every group back as a row,
projected it and sorted it, where the statement itself kept a few rows a
partition. The times and the rows it showed were of another plan than
the one that runs.

The top-N now passes those counts and keeps them
(`exec/parallel/grouped/top.rs`, `Counts`), so an analyzed statement
runs as the statement does. The grouping's count takes the groups its
tables made, which is what its estimate is read against. The count of
the projection over the part takes the rows the partitions kept for the
sort, as those are the rows that leave the part. Both take the time of
the part's run and of each row pulled. A part that gives way, and a sort
whose rows are not taken from the tables, count every group in both.

#### D1256. A sort by set functions alone picks its first groups of a partition before their rows are made

A sort that asks for its first rows over a grouping run in parallel takes
them from each partition's table (D1124). The partition gave every group
as a batch first, each set function finished of each group into a column
of results, and then kept the few rows the sort asks. Of a grouping of
very many groups, finishing every function of every group and holding
the columns of results was most of what the partition did, to keep a few
rows.

Where every key of the sort names a set function, the partition now
picks before it makes (`exec/parallel/grouped/top.rs`, `picked_of`). It
finishes the columns of those functions alone, takes its first rows by
them and by the first rows' numbers, and makes the rows of the groups
picked from its table (`exec/table/given.rs`, `row`). The rows and their
order are those the batch of every column gave, as the keys and the tie
by first row are the same.

A set function that no key names is still finished of every group, with
no value kept (`checked_but`). Its result may raise, as a sum past the
range of its type does [ISO/IEC 9075:1992 §6.5 GR2b iv], and the plan run
alone finishes every group and raises it, so the part raises it too. A
count raises nothing and is not finished. An exact total raises only
past the most digits a number has, and a mean only if its total written
at its result's scale is past them, so a column of totals is passed over
by their units, and only a total large enough to raise is finished to
know (`exec/table/states/typed/quiet.rs`). The least or greatest string
is given as it is, raises nothing, and is not finished either.

A sort with a key that names a grouping column or a constant sorts the
batch of every column, as before. A column of results is made at its
length, so its values do not move as it fills.

#### D1258. An abort record that cannot be appended stops the database

A rollback appends its abort record after the records of its transaction
already in the log, and ignored a failure of that append, on the ground
that recovery undoes a transaction with no commit record either way.
D1250 shows where that ground gives way. The records then stand in the
log with no end, the transaction is rolled back in memory and its locks
released, and if the log takes records again the next writer of its rows
commits after them. Recovery that reads so far back puts the rows back
over that commit.

Whether a log takes records after it refused one is the log's own
matter. The file log mostly does not. A write that fails, of the records
its buffer held or of the zeros written ahead, leaves the segment
refusing appends until the log is opened again (`BlockFile::publish`),
and a segment is begun only after an append that succeeded. Yet a change
of the log's formats begins one before the next append
(`rotate_for_formats`), and a record's own encoding can fail with
nothing written. A log is a plug-in, and `Log::append` promises nothing
of the appends after one that failed.

So the rule is kept above the log. A rollback whose abort record cannot
be appended, a record of its transaction having reached the log, stops
the database as a failed sync does (`Txn::log_abort`,
`Transactions::stop_changes`, D25). It takes no row change, no commit
that wrote, no definition and no checkpoint (SQLCODE -915, naming the
abort record) until it is opened again and recovered. Recovery then
undoes the transaction as one a crash interrupted, and rightly, nothing
having been committed over its rows since. Reads and rollbacks go on. A
transaction that would write those rows makes that write after the locks
on them are released, which follows the stop, and every row change,
load and commit record asks first whether the database takes changes. A
commit written and not yet synced as the database stops is in doubt, as
after a failed sync. The stop is told to the sink with the first change
refused.

The abort record is still not synced. The sync of a later commit makes
it durable first, being before it in the log, and a crash that loses it
loses every commit after it.

A commit record that cannot be appended needs no rule of its own. Its
transaction is rolled back, the run that failed having noted that a
record of it may have reached the log (`TxLog::write`), so its abort
record is appended after whatever was, or the database stops by this
rule. It stops so even where the log refused the whole run, as how
much of a run reached a log that failed is not known above it. With
the file log nothing is lost by that, a segment that refused a write
taking no append until the log is opened again.

#### D1259. A transaction dropped without its end is rolled back by its drop, or stops the database

A transaction ends by its commit or its rollback. One dropped with
neither released its table locks, its row waits and its snapshot, and
did nothing more. No change was undone, no engine was told, no end
record was written, and the records it held were discarded. Its versions
stayed in the row store as those of an open transaction. Readers went on
reading the versions before them. The next writer of one of its rows was
refused as by a writer still at work (SQLCODE -911) for the life of the
process, or with LOCKS.WAIT ON waited for an end already given. A
checkpoint captured the versions, the log holding no record of them, and
after a crash recovery had nothing to undo them by. The versions before
them were in the undo store, which does not outlive the process, so
every read of the table then failed (SQLCODE -916), its committed rows
with it.

A session's drop left its transaction so when no call could be entered:
the session left busy by a panic in a call's entry, its database
retired (D57) or opened again in place since. A client's disconnection,
a server's stop and a panic within a statement do not come to this. The
call's own guard is dropped first, and the session then rolls back. The
same state was reached where a commit or a rollback returned before it
undid anything, on a poisoned lock or a snapshot refused.

The drop now ends it (`txn/release.rs`). A transaction dropped still
open, its `open` mark not yet cleared by the release every commit and
every rollback makes, that joined an engine is rolled back by the steps
a session's rollback takes (`Txn::undo_whole`). Under the gate its
changes are undone, each engine it joined is told, the records it holds
are dropped and its abort record is written (D1250, D1258). One that
joined nothing, as the transactions that only hold a table's lock for a
definition, is left as it was. A session dropped with no call to enter
ends its transaction itself, its cursors closed first
(`Session::end_unentered`).

A rollback in a drop runs where nobody chose, so it may wait for nothing
its thread holds. It takes the gate, the transaction's own state, its
engines' latches and the log. A transaction is held by its session
alone, as its own, as the one its running call notes and in a routine's
host, and by the database's list of commits in doubt, which are not
open. No executor, cursor or plan holds one. So the last reference to an
open transaction that joined an engine is dropped in one of three
places. The first is the start of a session's drop, where a session
rolled back before too. The second is the end of a call that ends a
transaction, when the end returned early (`Session::rollback_in`,
`Session::commit_in`). The third is the return of a function that began
a transaction of its own, which ends it on every path but a failure of
the end itself (`db/assertions.rs`). The thread is in no engine at any
of them, and the gate taken again by its holder does not wait
(`sync::Gate`).

Where the rollback cannot be trusted, or fails, the database stops
taking changes as after a failed sync (`Transactions::stop_changes`,
D1258) and the tables whose locks the transaction holds are marked
damaged (D19). That is so while a panic unwinds, when a second panic
would end the process, with the lock of the transaction's state
poisoned, its bookkeeping left half changed, with its commit under way,
its participants already taken, when a change cannot be undone or an
engine refuses, and when the rollback itself panics, which the drop
catches. A database stopped takes no checkpoint, so no image holds a
version left so, and commits nothing, so nothing is committed over one.
Opening it again recovers it from its last checkpoint and its log.

For this a commit pays one load of the `open` mark, in its
transaction's drop, and takes no lock.

#### D1260. Morsels whose tables reduce nothing hand their rows to the partitions ungrouped

A grouping run in parallel groups each morsel in a table of its own and
hands the table's groups to the partitions, which merge them (D355,
D356). The table pays where it reduces: many rows leave as few groups,
and the partitions merge few. Where nearly every row of a morsel is a
group of its own, the table found nothing to merge. Every lookup missed
and every slot was taken for a group the partition finds again by the
same hash, so the morsel's table was work done twice.

The morsels of such a grouping now hand their rows on ungrouped
(`exec/batch/groups/morsel.rs`, `rows_apart`). Each row is made a group
of its own: its key appended, its hash kept, its first row its own
number, its set functions fed its one row. No group is looked for and no
slot is taken (`exec/table.rs`, `appended`). What is handed on has the
form a morsel's groups always had, so the partitions merge it, hold it
and spill it as before, and a key the morsel held twice is merged there.
The groups, their order and their results are unchanged. Only where a
row is first grouped differs.

Whether to group is the workers' own measurement, never the planner's
estimate (`exec/parallel/grouped/waves.rs`, `Reduction`). Each morsel's
table tells the groups it ended with of the rows it took. After a table
that left more than 750 groups a thousand rows the next morsels are
handed on ungrouped. A table spends a lookup and a slot on each row, and
saves, for each row it merges, the appending, the ordering by partition
and the lookup the partition would spend on it. Where the two meet was
measured, the hand-over forced on and forced off over groupings of
integer keys whose morsels leave from 640 to 1000 groups a thousand
rows. Where every group is new to its partition, the two were level at
640 and the hand-over was ahead at 790 and above. Where the keys are few
in all, so that the partitions merge the rows anyway into tables that
stay small, it was ahead at 730 and above. The bound sits between the
ratio measured level and the least measured ahead of both kinds.

One morsel in sixteen still makes a table. It gives back a sixteenth of
what the others save, and data that turns to few groups is grouped in
its morsels again within sixteen of them.

Two things follow from rows of one key arriving as several groups. A
partition's table finds a key the morsel holds twice in the group its
first made, as its merge gives a new group its slot before the next is
looked up (D1275, `exec/table/made.rs`). And a morsel that must go to
the spill as it is, the grant holding nothing more, is grouped first
(`waves.rs`, `regrouped`). A partition read back is split by its groups'
hashes where it outgrows the grant, and rows of one key share a hash, so
a key held many times must be one group there. Nothing written to the
spill holds a key twice, then, and its form needs no word for it.

#### D1262. A grouping's threads lead the statement's thread by more morsels while the grant has room for what they hold

A run gives its results in the order of its morsels and took no morsel
more than two a thread past the one its reader waits for (D290), so
that a reader stopping early left little read for nothing. Where the
morsels of a run cost unevenly, as under a filter that keeps the rows
of some and few of others, or its reader works in bursts, the threads
that finished early had taken the window's morsels and waited for the
one slow morsel the reader wanted, most of the processors idle
meanwhile.

A reader that holds all its input stops early of nothing, so its run
may lead it further. A grouping read by batch now asks its run a lead
(`exec/parallel/run.rs`, `Lead`, `grouped/waves.rs`), sixteen morsels
a thread in place of two. A sweep of 2 to 128 a thread, over groupings
of few groups and of many, whose morsels cost unevenly, and a join's
probe that makes several rows of each, on eight threads and on two,
falls to sixteen and is level past it, so the least that is level is
taken, as a longer lead only holds more. A stream stays at two, as its reader sets its
pace and the rows held ahead of it are bounded by the window (D1153).
A sort, a join's build and the partitioned operators stay at two as
well, their morsels charged to the grant as they are gathered (D1150).

What the threads of a grouping hold ahead of the statement's thread was
charged to nothing until it was read (D1155), which two morsels a
thread kept small. So the lead is metered. Each morsel's groups count
their bytes as its thread lands them and no longer once the reader is
given them, and a thread takes a morsel past the two a thread only
while the bytes so held are fewer than what the grant has left, its
bytes less those the grouping holds. At any moment, then, the bytes the
grouping holds and the bytes held ahead of its reader are within the
grant, but for the one morsel each thread is grouping at that moment,
as before. Of a small MEMORY.WORK_BYTES the lead narrows itself to the
two a thread it was.

The meter is apart from the grant's own count and decides nothing else.
The reader charges each morsel's groups as it takes them, in the order
of the morsels, as before, and by those charges alone a wave is merged,
a partition written to the spill or the grouping gives way. So how many
waves a grouping merges and how often it spills are the same whatever
its lead, and whatever the threads' timing. The order of the results is
kept as it was. Each partition merges its morsels in the order of their
numbers, so a set function whose state depends on the order of its
values, as MIN of strings equal under their collation and different in
their octets, gives what the plan run alone gives. Timing changes when
a thread waits, and nothing a statement can see.

#### D1267. A column read only for its octet length is given by its scan with its lengths and never decoded

OCTET_LENGTH of a column counted the octets of each value's text
(`functions/strings/counts.rs`), so the scan first made that text. Of a
column store that meant decoding every chunk the statement read, a
dictionary's entries checked and copied and texts coded by symbols
written out, to read from each value only how long it was. A chunk
holds that length without its text. A varying chunk has it between two
ends, a constant chunk in its one field, a dictionary in the ends of the
value's entry, and texts coded by symbols in the lengths of their codes'
symbols, an escaped octet counting one.

A column whose text no operator of a stream reads, nor whoever reads
the stream, is now asked of its scan measured
(`exec/batch/late.rs`, `Deferred::measuring`). The scan of a column
store reads the length of each row's value from the chunks it has open
(`engine/columns/encoded/lengths.rs`, `scan/lengths.rs`) and gives the
column late, as its rows' places (D361), with those lengths beside them
(`storage/batch/late/measured.rs`). OCTET_LENGTH of such a column reads
the lengths. `Batch::resolve` leaves the column late, so it is not
decoded at the stream's end, and it is measured whether or not an
operator drops rows.

Two readers do not read a column's text. One is OCTET_LENGTH of the
column itself, alone or within an expression. The other is a filter's
conjunct that compares the column with the empty string by octets,
neither padded, as a collation of NO PAD that orders strings as their
octets do compares them (D1183). Under that comparison alone a string
of no octets equals the empty string and every other string comes after
it, so the conjunct is the comparison of the string's octet length with
0, and the filter judges it of the lengths
(`exec/batch/judge/measured.rs`). The scan, told the same conjunct,
judges it of the lengths it takes of the run
(`engine/columns/judged/lengths.rs`), and the lengths of a run judged
whole are kept for the run's batch (`prepared/lengths.rs`), so a run's
chunks are read for their lengths once. This does not hold under a collation
that pads with spaces, where a string of spaces equals the empty string
whatever its length, nor for any other constant. Such a conjunct reads
the column's text, as CHAR_LENGTH, a grouping column and every other
expression do, and the column is then decoded as before. Readers that
ask for measured columns are a grouping, on one thread or many, by the
arguments of its set functions and its grouping columns, and a
projection that computes, of a statement or within a stream. A join's
operand asks for none.

The lengths are exact. A VARCHAR value is written in a chunk as the
octets of its text (D31), and texts coded by symbols decode to exactly
their symbols' octets, so the length read is the length of the text the
scan would have made. A null's length is null. Only VARCHAR is
measured, as a CHARACTER value is padded as it is read and no chunk
holds its padded length, and no chunk records how many characters its
octets make, so CHAR_LENGTH reads the text. A chunk whose ends lie
outside its octets, or whose codes name no symbol, gives no length, and
the run's column is then decoded, which raises what is malformed. What
is no longer done is the check that a chunk's octets are UTF-8, for a
chunk nobody reads as text (as D1251 leaves it for LIKE).

A column measured where its text is read after all is slow, never
wrong, and this holds by how the column is made, not by the choice of
when to ask. A measured column is still the late column of D361. It
keeps where its rows are and how to decode them, and its lengths are
only a second way to read one property of the same values. Every reader
of a late column that is not resolved reads its values decoded whole,
so a reader the plan did not foresee, or an expression evaluated again
a row at a time after its vectors gave none, reads what the scan would
have given. The tree's rows of a column store and the rows of a row
store are given as text, and the function measures the text it is
given.

The scan is asked through `TableStorage::scan_measured` and
`Split::morsel_measured`, whose defaults ask for nothing measured, so
an engine that does not measure answers as before.

#### D1270. A page of a B-link tree is read by its number only by code that holds proof of being in the tree's epoch

A leaf taken out of a B-link tree is freed once no operation that may
hold its number is left (D31, D814). Every operation is counted in the
tree's epoch as it begins, and that count is what keeps the page. The
paths under an operation took no part in this. The descent, a node's
lock and the read from a leaf remembered or noted each relied on their
caller having entered the epoch, and nothing checked that it had.

The tree's stress test called the descent itself, in no epoch, to find
a leaf to note. Between its read of a parent and its read of the leaf,
other threads could take the leaf out, move the epoch on twice and free
the page. The read was then refused as one of a page not allocated,
rarely, and on one platform's run of the checks first. The test had
made that call since it was written. It failed far more often once
sparse leaves were merged (D814), which takes leaves out more often
than emptying them did.

No operation of the engine made such a read. A build that reported
every read of a page by its number made by a thread counted in no epoch
of the tree named only the tree's own unit tests, over the unit tests
of the engines and the disk and over the integration suite.

A read outside the epoch risks more than a refusal. The page refused is
one freed and not yet given out again. Once it is another leaf of the
tree it is read as valid, since a descent checks a node's level and its
mark and not where its range begins. A leaf further right then answers
that a key the tree holds is absent, and a writer puts its key in a
leaf that is not the key's. Once it is another tree's it is read as
this tree's.

So the rule is in the types. `Within` (`engine/tree/reclaim.rs`) is
proof of being counted in a tree's epoch. An operation's guard lends
it, and so do the counts a scan and a pin hold, and it is made nowhere
else. Every path that reads or locks a page by a number a node gave, or
one remembered, takes one. They are `descend`, `move_right`, `lock`,
`page`, `edge_for`, `leaf_by_copies`, `at_noted`, the reads from a leaf
remembered and a leaf noted, and the paths that reach them. A call made
outside an epoch does not compile, in any build. `Within` has no size,
so passing it adds no instruction to a read or a write.

Two things stay conventions. `Within` does not say which tree's epoch
it proves, so one tree's lent to another tree's path compiles. An
operation works one tree and makes and uses the proof inside one call,
so that mistake has to be written out. And the count a scan or a pin
keeps (`Entered`) can be copied, so a copy kept past its `leave` would
still lend. Only `Scan` and `Pinned` hold one, each until it is dropped.

The meta page and the root are read and locked without the proof, as
neither is freed while the tree lives. So are the walks of a tree no one
else uses, its load and its freeing.

The tree's tests that called these paths directly enter the epoch as an
operation does, through one helper, `leaf_of`, where they ask for a
key's leaf.

#### D1271. A split that is refused a page gives back those it took

A split writes its right half to a new page, then its left half over
the old node, which links the new page in (D31). A half that does not
fit its page is split again, each part taking a page more (D500,
`engine/tree/fit.rs`). A file may refuse a page, as the file of a
database kept in memory does at its budget's limit (D38).

A split refused its first page failed with nothing taken. One refused
a later page left the pages before it allocated, with nothing linking
to them, for as long as the file lived. The first of them already held
the right half, a leaf of the tree in every byte. A read of a row
starts at the leaf noted for the row and trusts a page a frame holds
that is a leaf of the tree, not deleted, whose first key is at or below
the row's (D500). A note can name a number a leaf had before the page
was freed and taken again. Such a read could then have answered from
the page left behind, with the row as it was when the split failed.

A split that fails after it took a page now gives back every page it
took (`BLinkTree::give_back`). The old node is not yet written over, so
the tree is as it was. Each page is emptied first, so one that cannot
be freed is no node, and freed once no read holds it.

#### D1274. A table of groups compares integer keys by their words, and a lane that holds no null reads none

A table of groups finds a key by its hash and then compares it with
the group whose slot matched (D356). The compare went lane by lane
through cells. Each side's value was made a cell of its type, the two
were matched by type, and an integer was widened before it was
compared. That is right for every type and every pair of types, and it
is what a key of two integer columns paid for each of its lanes, in the
morsels' tables and again in the partitions'.

A lane of integers is now compared by its words where the key gives
words (`exec/table/keys/words.rs`). A key comes as a row of a batch or
as a group of another table. Where its value of the lane is read from a
vector of integers of the lane's scale, the two are equal as their
units are, and nulls are equal to each other alone. No cell is made and
no bytes are written. Any other pair, an integer of another scale, a
value, a lane of another type, is compared by cells as before, so the
keys that are equal are the same keys (D356).

A lane also notes whether any of its groups is null
(`exec/table/keys.rs`, `nulled`). While none is, it does not read its
vector of nulls to learn that a group's value is not one. In a table of
many groups a compare reads the group's place in each vector from
memory the processor does not hold, so a lane of integers with no null
now reads one word there where it read two.

#### D1275. A partition merges a morsel's groups in one pass, a new group given its slot as it is met

A partition's table merged a morsel's groups in two passes over its
slots (D1110). It looked every group up, then appended those that were
new and went over them again to give each its slot. That holds only
while no two of the morsel's groups share a key, since a group not yet
placed cannot be found by the one after it. Rows handed on ungrouped
(D1260) do share keys, so they were found or made one at a time, each
group's key, first row and states appended through its cells before the
next was looked up. Where every row is a new group that cost more than
the morsels' tables had saved.

The merge is now one pass for every morsel (`exec/table/made.rs`,
`looked_up`). Each group is looked up by its key and hash. One that is
new takes the next number, and its hash and slot are written at once,
so the slots stand as they would had it been made. Its key, first row
and states are not appended yet. A key looked up later that meets its
slot is compared with the key the morsel holds at that group's place,
so a key the morsel holds twice finds the group its first made. After
the pass the new groups' keys, first rows and states are appended a
column at a time, and each set function's states are merged in one
loop, as before.

The groups, their numbers and their slots are those that finding or
making each group in turn gives. A probe that grows past the longest a
table takes (D357) ends the pass after its group. What is new so far is
appended, the table hashes its keys anew, and the rest are found or made
one at a time by their keyed hashes, as a table placed so always merged
them.

#### D1276. A grouping whose statement thread's table went to the spill reads the spill at its end

A grouping run in parallel merges the morsels of few groups on the
statement's thread, in a table of its own (D356, D1247). At its end, if
no wave was merged and none waits, it took every group to be in that
table and gave the table's groups alone
(`exec/parallel/grouped/waves.rs`, `finished`). That was so while a
grouping past its grant gave way. Since the partitions are held in the
spill (D1226) it is not. A table of the statement's thread that outgrows
the grant is handed to the partitions, and where the grant cannot hold
it even with every partition spilled, it is written to the spill as it
is, with no wave merged. The end then still took the early path. It
gave the groups of the statement thread's last table and never read the
spill, so the statement returned some of its groups and no error.

A statement reached this with few groups a morsel and a table of them,
no more than EXECUTOR.MORSEL_ROWS groups, whose keys and states pass
MEMORY.WORK_BYTES. That takes a small grant, or states of long strings.

The end now takes the early path only if nothing was spilled. With a
spill it hands the table over as it does any other and reads each
partition back. A unit test hands every morsel whole under a grant the
table passes, and a statement whose groups of one morsel pass the
grant, by the states of many set functions, is compared with itself
run alone.

#### D1278. Sorting a grouping's input first is weighed with each form priced as it would run, by the groups of the rows built, and by least regret

A grouping under an ORDER BY of its keys is streamed over a sort of its
rows where that costs less than hashing them and sorting the groups
(D550), the rows weighed those of the input as built (D1208). Three
things were left as they had been, and a grouping of a table kept by
column, by an expression of a time, under an ORDER BY of it, showed
them. It was streamed over a sort of every row on the statement's
thread, where a part's threads had hashed the rows before.

The first is how each form runs. Both were priced as work of one
thread. But the marking pass makes a hashed grouping over a stream a
part its threads share (D291), and a sort a part only where a serial
scan by batch does not serve its stream better, which of a table kept
by column with no join it does. So the two forms of one grouping may
run on different numbers of threads, and the choice between them saw
none of it. Each is now priced as it would run
(`physical/streamed.rs`, `parallel/sides.rs`). The planner asks the
marking pass's own rule how many threads the hashed grouping it would
make, and a sort of the same rows, would each be given. What a part's
threads share, the sort of the rows, or their hashing and the making of
their groups, costs its share of them, each thread past the first
gaining what the stream's table lets a part gain, and the part's start
(D652). What the statement's thread does after costs it whole. That is
the comparing of the sorted rows as they stream, or the sort of the
groups. The weights are those the joins' costs use, and none is new. Of
an input no part could read on more threads than one, by its rows, both
forms run alone, with no plan made to ask, so a statement of few rows
is planned at no cost more.

The second is the groups. The rows weighed became the built input's,
and the groups stayed those the estimator counted of the logical
input. Where a scan is told a condition and reads only the zones that
may match, the plan carries fewer rows than the logical count, and the
groups counted of the larger number could come near the rows built or
pass them. Every row then looked a group of its own, and sorting the
rows once looked cheaper than hashing them and sorting as many groups.
The groups weighed are now those of the rows built, as the estimator's
own formula counts them of that many rows (`Estimates::groups_of`,
D370), and never more than it counted of the logical input, which
still bounds them where the plan's rows are the more.

The third is what the choice does where the two forms price near each
other. It took the cheaper at the groups estimated, by however little.
But the two do not answer alike to a count that is wrong. A count of
groups errs high. The values of several columns, or of an expression
of one, are taken as independent of each other and as likely each as
the next (D370, D1082), and what they share or favour only makes the
groups fewer. Of fewer groups than counted the hashed grouping costs
less, as it makes and sorts fewer, and the sort of the rows costs what
it did, every row still sorted. So the form is now taken by its regret
(D386, `robust.rs`), between the groups estimated and those over
PLANNER.ESTIMATE_MARGIN, at least one. A form's regret at a number of
groups is its cost there over the cheaper form's, and the form taken
is the one whose larger regret of the two ends is least. The hashed
grouping's cost only rises with its groups and the sort's does not
change, so the two ends hold each form's largest regret between them,
as they do of the joins' linear costs. Of equal regret the hashed
grouping is taken. The margin is the one the joins weigh their
estimates by, taken here the way a count of groups errs, as an index
range bounded by a scan is weighed by the table's rows over it
(`access/bounded.rs`). A margin of 1 restores the cheaper form at the
estimate.

So the sort of the rows is taken where it is the cheaper even of the
groups over the margin, or where hashing would lose more at the count
than the sort would at the fewer. That holds of few rows, each nearly
a group, as a DISTINCT of a short range of a key is, where a sort is
cheap whatever the count. Of many rows counted a group each, both
forms alone, the hashed grouping is now taken, as what it loses if the
count is right is less than what the sort loses if the count is high
by the margin.

None of the three changes what a grouping gives, as both forms give
the same groups in the order asked. How far the count of an
