expression's values is from the values it takes is the estimator's
matter (D1082, D1279) and is not settled here.

#### D1279. A grouping by an expression counts no more groups than its table's sample shows the expression to take values

A grouping by a deterministic expression counts no more groups than the
columns it reads take values together (D1082). That says nothing of
what the expression does to them. A time less its seconds takes a value
a minute, a number divided by a hundred a hundredth of its values, the
first two characters of a telephone number a few dozen, and the year of
a date one a year. Each was counted by its column, most of them a value
a row. With a group a row a sort of every row looked cheaper than
hashing them (D550, D1278), and what was planned above the grouping
was planned for as many rows.

No shape of expression is looked for. There is no node for a
truncation, and a list of the ways one is written would begin with the
statements at hand and end there. The expression is evaluated instead
on the rows of the sample its table's statistics keep (D382), as a
conjunction no synopsis answers is, and two things are read of the
values it gives (`cardinality/shown.rs`).

The first is how many differ. The values seen more than once are
counted as they are. A value seen once stands for the values the sample
missed, which may be as few as itself or as many as the rows a sampled
row stands for, and it is counted as the square root of those rows, the
mean of the two in ratio. This is the estimator GEE of Charikar,
Chaudhuri, Motwani and Narasayya ("Towards estimation error guarantees
for distinct values", PODS 2000). Its count is expected to err by about
that root at most either way, and the paper shows no count from a
sample to be sure of less. The estimator that counts a column's
distinct values from a statistics pass (Haas and Stokes, D31) is not
used here. It takes the values as equally common, which of a sample
this small counts an expression a few of whose values hold most rows,
with many rare ones after them, far below what it takes. A count of
groups is relied on to err high (D1278). A sample that is the whole
table holds every value.

GEE counts no more than the root of the sample's rows times the
table's, which is what it gives when every sampled value is seen once.
Of more values than that it falls short, by up to the same root, and a
single chance repeat among the sampled rows would pass for a merging.
So its count is taken only where at most half of the sampled rows hold
a value seen once. Of values equally common that is where they number
no more than the sampled rows over the natural logarithm of 2, about
the sample's own size and a half, and there GEE errs high or not at
all. Past it the sample holds less than a row a value and could only
guess, so it tells no count, and the lattice or the columns' bound
stands.

The second is the lattice the values lie on, of exact numbers of one
scale, datetimes and intervals. The step is the greatest that every
sampled value is whole steps from the first by, and between the least
and the greatest value the lattice has their distance over the step,
and one, places. A time less its seconds lies on a lattice of a
minute, whatever the way it is written, and so does a quotient, a
number rounded and a field of a date on theirs. The step is read, not
proved. A thousand values that all fall on a coarser lattice than the
expression's own are not a case to plan for, and the least and the
greatest seen are near those of the table where its values are spread
as the sample's are.

The lesser of the two counts is what the sample shows, a null one
place more of the lattice's, and the grouping counts the lesser of
that and the columns' bound, never more than it counted before. The
count then goes through Cardenas' formula with the grouping's rows as
any column's does (D370). It is of the table, not of the rows a
condition beside the expression keeps, so a grouping of two days of a
month's minutes is still counted by the month's.

The sample shows nothing, and the columns' bound stands alone, in each
of these cases.

- The table has no statistics, or they keep no sample.
- The expression reads the columns of more than one table, or cannot
  be evaluated on a row alone, as one of a `?`, a subquery, a sequence
  or a routine cannot (D382).
- The sample tells neither a count nor a lattice, as of strings most
  of which it holds once.
- No sampled row gives a value. A row whose evaluation raises is left
  out and nothing is raised, as planning raises nothing of what the
  statement evaluates (D15).
- No two sampled rows that differ in the columns read give one value.
  The sample then shows nothing merged, as of a number and one, and of
  the columns' own values the statistics, counted from many more rows
  or from an index, know more than the sample does.
- A column read may have been cut in a sampled row. A sampled row
  keeps the first 256 characters of a string, as many octets of a
  binary string, and no large object (D382). The value of an
  expression of what was cut is not the value of the expression of the
  whole, as the length of a string shows, so a string of 256 octets or
  more in a column read, or a large object, leaves the bound to the
  columns.
- The plan under the grouping has no more rows than the sample. The
  evaluation would cost what the statement's own does, so a statement
  of few rows plans at no cost more.

The count is the same whenever it is asked of the same statistics, as
the sample is fixed with them, so no plan depends on when it is made.
A statement evaluates the sample once for each expression, however
many plans it weighs, and keeps the answer (`Seen::shown`, D1089). The
answer is not kept in the sample for later statements, as a
conjunction's is. It counts by the table's rows, which change with
every row written, where a share of the sample does not. The
statement's key writes each function by the address of its handle
(D1299), and keeps the expression, so no handle is freed and its
address taken while the key is kept.

#### D1280. A part of a built-in set function reaches the second grouping as its column of states, merged slot by slot

A query with a DISTINCT set function is computed by two groupings
(D340), and a set function without DISTINCT beside it is computed in
parts (D341). The first grouping keeps a part of COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX or
MIN in that function's column of states (D1186). The second grouping,
made in a table of the first's groups given as a batch (D1123), took
each part as a value all the same. Every group of the first made a
binary string of each part, its function's state written after a tag.
The second kept an accumulator a group for each such function, sorted
the batch's rows by group to feed them, and each accumulator read the
bytes back. The first grouping holds a group for every distinct value
of every group of the second, so a query with three set functions
beside one DISTINCT function made and read three values for each of
them, and spent more on that than on both groupings.

A part's column now leaves the first's table as the column it is
(`exec/table/merged.rs`, `GroupTable::into_parts`). The second's table
keeps the function it merges in a column of the same kind, and the
first's column is added to it slot by slot, each state to the group its
group of the first fell in (`States::merge_part`). That is the loop by
which a partition merges a morsel's column into its own (D1110), so a
count, a total and an extreme are merged by the code that merged them
before the second grouping saw them. No value is made of a part, no
accumulator is kept for one, and the rows are not sorted.

A column is taken so when three things hold (`GroupTable::merged_by`).
The second's set function merges parts and has no filter. The column it
names is one the first's table still keeps as a part's. And that column
holds counts or exact totals, whose function writes its state, so each
group's part is that state and never a result. Such states are of
totals that do not depend on the order they are merged in, which is why
they are written at all (D341), so merging them a column at a time
gives what merging them in the order of the first's groups gave.

Every other part is given as its value and merged by an accumulator, as
before. That is a column that turned into accumulators when it was
given integers of another scale, a set function no column holds, as a
plug-in's or an extreme of texts, and a sum of approximate numbers,
which writes no state and is computed whole. A second grouping that
reads the first's groups a row at a time, as one with a filtered set
function does, is unchanged too. In one pair some parts may be taken as
columns and others as values.

The groups, their order, each result, the warnings and the errors are
as before. A null a set function eliminates warns where the first
grouping is fed it. A sum past the digits an exact number holds raises
what the partitions' merge raises of it. EXPLAIN shows the plan it
showed.

#### D1281. A sort's first rows over a pair of groupings are taken from the second's table of each partition

A sort that asks for its first rows over a grouping run in parallel
takes them from each partition's table (D1124), and where its keys are
set functions it picks them before any row is made (D1256). A pair of
groupings run as one part (D1113), as a DISTINCT set function makes
them (D340), was left out. Each partition's thread made the second's
groups in a table (D1123) and then a row of every one of them. The
statement's thread merged the partitions' rows in the order of their
first rows and projected each, and the sort kept its few. Of a second
grouping of very many groups that was a row allocated, moved, compared
and freed a group, most of it on one thread after the partitions were
done.

A partition's thread now takes the first rows from the second's table
(`exec/parallel/grouped/top.rs`, `of_part`). The table is made of the
partition's groups of the first as before (`regrouped.rs`,
`second_table`) and given to the code that takes the first rows from
the table of a grouping alone. The sort stands over the second grouping,
so its keys and the projection under it already name the columns of the
second's row. No row is made of a group the partition does not keep,
and the statement's thread sorts the partitions' few rows alone.

The rows given and their order are the plan's, by the argument of
D1124. The plan run alone gives the second's groups in the order each
is first met among the first's groups, and those come in the order of
their first rows. The sort is stable, so of two groups of equal keys it
gives the one met earlier. A group of the second is numbered by its
first group of the first (D1113), which is the number of the first row
that falls in it. No row falls in two groups, so no two groups share a
number, and the number as the last key orders any two groups of equal
keys as the plan does. The partitions are split by the second's
grouping columns alone, so a group of the second lies whole in one
partition, and that partition's table holds its one row, with its
number and its results as the plan computes them. A row among the first
of all is then among the first of its partition under the same keys, so
the statement's thread, sorting the partitions' rows by the keys and
then the number, gives the plan's rows in the plan's order.

It does so where each partition makes the second in a table and the
second crosses no partition (`Outer::in_tables`). A second that crosses
the partitions (D1133, D1219) has a group in several of them, a part of
its count in each, so no partition's table holds its row. A second that
no grouping by batch reads, as one with a filtered set function, is
made of rows (D1123). Both are read as before, every group given to the
sort. So is a pair under a HAVING condition, and a sort that asks the
peers of its last row.

Whether the first's groups lie in the order of their first rows is
known of each partition's table only as it is finished (D1123). A
partition where they do not makes the second's groups of rows put in
order, as before, and keeps the first of them under the same keys and
numbers (`of_groups`). Its rows are those its table would have given,
so the statement's thread reads them alike. A partition read back from
the spill (D1226) is finished by the same code and gives its first rows
the same way.

An analyzed plan counts the second grouping the groups its tables made,
and the projection the rows the partitions kept (D1254).

#### D1282. The runs that merge and finish a grouping's partitions lead their reader by every partition

A grouping run in parallel merges each wave's morsels into its
partitions, a thread a partition, and finishes the partitions the same
way at the end (D356). Those runs, as every run, gave their results in
the order of their numbers and took no partition more than two a thread
past the one their reader waited for (D290). D1262 widened that for the
run over the morsels and left the partitions' runs as they were.

Where one partition holds far more groups than the others, the window
made it cost twice. A grouping over another whose grouping columns hold
its own (D1113) splits the first's groups by the second's columns alone,
so one value of those columns that takes a large share of the groups
puts that share in one partition. Its thread merged it for as long as
that took. The other threads finished the partitions within the window
past it and then stood idle, as the reader took no result out of order
and no partition past the window could be started. Only once the long
partition was done were the rest merged. A profile over time showed one
thread busy and the others waiting, then all of them busy again.

The runs that merge a wave, that finish the partitions, and that merge
the partitions of a grouping read a row at a time now lead their reader
by every partition (`exec/parallel/run.rs`, `Lead::unmetered`,
`grouped/waves.rs`, `grouped.rs`). The partitions after a long one are
merged while it is, and the run ends when the long one does.

The lead is not metered as the morsels' is, and needs no meter. A
morsel's groups ahead of the reader were charged to nothing until read,
so D1262 counts their bytes against the grant. A partition's result is
held either way. The reader of each of these runs gathers every
partition's result before it gives one row or merges the next wave, so
a partition finished early holds nothing that would not be held a
moment later, and at the end of the run both orders hold the same. What
a partition's table holds between waves is charged as the wave ends, by
the bytes the run gives back, in the order of the partitions, as
before. So the waves a grouping merges and the times it writes its
partitions to the spill are the same at a lead of two a thread and of
every partition, which a test shows of a grant that holds the groups
only in waves and of one they pass.

No more threads run than before. The lead says how many partitions may
be taken past the reader's, not how many are merged at once, which is
the degree as it was (D1246). A statement cancelled or ended while the
partitions run drops the run, which waits for the partitions its
workers are in, one a worker, and lets go of its work and of every
result not read. That wait is of the same length at any lead. The
partitions read back from the spill a few at a time (D1226) keep their
window, as what they hold at once is what bounds them.

The groups, their order, each set function's result, the warnings and
the errors are unchanged. Results still come in the order of the
partitions, and a partition's morsels are merged in the order of their
numbers.

#### D1287. A chunk of 16-byte fields whose values 64 bits hold is read as integers

A column of an exact numeric type of 19 to 38 digits is kept in 16-byte
fields (D698) and was read a value at a time into a batch's values,
whatever it held. An identifier is often declared with 19 or 20 digits
while every value of it fits 64 bits. Such a column was tested by the
filter above the scan, hashed in 128 bits and summed a value at a time,
where a column of 18 digits is judged by the scan and computed by the
kernels (D360, D362).

A scan now reads a run of such a column as integers (`storage::Ints`),
at the type's scale, if the least and the greatest value of each chunk
the run reads fit 64 bits (`scan::ints_scale`). A chunk's zone holds
both, so every value of the chunk fits. Fixed fields are narrowed in one
loop that keeps each field's low half and tests at its end that every
high half was its sign alone. A dictionary's entries are narrowed once a
chunk (`prepared.rs`), and a constant once. A field 64 bits do not hold
is never cut to them. The reading gives none, and the run is read as
values, as before (`encoded/words.rs`). A constant of 16 bytes past 64
bits would otherwise have read as 0. The bounds are tested first, so a
column whose values do pass 64 bits pays that test alone and opens no
chunk for it. The scan judges a conjunct on such a column wherever the
run reads as integers, and leaves it to the filter where it does not
(`judged.rs`).

No operator reads a column's declared precision. Each reads the kind of
a batch's column and its values (D696, D699). So a column's type, the
types of its results, their values and the overflow of its sums are as
they were. A sum of integers is added in 128 bits and judged against
its result's precision at its end, as a sum of values is. One column may
reach an operator as integers in one batch and as values in the next.
Both hash alike and compare by value.

Nothing stored changes, so data frozen before is read so with no
reload. The grain is the chunk, so the chunks of a group that hold no
value past 64 bits are integers though another chunk of it holds one.

#### D1288. A join key that is a whole number of 64 bits is hashed by itself, and any other number by its nearest `f64`

A join hashed every number by the bits of its nearest `f64` (D368), so
that an exact key of any scale and an approximate one that match hash
alike. An `f64` keeps 53 bits. Whole numbers past 2^53 share their
nearest `f64` with their neighbours, 1,024 of them near 2^63. Keys one
after another there, as identifiers of 19 digits are, fell 1,024 to a
hash, and each probe compared its key with every row of its hash. Keys
of 18 digits fell 128 to a hash. A key of 2^51 or more was also made
its `f64` through its digits, a row at a time.

Two numbers match by their algebraic value, an exact one against an
approximate one too (`value::compare_numbers`). So the word a number is
hashed of can be chosen by the number alone, with no word of its type
or of the other side's. It is now the number itself if the number is a
whole number 64 bits hold, and the bits of its nearest `f64` if it is
not (`table/join/keys.rs`). An exact number is such a whole number if
its units divide by its scale's power of ten into 64 bits. An
approximate number is one if it has no fraction and lies within them,
read from its bits. A decimal floating-point number is first made the
exact number equal to it. Values that match are one number, so they
have one word, whatever their types, and nothing is decided as a join
is planned. A fraction, and a number past 64 bits, keep the nearest
`f64`, which is one for values that match.

A whole number below 2^51 keeps the bits of its `f64` as its word, which
is the number exactly, so a direct table reads its place of them as
before (D601). A wider one's word is its 64 bits crossed with the number
a null is given as to a direct table, so no key's word is a null's.
Such a word can be the bits of one small number's `f64`, so a wide key
near 4.6 × 10^18 may share its word with one small key. That is one
stray pair a key at most, told apart as keys are compared, and never a
run of keys in one hash. The
hashes a build makes of its keys' numbers are those a probe makes
(D1080). A vector of integers of scale 0 is hashed whole by the
kernels' hash of words (D1098) whatever its values, where one value of
2^51 or more sent the vector a row at a time before. The hash itself
is unchanged (D460).

Keys past 64 bits one after another still share their nearest `f64`.
A table of such keys compares more rows a probe, as before, and gives
the same rows.

#### D1289. A null's place in a vector of numbers has no meaning, and a window's lane holds 0 there

A batch's vector of integers, of approximate numbers or of datetimes
keeps a number in every place and marks its nulls beside them
(`storage::Ints`, `Floats`, `Datetimes`). Their documentation said a
null's place holds 0. A column store's chunk does not give that. A frame
of reference gives its least number there, runs give the run's number, a
dictionary gives its first entry, and only fixed fields give 0
(`engine/columns/encoded/words.rs`, which says so). Zeroing them as a
chunk is read would cost every nullable column a pass that almost no
reader needs. Every reader but one already left the place out. The set
functions add every place with a kernel and take the nulls' numbers off
again, a hash of a null is written over, and the kernels that select or
find the least and greatest take the nulls with the numbers.

So the rule is the store's. A null's place has no meaning, the
documentation of the three vectors says so now, and whatever reads a
place leaves out those its nulls mark. The one reader that did not is a
window's lane (`exec/window/batched/lanes.rs`). A lane said its nulls'
places hold 0, copied each vector as it was, and SUM and AVG over a
frame add every place of it by prefix sums (`sets.rs`). A lane now
writes 0 in each null's place as it copies a vector, of integers and of
approximate numbers alike, which makes true what it said and keeps the
prefix sums as they are.

No statement was found that gave a wrong sum before this change. A sort
below a window writes its rows out with 0 in each null's place, and a
window over a whole partition of a frozen table, which asks for no
order, gave the row store's results too
(`test/integration/window_nulls.rs`, which stays as the requirement's
test). Which step kept the store's numbers from the lane there was not
found. The lane's own test shows the place it now clears.

#### D1290. MAX and MIN compare character strings where they lie, and a grouping keeps each group's best in a column of states

A set function fed by batches is given a vector at a time. A vector of
character strings is one text with where each string ends, or the codes
of a dictionary's entries (D31), and `Accumulator::update_texts` hands
it over as it is. COUNT counted its strings so. MAX and MIN did not
override it, so the default made a value of every string of the batch,
the first time any group's accumulator asked, to compare each with the
best so far. Nearly all of those values lost and were dropped with the
batch.

MAX and MIN now find the best string of the vector where the strings
lie (`TextOrder::best_of`, `functions/extremes.rs`) and make a value of
it alone, and only if it betters the best so far.

- With no collation two strings compare with the shorter padded with
  spaces [X3.135-1986 §5.11 GR5], by `compare_strings`, as two values
  do. Of two that compare equal the one met first is kept, as before.
- Under a collation of NO PAD whose sort key is the text itself (D1183)
  they compare by their octets. A string given as a value compares by
  the same rule (`TextOrder::better`), so the two ways cannot differ.
- Under any other collation a sort key is made of each string's value,
  as before.

The rows asked of the vector are read in the order asked, and a null is
passed over. What an accumulator writes, merges and gives is unchanged.

A grouping by batch keeps COUNT, SUM, AVG, and MAX and MIN of exact
numbers in columns of states, a slot a group (D356). MAX and MIN of
character strings had no column, so each group held an accumulator on
the heap, and in it a value of the group's best string. Every batch's
rows were sorted by group to hand each accumulator its rows. Where the
grouping ran in parallel, every group of every morsel wrote its string
as a state for the partition's accumulator to read back as a value
(D1110), and each accumulator was made and dropped by itself.

They now keep a column (`Typed::Best`,
`exec/table/states/typed/best.rs`). It holds every group's best string
in one text, and where each group's lies in it. A row's string is
compared with its group's best where both lie, by the order of
`TextOrder`, and copied to the end of the text only when it wins.

- Which set function has the column is asked of its accumulator
  (`Accumulator::text_order`), as D1201 asks whether one keeps its first
  value. MAX and MIN with no collation answer for a result that is a
  character string held whole, and those under a collation whose key is
  the text itself answer by octets. Under a collation that makes sort
  keys they give none, as the keys would have to be kept beside the
  strings. Of a character large object they give none, as comparing two
  reads their chunks and may fail. No plug-in's function answers. A part
  of MAX or MIN (D341, D1280) gives none either, so the first of two
  groupings keeps accumulators of it and the second merges their
  written states, as before.
- A string bettered stays in the text, dead. Once the dead octets pass
  what the column holds beside them, its live octets and its groups'
  places, the live strings are copied to a text of their own
  (`Best::compact`). A copy moves the live octets and rewrites the
  places, and more than that many octets died since the last one, so
  copying costs less than one octet moved for each octet that died, and
  the column holds less than twice what it needs and one string more.
- Two tables' columns are merged in one loop, each group's best
  compared with the other's where they lie (D1110), with no state
  written. A column is gathered in another order, and written to a
  spill and read back (D1226) as each group's string and whether it has
  one. A state an accumulator wrote is merged as the accumulator merges
  it, and a group's result and written state are its accumulator's.
- A column fed anything but character strings and nulls turns into
  accumulators, each given its group's best, and is fed as they are.

#### D1291. A regular expression function over a dictionary's codes is run once of each entry a row reads

A column store gives a character string column's rows as the codes of
its chunks' dictionaries (D31, D1161), and many rows read one entry.
UPPER, LOWER, SUBSTRING and the lengths already run once an entry and
give their rows the same codes (D363, D1126). LIKE_REGEX and
TRANSLATE_REGEX read each row's string through its code and searched
it again for every row that read it (D1188).

Over a vector of codes they now run once of each entry a row reads
(`functions/regex/entries.rs`).

- One pass over the codes marks the entries a row that is not null
  reads. TRANSLATE_REGEX translates each marked entry once, in the
  entries' order, into one text, and its result is the rows' own codes
  over the translated entries, so a grouping by it goes by codes
  (D1161) and hashes each entry once. LIKE_REGEX matches each marked
  entry once and gives each row its entry's truth value.
- An entry no row reads is not run. A row a filter took out before the
  call leaves its entry in the dictionary, and a call may raise an
  error of one string and not of another, a result past the longest
  string [ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §6.33 SR12f i 2] or a search past its
  steps (D61). Run of every entry, a query could raise what none of its
  rows raises. A row that is null marks nothing.
- A row is given a null if it is null, or if its entry was given one,
  as where the start position is not of the string [§6.33 GR9b ii].
- A dictionary of more entries than the vector has rows is run a row
  at a time, as before, since marking its entries would cost more than
  the rows. A vector of texts one after another, and a call whose other
  operands are not all constants, are run as before too.

Which error a statement raises when several of its rows would raise
one is that of the entry met first, where it was that of the row met
first. The standard orders neither.

#### D1292. What a searcher keeps is left with its expression for the next searcher

A call over a vector of texts makes one searcher for the vector (D1188),
which keeps the expression's automaton, what its last window of
searches found and its scratch from one text to the next. The next
vector's searcher began with none of it. It built the automaton's
states again from the texts it read, and asked the automaton first for
a window of searches before it learned again what the last searcher
knew, that most of the column's texts match. A column is some tens of
thousands of vectors.

A searcher of text after text now leaves what it kept with its
expression as it is dropped (`searcher::Leavings`), and
`Regex::searcher` takes up what one left before it makes anything anew.
The automaton's states and the window's verdict so last as long as the
expression does, the statement's plan.

- A searcher takes one `Left` out and puts one back, so the expression
  holds no more of them than the searchers that were at work on it at
  one time, the threads of the statements that share it. Each is within
  the bound of one searcher (`dfa::OCTETS_MOST`,
  `bounded::MARKS_OCTETS`).
- Two searchers at work at once hold states of their own, and the lock
  is taken to take one up and to leave one, never during a search.
- An automaton that outgrew its states is left as none, so the
  expression's next searchers ask none, where each vector's searcher
  grew one to the bound before it gave up.
- A search of one text alone (`Regex::once`) takes up nothing and
  leaves nothing, as it makes no automaton.
- A copy of an expression starts with nothing left.

What a search finds is unchanged, as an automaton's states are of its
program alone and the scratch is cleared by each search.

#### D1293. A column store's scan does not judge a comparison that the bounds of every part of a run prove

A chunk of a frozen group is written with the least and the greatest of
its values and the count of its nulls, and with the same of each part of
1,024 of its rows (`engine/columns/group/zones.rs`). A scan read them one
way only. A part whose bounds a told conjunct cannot match is passed
over (`columns/scan.rs`). A part it may match was decoded and judged a
row at a time (D360), also where the bounds say it matches every row.

That case is common. A hash join tells its probing side's scan the
least and the greatest of its built keys (D369), and where the built
rows span the table's keys nearly every part lies inside that range. A
profile showed the two bounds of such a range judged of every row of the
probing table in most joins of the reference queries, by runs of a
column kept as runs, and it was the largest single cost of a semi join
over that table. A range of a column a table is written in the order of,
a day of a log, holds every part between its two ends.

So a run now asks its parts first (`columns/judged/proved.rs`). Of a
comparison of a column with a constant, the run is proved if every part
it lies in holds no null and has bounds that satisfy the comparison at
the end that decides it. `>=` is decided by the least value and `>` by
the least being above the constant. `<=` and `<` are decided by the
greatest in the same way. `=` needs both ends equal to the constant, and
`<>` needs the constant below the least or above the greatest. A
comparison proved keeps every row, so the scan does not decode its
column to judge it and tests no row. A null proves nothing, as no
comparison is true of one [X3.135-1986 §5.11 GR2]. A run must lie
wholly in chunks whose parts prove it, so a header that lacks a chunk
proves nothing of the rows it held. The bound of a sort's first rows is
proved as the comparison it is at that moment (D1241).

The bounds are those of every row frozen in a part. A run gives those
rows or fewer. A row changed or deleted since the freeze has an entry in
the tree, its frozen row is left out of the run, and what the tree holds
of it is given apart and judged by the filter alone
(`rows/frozen/batches.rs`). So the bounds cover every row a run gives,
whatever was written since, and no row is given that the scan would
have left out. The filter judges every row given as before (D15).

Only columns of exact numbers and of datetimes of no time zone are
proved so. Their bounds are their values whole, and a bound compares
with the constant as each value does (`value::compare`), at any scale. A
part whose bounds do not compare with the constant proves nothing. Texts
are left out, as are approximate numbers. A run asks two comparisons of
values a part and a conjunct, against a decode and a test of each of up
to 2,048 rows.

The tests ask each comparison at the bound its parts reach and one unit
past it, a part with a null, runs that are not whole parts and that
cross chunks, and a header with a chunk missing
(`judged/proved/tests.rs`). An integration test changes, deletes and
adds rows in parts whose stored bounds prove a comparison and compares
every answer with the row store's (`test/integration/proved_bounds.rs`).

#### D1294. A column store's scan asks a hash join's runtime filter's keys of each run before it decodes the other columns, while they keep few of its rows

A hash join tells the scan of its other operand the range of its built
keys, and judges its Bloom filter, key set or bitmap in a step over the
batches the scan gives (D369, D389, D600). The scan decoded every column
the pipeline reads of every row in the range before that step ran. A
semi join of the orders of one quarter with the lines of every order
showed the cost. The lines' scan decoded two dates of every row for a
filter over the scan, the filter judged every row, and only then did
the join's keys leave a few of them. The key's column is kept as runs
there, several rows a key, and each key was hashed and looked up a row
at a time.

A filter of an exact key now tells the scan its keys too
(`Conjunct::Among`, `storage::Members`): its bitmap, its key set, or, of
whole numbers, its Bloom filter's words with the seed of the hashes the
join made. A column store's scan asks them of the key's column
(`columns/judged/among.rs`), after its comparisons and before a LIKE,
once a run of equal keys where the column is kept as runs (D1084) and of
each row otherwise. The rows kept then go the way of any conjunct the
scan judges (D360, D366). A run of which fewer than one row in eight is
kept is decoded at those rows alone, so the filter over the scan and
the join see those rows and no others of it. A run of more is given
whole.

A row the scan leaves out is one no built row matches, which the join
drops. A bitmap and a key set are exact. A Bloom filter also keeps a
few rows no built key equals, and that is harmless only because the
rows are judged again. So the join's filter step and its probe stay
exactly where they were and judge every row the scan gives, and the
rows a statement gives, and the rows every operator above the join
counts, are unchanged. Only the rows a scan and the operators between
it and the join count in an analyzed plan fall. An integer the keys
cannot be asked of is kept: one of another scale than the built keys',
and under a Bloom filter one of 2^51 or more in magnitude, whose hash
the join made another way. A null is left out, as the keys are told
only of a key no null matches. Keys are told of a column of exact
numbers alone.

Asking costs a hash and a read of the filter a run or a row, and gains
nothing where the run is given whole. So the keys count the rows the
scan asked them of in its first 16 runs, the count a filter's own stop
uses (D369), and after those the scan asks them only while they kept
fewer than one row in eight of them, the share a run is given whole at
(D360). No constant is new. The counts are shared by the threads of a
statement and written only through those first runs.

D389 said a morsel's scan judges no Bloom filter, as judging one cost
more than the probes it spared. That was measured when a morsel's
batches were decoded whole whatever the filter kept, so a scan that
asked the filter saved the probe alone and paid a hash for it, and
every thread wrote the filter's counts for every batch. Both reasons
are gone. A scan now decodes the other columns at the rows kept, and
the counts are written through the first runs only. D389's paragraph is
rewritten to say so.

The tests ask each form of keys what it holds, compare the keys told
with what the filter itself keeps of the same rows, ask a scan's runs
of a group, by rows and by runs, and show a scan that stops asking keys
that keep one row in eight (`storage/condition/members/tests.rs`,
`exec/table/runtime.rs`, `columns/judged/among/tests.rs`). An
integration test counts the rows a scan gives under a join and a semi
join of few keys, with the filters off and on, and compares every
answer with the row store's and with the filters off
(`test/integration/scan_keys.rs`).

#### D1295. An IN list of exact constants is judged of integers by its units folded to their scale once, found by a bit or by halving

A column of exact numbers reaches a filter and a column store's scan as
a vector of integers of one scale (D31, D360). A comparison with a
constant was folded to that scale once and judged as integers (D354).
An IN list was not. The scan made a value of every integer and compared
it with each constant in turn (`Conjunct::matches_key`). The filter
compared a list of under eight constants in 128 bits, a constant at a
time, and looked a longer one up in a set of buckets, which made a value
and hashed it for every row (`logical/sets.rs`). A profile of a filter
of eight sizes on a table of parts showed both: the scan's judging and
the filter's second judging of the same rows were together a sixth of
the statement.

A list of exact constants is now folded once for a vector
(`storage/batch/listed.rs`). Each constant folds as an equality with it
does (`rescaled_bound`, D354). One of fewer fractional digits is scaled
up, one of more is divided where the scale divides it, and one the
scale cannot hold, or past 64 bits, equals no integer and is left out.
The units are kept in order, each once. Where the greatest lies fewer
than 64 above the least, they are the bits of one word counted from the
least, and a row is found by one subtraction and one bit. Otherwise it
is found by halving the list. Neither form has a length to tune. The
width of a word is the only bound, and it is the machine's.

NOT IN keeps the rows found in none, and no row at all if a constant is
null, as it is then unknown of every row not found [X3.135-1986 §5.13
GR2, §5.18]. A null row is kept by neither. A list with a constant that
is not an exact number, or too large to scale, is judged as before, by
the set if it is long and of the values if it is short. The filter's
list of pairs in 128 bits is gone, as every list it took is now folded.

Both readers use the one type, so a scan keeps what the filter keeps.
The tests compare each list, IN and NOT IN, with each value judged
against each constant: constants out of order and repeated, a null
among them, one the scale cannot hold, one past 64 bits, spans of 63, 64
and 65 units, the ends of an integer, and integers kept as runs
(`storage/batch/listed/tests.rs`, `columns/judged/tests.rs`,
`batch/judge/tests.rs`).

#### D1298. A dictionary chunk's entries are made text the first time a run asks for its rows as text, not when the chunk is opened

A scan opens each chunk it reads once for all the runs that read it
(D352). Opening a dictionary chunk of a character string column made
its entries text at once. The octets of every entry were judged UTF-8
and copied, and the text was kept for the runs that give the chunk's
rows as codes of those entries. Many readers of such a chunk ask for no
text. A conjunct
judged of the chunk where its octets lie (D360, D512, D1251, D1253), a
value read alone, and a row group passed over after its first chunks
all open the chunk and read its codes or its octets as written. Each
still paid for the check and the copy of entries nobody read.

The entries are now made text the first time a run asks for the chunk's
rows as text (`engine/columns/prepared.rs`, `Made::texts_of`), and kept
from then for the chunk's other runs as before. A chunk never asked for
text makes none.

Nothing a reader of the text is given changes. The text is made of the
same octets by the same function, and those octets are judged UTF-8 as
the text is made, before any of it is given, so a chunk with an entry
that is no text still gives none and its rows are read the way that
raises what is malformed. The text is held in a cell that is set once.
Two runs that ask for the text of one opened chunk make it once, and a
chunk whose entries were judged not to be text is not judged again. The
chunks opened belong to the one scan that reads them, or to one decoding
of a late column at a time (D361), so no two threads ask one cell at
once, and the cell would still make the text once if they did.

D1252 withdrew the cell. A run that asks for text copies the entries it
reads from the chunk into the run's own vector and judges them there,
so nothing is made of a dictionary of texts and nothing of it is kept.
A reader that asks for no text pays for none, as this decision meant.

#### D1299. A table's sample remembers a function by its handle, not by its name alone

A table's sample remembers what was asked of it under a fingerprint of
the question (D382). The fingerprint wrote a function by its name and
its arguments. A name does not tell a function. EXTRACT holds its
field, a CAST by a template holds the template, a field of a row its
number, a difference of two datetimes its interval qualifier, a query
of XML its expression, TRIM and the greatest and least of strings
their collation, and a type test its types. Each is one name whatever
it holds, about thirty kinds of function in all. So two conditions
that differed only in what such a function held were one question.
The second asked was given the answer of the first, and a condition on
the day of a date was estimated at the rows of a condition on its
month. The estimate was wrong, and it was whichever was asked first.

What does tell one function from another is its handle, as the rule
that makes a list of ORs one set already takes it (`logical/sets.rs`).
A function now writes its name and the address of its handle
(`estimate/fingerprint.rs`). An address is one function's only while
the function lives, and a sample outlives the statements that ask it.
So a key comes with the handles it wrote (`stats::sample::Asked`), and
the sample keeps them beside the answer. No function of a remembered
answer is freed, and its address taken by another, while the answer
may be given. The handles go when the sample forgets its answers, at
1,024 of them, or is dropped with its statistics.

What this costs is stated here so that it is not read later as a
loss. A function registered once, as the string and numeric functions
are, is one handle for the database's life, and its answers are shared
by every statement as before. A function the binder makes for a call,
as it makes EXTRACT for its field, is its statement's own. Its answers
are shared within the statement and by each planning of a plan that is
kept, and not by two statements written apart, each of which evaluates
the sample once. Before, two such statements shared an answer, and it
was the wrong one for one of them wherever they differed.

Told apart without the handle, a function would have to give what it
holds as part of its contract, a method of the function trait for
every function and plug-in to write. The handle needs none.

The count a grouping makes of an expression (D1279) writes its key the
same way and keeps the expression for its statement.

#### D1316. A run's texts have codes once one of its chunks shares entries among its rows, whatever the others' encodings, and never more entries than rows

A column store gives a run's character strings as codes of dictionary
entries where it can (`storage::Coded`), and what reads them works an
entry once and not a row once. Grouping finds a code's group once
(D1161), and a hash, a comparison, a LIKE and a regular expression
function are run of each entry (D1099, D1253, D1291). A run was given so
only if every chunk it read was a dictionary. A column of long strings
has a chunk to a page, and each chunk takes the encoding that is
smallest for it, so its runs read dictionaries, texts coded by symbols
and varying fields together. Such a run was given as plain text, and
each of its rows was hashed, compared and copied.

A run's texts are entries (D1252), and its rows are entries, one each,
until a chunk gives entries its rows share
(`engine/columns/texts.rs`). A dictionary gives its entries and each
row's code among them. A chunk of one value gives one entry. From the
first such chunk every row of the run has a code. The rows gathered
before it are given the codes of the entries they are, with nothing
copied, and the rows of a later chunk that shares nothing are each an
entry and its code. A run none of whose chunks shares entries is texts
and their ends as before, so a reader of plain text pays for no codes.

A dictionary asked for no fewer rows than it has entries gives its
entries whole. One asked for fewer gives only the entries those rows
read, each once, in the order the rows meet them. That is so of a run
that ends within the chunk and of the few rows a condition kept (D360).
A dictionary was given whole before whatever was asked of it, so a scan
that kept one row of a chunk copied every entry of the chunk. The entry
a code was given is kept by code while the chunk is read. An entry given
of a chunk lies after those the run held before the chunk, so what an
earlier chunk left by a code is told by its place, and nothing is
cleared between chunks.

So a run holds no more entries than rows. Each reader's rule that works
entries only where they are no more than the rows (D1161, D1291) holds
of every run a scan gives. Two chunks' entries of the same text are two
entries, as two dictionaries' were, and every reader already finds them
equal by their text.

More runs reach their readers as codes, so the two readers that searched
only plain text at once now search entries too. A LIKE of a piece
between two `%`s, judged by a filter (`exec/batch/judge/texts.rs`) or as
an expression (`exec/batch/expr/compare.rs`), searches a coded column's
entries as one arena (D1119) and takes each row by its code. A filter
asked of fewer rows than the column has entries judges each of those
rows' texts instead, as an entry no row asked reads is judged for
nothing. That holds of every conjunct a filter judges of texts.

A null's code is 0 and its row is marked null, as before. A null row
gathered before the run had codes is the empty entry of its place.

## 2. Project layout

```
Cargo.toml              workspace and package; lint levels (D10)
clippy.toml             lint thresholds
rustfmt.toml            formatting (D9)
rust-toolchain.toml     pinned toolchain (D8)
.cargo/config.toml      the `cargo xtask` alias
Dockerfile              the server's image (D241)
.dockerignore           what the image's build does not read
README.md               what turborel is; how to build and test it
RULES.md                this file
CONFORMANCE.md          what is implemented of the standards, and the
                        choices they leave to an implementation
TODO.md                 open work
CONTRIBUTING.md         changes, commit messages, pull requests, issues
SECURITY.md             how to report a vulnerability
AGENTS.md               the guide for coding agents
CLAUDE.md               points Claude Code to AGENTS.md
.github/                CI (workflows/), issue forms, pull request
                        template
src/                    the library (lib.rs); one concept per module
protocol/src/           the native wire protocol: messages, codec (D42)
client/src/             the client: a connection over the protocol (D42)
server/src/             the server, as a library (D42)
server/test/            the server's integration tests, with a client
turboreld/src/          the server program: command line, signals (D42)
turboreld/test/         the program's integration tests
cli/src/                the command-line client `turborel` (D46)
cli/test/               its integration tests
lz4/src/                LZ4 compression, an encoding plug-in (D48)
aes/src/                encryption (AES-256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) and
                        cryptographic hash functions (D26, D48)
support/src/            fixtures shared by the crates' tests (R-TEST-10)
replication/src/        the replication crate (D57)
doc/                    the manual (R-DOC-8)
test/integration/       the integration test binary: public API only
  main.rs               crate root and module list
  common.rs             shared fixtures and helpers
  <area>.rs             one module per area
bench/                  benchmarks, run by `cargo xtask bench`
  harness.rs            the harness every benchmark uses
xtask/                  project tools: verify, coverage, trace, bench,
                        mutate
```

`Cargo.toml` declares each test and benchmark target with its path, with
discovery off, so the directories are `test/` and `bench/`. Every other file
under a target's directory is a module of that target.

## 3. Code rules

### R-STYLE: formatting and idiom

| ID | Rule | Checked by |
|---|---|---|
| R-STYLE-1 | Code **shall** be formatted by `rustfmt`. | `cargo fmt --check` |
| R-STYLE-2 | Code **shall** pass clippy `pedantic` and restriction lints, `-D warnings`. | clippy |
| R-STYLE-3 | Names **shall** follow Rust API Guidelines casing; code implementing a production is named after it: `QuerySpecification`, `query_specification`. | review |
| R-STYLE-4 | Modules are `foo.rs`, submodules in `foo/`; no `mod.rs`. | `mod_module_files` |
| R-STYLE-5 | No wildcard imports, except `use super::*` in unit tests. | `wildcard_imports` |
| R-STYLE-6 | A name **shall not** shadow an unrelated binding. | `shadow_unrelated` |
| R-STYLE-7 | No `dbg!`; production code **shall not** print. | `dbg_macro`, `print_stdout`, `print_stderr` |

### R-SIZE: short functions and files

| ID | Rule | Checked by |
|---|---|---|
| R-SIZE-1 | A function **shall** have at most 50 lines of code. | `too_many_lines` |
| R-SIZE-2 | A source file **shall** have at most 600 lines; split by the standard's clauses or pipeline stages. | `cargo xtask file-length` |
| R-SIZE-3 | A function **shall** take at most 5 parameters, at most 1 a `bool`; else use a struct, tuple or enum. | `too_many_arguments`, `fn_params_excessive_bools` |
| R-SIZE-4 | A module **should** hold one concept, stated in its `//!` doc. | review |

### R-DOC: comments and documentation

| ID | Rule | Checked by |
|---|---|---|
| R-DOC-1 | Every public item **shall** have a doc comment, with `# Errors` if it returns `Result` and `# Panics` if it can panic. | `missing_docs`, `missing_errors_doc`, `missing_panics_doc` |
| R-DOC-2 | Comments **shall** say *why*: the rule implemented, the choice made, the invariant relied on. | review |
| R-DOC-3 | Documentation **shall** build without warnings. | `cargo doc` with `-D warnings` |
| R-DOC-4 | Behaviour the standard governs **shall** cite it as printed: `[X3.135-1986 §8.6 GR2]`, `[ISO/IEC 9075:1992 §11.19 SR13]`, `[ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 §9.15 SR4e]`. Implementation-defined choices say so and state the choice. Beyond the standards: `[EXTENSION]`; ungoverned internals: `[DESIGN]`. BNF in doc comments goes in backticks. | review |
| R-DOC-5 | No commented-out code, no `TODO` or `FIXME` comments: open work goes in TODO.md, and code never cites TODO.md. | review; `cargo xtask verify` |
| R-DOC-6 | Every file **shall** start with a `//!` doc giving its responsibility and clauses implemented. | review |
| R-DOC-7 | Each implementation-defined choice **shall** be listed in CONFORMANCE.md with its implementing file. | review |
| R-DOC-8 | A change visible to a user, operator or program **shall** update the manual, `doc/`, in the same commit: every page stating what changed, in its format (statement pages: NAME, SYNOPSIS, DESCRIPTION, RULES, PRIVILEGES, ERRORS, EXAMPLES, STANDARD, SEE ALSO; chapters: sections). New statements, settings, program options and events get a page or entry. Claims are checked against the code; examples are run, with the changed output pasted. | review |
| R-DOC-9 | README.md's "What it has" **shall** name each area of capability a user would look for in one short line that says what can be done and nothing of how it is built, in no more than 24 lines. A major feature of an area already named extends that line by a few words or leaves it alone, and a line is added only for a new area. How a feature works belongs to the manuals, and CONFORMANCE.md lists every feature. | review |

### R-CONST: no magic numbers or strings

| ID | Rule | Checked by |
|---|---|---|
| R-CONST-1 | Production numeric literals other than `0` or `1` **shall** be named `const`s, documenting the value's source. | review; `default_numeric_fallback` |
| R-CONST-2 | Strings matched or looked up (key words, plug-in names, settings, paths) **shall** be named `const`s, defined once. Messages for people are not, but cite their rule (R-ERR-2). | review |
| R-CONST-3 | Related constants **shall** live together in the concept's module, under a header naming their source. | review |
| R-CONST-4 | Tests may use literal fixtures; expected values restating a constant **should** use it. | review |

### R-ERR: errors, not panics

| ID | Rule | Checked by |
|---|---|---|
| R-ERR-1 | Production code **shall not** panic: no `unwrap`, `expect`, `panic!`, `unreachable!`, `todo!`, `unimplemented!`, indexing, slicing or `process::exit`. | clippy restriction lints |
| R-ERR-2 | Every failure **shall** be a `SqlError` with a SQLCODE and a plain-words message. In source, a message begins with the broken rule, `"[X3.135-1986 §8.3 SR6] ..."`, kept apart as the error's `rule`; or, if no standard governs, `[DESIGN]` or `[EXTENSION]`, which the error drops. Format errors name tokens instead (D24). | review; `error.rs` tests |
| R-ERR-3 | No `Result` **shall** be silently discarded: `let _ = fallible()` needs a comment on why the error cannot matter. | `unused_must_use`; review |
| R-ERR-4 | A `RefCell` borrow or lock guard **shall** be scoped to the block needing it, never held across a plug-in call or any call that could take it again. A poisoned lock is reported (SQLCODE -910), never unwrapped. | review |
| R-ERR-5 | A failed statement **shall** leave no effect [X3.135-1986 §3.3]; writes go through the transaction coordinator's undo. | tests |

### R-NUM: arithmetic and conversions

| ID | Rule | Checked by |
|---|---|---|
| R-NUM-1 | Integer arithmetic **shall** be explicit about overflow: `checked_*`, `wrapping_*`, `saturating_*` or `overflowing_*`. | `arithmetic_side_effects` |
| R-NUM-2 | `as` **shall not** be used on numbers; use `From`, `TryFrom` or a checked helper. | `as_conversions`, `cast_*` |
| R-NUM-3 | A divisor **shall** be shown non-zero, and `MIN / -1` handled. | `integer_division`; review |
| R-NUM-4 | Floats **shall not** be compared for equality except by the standard's comparison rules in `value.rs`. | `float_cmp`; review |
| R-NUM-5 | A numeric literal whose type would default **shall** carry a suffix or typed binding. | `default_numeric_fallback` |

### R-CF: control flow testable to MC/DC

| ID | Rule | Checked by |
|---|---|---|
| R-CF-1 | A boolean decision **shall** have at most 4 conditions; else extract a named predicate. | review |
| R-CF-2 | Cognitive complexity **shall** be at most 15, block nesting at most 5. | `cognitive_complexity`, `excessive_nesting` |
| R-CF-3 | A `match` on an enum **shall** list every variant, with no `_`. | `wildcard_enum_match_arm` |
| R-CF-4 | Conditions **shall** have no side effects, except R-DEV-5's consuming idioms. | review |
| R-CF-5 | Or-patterns **should** appear only at a pattern's root, and match guards **should** be avoided: both hide conditions from MC/DC test design. | review |
| R-CF-6 | Recursion **shall** be bounded by a named depth constant, failing with a `SqlError` past it. | review; tests |

### R-SAFE: language subset and resources

| ID | Rule | Checked by |
|---|---|---|
| R-SAFE-1 | No `unsafe` code, but in the crate `turborel-simd` (D460), where each block **shall** follow a check of the processor's features and carry a SAFETY comment. | `unsafe_code = "forbid"`; `undocumented_unsafe_blocks` in `simd/` |
| R-SAFE-2 | No `mem::forget`, `process::exit` or global mutable state. | `mem_forget`, `exit`; review |
| R-SAFE-3 | `dyn Trait` **shall** appear only at the extension points listed atop `src/db.rs`, the traits they hand out, the storage foundation's traits (D30), and row streams, and at a boundary that keeps a proof of `Send` or `Sync` within the compiler's default recursion limit, marked `[DESIGN]`. Each extension trait **shall** document its contract; every built-in implementation **shall** pass the same contract tests. | review; tests |
| R-SAFE-4 | Each dependency **shall** have a §1 decision covering rationale, version, license and review; only cryptography and compression plug-ins, the server crate and the command-line client may have any (D3, D26, D42, D46, D48). | review |
| R-SAFE-5 | No thread **shall** be started except through the thread manager (`src/threads.rs`, D55), and none unnamed. | xtask; review |
| R-SAFE-6 | Every hash table, filter, partitioner, sketch, sampler and digest **shall** hash by XXH3 or XXH64 (`src/hash/xxhash.rs`), a checksum by them or the CRC family, and an attacker's keys by SipHash where D357 falls back to it; none by an identity, a bare multiply, FNV or a mix of its own (D460). | review only: clippy cannot tell a hash from arithmetic |

## 4. Test rules

### R-TEST: levels and layout

| ID | Rule | Checked by |
|---|---|---|
| R-TEST-1 | Each test **shall** sit at the lowest level showing its requirement: unit (`#[cfg(test)] mod tests`, private logic), integration (`test/integration/`, public API only) or doc (examples in `///` docs). | review |
| R-TEST-2 | Tests **shall** derive from requirements, not code: normal-range (boundaries included) and robustness (invalid inputs, exact SQLCODE expected). | review |
| R-TEST-3 | A test's name **shall** say the behaviour checked; an integration test may end in its clause: `fetch_targets_8_6`. | review |
| R-TEST-4 | Test code may `unwrap`, index and panic: a panic is a failure. Every other rule applies. | lints |
| R-TEST-5 | Tests **shall** be deterministic and independent: no clock, randomness, network beyond loopback (the server's tests, D42) or order dependence; each builds its own `Database`. Case generators use a fixed seed, so every run makes the same cases (`test/integration/random_queries.rs`). | review |
| R-TEST-7 | Every fixed defect **shall** get a regression test, failing without the fix, its doc comment saying so. | review |
| R-TEST-8 | New decisions of two or more conditions **shall** have tests showing MC/DC, naming the condition pairs in doc comments. | review |
| R-TEST-9 | Tests **should** be mutation-checked periodically. `cargo xtask mutate [NAME]` applies each mutation in `xtask/src/mutate/list.rs` and its submodules (package, file, snippet occurring once, replacement, tests that must fail) in turn, runs its tests, restores the file, and reports uncaught mutations and named tests that passed. Run it when changing a mechanism the list breaks; a new mechanism adds a mutation. | `cargo xtask mutate`, periodic; `verify` checks each mutation still applies |
| R-TEST-10 | A fixture or helper shared by modules **shall** be written once: in the test binary's `common.rs`, or, if shared by crates, in `turborel-test-support` (`support/`). Tests use `#[test]`, no other framework. | review |

R-TEST-6 was withdrawn with the golden-file tests (D6).

### R-TRACE: traceability

| ID | Rule | Checked by |
|---|---|---|
| R-TRACE-1 | Every test **shall** have a `/// Verifies:` paragraph starting with a tag: `[X3.135-1986 §…]`, `[ISO/IEC 9075…]` of any part, `[ISO/IEC 13249…]` (SQL/MM) of any part, `[OGC 06-10…]` (Simple feature access) of either part, `[EXTENSION]`, `[DESIGN]` or `[TOOL] R-…`. | `cargo xtask verify` |
| R-TRACE-2 | Code implementing a requirement **shall** cite it (R-DOC-4). `cargo xtask trace '§8.6'` lists a clause's tests. | review; `xtask trace` |
| R-TRACE-3 | CONFORMANCE.md **shall** change with the change implementing or changing a clause. | review |

### R-BENCH: benchmarks

| ID | Rule | Checked by |
|---|---|---|
| R-BENCH-1 | Every benchmark **shall** run on `bench/harness.rs`: benchmarks hold workloads; the harness times, reports and keeps them, and holds what they share. | review |
| R-BENCH-2 | Benchmarks measure, not test: no timing assertions; `verify` skips them. A performance claim **shall** cite `cargo xtask bench --compare` against the prior code. | review |

## 5. Structural coverage and MC/DC

| ID | Rule | Checked by |
|---|---|---|
| R-COV-1 | Coverage **shall** be measured by `cargo xtask coverage` over unit and integration tests, for `src/`. On the pinned toolchain, doc tests are excluded and unit-test modules count as covered code. | `xtask coverage` |
| R-COV-2 | Coverage **shall not** fall below the floors in `xtask/src/baseline.rs`; a change raising it **should** raise them. | `xtask coverage` |
| R-COV-3 | Target: 100 % statement, decision and MC/DC coverage (D2). Close gaps by requirements-based tests, removing dead code, or documenting deactivated code; never by requirement-less tests. | review |
| R-COV-4 | MC/DC **shall** be shown by test design (R-TEST-8) and checked in review (D22). | review |
| R-COV-5 | A coverage tool used for credit **shall** first be qualified (DO-330, TQL-5). | process |

Stable rustc gives region, line and function coverage, approximating
statement coverage. Branch coverage needs nightly, and MC/DC can't be
measured (D22). Masking MC/DC is acceptable (CAST-6), which matters for
Rust's short-circuit `&&` and `||`.

| ID | Rule | Checked by |
|---|---|---|
| R-DEV-1 | Every `#[allow]` and `#[expect]` **shall** carry a `reason` citing the rule and justification. | `allow_attributes_without_reason` |
| R-DEV-2 | Lint baseline counts **shall never** rise, nor lints be added; record lower counts with `cargo xtask lint-audit --write` (D11, D20). | `cargo xtask lint-audit` |
| R-DEV-3 | Permanent deviations, each with its reason in code: printing in `xtask`; test-code allowances (R-TEST-4); `as` in the two float roundings std lacks (`value::round_to_single`, `value::decimal::nearest_f64`); `Code::sqlcode`, an enum whose discriminant is its SQLCODE. | lints |

## 7. Process and tools

| ID | Rule | Checked by |
|---|---|---|
| R-PROC-1 | `cargo xtask verify` **shall** pass before every commit: format, lints, lint baselines, docs, file length, traceability and citations, no merge conflict marker in a source or document, threads, the claimed features SQL_FEATURES shows, every test. `--coverage` adds coverage. | pre-commit hook; CI |
| R-PROC-2 | Every change **shall** be reviewed against the checklist below. | review |
| R-PROC-3 | Commits **should** be small and single-purpose, in CONTRIBUTING.md's form (`area: summary`, then why), citing rules applied or changed. | review |
| R-PROC-4 | A threshold change **shall** change RULES.md, `clippy.toml` and `xtask` together. | review |
| R-PROC-5 | A release's crates **shall** be published together at its number, from a pushed commit passing `cargo xtask verify --coverage`, dry run first, per VERSIONING.md. | review |
| R-TOOL-1 | Project automation **shall** be Rust in `xtask/`, never shell scripts (D7). | review |
| R-TOOL-2 | `xtask` **shall** follow these rules, use only std, and test its own decisions (`[TOOL]` requirements). | `xtask verify` |
| R-CM-1 | The toolchain is pinned (D8), and the Dockerfile's build image with it (D241); a change **shall** be its own commit, changing both, passing `cargo xtask verify --coverage`. | review |
| R-CM-2 | `Cargo.lock` and the baselines **shall** be under version control. | review |

The review checklist:

- requirement cited in code (R-DOC-4) and tests (R-TRACE-1);
- normal-range and robustness tests (R-TEST-2); MC/DC pairs for new
  decisions (R-TEST-8);
- no magic numbers or strings (R-CONST);
- comments explain why (R-DOC-2);
- conditions without side effects (R-CF-4); borrows and locks scoped
  (R-ERR-4);
- CONFORMANCE.md updated (R-TRACE-3), and TODO.md where open work
  changed.

## 8. DO-178C

These rules make the code and its verification acceptable DO-178C inputs,
but not certifiable alone. Certification belongs to a process run under
plans agreed with the authority. Meeting DO-178C as written here also meets
DO-178B.

| DO-178C item | Covered by |
|---|---|
| Software Code Standards (11.8) | §3 |
| High-level requirements | The standards' clauses; CONFORMANCE.md is their status |
| Derived requirements | `[EXTENSION]` and `[DESIGN]` tags |
| Requirements-based testing (6.4.2) | R-TEST-2 |
| Traceability, requirements ↔ code ↔ tests | R-DOC-4, R-TRACE |
| Structural coverage (6.4.4.2) | R-COV; statement coverage approximated by regions, MC/DC by design |
| Dead and deactivated code (6.4.4.3) | R-COV-3, R-DOC-5 |
| Configuration management of tools and baselines | R-CM |
| DO-332, dynamic dispatch | R-SAFE-3 |

These items are outside the rules.

1. Plans (PSAC, SDP, SVP, SCMP, SQAP) are not written. This file feeds the
   SDP and SVP.
2. Doc comments and unit tests stand in for low-level requirements.
3. Data and control coupling analysis is not done.
4. Source to object code traceability (Level A) is not done.
5. The compiler and coverage tools are not qualified (R-COV-5).
6. Independence of verification needs an organisation, not a rule.
7. The engine heap-allocates throughout, a DO-332 vulnerability area, so
   airborne use needs bounded allocation or analysis.

These rules were adopted on 2026-10-23 with a code audit. Every finding
was fixed that week, and lint baselines and over-long files were paid down.
